docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A point \(x_0\) is called a singularity of a function \(f\) if \(f\) fails to be defined or continuous at \(x=x_0\text{,}\) while being defined and continuous in a punctured neighbourhood of \(x_0\text{.}\)

Lecture 5 classifies these problem points by their one-sided limits:

  • Removable: the finite limit exists, but \(f(x_0)\) is missing or has the wrong value.
  • Jump: both one-sided limits are finite but unequal.
  • Infinite: at least one one-sided limit is \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\text{.}\)
  • Oscillatory: a one-sided limit fails because of persistent oscillation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A singularity marks a point where a function fails to behave regularly, despite being well behaved arbitrarily close to that point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At an interior point, \(f\) is continuous if and only if \(f(x_0^-)=f(x_0^+)=f(x_0)\text{;}\) a discontinuity is exactly a failure of this equality.
  • Several distinct things can go wrong at \(x_0\text{:}\) \(f(x_0)\) may be undefined while nearby values behave well; \(f\) may be defined but not continuous; nearby values may become unbounded; or nearby values may oscillate without approaching anything.
  • The word singularity returns in Lecture 12 for improper integrals: an integrand may be unbounded at an interior singularity, and the integral is then split there.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1)\) has a removable discontinuity at \(x=1\text{.}\)
  • The piecewise function \(f(x)=x\) for \(x\leq 0\) and \(f(x)=x+1\) for \(x>0\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x=0\text{;}\) so does the signum function at the origin.
  • The function \(f(x)=1/x\) has an infinite discontinuity at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x) = \sin(1/x)\) has an oscillatory discontinuity at \(x=0\text{.}\)

The three graphs illustrate singularities at \(x=0\). The first is removable because changing the assigned value \(-1\) to the limit \(0\) restores continuity; the second has unequal one-sided limits \(0.5\) and \(1\); and the third, \(1/x\), has an infinite singularity.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Suppose that \(g(x)\leq f(x)\leq h(x)\) for every \(x\) sufficiently close to \(x_0\) (possibly only from one side), except perhaps at \(x=x_0\) itself. If

\[ \lim_{x\to x_0}g(x)=\lim_{x\to x_0}h(x)=L, \]

then \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)=L\text{.}\)

The same statement holds for limits as \(x\to+\infty\) or \(x\to-\infty\): the inequalities need only hold for sufficiently large \(|x|\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The squeeze theorem shows that a function inherits its limit from two bounding functions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The function must be bounded above and below by convergent functions.
  • Equality of the bounding limits forces convergence.
  • The theorem applies even when the middle function is difficult to analyse directly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}x^2\sin(1/x)=0\) follows from squeezing between \(\pm x^2\text{.}\)

  • Oscillatory functions can converge when tightly bounded.

Zoom in on \(x_0=0\): however fast \(x^2\sin(1/x)\) oscillates, it stays between \(-x^2\) and \(x^2\), which both tend to \(0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\text{,}\) \((b_n)_{n=1}^\infty\text{,}\) and \((c_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be sequences of real numbers such that \(a_n\leq b_n\leq c_n\) for all \(n \geq 1\text{.}\) Suppose also that \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((c_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converge to the same limit \(L\text{.}\) Then \((b_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) also converges to \(L\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The squeeze theorem for sequences establishes convergence using termwise inequalities.

It reduces convergence questions to bounding arguments.

Shrink \(\varepsilon\): from the index where both \(a_n\) and \(c_n\) are inside the band, \(b_n\) is trapped inside too, so it converges to the same \(L\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The bounded sequence must lie between two convergent sequences.
  • Equality of outer limits enforces convergence of the middle sequence.
  • The theorem does not require monotonicity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(-1/n \le b_n \le 1/n\text{,}\) then \(b_n\to 0\text{.}\)
  • \(\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\left(n \cdot\sin(1/n)\right)= 1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a differentiable function \(f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) a stationary point of \(f\) is a point on the graph of \(f\) where its derivative is zero, i.e., \(f'(x_0)=0\text{,}\) for \(x_0\in X\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A stationary point is where local change temporarily vanishes.

It identifies candidates for local extrema.

Every stationary point has a horizontal tangent. Most here are peaks or valleys, but \(x^3\) shows a stationary point that is neither.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Not every stationary point corresponds to an extremum.
  • Stationary points must be analysed further to determine behaviour.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^2\) has a stationary point at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=x^3\) has a stationary point that is not an extremum.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Where this appears in the course

Subsequences are not defined in the 2026-27 lectures. The definition is given inside the tutorial question that uses it (Tutorial 2), and this page records it in the same form.

Let \((a_n)_{n\ge m}\) be a sequence. A subsequence of \((a_n)\) is a new sequence \((a_{n_k})_{k\ge 1}\) obtained by selecting terms of \((a_n)\) along a strictly increasing sequence of indices \((n_k)_{k\ge 1}\) with \(n_k \ge m\):

\[ (a_{n_k})_{k\ge 1} = a_{n_1},\,a_{n_2},\,a_{n_3},\,\dots, \]

where \(m \le n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A subsequence is what you get when you “thin out” a sequence while keeping the original order.

You are not allowed to reorder terms. You only choose some of them, further and further along the sequence.

Choose the indices \(n_k\): the even and odd subsequences of \(a_n=(-1)^n\left(1+\frac1n\right)\) converge to different limits, which is why the whole sequence diverges.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every subsequence of a sequence uses terms from the original sequence, but with a new index set \(n_1<n_2<\cdots\text{.}\)
  • If \(a_n \to L\text{,}\) then every subsequence \(a_{n_k}\) also converges to \(L\text{.}\)
  • Subsequence limits help detect non-convergence: if two subsequences converge to different limits, then the original sequence does not converge.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(a_n = (-1)^n\text{,}\) then \((a_{2k})_{k\ge 1} = 1,1,1,\dots\) and \((a_{2k-1})_{k\ge 1} = -1,-1,-1,\dots\) are subsequences.
  • If \(a_n = \dfrac{1}{n}\text{,}\) then \(a_{2k}=\dfrac{1}{2k}\) is a subsequence, and it still converges to \(0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\text{,}\) \(B\) be sets. We say that \(A\) is a subset of \(B\text{,}\) denoted \(A\subseteq B\text{,}\) if every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(B\text{,}\) i.e.,

\[ \text{for any object }x,\; x\in A \; \implies\; x\in B. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A subset describes containment between collections of objects.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every set is a subset of itself.
  • Subset relations are transitive, i.e., \(A\subseteq B\) and \(B\subseteq C\) implies \(A\subseteq C\text{.}\)
  • Proper subsets exclude equality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\{1,\,2\}\subseteq\{1,\,2,\,3\}\text{.}\)
  • \(\varnothing\) is a subset of every set.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The operation of subtraction \(x-y\) of two integers \(x\) and \(y\) is defined as

\[ x-y=x+(-y). \]

The result is called the difference between \(x\) and \(y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Subtraction measures how one quantity differs from another.

It is defined using addition and negation to ensure algebraic consistency.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Subtraction is not commutative.
  • The difference \(x-y\) equals \(x+(-y)\text{.}\)
  • Subtraction extends addition within the integers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(E\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be nonempty and bounded above. The supremum of \(E\) is its least upper bound, denoted by \(\sup E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The supremum captures the smallest value that bounds a set from above.

It allows precise description of upper limits even when no maximum exists.

Move the candidate \(u\): every number at or above \(\sup E\) is an upper bound, and for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some element of \(E\) lies within \(\varepsilon\) below it, which is what makes it the least one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A supremum need not belong to the set.
  • By the least-upper-bound property of \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) every nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) that is bounded above has a unique supremum.
  • In the extended real numbers, one uses the conventions \(\sup E=+\infty\) for a nonempty set with no upper bound and \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\text{;}\) neither \(+\infty\) nor \(-\infty\) is a real number.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The supremum of \((0,1)\) is \(1\text{.}\)
  • The supremum of \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon x<2\}\) is \(2\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A function \(f\colon X\to Y\) is surjective if for every \(y \in Y\text{,}\) there exists an \(x \in X\) such that \(f (x) = y\text{.}\) In other words, a function is onto if its codomain is exactly its range.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Surjectivity describes how completely a function covers its codomain.

A surjective function ensures that no element of the codomain is left unused.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A function is surjective if every element of the codomain is attained.
  • Surjectivity depends on both the function rule and the chosen codomain.
  • Changing the codomain may change surjectivity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=x^3\) from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is surjective.
  • The function \(f(x)=x^2\) from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is not surjective.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\text{,}\)

\[ |x+y|\leq |x|+|y|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The triangle inequality bounds the size of a sum by the sizes of its components.

It formalises the idea that direct paths are shorter than indirect ones.

In the top diagram, \(x\) and \(y\) have the same sign, so \(|x+y|=|x|+|y|\). In the bottom diagram their signs are opposite, so the displacements partly cancel. In general, equality holds precisely when \(xy\ge0\), including the case where either value is zero.

Walk \(x\), then \(y\): when they have the same sign the lengths add up exactly, and when the signs differ part of the walk is undone, so \(|x+y|<|x|+|y|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Absolute values interact subadditively under addition.
  • The inequality provides fundamental bounds in analysis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(|3+(-1)|\le |3|+|{-1}|\text{.}\)
  • \(|x-y|\le |x|+|y|\) for all real numbers \(x,y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For any two real numbers \(x\) and \(y\text{,}\) exactly one of the following is true: \(x<y\text{,}\) \(x=y\text{,}\) or \(x>y\text{.}\) Equivalently, for any real number \(x\text{,}\) exactly one of the following is true: \(x\) is zero, \(x\) is positive, or \(x\) is negative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Trichotomy states that real numbers are totally ordered.

It ensures that comparisons between real numbers are always decisive.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Exactly one of three relations holds between any two real numbers.
  • Trichotomy underpins order-based arguments.
  • Many proofs rely on splitting cases via trichotomy.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Complex numbers do not have this property: there is no compatible total order on \(\mathbb{C}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(x \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Consider the point \((\cos x, \sin x)\) on the unit circle \(\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^2 \colon u^2+v^2=1\}\) obtained by rotating the point \((1,0)\) counterclockwise by an angle \(x\) (measured in radians). The functions \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) are defined as the second and first coordinates of this point, respectively.

For all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\cos x \neq 0\text{,}\) the tangent function is defined by \(\displaystyle \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Trigonometric functions encode angular relationships using coordinates on the unit circle.

They provide periodic models for oscillatory behavior.

The point at angle \(x\) on the unit circle is \((\cos x,\sin x)\): \(\cos x\) is its horizontal coordinate (red dashed), \(\sin x\) its vertical one (green dashed), and \(\tan x=\sin x/\cos x\).

Turn the angle \(x\) (or press play): the coordinates of the point on the unit circle trace out \(\cos x\) and \(\sin x\) on the right. Show \(\tan x\) to see it blow up where \(\cos x=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Sine and cosine are defined for all real numbers.
  • Trigonometric functions are periodic.
  • Tangent is defined only where cosine is nonzero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\sin 0=0\) and \(\cos 0=1\text{.}\)
  • \(\tan x\) is undefined at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+\pi k\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Given two sets \(A\) and \(B\text{,}\) the union \(A\cup B\) of \(A\) and \(B\) is a set whose elements consist of all the elements which belong to \(A\) or \(B\) or both,

\[ \begin{aligned} x\in A\cup B \; &\iff \; x\in A \text{ or } x\in B\\ \;&\iff \; (x\in A)\lor (x\in B). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The union of sets combines elements from multiple collections.

It formalises logical disjunction in set-theoretic language.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Elements belong to the union if they belong to at least one set.
  • Union is commutative and associative, i.e., we have \(A\cup B=B\cup A\) and \(A\cup(B\cup C)=(A\cup B)\cup C\text{.}\)
  • The union with the empty set leaves a set unchanged.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(E\) be a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and let \(M\) be a real number. We say that \(M\) is an upper bound for \(E\) if we have \(x \leq M\) for every element \(x\) in \(E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An upper bound limits a set from above without requiring attainment.

It formalises constraints that restrict growth.

Every \(M\ge 1.1\) is an upper bound; the least one, \(\sup S=1.1\), is also \(\max S\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set may have many upper bounds.
  • Upper bounds need not belong to the set.
  • Upper bounds are not unique.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \((0,1)\) has upper bound \(1\text{.}\)
  • Any number greater than \(1\) is also an upper bound for \((0,1)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) The vertical line \(x=x_0\) is called a vertical asymptote of the curve \(y=f(x)\) if at least one of the following holds:

\[ \begin{aligned} \lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)&=+\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^+}f(x)&=+\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^-}f(x)&=+\infty,\\[6pt] \lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)&=-\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^+}f(x)&=-\infty,\\ \lim_{x\to x_0^-}f(x)&=-\infty. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A vertical asymptote describes unbounded behaviour near a finite input value.

\(f(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\to1^+\) and \(f(x)\to-\infty\) as \(x\to1^-\): the line \(x=1\) is a vertical asymptote.

Shrink \(h\) and watch \(f(x_0-h)\) and \(f(x_0+h)\): the values run off to \(+\infty\) on one side and \(-\infty\) on the other. Change the sign of \(k\) to swap the sides.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Vertical asymptotes arise from divergence at finite points.
  • One-sided divergence is sufficient.
  • Vertical asymptotes are detected using limits.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=1/x\) has a vertical asymptote at \(x=0\text{.}\)
  • Rational functions often exhibit vertical asymptotes at zeros of the denominator.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A zero of a function (also called a root or \(\boldsymbol{x}\)-intercept) is any input value that makes the function's output equal to zero

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Graphically, a zero of function is where the function's graph crosses or touches the \(x\)-axis.

The zeros of \(f\) are the \(x\)-intercepts of its graph: \(f(x_1)=f(x_2)=f(x_3)=0\) for \(f(x)=x^3-3x+1\).

Shift the graph with \(c\) and count the zeros: three crossings become a touch and then a single crossing. At a touching zero the graph meets the \(x\)-axis without crossing it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A zero of a function is a solution to the equation \(f(x)=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The zeros of the quadratic polynomial \(f(x)=x^2-1\) are \(x=1\) and \(x=-1\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f(x)=2^x\) does not have any zeros.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An algorithm is a prescribed sequence of computational rules for solving a problem. In the iterative methods considered in the course, these rules are applied repeatedly; each repetition is an iteration.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An algorithm replaces an unavailable closed-form answer with a sequence of manageable calculations. A stopping condition specifies when the required answer has been obtained.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The simplex method, network algorithms, and dynamic programming use different problem structures.
  • An iteration need not strictly improve the objective: a degenerate simplex pivot can leave its value unchanged.
  • A heuristic is a solution procedure without a general guarantee of optimality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Simplex checks its objective-row sign condition; the shortest-path method settles vertices until the destination is reached; flow augmentation stops when no augmenting path remains; dynamic programming advances through stages.

  • A simplex iteration exchanges a basic and a nonbasic variable.
  • A spanning-tree algorithm repeatedly adds an eligible edge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The ambulance location model selects a minimum number of station towns while ensuring that every town is within 18 minutes of a selected station. Let \(y_j=1\) if a station is placed at town \(j\), and let \(N_i=\{j:t_{ij}\le18\}\). Then

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{j=1}^6y_j,\\ \sum_{j\in N_i}y_j\ge1\ (i=1,\ldots,6),\\ y_j\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Each coverage constraint requires at least one sufficiently close station. A station may cover several towns and a town may be covered by several stations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Include the town itself because its travel time to itself is zero.
  • The threshold includes exactly 18 minutes.
  • This is the set-covering structure illustrated by the exercise; no station-capacity limit is specified.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The dashed links indicate travel times at most 18 minutes; the displayed positions are schematic rather than a geographical scale.

  • Town 1 can be covered from towns 1 or 4, giving \(y_1+y_4\ge1\).
  • Town 3 can be covered from towns 3 or 5, giving \(y_3+y_5\ge1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An artificial variable \(R_i\ge0\) is introduced temporarily into an equality or a converted \(\ge\) constraint to construct an initial basis. It is added with coefficient \(+1\) and initially takes the nonnegative right-hand-side value while the other variables in that row are zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Artificial variables make the auxiliary starting problem feasible. They have no physical interpretation and must be driven to zero to satisfy the original equations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• They differ from slack and surplus variables, which record genuine inequalities.
  • The first phase maximizes the negative sum of artificial variables.
  • The original constraints are recovered when every artificial variable is zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, setting \(x_A=x_B=S_1=0\) gives the initial artificial basis \(R_1=R_2=6\). Minimizing \(R_1+R_2\) is equivalent to maximizing its negative, as used in Phase I.

  • \(2x_1+3x_2=6\) becomes \(2x_1+3x_2+R_1=6\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: In a square one-to-one assignment problem, adding a constant \(a_i\) to every cost in row \(i\), or a constant \(b_j\) to every cost in column \(j\), preserves the set of optimal assignments. Every complete assignment's cost changes by the same total \(\sum_i a_i+\sum_j b_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Every assignment uses each row and each column exactly once. Uniform changes along a row or column therefore change the baseline cost without changing which assignment is best.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Subtracting row and column minima is a valid transformation.
  • The Hungarian uncovered-entry adjustment is equivalent to suitable row and column changes.
  • For a maximum-profit assignment, negate profits and add a constant large enough to make the resulting costs nonnegative.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, subtracting \(a_1=2\) from row 1 lowers each complete assignment cost by 2. More generally, subtracting row amounts \(a_i\) and column amounts \(b_j\) changes every complete total by \(-\sum_i a_i-\sum_j b_j\).

Assignment pairs Original total Transformed total \((1,1),(2,3),(3,2)\) \(4+7+1=12\) \(2+7+1=10\) \((1,2),(2,1),(3,3)\) \(2+4+6=12\) \(0+4+6=10\) \((1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\) \(8+3+3=14\) \(6+3+3=12\)
  • If row minima are 2, 5, 6, and 4, subtracting them reduces every assignment cost by 17.
  • Transforming profits \(p_{ij}\) into costs \(M-p_{ij}\) changes a complete assignment objective to \(nM-\sum_i p_{i,\pi(i)}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The assignment problem pairs \(n\) agents with \(n\) tasks so that each agent receives exactly one task and each task exactly one agent. If \(c_{ij}\) is the cost of assigning agent \(i\) to task \(j\), a binary model is

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^nc_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad \sum_jx_{ij}=1,\\ \sum_ix_{ij}=1,\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: One-to-one matching couples the choices: assigning a task to one agent removes that task from consideration for the others. The Hungarian algorithm solves this structure directly.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Costs can represent execution times as well as monetary amounts.
  • Unequal numbers of agents and tasks can be handled with dummy entries.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The augmented form of the course's initial LP models replaces each \(\le\) functional constraint by an equality with a nonnegative slack variable. For \(Ax\le b\), \(x\ge0\), this gives

\[ Ax+s=b,\qquad x\ge0,\quad s\ge0, \]

with the same objective in the original variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Adding slacks changes the algebraic representation, not the allowed original decisions. Each original feasible vector determines exactly one vector of slack values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Count auxiliary variables when determining the dimension of the equality system used for a basis.
  • For \(m\) independent equalities in \(n\) augmented variables, a basis contains \(m\) variables.
  • Artificial variables used for other constraint types require a feasibility phase; they cannot simply remain free in the final model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \(s_1\) measures unused finishing hours, \(s_2\) unused carpentry hours, and \(s_3\) unused soldier-demand allowance. The three equations contain five variables, so a basis sets two nonbasic variables to zero.

  • Two original variables and two slack variables give four augmented variables.
  • The constraints \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\) and \(x_1+3x_2+s_2=15\) have initial solution \((0,0,10,15)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The augmenting path algorithm starts with a feasible flow, initially zero in the course examples. Find a source-to-sink augmenting path, augment by its bottleneck \(\delta\), decrease each traversed residual capacity by \(\delta\), increase the opposite residual capacity by \(\delta\), and repeat. If no augmenting path remains, the current flow is maximum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The residual network allows both new routing and correction of earlier routing. The stopping condition certifies that no further flow increase is possible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Maintain flow conservation after every augmentation.
  • The integer capacities in the exercises allow integer augmentations and finite termination.
  • Recover original flows from the final residual values, taking edge directions into account.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
On an original forward edge the augmentation adds \(\delta\) to its flow; on a backward residual edge it subtracts \(\delta\). With integer capacities and an integral starting flow, each augmentation increases the value by at least 1, so only finitely many are possible.

  • The main example augments by \(5,2,1,4,1,2\), totalling 15.
  • The last residual network cannot reach T from S through positive residual directions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An augmenting path is a source-to-sink path in the residual network with strictly positive residual capacity in every traversed direction. Its residual capacity, or bottleneck, is

\[ \delta=\min\{r_e:e\text{ is traversed along the path}\}. \]

An additional \(\delta\) units of net source-to-sink flow can be assigned along it.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The smallest remaining capacity limits the whole path. A backward residual segment reduces an original flow while still increasing the total source-to-sink value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• All residual directions on the path must be feasible.
  • Augmenting by the bottleneck saturates at least one residual direction.
  • A path may use both forward and reverse directions relative to original edges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated edge labels are flow/capacity. The red path \(A-C-E-F\) has residual capacities \(3,4,3\), so \(\delta=\min(3,4,3)=3\) increases total flow from 5 to 8. A feasible flow is maximum exactly when no source-to-sink augmenting path remains.

  • The first S-A-D-T augmentation in the video has bottleneck 5.
  • A later S-B-E-D-A-C-T path cancels part of the earlier A-D flow and adds two units overall.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A basic feasible solution is a basic solution of an equality-form LP with all its variables nonnegative. A basic solution with a negative variable is a basic infeasible solution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Simplex maintains this combination of algebraic structure and feasibility. It can then improve the objective without leaving the allowed region.

Each intersection of two boundaries corresponds to a basic solution. The feasible ones (filled) are the basic feasible solutions; the hollow ones are basic but infeasible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonbasic variables are set to zero; feasibility is checked through the resulting basic values.
  • A basic variable may be zero in a degenerate solution.
  • For the course LPs with a finite optimum, an optimal basic feasible solution exists.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The filled points in the illustrated region \(F\) are its feasible corners; the hollow boundary intersections violate at least one nonnegativity restriction in the augmented system.

  • \((x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2)=(0,0,10,15)\) is basic feasible in the main simplex example.
  • \((0,10,0,-15)\) is basic but infeasible.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For \(m\) independent linear equality constraints in \(n\) variables, a basic solution is obtained by choosing \(n-m\) variables to be nonbasic and setting them to zero, then uniquely solving for the other \(m\) variables. The chosen basic columns must be linearly independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Choosing a basis selects an algebraic candidate for a corner. Some choices fail to give a unique solution and some give negative values, so not every choice is a feasible candidate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There are at most \(\binom{n}{m}\) basis choices.
  • A basic solution may be feasible or infeasible.
  • Different bases can represent the same degenerate solution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated system has \(m=3\) equations and \(n=5\) variables:

\[ \begin{aligned} 2x_s+x_t+s_1&=100,\\ x_s+x_t+s_2&=80,\\ x_s+s_3&=40. \end{aligned} \]

Setting two nonbasic variables to zero gives the following basic solutions. The nonnegative solutions are corners of the shaded feasible region; negative slack values identify the red, infeasible points.

Variables set to zero \((x_s,x_t)\) \((s_1,s_2,s_3)\) Feasible? \(x_s,x_t\) \((0,0)\) \((100,80,40)\) Yes \(s_1,s_2\) \((20,60)\) \((0,0,20)\) Yes \(x_t,s_3\) \((40,0)\) \((20,40,0)\) Yes \(s_2,s_3\) \((40,40)\) \((-20,0,0)\) No \(x_t,s_1\) \((50,0)\) \((0,30,-10)\) No

There are at most \(\binom53=10\) basis choices for this system. The figure shows five of their corresponding basic solutions.

  • The four-variable example has at most \(\binom42=6\) bases.
  • Week 2 practice 4 has five variables and two equalities, but only eight basic solutions from ten candidate choices.

docs.title: Definition

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The bin packing problem assigns every item to a container, subject to a common capacity per container, and minimizes the number of containers used. If item \(i\) has weight \(w_i\) and a container has capacity \(C\), the weights assigned to each container must sum to at most \(C\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Combining items efficiently can reduce the number of containers. A simple packing rule is easy to apply, but need not find the best combination.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each item must be packed exactly once without splitting it.
  • Any feasible packing provides an upper bound on the minimum number of containers.
  • The total-weight bound is \(\lceil\sum_i w_i/C\rceil\); it need not be attainable. This follows by aggregating the capacity requirements.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure is a separate four-item illustration with weights \(15,30,20,35\) and capacity \(C=50\). Its lower bound is \(\lceil100/50\rceil=2\), attained by the displayed packing \(\{15,35\}\) and \(\{30,20\}\). This proves optimality for the illustrated instance, rather than for the 15-item course exercise.

  • The exercise has 15 items and container capacity 50.
  • First-fit uses five containers, while the solution sheet states that four suffice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A binary integer program (BIP) is a linear optimization model in which all decision variables are binary. For variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), the domain is \(y\in\{0,1\}^n\) before imposing the remaining constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: BIPs describe combinations of yes-or-no choices. Even a moderate number of choices creates many candidate combinations, motivating methods such as branch-and-bound.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There are \(2^n\) binary assignments before functional constraints eliminate infeasible combinations.
  • Its LP relaxation replaces each binary restriction by \(0\le y_j\le1\).
  • The objective can count selected alternatives or weight them by costs or returns.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Project selection maximizes the return from projects under yearly budgets.
  • Ambulance location minimizes the number of selected station sites.

docs.title: Definition

A binary variable is a decision variable restricted to \(\{0,1\}\). For a yes-or-no choice \(j\), the course convention is

\[ y_j=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if decision }j\text{ is yes},\\0,&\text{if decision }j\text{ is no}.\end{cases} \]

  • Summing binary variables counts the selected decisions.
  • Auxiliary binary variables can activate or relax constraints.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A bipartite matching pairs entities from two distinct groups, with each selected pair containing one member of each group and no entity used in more than one pair. A complete one-to-one assignment between equally sized groups is a perfect bipartite matching.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The separation into two groups distinguishes assignment from pairing odd-degree vertices in the Chinese postman problem. This special structure supports the Hungarian algorithm.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Agents and tasks form the two groups in an assignment problem.
  • A matching need not use every entity unless completeness is required.
  • Maximum zero-cost matching can be represented as a unit-capacity flow problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Grey edges are allowed pairs and green edges form the matching. It contains \(|M|=3\) pairs, equal to the number of jobs, so no larger matching is possible; the fourth worker remains unmatched. A perfect matching would cover every vertex on both sides and requires equal group sizes.

  • A machine-job pair connects the machine group to the job group.
  • The CPP odd-vertex pairing is nonbipartite because all paired vertices belong to one common set.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For a maximization integer program with incumbent value \(L\), a branch-and-bound node can be pruned if its LP relaxation is infeasible, its relaxed optimizer satisfies all integer restrictions, or its relaxed upper bound \(U\) satisfies \(U\le L\). In the integral case, update the incumbent if appropriate. For minimization, reverse the bound comparison.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Each condition proves that further subdivision of that node cannot improve the best known value. This is what makes the method more efficient than full enumeration.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For maximization, a valid global upper bound is the maximum of the incumbent value and the LP bounds of active unresolved nodes.
  • At completion the incumbent proves the optimal value.
  • Pruning equality with the incumbent is sufficient to find the optimum value, but can discard other equally optimal solutions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For minimization, prune a node when its relaxed lower bound \(z_R\) is at least the incumbent value.

  • A node with upper bound 3.3 can be discarded once the incumbent is 3.4.
  • In week 3 practice 9, the branch \(x_3\ge7\) is infeasible because \(x_2+3x_3\le20\) and \(x_2\ge0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Branch-and-bound solves an integer program by solving LP relaxations of subproblems, splitting subproblems when restricted variables are fractional, and discarding subproblems whose bounds cannot improve the best feasible integer solution. If \(x_j=v\) is fractional, branch into

\[ x_j\le\lfloor v\rfloor\qquad\text{and}\qquad x_j\ge\lceil v\rceil. \]

For a binary variable these branches fix it to 0 and 1.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The branches retain every possible integer solution while excluding the current fractional value. Bounds prevent unnecessary exploration of parts of the search tree.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Carry all ancestor branching constraints into each child.
  • Prune for infeasibility, an integral relaxed optimum, or an uncompetitive bound.
  • Continue until every remaining possibility is resolved or bounded by the incumbent.
  • Branching choices affect the work required but not the correctly proven optimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure branches on \(x_2=1.25\), giving \(x_2\le\lfloor1.25\rfloor=1\) or \(x_2\ge\lceil1.25\rceil=2\).

  • A fractional value \(x_1=3.3\) yields branches \(x_1\le3\) and \(x_1\ge4\).
  • The development-project model has optimum 3.4; the supplied tree has incorrect intermediate LP values, documented in coverage.md.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The bus scheduling model chooses nonnegative integer counts \(x_i\) of buses starting in each of six consecutive four-hour intervals. Each bus operates for two intervals. With requirements \(d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)\), the cyclic model is

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{i=1}^6x_i,\\ x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i\ (i=1,\ldots,6),\\ x_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}, \end{gathered} \]

where \(x_0=x_6\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The variables count shift starts, while each coverage constraint counts all buses operating in an interval. The wrap-around term links the last daily shift to the first interval.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Eight-hour operation covers exactly two consecutive four-hour intervals.
  • Coverage may exceed the minimum demand.
  • The repeating daily interpretation is the assumption used to formulate the midnight boundary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The midnight-to-4 AM constraint is \(x_6+x_1\ge4\).
  • The 4 PM-to-8 PM requirement gives \(x_4+x_5\ge12\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Chinese postman problem (CPP) finds a minimum-length closed route traversing every edge at least once in a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths. To solve the course version, find a minimum-cost pairing of the odd-degree vertices using shortest-path distances, duplicate the corresponding paths, and construct an Euler tour in the resulting network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Every street must be covered. Repeated edges are necessary only to make a closed covering route possible, and the matching step chooses a minimum total extra length.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If every vertex already has even degree, any Euler tour is optimal.
  • The optimal cost is the sum of original edge lengths plus the minimum pairing cost.
  • The shortest path between paired vertices can contain intermediate vertices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \(A\) and \(C\) are the two odd-degree vertices. Their direct edge costs 4, compared with \(2+3=5\) via \(D\) or \(3+2=5\) via \(B\). Duplicating the direct edge gives route length \(14+4=18\). The dashed edge denotes this extra copy.

  • The five-vertex example has total edge length 25 and minimum pairing cost 7, giving CPP value 32.
  • Pairing A with D duplicates A-C-D, while pairing B with E duplicates B-E.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The classical EOQ model assumes deterministic constant demand rate \(D>0\), instantaneous batch replenishment, no shortages, fixed setup cost \(K>0\) per order, and holding cost \(h>0\) per unit per unit time. A constant unit purchasing price can be excluded when optimizing. For batch size \(y>0\), relevant cost per unit time is

\[ TCU(y)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inventory repeatedly drops linearly from the batch size to zero. Large batches reduce setup frequency but increase average stock.

Move \(y\): the setup cost rate \(KD/y\) falls and the holding cost rate \(hy/2\) rises. The right panel shows the inventory sawtooth for this batch size.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Average stock is \(y/2\) and cycle length is \(y/D\).
  • The cost is strictly convex for positive \(y\).
  • The model optimizes a continuous order quantity; discrete purchasing units require checking feasible nearby quantities.
  • Using a mean demand to approximate stochastic demand does not incorporate its variability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The phone data \(D=2\), \(K=605\), \(h=5\) give an optimal batch of 22.

docs.title: Definition

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A constraint is a requirement that an allowed decision must satisfy. A linear functional constraint has the form

\[ a_{i1}x_1+\cdots+a_{in}x_n\le b_i, \]

or the corresponding equality or \(\ge\) inequality. The \(a_{ij}\) are constraint coefficients and \(b_i\) is the right-hand side.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Constraints translate capacity limits, demand requirements, and other restrictions into mathematics. Feasibility requires all constraints to hold together.

The objective function \(f(x)\) is the quantity to maximise (for example, profit) or minimise (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(x)\) subject to \(x\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A capacity limit commonly gives a \(\le\) constraint; a minimum requirement commonly gives a \(\ge\) constraint.
  • An equality represents an exact requirement or balance.
  • Multiplication by a negative number reverses an inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s+x_t\le80\) limits carpentry use.
  • \(800x_A+1000x_B\ge8000\) requires enough calories.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Contingent decisions are binary choices whose admissibility depends on other choices. If decision 2 is allowed only when decision 1 is yes, the implication is represented by

\[ y_2\le y_1,\qquad y_1,y_2\in\{0,1\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The inequality prohibits precisely the combination “decision 2 yes, decision 1 no.” It does not force decision 2 to be selected when decision 1 is selected.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If decision 2 must be yes when decision 1 is no, use \(y_1+y_2\ge1\).
  • If decision 3 is allowed only when both decisions 1 and 2 are yes, use \(y_3\le y_1\) and \(y_3\le y_2\).
  • If \(y_1=1\) and \(y_2=0\) must imply \(y_3=0\), use \(y_1-y_2+y_3\le1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(W_{LA}\le F_{LA}\) requires a local factory before a warehouse can be built.
  • \(y_1+y_2+y_3\le2\) rules out all three yes decisions together.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For continuous demand with finite mean and CDF \(F\), the newsvendor expected cost satisfies

\[ G'(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b. \]

If \(F\) is continuous and strictly increasing through \(\beta=b/(b+h)\) and that quantile lies in the allowed quantity domain, the unique optimum is

\[ y^*=F^{-1}(\beta). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The optimal stock is a quantile of demand, determined by the cost balance. Continuity alone does not guarantee uniqueness if the CDF has a flat segment at the critical probability.

Where \(G'(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b\) is zero the CDF equals \(\beta\); read \(y^*=F^{-1}(\beta)\) off the right panel.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For uniform demand on \([a,u]\), the optimum is \(a+(u-a)\beta\).
  • For the course normal approximation, it is \(\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\).
  • A continuous demand approximation may give a noninteger answer even when actual items are indivisible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Meal demand uniform on \([80,120]\) with \(\beta=0.6\) gives 104 meals.
  • Normal meal demand with mean 100 and standard deviation 20 gives about 105.07.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
If \(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(k)}\) are optimal solutions of the same LP and \(\alpha_j\ge0\) with \(\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j=1\), then

\[ x=\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_jx^{(j)} \]

is also optimal. Such a weighted average is a convex combination.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Linear constraints are preserved by these weighted averages, and the linear objective remains equal to the common optimum. Two optimal corners therefore generate an entire optimal segment.

For any \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) the mixture \(\alpha x^{(1)}+(1-\alpha)x^{(2)}\) of the two optimal corners is feasible and has the same optimal \(z\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Weights must be nonnegative and sum to one.
  • For two points use \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\), with \(0\le\alpha\le1\).
  • The property concerns continuous LP feasibility; averaging integer solutions need not preserve integrality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective \(2x_s+2x_t\), the edge between \((0,80)\) and \((20,60)\) is optimal with value 160. The displayed combination \(\tfrac14(0,80)+\tfrac34(20,60)=(15,65)\) has the same value. In general, the combined value is \(\sum_j\alpha_jz^*=z^*\).

  • Combining \((5,0)\) and \((3,4)\) gives \((3+2\alpha,4-4\alpha)\), all with value 20.
  • Combining \((2,3)\) and \((0,6)\) gives \((2\alpha,6-3\alpha)\); \(\alpha=1/2\) gives \((1,9/2)\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For the LPs in the course with a nonempty feasible region in nonnegative variables, if a finite optimum exists, at least one feasible corner point attains it. Consequently, a unique optimal solution must be a feasible corner point. If a bounded feasible region has multiple optimal solutions, at least two of its corner points are optimal.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This result allows an LP to be solved without testing every point in its feasible region. Simplex uses the algebraic counterparts of these corners.

Turn the objective with \(c_1\) and \(c_2\): whenever a finite optimum exists, some feasible corner attains it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The existence of a finite optimum is essential.
  • The bounded-region qualification in the multiple-corner statement matters when the feasible region has rays.
  • Every convex combination of optimal corners is optimal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure evaluates \(z=3x_s+2x_t\) at its five feasible corners: the values are \(0,120,160,180,160\). The largest is 180 at \((20,60)\), and the orange line is the objective line through that point.

  • The manufacturing optimum \((2,5)\) is a feasible corner.
  • For the course LP with objective \(4x_1+2x_2\) and boundary \(2x_1+x_2\le11\), an entire feasible boundary segment attains 22.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In an LP with \(n\) decision variables, a corner point is a point determined by the intersection of constraint boundaries with \(n\) independent boundary equations. At least \(n\) constraints are therefore active there, counting nonnegativity boundaries. A corner point is feasible only if it satisfies all constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Corner points are the finite candidates exploited by the graphical and simplex methods in the course. Merely counting repeated or dependent constraints does not determine a corner.

Every intersection of two boundaries is a candidate corner. Filled points are feasible corners; hollow ones lie outside the region.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In two dimensions, two nonparallel active boundaries determine a corner.
  • Extra active constraints can occur at a degenerate corner.
  • Not every intersection of boundaries is feasible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated feasible corner \((20,60)\) solves \(2x_s+x_t=100\) and \(x_s+x_t=80\). The boundary intersection \((50,0)\) is infeasible because it violates the soldier-demand limit; it is not an extreme point of the feasible set. Feasible corners correspond to basic feasible solutions of the augmented model.

  • The lines \(x_2=5\) and \(2x_1+x_2=9\) intersect at \((2,5)\).
  • The nonnegativity boundaries meet at the origin \((0,0)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For newsvendor overage cost \(h>0\) and underage cost \(b>0\), the critical ratio is

\[ \beta=\frac{b}{b+h}=\frac{p-c}{p-s},\qquad 0<\beta<1. \]

It is the cumulative-demand probability used to select the optimal stock quantile.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A large underage cost justifies a higher demand quantile; a large overage cost justifies a lower one. The ratio balances the two marginal risks.

Change \(p\), \(c\) and \(s\): \(\beta=b/(b+h)\) moves, and the optimal stock is the demand quantile where the CDF reaches \(\beta\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For integer demand, increasing from \(y\) to \(y+1\) helps while \(F(y)<\beta\).
  • For the continuous strictly increasing CDFs used in the examples, the optimum solves \(F(y^*)=\beta\).
  • The ratio is not the expected fraction of demand served.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Newspapers with \(b=1.5\) and \(h=2\) have \(\beta=3/7\).
  • Meals with \(b=3.3\) and \(h=2.2\) have \(\beta=0.6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's network terminology, a cycle or tour is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex. Because its path convention requires distinct edges, no edge is repeated within such a cycle.

docs.title: Interpretation

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A decision variable represents a quantity or choice that the model is intended to determine. Its definition specifies its practical meaning, unit, and allowed values. A solution assigns a value to every decision variable.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A clear variable definition connects a mathematical expression to a real decision. It also determines whether fractions, negative values, or only yes-or-no choices make sense.

The objective function \(f(x)\) is the quantity to maximise (for example, profit) or minimise (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(x)\) subject to \(x\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of decision variables is the dimension of the original optimization problem.
  • Input data such as available hours are parameters rather than decisions.
  • Variable restrictions must be stated explicitly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s\) denotes the number of wooden soldiers to produce.
  • \(x_A\) denotes pounds of feed A in a pig diet.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A degenerate basic feasible solution has at least one basic variable equal to zero. A degenerate pivot has a zero step length and can change the basis without changing the solution vector or objective value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: At a degenerate point, several constraints become active together. More than one basis may describe the same point, so a simplex iteration need not correspond to visible movement.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A tie for the minimum ratio can produce a degenerate basic feasible solution.
  • Zero ratios must be considered when the pivot-column coefficient is positive.
  • The basic/nonbasic distinction is determined by the basis, not by whether a value is zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
At the illustrated point \((20,60)\), \(s_1=s_2=s_4=0\). The augmented model has two nonbasic variables, so at least one of these three zeros is basic. Without an anti-cycling rule, repeated degenerate pivots can cause simplex to cycle.

  • With \(x_1-x_2\le1\) and \(2x_1+x_2\le2\), increasing \(x_1\) gives tied ratios of 1.
  • At \((x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2)=(1,0,0,0)\), exchanging \(s_2\) for \(x_2\) leaves the point and \(z=3\) unchanged.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's diet problem chooses pounds \(x_A,x_B\) of two feeds to minimize daily feed cost while satisfying calorie, vitamin, and composition requirements:

\[ \begin{aligned} \min\quad &0.4x_A+0.8x_B\\ \text{subject to}\quad &800x_A+1000x_B\ge8000,\\ &140x_A+70x_B\ge700,\\ &2x_A-x_B\le0,\\ &x_A,x_B\ge0. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This is a minimum-cost mixture model. The composition restriction prevents cheap feed A from exceeding one-third of total feed weight.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The share constraint follows from \(x_A\le(x_A+x_B)/3\).
  • Nutrient requirements are lower bounds, so their inequalities point toward greater nutrient intake.
  • The optimal solution is \(x_A=20/7\), \(x_B=40/7\), with cost \(40/7\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure uses a simplified illustrative diet model, distinct from the course-data formulation above: minimize \(2x_A+3x_B\) subject to \(x_A+2x_B\ge6\), \(3x_A+x_B\ge6\) and \(x_A,x_B\ge0\). The variables still represent pounds of feeds A and B. Sliding the cost line towards the origin gives the illustrated optimum \((1.2,2.4)\) with cost 9.6.

  • The optimal mixture contains exactly one-third feed A.
  • At the optimum the calorie requirement is tight, while vitamin intake is \(800\ge700\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Dijkstra-Prim method constructs a minimum spanning tree in a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths. Start with an arbitrary vertex in \(U\) and no selected edges. Repeatedly select a shortest edge joining a vertex in \(U\) to a vertex outside \(U\), add that edge, and add the outside endpoint to \(U\). Stop when every vertex belongs to \(U\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The method grows one connected tree. Each new edge connects one previously unreached vertex at the smallest available joining cost.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compare edges crossing from the whole set \(U\), not only from the last added vertex.
  • Ties can be broken arbitrarily.
  • The starting vertex can change the construction order without changing the minimum total value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, each green edge label gives its weight and selection step in brackets. After reaching \(U=\{A,B,C\}\), \(BD=5\) is cheaper than \(CD=8\) or \(CE=10\); \(AB\) is ineligible because both endpoints are already in \(U\). The five selected edges have total length 13.

  • In the Euclidean example, starting with \(U=\{1\}\) selects edge \(1-7\) of length \(\sqrt{13}\).
  • The next edge is \(1-4\), of length 5.

  • Maximum-flow constraints respect the original edge directions.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let demand be a nonnegative integer-valued random variable with CDF \(F\), finite mean, and newsvendor costs \(b,h>0\). Over nonnegative integer order quantities, a smallest optimal quantity is

\[ \begin{gathered} y^*=\min\{y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:F(y)\ge\beta\},\\ \beta=\frac{b}{b+h}. \end{gathered} \]

The marginal expected-cost difference is

\[ G(y+1)-G(y)=(b+h)F(y)-b. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Add another item while its expected lost-margin saving exceeds its expected leftover loss. Stop at the first CDF value reaching the critical ratio.

With integer demand, increase \(y\) while \(F(y)<\beta\): the first \(y\) with \(F(y)\ge\beta\) is optimal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(F(y)=\beta\), quantities \(y\) and \(y+1\) have equal expected cost.
  • All integer optimal quantities satisfy \(F(y-1)\le\beta\le F(y)\), taking \(F(-1)=0\).
  • Compute the expected cost with the actual discrete probabilities, not only the critical ratio.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The drawn CDF steps other than \(F(9)\) and \(F(10)\) are schematic; they do not specify additional probabilities for the dress example.

  • For the newspaper distribution, \(F(16)=0.25<3/7\le F(17)=0.50\), so the smallest optimum is 17; expected cost is 1.975.
  • The dress example has \(\beta=0.75\), optimal quantity 10, and expected cost 138.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The dynamic lot-size model chooses order quantities over \(n\) discrete periods with known varying demands, no shortages, and no lead time. In the detailed course notation, \(y_i\) is the period-\(i\) order, \(D_i\) demand, \(x_i\) starting stock, \(K_i\) setup cost, and \(h_i\) holding cost per unit carried to the next period. Then

\[ \begin{gathered} x_{i+1}=x_i+y_i-D_i\ge0,\\ C_i(y_i)=\begin{cases}0,&y_i=0,\\K_i+c_i(y_i),&y_i>0.\end{cases} \end{gathered} \]

Minimize \(\sum_{i=1}^n[C_i(y_i)+h_ix_{i+1}]\), with given \(x_1\) and terminal stock \(x_{n+1}=0\) in the course examples.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The model balances setup costs against carrying inventory into later periods. Unlike EOQ, demand and costs can change over the finite planning horizon.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course tables enumerate nonnegative integer order and stock quantities.
  • Variable ordering cost \(c_i(y_i)\) may depend nonlinearly on the batch size.
  • The model is introduced in the week 5 overview and developed in week 6.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated three-period policy, the period-2 order exceeds that period’s demand by one unit. Carrying it into period 3 gives the displayed total cost 79.

  • For demands \((2,1,3)\), the worked optimum orders \((2,2,2)\) at total cost 79.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Under the classical EOQ assumptions with \(D,K,h>0\), the unique order quantity minimizing \(TCU(y)=KD/y+hy/2\) over \(y>0\) is

\[ y^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}},\qquad t_0^*=\frac{y^*}{D}=\sqrt{\frac{2K}{Dh}}. \]

The optimal policy orders \(y^*\) units when stock reaches zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The formula balances the two policy-dependent cost components. Demand and setup cost favour larger batches; expensive holding favours smaller ones.

Change \(D\), \(K\) and \(h\): the minimum of \(TCU(y)\) sits where the two cost rates are equal, at \(y^*=\sqrt{2KD/h}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At the optimum, \(KD/y^*=hy^*/2\).
  • The minimum relevant cost rate is \(\sqrt{2KDh}\).
  • Increasing demand raises the batch size but shortens the cycle.
  • The formula follows from \(-KD/y^2+h/2=0\) and strict convexity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the illustrated phone shop, \(K=605\), \(D=2\) per day and \(h=5\) per unit per day give \(y^*=\sqrt{2\cdot605\cdot2/5}=22\). It orders every \(22/2=11\) days; setup and holding each cost \(55\) per day, giving relevant daily cost \(110\).
  • The snack bar obtains \(y^*=\sqrt{2(50)(10)/(3/7)}\approx48.30\) kilograms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a repeating EOQ cycle of length \(t_0^*>0\) and fixed lead time \(L\ge0\), the effective lead time is

\[ L_e=L-nt_0^*,\qquad n=\left\lfloor\frac{L}{t_0^*}\right\rfloor. \]

Thus \(0\le L_e<t_0^*\). The course's on-hand reorder level is \(DL_e\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The formula removes complete ordering cycles from the delay. It locates the ordering moment within a repeating stock cycle when orders from earlier cycles can still be in transit.

Whole cycles inside \(L\) do not matter for the reorder level: only \(L_e=L-nt_0^*\) does. Make \(L\) longer than a cycle to see orders overlap.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a lead time shorter than a cycle, \(L_e=L\).
  • The quantity \(L_e\) is a cycle remainder, not a shorter physical delivery delay.
  • If the delay is an exact multiple of the cycle, the remainder is zero; ordering and receipt events must be interpreted at that common cycle boundary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
To require at least one of \(a^Tx\le b\) and \(d^Tx\le e\), introduce \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and write

\[ a^Tx\le b+My,\qquad d^Tx\le e+M(1-y). \]

The finite constant \(M\) must be large enough that the relaxed inequality imposes no unintended restriction over the relevant variable domain.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: One inequality is enforced while the other is allowed to relax. Both original inequalities may still hold, so this formulation expresses inclusive “or.”

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(y=0\), the first inequality is enforced; for \(y=1\), the second is enforced.
  • A valid value of \(M\) requires information about bounds on the expressions being relaxed.
  • This is a modelling device; it does not mean multiplying two decision variables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The blue inequality is enforced when \(y=0\), and the red one when \(y=1\). The illustrated union is nonconvex, so it cannot be represented by one system of continuous linear inequalities in \(x\) alone.

  • \(3x_1+2x_2\le18+My\) and \(x_1+4x_2\le16+M(1-y)\) implement the video example.
  • The week 3 exercise applies the same switch to two inequalities involving four variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's maximization simplex tableau, the entering variable rule selects a nonbasic variable with the most negative coefficient in the objective row. If several coefficients tie for most negative, any tied variable may be chosen.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Because the objective row is written with the objective on the left, a more negative coefficient corresponds to a higher improvement rate per unit increase of that variable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The selected variable defines the pivot column.
  • The greatest improvement rate is not necessarily the greatest total improvement, because allowable step sizes differ.
  • The ratio test determines how far the entering variable can increase while preserving feasibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated row is \(z-3x_s-2x_t=0\), so \(x_s\) has the largest objective improvement rate per unit, \(3>2\), and enters. Choosing the smallest index is one possible tie convention; it is not required by the course rule. A feasible canonical tableau with no negative nonbasic objective-row coefficient is already optimal.

  • From \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\), choose \(x_1\).
  • From \(z-(1/2)x_2+(3/2)s_1=15\), choose \(x_2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The EOQ model with lead times retains constant known demand, no shortages, and the classical setup and holding costs, but an order arrives after a fixed delay \(L\ge0\). The optimal quantity remains \(y^*=\sqrt{2KD/h}\). In the course's repeating on-hand-stock convention, order when stock falls to \(DL_e\), where \(L_e\) is the effective lead time.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Lead time changes when an order must be placed so that replenishment arrives at the required moment. It does not change the EOQ under these deterministic assumptions.

Change the lead time \(L\): the batch size stays \(y^*\), but the order must be placed when stock reaches \(DL_e\) (dashed).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(L<t_0^*\), the reorder stock level is \(DL\).
  • If lead time exceeds a cycle, several orders can be outstanding; use the course effective-lead-time construction.
  • The on-hand trigger describes steady-state cycles, not the initial setup of an empty supply pipeline.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated pencil inventory, demand is \(D=100\) per day, each order costs \(K=180\), and holding one pencil costs \(h=0.001\) per day. The optimal order quantity and relevant daily cost are

\[ y^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\cdot180\cdot100}{0.001}}=6000, \qquad \sqrt{2KDh}=6. \]

The cycle lasts \(t_0^*=y^*/D=60\) days. With a 12-day lead time, the reorder level is \(DL=1200\): place the order on day 48 so that it arrives on day 60, when the stock runs out. The order quantity and cost remain unchanged.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The EOQ model with planned shortages allows all unmet demand to be backordered until instantaneous replenishment. With constant \(D>0\), setup \(K>0\), holding rate \(h>0\), and backlog penalty \(p>0\), choose batch size \(y>0\) and stock just after replenishment \(0\le s\le y\). Maximum backlog is \(y-s\), and

\[ TCU(y,s)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hs^2}{2y}+\frac{p(y-s)^2}{2y}. \]

The optimum is

\[ \begin{aligned} y^*&=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p+h}{p}},\\ s^*&=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p}{p+h}}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The policy deliberately balances periods with positive stock and periods with waiting customers. Replenishment first clears the backlog, leaving \(s\) units on hand.

Choose the batch size \(y\) and the stock \(s\) after replenishment. The level curves of \(TCU(y,s)\) (left) surround the optimum; the right panel shows stock and backlog.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Order \(y^*\) when backlog reaches \(y^*-s^*\).
  • Cycle length is \(y^*/D\); the fraction of time without shortage is \(p/(p+h)\).
  • The stock-phase mean \(s/2\) is not the whole-cycle average; the latter is \(s^2/(2y)\).
  • For finite positive \(p\), the optimal batch is larger than the classical EOQ.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the illustrated phone example, \(D=2\) per day, \(K=605\), \(h=5\) per phone per day and \(p=6\) per backlogged phone per day give \(y^*=22\sqrt{11/6}\approx29.79\) and \(s^*=22\sqrt{6/11}\approx16.25\). Order when the backlog reaches \(y^*-s^*\approx13.54\). The cycle lasts about \(14.9\) days: stock is positive for about \(8.1\) days and backlogged for about \(6.8\) days, with stock-positive fraction \(6/11\).
  • With \(p=h\), the model is out of stock for half the cycle.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's EOQ model with price breaks gives an all-unit discount: every ordered unit has price \(c_2<c_1\) when the batch meets a threshold \(q\). Following the “at least” convention of the worked examples,

\[ \begin{gathered} c(y)=\begin{cases}c_1,&0<y<q,\\c_2,&y\ge q,\end{cases}\\ TCU(y)=Dc(y)+\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hy}{2}. \end{gathered} \]

Holding rate \(h\) is fixed across price levels; demand is constant, replenishment instantaneous, and shortages prohibited.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A larger batch may be worth buying to reduce the price of every unit. Purchasing cost must therefore be included in the comparison.

From the break \(q\) on, every unit costs \(c_2<c_1\), so the total cost curve jumps down. Compare the best quantity on each side of \(q\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Let \(y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}\). If \(y_m\ge q\), order \(y_m\) at the discount price.
  • If \(y_m<q\), compare the full costs at \(y_m\) and \(q\) and choose the cheaper; both are optimal at equality.
  • The introductory PDF uses \(y>q\), inconsistent with its later recommendation \(y=q\). This page explicitly follows the worked-example convention.
  • The discount is all-unit, not a discount only on units above the threshold.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For phones, \(y_m=22\): cost at 22 is 450 per day, while cost at the qualifying 35 is about 442.07; order 35.
  • For the snack bar, the 100-kilogram threshold is not worthwhile; the optimal quantity remains about 48.30.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the course's Euclidean network, cities have plane coordinates \((x_i,y_i)\), an edge may join every pair of cities, and its length is

\[ d_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}. \]

The resulting distances provide the weights for the minimum spanning tree problem.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Coordinates turn a location problem into a complete weighted network. Distances are straight-line lengths rather than road travel times.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Distances are symmetric: \(d_{ij}=d_{ji}\).
  • Use sufficient precision when comparing close distances.
  • The usual spanning-tree algorithms apply once the distance matrix is computed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The red edge has length \(\ell_{12}=\sqrt{3^2+2^2}=\sqrt{13}\). Euclidean distances satisfy the triangle inequality and can also be used as routing costs.

  • Between \((13,6)\) and \((15,9)\) the distance is \(\sqrt{13}\approx3.61\).
  • The seven-city example has tree length about 27.29 using the displayed rounded distances.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: A finite connected undirected network has an Euler tour if and only if every vertex has even degree. Such a network is called an Euler network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Even degree is necessary because each arrival along an edge must be paired with a departure. The cycle-splicing construction establishes sufficiency.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• One odd-degree vertex is enough to rule out an Euler tour.
  • Connectedness is required to traverse all edges in one tour.
  • Parallel copies introduced by the Chinese postman construction are counted as separate edges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The seven-bridge network violates the even-degree condition.
  • Duplicating suitable paths between odd-degree vertices makes their endpoint degrees even.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a connected undirected Euler network, the course's Euler tour algorithm starts at a vertex \(s\), follows unused edges until returning to \(s\), and calls the resulting cycle \(\Omega\). If unused edges remain, choose a vertex \(v\) on \(\Omega\) incident to an unused edge, build another closed unused-edge traversal \(\Omega_1\) from \(v\), and splice \(\Omega_1\) into \(\Omega\) at \(v\). Repeat until every edge is used.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The method builds a complete tour from smaller cycles. Even degree ensures that an unused-edge excursion can close at its starting vertex.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Keep track of used edge identities, especially with parallel copies.
  • The splice inserts one closed excursion into another without losing any previously used edge.
  • Arbitrary eligible choices can give different valid Euler tours.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, the first cycle is \(\Omega=A-B-C-A\). The remaining cycle \(A-D-E-A\) is spliced at \(A\), giving \(A-B-C-A-D-E-A\). The even-degree condition permits these closed excursions.

  • The worked example begins its first cycle at A.
  • It later adds a cycle through B and then one through D to include all 12 edges.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An Euler tour is a closed traversal of a network that uses every edge exactly once. Vertices may be revisited. A network possessing an Euler tour is called an Euler network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The requirement concerns visiting edges, not visiting each vertex once. It models a route that covers every street without retracing an edge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At each vertex, arrivals and departures balance.
  • For connected undirected networks, an Euler tour exists exactly when every vertex has even degree.
  • In a weighted Euler network, every Euler tour has length equal to the sum of all edge lengths.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated Euler network, \(\deg A=4\) and every other degree is 2. The tour returns to its start while using every edge once.

  • The Königsberg bridge network has no Euler tour because its vertices have odd degree.
  • The course weighted Euler example has total edge length 24, so its Euler tours have length 24.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The feasible region is the set of all feasible solutions of a model:

\[ F=\{x:x\text{ satisfies every model constraint}\}. \]

For a two-variable LP it is obtained by intersecting the allowed half-planes and equality lines, including variable-domain restrictions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The feasible region shows the choices available before the objective is considered. Each extra constraint can retain or reduce this set.

Drag the decision point: it is feasible exactly when it satisfies every constraint, including \(x_s,x_t\ge0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Removing a constraint cannot shrink the feasible region.
  • An empty feasible region means the model is infeasible.
  • An unbounded feasible region does not by itself imply an unbounded objective value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated upper-bound model, \(F=\{x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\). It is an intersection of half-planes in two dimensions, or a convex polyhedron in \(\mathbb R^n\); an LP feasible set may be bounded, unbounded or empty.

  • \(x_1,x_2\ge0\) restrict the region to the first quadrant.
  • The diet requirements define the intersection of calorie, vitamin, and feed-share half-planes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A feasible solution assigns values to all decision variables and satisfies every constraint, including their domain restrictions. A solution violating at least one constraint is infeasible.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Feasibility asks whether a decision is allowed. It must be checked before the decision's objective value can be used as a practical candidate.

Drag the point and read each constraint: a single violated inequality makes the decision infeasible, however good its objective value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An attractive objective value does not compensate for a violated constraint.
  • An LP-feasible fractional solution may be infeasible after integer restrictions are imposed.
  • Every optimal solution is feasible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \((15,40)\) satisfies \(70\le100\), \(55\le80\) and \(15\le40\); \((40,20)\) is also feasible. By contrast, \((30,50)\) requires \(2\cdot30+50=110>100\) finishing hours, and any \(x_s<0\) violates nonnegativity.

  • For \(x_1\le4\), \(x_2\le5\), \(2x_1+x_2\le9\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\), \((2,5)\) is feasible.
  • In the same model, \((4,5)\) is infeasible because \(2(4)+5=13>9\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear expression can be restricted to one of the listed values \(d_1,\ldots,d_N\) by introducing binary variables \(y_i\) and writing

\[ \begin{gathered} a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=\sum_{i=1}^Nd_iy_i,\\ \sum_{i=1}^Ny_i=1,\qquad y_i\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Exactly one indicator selects the allowed value of the expression. This avoids writing a separate alternative constraint for every possible value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sum-to-one equality ensures that a value is actually selected.
  • The \(d_i\) are fixed data, so \(d_iy_i\) is linear.
  • Relaxing the indicators to continuous fractions would generally allow values between the listed values.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The light band shows intermediate totals made possible by fractional selector values; the binary selectors permit only the listed totals.

  • For allowed totals 3, 5, or 8, write \(x_1+x_2=3y_1+5y_2+8y_3\).
  • An even number of three yes decisions can take only the values 0 and 2.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The first-fit heuristic processes packing items in their given order. Place the current item into the first previously opened container with enough unused capacity. If no such container exists, open a new container and place the item there. Assume every item individually fits in a container.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The rule makes each placement using the current packing, without searching all arrangements. Both item order and container order affect its decisions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every produced packing respects capacity.
  • Its container count is an upper bound, not a proof of optimality.
  • The exercise gives this procedure without a name; first-fit is its conventional search name.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated order \(15,30,20,35\) with capacity 50 uses three containers under first fit. Two suffice with \(\{15,35\}\) and \(\{30,20\}\), so that first-fit result is not optimal. Reordering the same items as \(35,30,20,15\) makes first fit use two containers here.

  • In the course exercise, items 1, 2, 3, and 9 fill container 1 to weight 49.
  • Items 6, 7, and 8 fill another container to weight 49; the full heuristic packing uses five containers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A forbidden assignment is an agent-task pair that is not allowed. In the course's Hungarian cost matrix, represent this pair by \(\infty\) and leave that entry infinite during all transformations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The infinite cost acts as a prohibition rather than an expensive ordinary choice. A finite feasible complete assignment must avoid every prohibited pair.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Do not apply finite row or column adjustments as if they made an infinite entry available.
  • If no complete assignment avoiding forbidden pairs exists, the intended assignment problem is infeasible.
  • In a binary formulation, the equivalent restriction is \(x_{ij}=0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, prohibiting \((2,2)\) gives the highlighted assignment \(A_1\to T_1\), \(A_2\to T_3\), \(A_3\to T_2\) with cost \(2+4+6=12\), compared with diagonal cost \(2+3+2=7\) without the ban. A finite penalty \(M\) represents a prohibition only if it is sufficiently large and an allowed complete assignment exists; \(x_{22}=0\) enforces the ban directly.

  • A machine unable to process job 3 receives an infinite entry in that job's column.
  • A feasible assignment must choose another machine for that job.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Graphical integer programming solves a two-variable integer model by plotting its continuous constraints and considering only the lattice points satisfying all restrictions. Evaluate the objective at feasible integer points to identify the best value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The continuous feasible region helps locate the permitted integer points. Unlike an LP, the best integer point need not be a corner of that continuous region.

Only the lattice points count. The best integer point (ringed) need not be a corner of the continuous region: here it lies on an edge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both coordinates must satisfy the stated integrality restrictions.
  • An LP-optimal fractional corner is not an integer-feasible decision.
  • For a small bounded example, explicit comparison of feasible lattice points proves optimality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure uses the illustrative model \(\max(3x_1+2x_2)\) subject to \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\), \(x_1\le3.5\) and \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2\). Its best lattice point is \((3,1)\) with value 11; it is not a corner of the continuous polygon.

  • The integer work-order model uses \(3.2T+2.4S\le16\) and \(2T+3S\le15\).
