docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The graphical method solves a two-variable LP by drawing each constraint boundary, identifying the common feasible region, drawing a constant-objective line, and moving that line in the direction of improvement until the best feasible contact is reached. Intersecting the relevant boundary equations gives exact coordinates.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The method makes feasibility and optimality visible. It also reveals whether the best value is attained at one point or along a segment.

The numbered markers illustrate the method for the objective \(z=3x_s+2x_t\):

  1. Draw the boundaries \(2x_s+x_t=100\), \(x_s+x_t=80\) and \(x_s=40\).
  2. Shade their common feasible region, including the restrictions \(x_s,x_t\ge0\).
  3. Draw a constant-objective line, such as the dashed line \(3x_s+2x_t=90\).
  4. Move the line in the improving direction \((3,2)\) while it still touches the feasible region.
  5. The last contact is the optimum, here the corner \((20,60)\).

Push the objective line \(z=\bar z\) in the direction of the arrow until it last touches the feasible region; press the button to jump there. Here the last contact is the corner \((20,60)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Determine the allowed side of each boundary from the inequality; do not assume it is always below the line.
  • Check the direction of improvement from the objective, especially with negative coefficients.
  • Also allow for an empty feasible region or an objective that can improve without bound.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Maximizing \(x_1+2x_2\) with \(x_1\le4\), \(x_2\le5\), \(2x_1+x_2\le9\) gives \((2,5)\).
  • For \(z=2x_1-3x_2\), increasing \(z\) moves its objective line downward.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A heuristic is a solution method designed to obtain a good feasible solution without a general guarantee that it is optimal. In this course, a heuristic solution is required to satisfy the original problem's constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Heuristics are useful when finding an exact optimum is too difficult or time-consuming. A good feasible decision can be valuable even before its distance from optimality is known.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For minimization, a feasible heuristic value is an upper bound on the optimum.
  • For maximization, a feasible heuristic value is a lower bound.
  • A relaxation can supply an opposing bound that measures solution quality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For maximization, improved incumbents raise the feasible lower bound. Resolving branch-and-bound nodes can reduce the global upper bound formed from the incumbent and the remaining open-node relaxation bounds.

  • Visiting each routing location separately from the depot gives a feasible starting plan.
  • First-fit packs items into the first container with enough remaining capacity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A holding cost charges for inventory kept in stock. In the continuous-time EOQ model, \(h\) is the cost per unit held per unit of time. With average inventory \(\bar I\), the average holding cost rate is \(h\bar I\). In the discrete-time models, \(h_i\) charges each unit carried from period \(i\) to \(i+1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Holding cost makes early or large replenishment costly. Its time unit must match the demand rate and other rates in the calculation.

The average stock in the sawtooth is \(y/2\) (dashed line), so the holding cost rate is \(hy/2\). Raise \(h\) to see \(y^*\) fall.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Hungarian algorithm solves the square minimum-cost assignment problem. Subtract each row minimum, then each column minimum. Cover all zeros of the resulting matrix with a minimum number of rows and columns. If \(n\) lines are needed, select \(n\) independent zeros, one per row and column. Otherwise let \(k\) be the smallest uncovered entry, subtract \(k\) from uncovered entries, add \(k\) to doubly covered entries, leave singly covered entries unchanged, and repeat the covering step.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The transformations preserve the optimal assignment while creating enough zero entries for a complete assignment. The final cost must be evaluated in the original matrix.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero cover must use the minimum number of lines.
  • A set of independent zeros has no two in the same row or column.
  • The minimum line-cover size equals the maximum number of independent zero assignments in this construction.
  • Do not add together transformed zero costs to report the original objective value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, the smallest uncovered entry is 1: subtract 1 from uncovered entries, add 1 at double intersections, and leave singly covered entries unchanged. The final zero assignment \((1,1),(2,3),(3,2)\) has original cost \(4+7+1=12\).

  • The worked four-machine matrix initially needs three covering lines; an adjustment with k=2 enables a complete assignment.
  • The final original cost is \(2+5+6+7=20\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The incumbent solution in branch-and-bound is the best feasible solution of the original integer problem found so far. Its objective value supplies a lower bound for maximization and an upper bound for minimization.

docs.title: Interpretation

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An infeasible linear program has no decision vector satisfying all its constraints. Equivalently, its feasible region is empty. In the two-phase method, a negative optimal value of \(r=-\sum_iR_i\) proves infeasibility.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conflicting requirements can make a model impossible even when each requirement is individually sensible. The objective cannot resolve this conflict.

The two constraints cannot hold together, so no decision is feasible. Lower \(b_2\) until the requirements become compatible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An infeasible model has no optimal feasible solution.
  • A positive remaining artificial variable at the phase-I optimum indicates an unsatisfied original requirement.
  • Infeasibility differs from an unbounded objective, which requires feasible points.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\le2\), \(3x_1+4x_2\ge12\), \(x_1,x_2\ge0\) is infeasible: the first constraint implies \(3x_1+4x_2\le8\).
  • A negative phase-I optimum, such as \(r^*=-4\), cannot be repaired by beginning Phase II.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An integer linear program (ILP) is a linear optimization model in which some or all decision variables must take integer values. The linear objective and functional constraints are retained, with restrictions such as \(x_j\in\mathbb Z\) added to the specified variables.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Integrality represents indivisible decisions and also supports modelling of logical conditions. It changes the feasible set and can make the problem substantially harder to solve.

Change the objective and compare the LP optimum with the best feasible lattice point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pure integer programs require all decision variables to be integer.
  • Mixed integer programs include both integer and continuous variables.
  • Binary integer programs restrict every decision variable to 0 or 1.
  • Rounding an LP solution need not preserve feasibility or optimality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure uses the illustrative objective \(3x_1+2x_2\) and restrictions \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\), \(x_1\le3.5\), \(x\ge0\). Its continuous optimum \((3.5,1.25)\) has value 13, whereas requiring both variables to be integers gives \((3,1)\) with value 11. Branch-and-bound on LP relaxations is an exact method; arbitrary rounding is not.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An inventory policy specifies when to replenish stock and how much to order. Inventory theory constructs and analyses models to choose these decisions while accounting for demand and relevant costs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Ordering frequently reduces stock held but increases the number of setups. Larger, less frequent orders reverse that trade-off. The appropriate model depends on the demand setting.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The EOQ models use a constant deterministic demand rate.
  • Dynamic lot sizing uses known demand varying by discrete period.
  • The newsvendor model uses stochastic demand for one selling period.
  • A complete policy states both the quantity and the ordering trigger or period.

docs.title: Examples

  • The right panel shows a newsvendor policy: choose one stock quantity before demand is observed, using the critical-ratio quantile \(F^{-1}(\beta)\) under the continuous, strictly increasing distribution assumptions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The job sequencing model orders nonpreemptive jobs on one machine to minimize total lateness penalties. Let \(s_i\ge0\) be job \(i\)'s start, \(p_i\) its duration, \(d_i\) its due date, \(T_i\ge0\) its tardiness, and \(w_i\) its penalty rate. Minimize \(\sum_iw_iT_i\) subject to \(T_i\ge s_i+p_i-d_i\). For each pair \(i<j\), impose

\[ \begin{gathered} s_i+p_i\le s_j+M(1-y_{ij}),\\ s_j+p_j\le s_i+My_{ij},\qquad y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

Here \(y_{ij}=1\) means \(i\) precedes \(j\), and \(M\) must be valid for the scheduling horizon.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Pairwise alternatives prevent overlapping processing. Tardiness variables charge for finishing after the due date while imposing no penalty for early completion.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For the supplied three jobs, total processing time is 40; a no-idle schedule starts at zero and lies within that horizon.
  • Nonnegative penalty rates make unnecessary idle time avoidable.
  • This formulation is derived from the exercise and the preceding either-or technique; the video PDF contains the problem statement only.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The course has processing times \((5,20,15)\) and due dates \((24,22,35)\).
  • Sequence \(2,1,3\) completes at 20, 25, 40 and incurs \(12(0)+19(1)+34(5)=189\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
To require at least \(K\) of \(N\) inequalities \(a_i^Tx\le d_i\), introduce binary relaxation indicators \(y_i\) and impose

\[ \begin{gathered} a_i^Tx\le d_i+My_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,N),\\ \sum_{i=1}^Ny_i\le N-K. \end{gathered} \]

Here \(0\le K\le N\) and \(M\) must validly relax each marked inequality. The video's equality \(\sum_i y_i=N-K\) gives the same allowed \(x\) values when such relaxation is valid.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: At most \(N-K\) inequalities may be released, so at least \(K\) remain enforced. A released inequality is allowed to hold as well.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The formulation does not require exactly \(K\) original inequalities to be true.
  • The practice solution uses the inequality version; the video uses equality.
  • For \(K=N\), no constraint may be relaxed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure sets \(N=4\), \(K=2\): the binary bound \(y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4\le2\) allows at most two released inequalities, leaving at least two enforced. The constant \(M\) must be large enough to remove unintended restrictions from every released inequality.

  • At least two of four constraints can be enforced using \(y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4\le2\).
  • At least two of three constraints leave at most one relaxation indicator equal to 1.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Königsberg bridge problem asks whether a closed walk can cross each of the city's seven bridges exactly once. Represent each land region by a vertex and each bridge by an edge. The resulting four-vertex network asks whether an Euler tour exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The geographical details are reduced to a connection problem. The impossibility follows from vertex degrees rather than from testing every possible walk.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Parallel bridges are separate edges between the same vertices.
  • The illustrated degrees are 5, 3, 3, and 3, so the even-degree condition fails.
  • The requested return to the starting point is part of the problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The four vertices represent the land areas: island \(A\), banks \(B,C\) and area \(D\). Four odd-degree vertices also rule out an open edge-once trail: such a trail has exactly two odd endpoints, or none if closed. Euler’s 1736 analysis is conventionally regarded as the beginning of graph theory.

  • The central land region has five incident bridge edges.
  • At an odd-degree region, a closed traversal cannot pair all arrivals and departures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Kruskal method constructs a minimum spanning tree by starting with no selected edges and repeatedly choosing a shortest unselected edge that does not create a cycle with the already selected edges. Stop once the selected edges connect all vertices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The selected edges may initially form several separate pieces. The method joins those pieces while avoiding unnecessary loops.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equivalently, inspect edges in nondecreasing order and reject any that create a cycle.
  • For \(n\) vertices, a completed tree has \(n-1\) selected edges.
  • Equal-length eligible edges may be chosen in any order.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the figure, the sorted weights are \(1,2,2,3,4,5,6,8,10\). Accept \(BC,AC,DE,EF\), reject \(AB\) because it closes \(A-B-C-A\), then accept \(BD\). These \(n-1=5\) edges have total length 13.

  • If A-B and B-C are already selected, adding A-C would create a cycle and must be rejected.
  • Week 4 practice 3 has three independent binary tie choices, giving \(2^3=8\) minimum trees.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A linear program (LP) maximizes or minimizes a linear objective function subject to linear equality and/or inequality constraints. Its decision variables are continuous unless additional integer restrictions are imposed. For example,

\[ \begin{gathered} \max z=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j,\\ \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j\le b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\\ x_j\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

Other inequality directions and equalities are also allowed in an LP.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Linearity makes large planning models tractable by methods such as simplex. A model with indivisible decisions needs explicit integer restrictions to rule out fractional choices.

Change the objective coefficients \(c_1,c_2\): the feasible region stays put, and the optimum jumps from corner to corner.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Products of decision variables and powers such as \(x_j^2\) are not linear.
  • Negative coefficients are allowed.
  • The graphical method is useful for two variables; simplex handles larger models.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated Giapetto LP has objective \(3x_s+2x_t\) and attains value 180 at \((20,60)\). Its original quantities are continuous; no integrality restriction is included.

  • Giapetto maximizes \(3x_s+2x_t\) under linear labour and demand limits.
  • The feeding-pigs model minimizes cost under nutrient and composition requirements.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f_i(x_{i+1})\) be the minimum cost through period \(i\), including its ending-stock holding cost, conditional on stock \(x_{i+1}\). For given initial stock \(x_1\), the course's forward lot-size recursion is

\[ f_1(x_2)=C_1(D_1+x_2-x_1)+h_1x_2 \]

when the required order is nonnegative, and \(+\infty\) otherwise. For \(i\ge2\),

\[ \begin{aligned} &f_i(x_{i+1})\\ &\quad=\min_{0\le y_i\le D_i+x_{i+1}} \left\{C_i(y_i)+h_ix_{i+1}\right.\\ &\qquad\left.{}+f_{i-1}(x_{i+1}+D_i-y_i)\right\}. \end{aligned} \]

Use integer states and decisions in the course tables; unreachable predecessor states have value \(+\infty\). The required final value is \(f_n(0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The previous stock level is inferred from the ending stock and current order. The recursion compares all feasible ways to reach the same ending state.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The bound on \(y_i\) ensures nonnegative predecessor inventory.
  • Reconstruct from \(x_{n+1}=0\) using stored minimizers and \(x_i=x_{i+1}+D_i-y_i\).
  • In the course examples, states need not exceed the remaining future demand.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The three-period example gives \(f_2(1)=53\) and \(f_3(0)=26+53=79\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The LP relaxation of an integer linear program removes its integrality requirements and keeps the objective and all other restrictions. In particular, a binary variable becomes a continuous variable satisfying \(0\le x_j\le1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The relaxation is easier to solve and includes every integer-feasible decision. Its optimum bounds the original integer optimum.

Dropping integrality enlarges the feasible set, so the relaxed optimum \(z_{LP}\) is an upper bound on the integer optimum \(z_{IP}\) for this maximization.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Its value is an upper bound for maximization and a lower bound for minimization.
  • If a relaxed optimizer satisfies every original integrality restriction, it is also integer-optimal.
  • Do not drop binary upper bounds when dropping binarity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated model, the relaxed optimum \((3.5,1.25)\) gives value 13. Rounding to \((4,1)\) violates the constraints; \((3,1)\) is feasible and happens to be integer-optimal with value 11. That success does not establish a general rounding rule.

  • The project-selection relaxation allows \(x_3=0.2\) and obtains 3.52 at the root.
  • An integral relaxed solution such as \((1,0,1,1,0)\) is a feasible candidate for the original project model.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For the course network with only outgoing source edges and only incoming sink edges, the maximum flow LP uses continuous variables \(x_{ij}\) and solves

\[ \begin{aligned} &\max\quad \sum_jx_{sj}\\ &\text{subject to}\\ &\quad\sum_jx_{ji}=\sum_jx_{ij}\quad(i\ne s,t),\\ &\quad0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\\ &\qquad\text{for every directed edge }(i,j). \end{aligned} \]

Here \(c_{ij}\) is the edge capacity and sums run over existing edges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The formulation separates the objective at the source from conservation at intermediate vertices. Capacities constrain individual directed flows.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Source outflow equals sink inflow by summing conservation equations.
  • No binary selection variable is needed: an edge may carry any feasible flow amount.
  • The formulation is derived from the video prompt and the previously taught flow conditions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, maximize \(x_{AB}+x_{AC}\) with the displayed edge capacities. The intermediate balances are

\[ \begin{aligned}x_{AB}&=x_{BC}+x_{BD},\\x_{AC}+x_{BC}&=x_{CD}+x_{CE},\\x_{BD}+x_{CD}&=x_{DF},\\x_{CE}&=x_{EF}.\end{aligned} \]

The optimum is 8. For a maximum-flow formulation with integer capacities, an integral optimal flow exists; this is a property of this network formulation, not of arbitrary LPs with integer data.

  • The example objective is \(x_{SA}+x_{SB}\).
  • At A, conservation is \(x_{SA}=x_{AB}+x_{AC}+x_{AD}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The maximum flow problem assigns nonnegative flow \(x_{ij}\) to the edges of a directed network, subject to capacities \(x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\) and flow conservation at every transshipment vertex. The course assumes the source has only outgoing edges and the sink only incoming edges. The objective is to maximize total source outflow, equivalently total sink inflow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Intermediate vertices pass flow through the network rather than create or consume it. Capacities limit how much can travel on each directed connection.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Flow into each intermediate vertex equals flow out.
  • The same maximum value can have several feasible edge-flow assignments.
  • Residual reverse capacity permits earlier routing choices to be revised.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated flow has source outflow \(3+5=8\). The cut separating \(\{A,B,C,E\}\) from \(\{D,F\}\) has capacity \(3+2+3=8\), so no feasible flow can exceed 8. Attaining that cut bound certifies maximality.

  • The main example sends maximum flow 15 from S to T.
  • Week 4 practice 7 reaches 16, with 9 entering T from D and 7 from E.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: Over the same feasible set, minimizing \(f(x)\) is equivalent to maximizing \(-f(x)\). The two problems have the same optimal solution vectors, and their optimal objective values have opposite signs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The course presents simplex for maximization. Negating a minimization objective allows that procedure to be used while leaving the constraints unchanged.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Negate every objective coefficient.
  • Recover the original optimal value by changing the sign back.
  • Only the objective changes; the allowed decisions remain the same.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Minimizing \(3x_1-5x_2\) becomes maximizing \(-3x_1+5x_2\).
  • In week 2 practice 8, transformed value 10 corresponds to original minimum \(-10\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a feasible canonical tableau and an entering variable with constraint-column coefficients \(a_{ik}\) and right-hand sides \(b_i\ge0\), the minimum-ratio test selects

\[ \theta=\min_{i:a_{ik}>0}\frac{b_i}{a_{ik}}. \]

A row attaining the minimum supplies the leaving basic variable. Zero ratios are eligible; only the denominator must be strictly positive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The test finds the first basic variable that reaches zero as the entering variable increases. A larger step would violate nonnegativity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rows with zero or negative pivot-column coefficients do not restrict the increase.
  • A tie may be broken arbitrarily in the course procedure and can lead to degeneracy.
  • If there is no positive coefficient and the objective improves along this column, the objective is unbounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated tableau, increasing \(x_s\) gives \(s_1=100-2x_s\), \(s_2=80-x_s\) and \(s_3=40-x_s\). The limits \(50,80,40\) give step length 40, so \(s_3\) leaves.

  • The initial ratios \(10/2=5\) and \(15/1=15\) make \(s_1\) leave.
  • The next ratios are \(5/(1/2)=10\) and \(10/(5/2)=4\), so \(s_2\) leaves.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, a minimum spanning tree is a spanning tree whose total selected edge length is smallest among all spanning trees of that network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The objective is to connect every location at minimum total construction length. It does not minimize travel distance from one selected origin.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both Dijkstra-Prim and Kruskal methods produce a minimum spanning tree.
  • There may be several minimum trees with the same total length.
  • Tie choices may be explored to identify alternative minimum trees.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The green edges in the figure have total length \(1+2+2+3+5=13\). They form a minimum spanning tree.

  • Roads can be selected to connect all cities while minimizing total road length.
  • Week 4 practice 1 has two minimum spanning trees, differing by the choice B-F or F-G.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the CPP construction, a minimum-weight perfect matching pairs the odd-degree vertices so that each belongs to exactly one pair and the sum of pair costs is minimized. The cost \(d_{ij}\) of a pair is its shortest-path distance. With a binary variable for each unordered pair,

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{i<j}d_{ij}x_{ij},\\ \sum_{j<i}x_{ji}+\sum_{j>i}x_{ij}=1\\ \text{for each odd vertex }i. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This selects which odd vertices should be linked by duplicated paths. Pairing must be optimized jointly, since a locally cheap pair may leave expensive remaining pairs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each pair variable is binary.
  • For four odd vertices there are three complete pairings to compare.
  • This is a nonbipartite matching problem because the vertices are not separated into two assignment groups.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated four odd vertices, the alternative pairing \(\{PR,QS\}\) costs 13. The minimum-cost pairing determines which shortest paths are duplicated in the CPP construction.

  • The pairings AB/DE, AD/BE, and AE/BD cost 8, 7, and 8.
  • The optimum selects \(x_{AD}=x_{BE}=1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A minimum zero cover is a smallest set of matrix rows and columns covering all zero entries. Starting from a maximum independent zero assignment, mark all unassigned rows; repeatedly mark columns containing zeros in marked rows and rows assigned to marked columns. When marking stops, cover all marked columns and all unmarked rows.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This procedure supplies the minimum line cover required by the Hungarian algorithm. A merely maximal partial assignment is insufficient; use a maximum one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For an \(n\times n\) matrix, \(n\) required covering lines indicate that a complete zero-cost assignment exists.
  • The cover size equals the size of the maximum independent zero assignment.
  • Rows and columns marked during the search are not the same as the final lines: the final rows are the unmarked ones.
  • If fewer than \(n\) lines are needed, subtract the smallest uncovered entry from all uncovered entries and add it to entries at intersections of covering lines. Repeat the assignment and covering steps until \(n\) lines are needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the illustrated matrix, the independent zeros at \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) form a maximum assignment of size \(2\). Row 2 and column 2 cover every zero with two lines. Their equal sizes illustrate Kőnig's theorem; since \(2<3\), the matrix still needs adjustment before a complete zero assignment is possible.
  • Week 5 practice 5(b) covers columns 1 and 2 and rows 2 and 3.
  • The ten-job example covers columns 1, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9 and rows 2, 10: eight lines.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A mixed integer program (MIP) is an integer linear program containing both integer-restricted decision variables and continuous decision variables. Binary variables may be used for the discrete decisions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A single model can select a discrete action and determine continuous quantities conditional on it. The domain of each variable must therefore be stated individually.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An LP relaxation removes integrality only from the restricted variables.
  • Continuous variables should not accidentally be forced to integer values.
  • Logical modelling often introduces auxiliary binary variables alongside quantities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure maximizes \(3x_1+2x_2\) under \(2x_1+2x_2\le9.5\), \(x_1\le3.5\) and \(x\ge0\), with only \(x_1\) integer. Its optimum \((3,1.75)\) has value 12.5, between the pure-integer value 11 and the continuous relaxation value 13.

  • \(x_1+x_2\le100+50y\) combines continuous production with a binary machine-purchase decision.
  • Continuous job start times can be combined with binary variables specifying which job comes first.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A model parameter is a given numerical input to the optimization model. In the course's LP notation, parameters include objective coefficients \(c_j\), constraint coefficients \(a_{ij}\), and right-hand sides \(b_i\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Parameters describe the circumstances under which decisions are made. A parameter may be an estimate even though the optimization treats its supplied value as fixed.

The objective function \(f(x)\) is the quantity to maximise (for example, profit) or minimise (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(x)\) subject to \(x\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Changing parameters can change both the optimal decision and the optimal value.
  • Units must agree within an equation or inequality.
  • Sensitivity analysis investigates the effect of parameter changes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The coefficient \(3\) in \(3x_s+2x_t\) is profit per soldier.
  • The right-hand side \(100\) in \(2x_s+x_t\le100\) is available painting time.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An optimization problem has multiple optimal solutions if distinct feasible decision vectors attain the same optimal objective value. In an LP, every convex combination of two optimal solutions is also optimal.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Different decisions can be equally good under the stated objective. In a two-variable LP, this often appears as an objective line coinciding with a feasible boundary segment.

With \(z=4x_s+2x_t\) the objective line is parallel to the finishing constraint, so every point of an edge is optimal. Move \(\alpha\) along it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero objective-row coefficient for a nonbasic variable in an optimal simplex tableau suggests an alternative optimum.
  • A positive feasible movement in that direction produces a distinct optimum; a zero-length degenerate pivot alone does not establish a different decision vector.
  • Additional requirements can select one point from an optimal segment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective \(2x_s+2x_t\), the feasible part of \(x_s+x_t=80\) between \((0,80)\) and \((20,60)\) is optimal. It includes \((10,70)\); every point on the segment has value 160.

  • In the week 3 example, \((5,0)\) and \((3,4)\) both give \(4x_1+2x_2=20\).
  • In practice exercise 3 of week 3, imposing \(x_1=1\) selects \((1,9/2)\) from the optimal segment.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For binary variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_k\), mutually exclusive decisions allow at most one variable to equal 1:

\[ \sum_{j=1}^ky_j\le1. \]

If one alternative must be chosen, use \(\sum_{j=1}^ky_j=1\) instead.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The inequality permits choosing none, while the equality requires one choice. This distinction matters when translating phrases such as “at most one” and “exactly one.”

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Binarity is essential to interpret the sum as the number of yes decisions.
  • Exactly one implies at most one, but the reverse is false.
  • This restriction concerns decisions, not an either-or condition on continuous inequalities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(W_{LA}+W_{SF}\le1\) permits at most one warehouse.
  • \(y_1+y_2+y_3=1\) selects exactly one allowed quantity value.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A network consists of a set of vertices and edges connecting specified pairs of vertices. Vertices represent entities or locations; edges represent connections. Depending on the problem, edges may have directions and numerical values such as distances, costs, or capacities.

  • The meaning of an edge value depends on the problem: distance and capacity are different quantities.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The newsvendor model chooses a single order quantity \(y\ge0\) before observing random demand \(D\). With unit purchase cost \(c\), selling price \(p>c\), and salvage value \(s<c\), define overage cost \(h=c-s\) and underage cost \(b=p-c\). Minimize

\[ G(y)=h\,\mathbb E[(y-D)^+]+b\,\mathbb E[(D-y)^+], \]

where \(u^+=\max\{u,0\}\) and the expectations are finite. Sales equal \(\min\{y,D\}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Too much stock leaves costly leftovers; too little misses profitable demand. The optimal quantity balances those risks through the demand distribution.

Move \(y\): the expected overage cost rises and the expected underage cost falls. Their sum \(G(y)\) is smallest at the \(\beta\)-quantile of demand (right).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Salvage value can be zero or negative.
  • \(G(y)\) is convex; an optimum occurs where increasing stock stops reducing expected cost.
  • \(G(y)\) measures overage and underage loss, not gross purchasing expenditure.
  • The model is introduced in the week 5 overview and developed in week 6.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated meal-demand example is uniform on \([80,120]\) with critical ratio \(\beta=0.6\). Its optimal stock is \(y^*=104\), for which \(F(104)=0.6\).

  • A newsvendor chooses newspaper stock before daily demand is known.
  • A shop chooses seasonal dress inventory; a canteen prepares meals before evening demand.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For a fixed integer quantity \(y\) and fixed purchase cost \(c\) and salvage value \(s<c\), newsvendor price sensitivity finds selling prices \(p>c\) for which \(y\) remains optimal. The condition is

\[ F(y-1)\le\frac{p-c}{p-s}\le F(y). \]

The endpoints include ties with neighbouring quantities.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A higher selling price raises the opportunity cost of unmet demand. The interval identifies how far the price can move before the chosen stock level stops being optimal.

Fix the quantity \(y\) and vary the price \(p\): \(y\) stays optimal while \(F(y-1)\le\frac{p-c}{p-s}\le F(y)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The condition is for being an optimum, not necessarily the smallest optimum.
  • At the lower boundary, \(y-1\) can tie with \(y\).
  • This analysis holds the demand distribution fixed, as the exercise does.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
At \(p=250\), quantities 9 and 10 tie; at \(p=450\), quantities 10 and 11 tie. Increasing price past the upper endpoint calls for additional stock, with demand distribution held fixed.

  • The dress solution uses effective unit cost \(c=80+30=110\) and salvage \(s=50\).
  • For \(y=10\), \(F(9)=0.70\) and \(F(10)=0.85\) give \(250\le p\le450\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A nonbasic variable is a variable outside the chosen basis and is set to zero when the associated basic solution is read. For \(m\) independent equations in \(n\) variables, there are \(n-m\) nonbasic variables.

docs.text:
• A zero value alone does not establish that a variable is nonbasic; basic variables can also be zero.
  • The objective row expresses the effect of changing nonbasic variables.
  • The entering variable becomes basic after a pivot.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Nonconvex region modelling represents a union of allowed regions using binary variables that select which region's inequalities are enforced. The selected region must satisfy all its defining inequalities; common constraints remain active for every selection.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A single system of continuous linear inequalities cannot describe separated allowed regions exactly. Binary switches can exclude the gaps between them.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use one indicator per region and require exactly one selected region.
  • Relax every inequality belonging only to an unselected region with a valid \(M\).
  • Keep nonnegativity and shared boundaries outside the switches.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated switch is \(x_2\le1+My\), \(x_2\ge2-M(1-y)\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\). The common restrictions \(x_1+x_2\le3\) and \(x\ge0\) remain active for both choices.

  • The video region is \(x_1,x_2\ge0\), \(x_1+x_2\le3\), with either \(x_2\le1\) or \(x_2\ge2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A nonnegativity constraint requires a decision variable to satisfy \(x_j\ge0\). It excludes negative quantities while permitting zero. For a vector of variables, \(x\ge0\) means \(x_j\ge0\) for every component \(j\). In the course's augmented simplex models, all original and auxiliary variables are nonnegative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Production and shipment quantities are normally nonnegative. Variables representing signed quantities need a different domain or a transformation.

With two nonnegative variables \(x,y\ge0\) the feasible region lies in the first quadrant. Drag the peak of the objective to the left of the \(y\)-axis: the optimum moves onto the axis and the constraint \(x\ge0\) binds.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonnegativity is a constraint, not an automatic consequence of a variable name.
  • With two nonnegative variables, feasible points lie in the first quadrant.
  • Nonnegative continuous variables may still take fractional values.
  • At an optimum a nonnegativity constraint is either slack (\(x_j^\ast>0\)) or binding (\(x_j^\ast=0\)); in nonlinear problems this is what the Kuhn-Tucker conditions with nonnegativity constraints handle.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x_s\ge0\) prevents negative soldier production.
  • \(s_1\ge0\) ensures that a slack variable represents unused rather than exceeded capacity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the course's normal demand approximation, \(D\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with standard deviation \(\sigma>0\). If \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF, then

\[ \begin{gathered} F(y)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right),\\ y^*=\max\!\left\{0,\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\right\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The mean sets the central demand level, while the standard deviation scales the distance to the required quantile. The examples use the normal model as an approximation to practical demand.

With \(D\sim N(100,20^2)\) the optimal stock is \(\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\beta)\): above the mean when \(\beta>1/2\), below it when \(\beta<1/2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use the standard deviation \(\sigma\), not the variance \(\sigma^2\), in the quantile formula.
  • The order quantity must satisfy \(y\ge0\). Use the normal quantile when it is nonnegative; otherwise the constrained optimum is \(y^*=0\).
  • The untruncated normal distribution allows negative values; the course examples retain that approximation.
  • The normal table gives rounded quantiles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The shaded area in the figure is \(P(D\le y^*)=0.6\). Table values \(\Phi(0.25)=0.5987\) and \(\Phi(0.26)=0.6026\) bracket the standardized quantile between 0.25 and 0.26.

  • Meal demand with \(\mu=100\), \(\sigma=20\) and \(\beta=0.6\) gives about 105.07.
  • For apples, \(\beta=1.8/2.2\approx0.8182\) and the source table approximation \(z\approx0.91\) gives 82.75 kilograms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An objective coefficient range is an interval of values for one objective coefficient over which the current optimal basis remains optimal while all other data stay fixed. A report with coefficient \(c_j\), allowable decrease \(d_j\), and allowable increase \(u_j\) gives

\[ c_j-d_j\le c_j^{\mathrm{new}}\le c_j+u_j. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Within this interval the reported decision vector remains an optimum. Its objective value changes because the same quantity now earns a different unit return.

Change the profit per soldier \(c_s\): within the shown range the corner \((20,60)\) stays optimal and only \(z^*\) changes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a change \(\Delta c_j\) within the range, the value changes by \(x_j^*\Delta c_j\).
  • At a range endpoint, additional optimal solutions may become available.
  • Separate reported ranges do not justify simultaneous changes automatically.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective \(c_1x_s+2x_t\), the coefficient \(c_1=3\) may decrease or increase by 1, giving \([2,4]\). The corner \((20,60)\) remains optimal, while its value becomes \(20c_1+120\); endpoint values may admit other optima.

  • The small-pipe profit coefficient 5 has allowable decrease 1 and increase 3, giving \([4,8]\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The objective function assigns a numerical value to a decision vector. The model specifies whether this value should be maximized or minimized. In an LP it has the form

\[ z=c_1x_1+\cdots+c_nx_n, \]

where the \(c_j\) are given objective coefficients.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The objective expresses the criterion used to compare feasible choices. Profit maximization and cost minimization are common, but the course also considers distance, time, and flow.

The objective function \(f(x)\) is the quantity to maximise (for example, profit) or minimise (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(x)\) subject to \(x\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An objective value is a number; an optimal solution is a vector of decisions.
  • In a profit objective, use revenues minus relevant costs.
  • The direction of optimization determines what constitutes an improvement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Giapetto maximizes \(z=3x_s+2x_t\).
  • The pig diet minimizes \(z=0.4x_A+0.8x_B\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a two-variable linear objective \(z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2\) with at least one nonzero coefficient, an objective line is the set of points giving a fixed value \(z=\bar z\). If \(c_2\ne0\), its slope-intercept form is

\[ x_2=-\frac{c_1}{c_2}x_1+\frac{\bar z}{c_2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Changing the objective value translates the line without changing its slope. This is the geometric basis of the graphical solution method.

Change \(\bar z\) to translate the line and \(c_1,c_2\) to turn it: all lines for one objective are parallel, with slope \(-c_1/c_2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• All constant-objective lines for a fixed objective are parallel.
  • If \(c_2<0\), a larger objective value lowers the vertical intercept.
  • When \(c_2=0\), the objective lines are vertical.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Translating a line in the direction \((c_1,c_2)\) raises its objective value. When a finite maximum is attained, the last objective line meeting the feasible region identifies it.

  • \(z=x_1+2x_2\) gives \(x_2=-x_1/2+z/2\).
  • \(z=2x_1-3x_2\) gives \(x_2=2x_1/3-z/3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Operations research (OR) uses mathematical models and analytical solution methods to support optimal, or sufficiently good, decisions in practical situations. The decision problem includes an objective, available choices, and restrictions on those choices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: OR turns a practical planning question into a problem that can be analysed systematically. The usefulness of the answer depends on how well the model represents the situation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Applications include production, transport, scheduling, maintenance, and inventory management.
  • An optimal model solution must still be checked against the practical situation.
  • Difficult problems may require a heuristic instead of an exact solution method.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Any stage can prompt a return to an earlier stage if validation shows that the simplified representation is inadequate.

  • Lecture scheduling allocates teaching activities to times and rooms.
  • A warehouse chooses replenishment quantities and ordering times.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a minimization problem with feasible set \(F\), a feasible vector \(x^*\) is an optimal solution if

\[ f(x^*)\le f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in F. \]

For maximization the inequality is reversed. The number \(z^*=f(x^*)\) is the optimal value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Optimality compares a feasible decision with every allowed alternative. There may be several equally good decisions, even when the optimal value is fixed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A model may have no feasible solution or no finite optimum.
  • The optimal value and the vector attaining it are different objects.
  • An optimum is relative to the specified objective, constraints, and input data.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated Giapetto objective, the optimal point \((20,60)\) has value \(3\cdot20+2\cdot60=180\).

  • The manufacturing example has \(x_1^*=2\), \(x_2^*=5\), and \(z^*=12\).
  • The practice LP with objective \(2x_1+2x_2\) has optimum \((3,4)\) and value 14.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Suppose an optimization problem has a finite optimal value \(z^*\). Let \(z_H\) be the value of a feasible solution and \(z_R\) the finite optimal value of a relaxation with the same objective. Then

\[ z_R\le z^*\le z_H\quad\text{for minimization}, \] \[ z_H\le z^*\le z_R\quad\text{for maximization}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The two bounds enclose the unknown optimum. Their difference limits how much the current feasible solution could still be improved.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a minimization problem, \(z_H-z^*\le z_H-z_R\).
  • If the feasible and relaxed values coincide, the feasible solution is proven optimal.
  • A feasible solution of a relaxation alone is not generally an opposing bound; its optimal value is needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For maximization, improved incumbents raise the feasible lower bound. Resolving branch-and-bound nodes can reduce the global upper bound formed from the incumbent and the remaining open-node relaxation bounds.

  • The routing example gives \(202\le z^*\le214\), so the remaining improvement is at most 12 miles.
  • A 232-mile route is also an upper bound, but 214 is tighter.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An optimization model specifies decision variables \(x\), an objective function \(f(x)\) to maximize or minimize, and constraints defining the allowed decisions. Writing the feasible set as \(F\), its form is

\[ \min_{x\in F} f(x)\qquad\text{or}\qquad\max_{x\in F} f(x). \]

The coefficients and other given inputs are model parameters.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The model states what can be chosen, what counts as better, and which choices are allowed. Solving it selects the best allowed decision according to the chosen objective.

The objective function \(f(x)\) is the quantity to maximise (for example, profit) or minimise (for example, cost). Functional constraints describe what an allowed decision must satisfy, such as resource limits or demand requirements. Domain restrictions specify signs or integrality.

In the diagram, blue identifies decision variables, whose values the model determines; red identifies model parameters, the given data \(c_j\), \(a_{ij}\) and \(b_i\). In general, the model is \(\max/\min\ f(x)\) subject to \(x\in F\), where the constraints define the feasible set \(F\). A solution assigns values to all variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The objective and constraints need not be linear in a general OR model.
  • Some simple models have a closed-form solution; many require an algorithm.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\min\{x^2+bx+c:x\ge d\}\), the optimum is \(x^*=\max\{-b/2,d\}\).
  • Giapetto chooses soldier and train production to maximize profit under labour limits.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The OR study cycle moves from a real situation to an assumed representation of it, then to a mathematical model, a solution, validation, and implementation. Validation checks whether the model and its solution adequately represent the practical decision problem.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A mathematically correct answer can be unsuitable if the modelling assumptions omit an essential feature. Model building and validation therefore belong to the same decision process.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Additional detail may improve realism but also increase data requirements and solution difficulty.
  • The required data must be available or obtainable.
  • Validation can reveal a need to revise assumptions before implementation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Any stage can prompt a return to an earlier stage if validation shows that the simplified representation is inadequate.

  • A route model may initially approximate travel distances by straight lines.
  • Road layout and time-dependent traffic may require a more detailed route model.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In the constant-demand EOQ setting, the ordering cycle length \(t_0\) is the time between consecutive orders. If each order contains \(y\) units and demand occurs at rate \(D>0\), then

\[ t_0=\frac{y}{D}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A batch supports exactly one cycle's demand in the repeating policy. The same identity holds with planned backorders because each batch still covers total demand over a cycle.

One batch of \(y\) units lasts \(t_0=y/D\): change \(y\) or \(D\) and watch the sawtooth's teeth stretch or shrink.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Orders per unit time equal \(D/y\).
  • Cycle length and lead time are different: one measures spacing of orders, the other order-to-receipt delay.
  • Convert demand and time consistently.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Ordering 22 phones at demand two per day gives an 11-day cycle.
  • In the figure, time is measured in days. Ordering \(6{,}000\) pencils at demand \(D=100\) per day gives a \(60\)-day cycle and \(D/y=1/60\) orders per day.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The overage cost in the newsvendor model is the net loss on one unit ordered but not sold at its regular price:

\[ h=c-s>0, \]

where \(c\) is its unit cost and \(s\) its salvage value. Total expected overage cost at order quantity \(y\) is \(h\mathbb E[(y-D)^+]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The salvage recovery offsets part of the cost of excess stock. A negative salvage value represents an additional disposal cost.

Each unsold unit loses \(h=c-s\). A low or negative salvage value \(s\) pushes \(y^*\) down.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only leftover units incur overage loss.
  • Increasing salvage value lowers overage cost.
  • This is a single-period per-unit loss, whereas EOQ holding cost is charged per unit per unit time.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated newspaper data give overage cost \(h=2\) and underage cost \(b=1.5\), hence critical ratio \(\beta=1.5/3.5=3/7\). These are single-period per-unit losses, rather than EOQ cost rates.

  • Newspapers costing 3.50 and salvaged for 1.50 have \(h=2\).
  • Meals costing 2.20 with zero salvage have \(h=2.20\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For three binary decisions \(y_1,y_2,y_3\), requiring an even number of yes decisions is equivalent to

\[ y_1+y_2+y_3=2x,\qquad x\in\{0,1\}. \]

The sum can therefore be 0 or 2, the only even values possible for three binary decisions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An auxiliary variable encodes the allowed count. The equality imposes a logical restriction using only linear expressions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• When \(x=0\), all three decisions are no.
  • When \(x=1\), exactly two decisions are yes.
  • Allowing \(x\) to be continuous would remove the parity restriction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((y_1,y_2,y_3)=(1,1,0)\) is allowed with \(x=1\).
  • \((1,1,1)\) is excluded because it would require \(x=3/2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's terminology, a path is a sequence of distinct edges connecting a starting vertex to an ending vertex, with consecutive edges joined through their shared vertices. For directed edges, traversal respects their directions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A path describes a connected route through a network. The course definition requires distinct edges; it does not add a requirement that all visited vertices be distinct. In graph theory such an edge-distinct walk is usually called a trail, and path is kept for walks that also visit every vertex at most once; this course uses path for the edge-distinct version.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The length of a weighted path is the sum of the lengths of the traversed edges.
  • The course convention corresponds to what some texts call a trail.
  • A path whose first and last vertices coincide is called a cycle or tour in the terminology video.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The highlighted path is \(A-C-B-D-E-F\), with length \(2+1+5+2+3=13\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a real number \(u\), its positive part is

\[ u^+=\max\{u,0\}=\begin{cases}u,&u\ge0,\\0,&u<0.\end{cases} \]

In the newsvendor model, \((y-D)^+\) is leftover stock and \((D-y)^+\) is unmet demand.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The operator keeps a positive excess and replaces a negative excess with zero. It allows the two different demand cases to be expressed in a single formula.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both leftover and shortage quantities are nonnegative.
  • For a fixed realized demand, at least one of them is zero.
  • For discrete demand, expectations are computed by probability-weighting the positive parts for every demand outcome.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Defining the negative part by \(u^-=\max\{-u,0\}\) gives the identity \(u=u^+-u^-\).

  • If \(y=10\) and \(D=7\), leftovers are 3 and unmet demand is zero.
  • If \(y=10\) and \(D=12\), leftovers are zero and unmet demand is 2.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}\) and \(TCU_j(y)=Dc_j+KD/y+hy/2\), with \(c_1>c_2\). The price-break indifference quantity \(Q>y_m\) solves

\[ TCU_2(Q)=TCU_1(y_m), \]

or equivalently

\[ Q^2+\frac{2(c_2D-TCU_1(y_m))}{h}Q+\frac{2KD}{h}=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The larger root marks how far the qualifying order threshold can exceed the ordinary EOQ before extra holding costs outweigh the purchasing discount.

\(Q\) is where the discounted cost curve climbs back to the best cost without discount, \(TCU_1(y_m)\). Move \(q\) past \(y_m\) and past \(Q\) to see the three cases.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With the worked-example convention that \(q\) qualifies, a threshold \(y_m<q<Q\) favours ordering \(q\).
  • For \(q>Q\), retain \(y_m\); for \(q<y_m\), \(y_m\) already receives the discount.
  • At \(q=Q\), the two candidates tie.
  • Directly comparing candidate costs avoids solving for \(Q\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The snack-bar exercise gives \(Q\approx89.07\) kilograms; its threshold 100 is too high.
  • For the phone example, \(Q\approx39.86\), and threshold 35 lies between \(y_m=22\) and \(Q\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A production-inventory model chooses production \(P_t\) and end-of-period stock \(I_t\) to meet known demands \(d_t\) across periods. With given initial stock \(I_0\), unit production costs \(c_t\), and end-of-period holding costs \(h_t\), the course problem is represented by

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{t=1}^T(c_tP_t+h_tI_t),\\ I_{t-1}+P_t-d_t=I_t,\qquad P_t,I_t\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Production in a cheaper month may be stored for a later month. The inventory balance ensures that every unit sold comes from current production or previously held stock.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Nonnegative inventory rules out shortages.
  • The PDF charges 8 per window per month on end-of-month inventory.
  • The six-month exercise does not specify initial stock; taking \(I_0=0\) is an explicit modelling assumption.
  • With positive production and holding costs and no required final stock, surplus final inventory is unnecessary.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Month 1 requires 100 windows; producing 120 from zero stock leaves 20.
  • Producing a month-3 window in month 2 costs 45 plus 8 holding, compared with 55 in month 3.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's project longest path model uses a directed acyclic activity network with start \(S\) and finish \(T\). Each edge has an activity duration; an outgoing activity may start only after all activities entering its starting vertex finish. Under these precedence rules and without additional resource restrictions, project duration is the length of a longest \(S\)-to-\(T\) path.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The longest chain of dependent activities determines the earliest possible project completion. The exercise models this chain with binary edge-selection variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Maximize the sum of selected activity durations.
  • Use one unit of source-to-sink binary flow with balance at intermediate vertices.
  • Acyclicity matters: in a general cyclic network, flow balance alone could allow unrelated selected cycles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure’s critical path \(S-2-3-T\) has duration \(2+5+2=9\), compared with 8 for \(S-2-T\). Negating the activity lengths turns this acyclic longest-path calculation into a shortest-path calculation; the lack of cycles permits the negative lengths.

  • In the exercise, \(S-A-D-F-T\) has duration \(5+2+6+4=17\).
  • \(S-B-D-F-T\) has duration \(3+3+6+4=16\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The project selection model chooses complete projects under resource budgets. Let \(y_j=1\) if project \(j\) is selected, \(r_j\) be its return, \(a_{tj}\) its expenditure in year \(t\), and \(B_t\) that year's budget. Then

\[ \begin{gathered} \max\sum_jr_jy_j,\\ \sum_ja_{tj}y_j\le B_t\ \text{for every }t,\\ y_j\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A project uses resources in each relevant year and contributes its full return only when selected. Fractional project funding is excluded in this model.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A separate budget constraint is needed for each year.
  • The later development-project example uses one capital budget.
  • Relaxing a binary variable to a fraction supplies a bound but not an implementable partial project.

The green columns in the figure represent selected projects, \(y_j=1\); each budget row sums only their expenditures.

docs.title: Definition

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A pure integer program is an integer linear program in which every decision variable is restricted to integer values. Nonnegativity, upper bounds, and other restrictions remain separate model constraints.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This model type fits decisions consisting entirely of counts. A linear objective alone does not permit fractional values once integrality has been imposed.

docs.text:
• If there are \(n\) variables, each of the \(n\) original decision variables is integer.
  • Binary integer programs are a special case with the additional bounds 0 and 1.
  • Dropping integrality gives its LP relaxation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the course's maximization sensitivity report, the reduced cost of a currently zero-valued variable is the marginal change in the objective when that variable is increased and the other variables adjust through the current basis. If the tableau row is \(z+q_jx_j+\cdots=z_0\), the corresponding reduced cost is \(-q_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The number measures the opportunity cost of forcing an unused activity into the plan. A negative value means that a small forced increase reduces profit.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Do not confuse a reported reduced cost with the original objective coefficient.
  • The sign is opposite to the coefficient in the course maximization tableau.
  • The interpretation is local and relies on a feasible basis adjustment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, a third product \(x_c\) earns 4 and uses 3 finishing and 2 carpentry hours. At shadow prices 1 and 1, its reduced cost is \(4-(3\cdot1+2\cdot1)=-1\). A small forced increase therefore costs 1 unit of profit per unit produced while the basis remains feasible. Raising its profit by 1 removes that marginal disadvantage; a tie need not force it into every optimal solution.

  • Sheets have reported reduced cost -3.3 in the pipes-and-sheets example.
  • Their profit coefficient is 4 and its allowable increase is 3.3 before the current optimal basis can cease to be optimal.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A relaxation retains a problem's objective and removes or weakens constraints to obtain an easier problem. If \(F\) and \(F_R\) are the original and relaxed feasible sets, then \(F\subseteq F_R\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The larger feasible set gives a benchmark that may be unattainable in the original problem. Its optimum helps assess a feasible solution obtained by another method.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For minimization, the relaxed optimum is no greater than the original optimum; for maximization, it is no smaller.
  • A relaxed optimum that is also feasible for the original problem is optimal for the original problem.
  • An infeasible relaxed optimizer need not have a strictly better value; equality can occur.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective \(4x_s+x_t\), dropping \(x_s\le40\) changes the optimum from \((40,20)\) with value 180 to \((50,0)\) with relaxed value 200.

  • Ignore the 100-mile refuelling limit in the routing example.
  • Remove integrality restrictions from an integer program while keeping its other constraints.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For an original directed edge \(i\to j\) with capacity \(c_{ij}\) and assigned flow \(x_{ij}\), its residual capacities are \(c_{ij}-x_{ij}\) in the forward direction and \(x_{ij}\) in the reverse direction. The residual network records these possibilities for increasing or cancelling current flow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Reverse residual movement revises an earlier flow assignment. It is essential because a good final routing may require undoing part of an initially chosen path.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course draws a connection with two directional residual labels; it must not be interpreted as equal capacity in both directions.
  • Only directions with positive residual capacity can be used by an augmenting path.
  • A forward augmentation decreases forward residual capacity and increases reverse residual capacity by the same amount.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A saturated original edge has no forward residual capacity; its backward residual direction permits cancelling its assigned flow.

  • Capacity 6 and flow 2 on A-B give residual capacities 4 forward and 2 backward.
  • Cancelling one unit changes those residual capacities to 5 forward and 1 backward.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A right-hand-side sensitivity range is the interval for one constraint's right-hand side over which the current optimal basis remains feasible and optimal, with other parameters fixed. Within this range, its shadow price gives the exact linear change in optimal value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The same basis can represent different production quantities as a resource changes. Thus a valid shadow price does not imply an unchanged solution vector.

Change the finishing hours \(b_1\): inside the shaded range the same constraints stay binding, and \(z^*\) grows linearly in \(b_1\) (right).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use \(b_i-d_i\le b_i^{\mathrm{new}}\le b_i+u_i\) from the report.
  • A slack resource can often be reduced by its unused amount without affecting the current decision.
  • A change beyond the range cannot generally be valued by multiplying the full change by the old shadow price.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated finishing RHS \(b_1\), the valid range is \([80,120]\). The intersection with \(x_s+x_t=80\) moves from \((0,80)\) to \((40,40)\); at the upper endpoint the demand limit also binds. With the illustrated objective, the shadow price is 1 per added finishing hour throughout the range.

  • The metal RHS is 960, with allowable increase 240 and decrease 360; the range is 600 to 1,200.
  • Milk availability can fall from 200 to 180 in the ice-cream example without changing its plan or value.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A rounding heuristic solves an integer program's LP relaxation and converts fractional variable values to nearby integers. The rounded vector is only a candidate: all original constraints must be checked before accepting it as a feasible solution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Rounding is simple and may be useful when quantities are large. Coupled constraints can make the nearest rounded decisions infeasible or substantially worse than an integer optimum.

The four lattice points around the LP optimum are the rounding candidates. Some violate a constraint, and none needs to be optimal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Rounding up can violate resource upper bounds.
  • Rounding down can violate minimum requirements or equalities.
  • Even a feasible rounded solution need not be optimal.
  • The video's numerical rounding illustration has inconsistent written constraints and a plotted feasible region; its claimed optimum is not used here.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Rounding \((2.6,1.6)\) upward to \((3,2)\) violates \(4x_1+x_2\le12\) because the left-hand side is 14.
  • The nearby vector \((2,2)\) satisfies that capacity inequality, but its objective value alone does not prove optimality.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Sensitivity analysis examines how changes in model parameters affect an LP's optimal solution and optimal value. The course studies changes to objective coefficients and resource right-hand sides using final simplex tableaux and Excel sensitivity reports.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inputs may be estimates, and additional resources may be purchasable. Sensitivity information helps assess whether the current decision remains suitable after an input changes.

Vary one objective coefficient at a time and watch when the optimal corner changes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The reported allowable ranges apply to one parameter change at a time.
  • Changing an objective coefficient can preserve the solution vector while changing profit.
  • Changing a right-hand side can change the solution vector even while the same basis and shadow prices remain valid.
  • Outside a valid range, reoptimization may be needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated objective with \(c_2>0\), \((20,60)\) remains optimal when \(1\le c_1/c_2\le2\). Changing the finishing RHS from 100 to 110 instead moves the optimum to \((30,50)\) while preserving the basis. Within the applicable one-parameter range, \(\Delta z=y_i^*\Delta b_i\).

  • A change in banana ice-cream profit from 0.95 to 0.92 leaves the given production plan optimal.
  • Losing three gallons of cream changes the ice-cream quantities and reduces optimal profit by 3.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A setup cost is a fixed charge incurred whenever an order is placed, regardless of the order quantity. In the EOQ model it is denoted by \(K\). With demand rate \(D\) and batch size \(y\), its average rate is

\[ \frac{K}{y/D}=\frac{KD}{y}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Larger orders spread one fixed charge over more units and reduce ordering frequency. This saving must be balanced against extra holding cost.

Each order costs \(K\) and there are \(D/y\) orders per unit time, so setups cost \(KD/y\). Raise \(K\) to make larger batches worthwhile.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The charge is per order, not per inventory unit.
  • A period with no order incurs no setup in the dynamic lot-size model.
  • Increasing \(K\) increases the classical optimal order size.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For the illustrated phone shop, \(K=605\) per order and \(D=2\) per day. The two panels cover the same \(33\) days:

Batch size Number of setups Setup cost per day \(y=11\) (left) \(6\) \(KD/y=1210/11=110\) \(y=22\) (right) \(3\) \(KD/y=1210/22=55\)

Doubling the batch size halves the setup frequency and its cost rate, but doubles average stock.

  • The snack bar pays 50 per order in addition to a per-kilogram purchase price.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The shadow price \(y_i^*\) of resource \(i\) is the rate of change of the optimal objective value when its right-hand side \(b_i\) increases slightly. Within the applicable sensitivity range,

\[ z^*(b_i+\Delta)=z^*(b_i)+y_i^*\Delta. \]

For the course's maximization LPs with \(\le\) resource constraints, it equals the coefficient of slack \(s_i\) in the final objective row.

The same marginal value is defined for nonlinear problems as the shadow price in constrained optimization, where it is given by a Lagrange multiplier; the linear-programming case is the one treated here.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A shadow price measures the marginal value of more resource under the current model. It can be compared with the cost of acquiring that resource.

The slope of \(z^*(b_1)\) on the right is the shadow price \(y_1^*\). It is valid only within the range where the basis stays the same.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The rate is valid only over its allowable right-hand-side range.
  • At a degenerate optimum the rates for increasing and for decreasing \(b_i\) can differ, so the tableau value is then only a one-sided shadow price.
  • An unused resource has zero marginal value in the illustrated resource-allocation setting.
  • A binding constraint does not by itself guarantee a positive shadow price.
  • The tableau sign interpretation must be adjusted if the model or objective convention changes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Malt and barley have shadow prices 1, while hops has shadow price 0 in the beer-and-ale example.
  • In the drinks example, an additional unit of sugar is worth 0.5 within the valid range.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A shortage cost penalizes unmet demand. In the EOQ model with planned shortages, customers wait for replenishment and the parameter \(p\) charges each outstanding unit per unit of waiting time. With maximum backlog \(y-s\), the average shortage cost rate is

\[ p\frac{(y-s)^2}{2y}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The penalty permits a trade-off between holding stock and making customers wait. This time-based backlog penalty differs from the single-period lost-margin measure in the newsvendor model.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The red triangle has area \((y-s)^2/(2D)\). Multiplying by \(p\) gives shortage cost \(p(y-s)^2/(2D)\) per cycle; dividing by \(t_0=y/D\) gives the cost rate \(p(y-s)^2/(2y)\).
  • Demand is backordered and later filled: the arriving batch first clears the backlog \(y-s\) and leaves \(s\) units on hand.
  • Use the same time unit for \(p\), \(h\), and \(D\).
  • In the newsvendor notation, \(p\) instead denotes selling price; symbols must be interpreted within their model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The phone shop compensates waiting customers by 6 per phone per day.
  • The EOQ practice exercise permits planned shortages at 10 per unit per week.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For nonnegative edge lengths, the course's shortest path algorithm sets \(d(s)=0\) and \(U=\{s\}\). Repeatedly choose an edge \(u-v\) with \(u\in U\), \(v\notin U\) minimizing

\[ d(u)+\ell_{uv}. \]

Set \(d(v)\) equal to this value, record predecessor \(u\), and add \(v\) to \(U\). Stop when the destination is added, or continue to obtain distances to all vertices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Vertices enter the settled set in order of their shortest distance from the origin. Predecessors recover the actual route after the distance has been computed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compare complete distances from the origin, not just individual edge lengths.
  • Ties can be broken arbitrarily when one shortest path is sufficient.
  • Backtrack from the destination through predecessors and reverse the sequence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure settles vertices in the order \(A,C,B,D,E,F\). The recorded predecessor edges form a shortest-path tree rooted at \(A\).

  • The worked labels are \(d(B)=2\), \(d(A)=3\), \(d(D)=6\), \(d(C)=7\), \(d(E)=8\), \(d(T)=12\).
  • The predecessor chain \(T,E,D,A,B,S\) recovers the route of length 12.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A shortest path binary formulation assigns \(x_{ij}=1\) if a directed edge is selected. For the undirected course network, create both directed orientations of each edge. With origin \(s\), destination \(t\), and edge lengths \(\ell_{ij}\), use

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_{(i,j)}\ell_{ij}x_{ij},\\ \sum_jx_{ij}-\sum_jx_{ji}=\begin{cases}1,&i=s,\\-1,&i=t,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\\ x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

Sums include only existing directed orientations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A unit of selected flow connects the origin to the destination. The objective chooses its least-cost route. This is the formulation derived from the video exercise.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With strictly positive lengths as in the exercise, an optimum contains no unnecessary cycle.
  • If zero-cost edges are allowed, an optimal binary solution may contain removable zero-cost cycles.
  • The balances alone must not be claimed to prohibit every possible cycle.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For a feasible network with nonnegative edge lengths, the unit-flow LP relaxation admits an integral optimal solution. Removing any zero-cost cycles leaves a shortest path; arbitrary optimal flow representations need not themselves be cycle-free.

  • The route S-B-A-D-E-T selects its five directed edges and has cost 12.
  • At A on that route, \(x_{BA}=x_{AD}=1\) balances one incoming and one outgoing edge.

docs.title: Definition

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Silver-Meal heuristic chooses consecutive periods to cover with each order when the variable unit ordering cost is constant and identical across periods. For an order in period \(i\) covering through \(t\), define

\[ \begin{gathered} TC(i,t)=K_i+\sum_{j=i+1}^tD_j\sum_{k=i}^{j-1}h_k,\\ TCU(i,t)=\frac{TC(i,t)}{t-i+1}. \end{gathered} \]

Starting at the first uncovered period, extend coverage while average cost decreases, select the first local minimum, order \(\sum_{j=i}^{t^*}D_j\), and restart at \(i=t^*+1\). Stop at the horizon; on a flat tie, selecting the first local minimum is the convention used here.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The rule compares setup-plus-holding cost per covered period. It is simpler than full dynamic programming but does not guarantee the optimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Purchasing cost is omitted from the comparisons because the common unit price gives the same total for every complete demand-covering policy.
  • Add that constant purchasing cost when reporting a total that includes it.
  • At the start or end of the horizon, use only available neighbouring average-cost comparisons.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure’s first order covers \(D_1+D_2+D_3\); the rule then restarts at period 4. The displayed values are illustrative rather than the complete course exercise data.

  • The six-period video orders \((32,0,0,20,13,25)\), with setup and holding cost 122.
  • Week 6 practice 4 orders \((9,22,0,0)\) and costs 169 including purchases; the exact DP cost is 152.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The simplex method solves an LP by moving between basic feasible solutions through basis exchanges. In the course's maximization tableau convention, start with a feasible basis, test the objective row, select an improving entering variable, apply the minimum-ratio test to select a leaving variable, pivot, and repeat until optimality or unboundedness is established.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Simplex uses the structure of an LP instead of enumerating all possible corners. Algebraic row operations implement movement between feasible corners.

Step through the iterations: starting from the slack basis at the origin, each pivot moves along an edge to a better corner until no improving variable is left.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The elementary starting form uses equality constraints, nonnegative right-hand sides, and nonnegative variables.
  • A slack basis starts the method for \(\le\) constraints with nonnegative right-hand sides.
  • The two-phase method supplies a feasible basis when one is not immediately available.
  • Degenerate pivots can change the basis without moving the decision vector.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
For maximization, a feasible pivot does not decrease the objective. Degenerate pivots may leave it unchanged; an anti-cycling rule is needed to guarantee termination rather than relying only on the finite number of bases.

  • The two-variable example visits \((0,0)\), \((5,0)\), and \((3,4)\), with values 0, 15, and 17.
  • The three-variable example ends at \((0,5,4)\) with value 33.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For a maximization LP with a feasible canonical tableau written as \(z+\sum_{j\in N}q_jx_j=z_0\), if \(q_j\ge0\) for every nonbasic variable, the current basic feasible solution is optimal. Here \(N\) is the nonbasic index set and every variable is nonnegative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Every allowed increase of a nonbasic variable then leaves the objective unchanged or reduces it. The tableau therefore certifies that the current value cannot be exceeded.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sign test depends on the course objective-row convention.
  • Feasibility and canonical form are required before applying the test.
  • A negative coefficient calls for further simplex analysis; degeneracy means it does not alone prove that a strictly better feasible vector exists.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, \(z=180-s_1-s_2\) and \(s_1,s_2\ge0\) certify \(z\le180\). Setting both nonbasic slacks to zero gives \(x_s=20\), \(x_t=60\), \(s_3=20\), attaining 180. A zero nonbasic objective coefficient can indicate an alternative optimum, but a distinct solution requires a positive feasible movement; a degenerate zero-length pivot is insufficient.

  • \(z+(7/5)s_1+(1/5)s_2=17\) proves \(z\le17\).
  • \(z-(1/2)x_2+(3/2)s_1=15\) still has a negative coefficient to investigate.
