docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A simplex pivot replaces the leaving basic variable with the entering variable. Divide the selected pivot row by the nonzero pivot element, then subtract appropriate multiples of that normalized row from every other row, including the objective row, so that the pivot column is a unit column.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
These Gauss-Jordan operations preserve the equations while expressing them in terms of a new basis. The updated tableau can be used for the next iteration.

Each pivot exchanges one basic variable for another; geometrically it moves to an adjacent corner of the feasible region.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pivot element is the intersection of the entering column and leaving row.
  • Update all coefficients and the right-hand side during each row operation.
  • Update the basic-variable label as well as the numerical entries.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the illustrated Giapetto pivot, the row operations are

\[ \begin{aligned}R_{s_3}&\leftarrow R_{s_3}/1,\\R_z&\leftarrow R_z+3R_{s_3},\\R_{s_1}&\leftarrow R_{s_1}-2R_{s_3},\\R_{s_2}&\leftarrow R_{s_2}-R_{s_3}.\end{aligned} \]

The new point is \((x_s,x_t)=(40,0)\) with \(z=120\); the next entering variable is \(x_t\).

  • Take the objective row \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\) with the constraints of the augmented-form example. Then \(x_1\) enters and the minimum-ratio test picks the row of \(s_1\), so divide the pivot row \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\) by 2.
  • Add three times that normalized row to \(z-3x_1-2x_2=0\) to eliminate \(x_1\) from the objective row.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A simplex tableau records the variable coefficients, right-hand sides, and basic-variable labels of the current simplex equations. In the course convention, the first row writes the objective as

\[ z+\sum_jq_jx_j=z_0. \]

In proper form, basic-variable columns form unit columns and have zero objective-row coefficients.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The tableau stores the equations compactly so that each pivot can be performed through row operations. It also makes the current solution and improvement directions easy to read.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Set nonbasic variables to zero and read basic values from the solution column.
  • The objective-row right-hand side is the current objective value.
  • A negative nonbasic coefficient indicates an improving direction for maximization.

The illustrated system is \(2x_s+x_t+s_1=100\), \(x_s+x_t+s_2=80\), \(x_s+s_3=40\), with objective \(z-3x_s-2x_t=0\). The orange objective row places coefficients on the left, and the blue basic columns form the identity. Setting \(x_s=x_t=0\) gives \(s_1=100\), \(s_2=80\), \(s_3=40\), \(z=0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a constraint \(\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\le b_i\), a slack variable \(s_i\) converts it into

\[ \sum_ja_{ij}x_j+s_i=b_i,\qquad s_i\ge0. \]

Thus \(s_i=b_i-\sum_ja_{ij}x_j\) measures the unused allowance in the inequality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The equality records both the amount used and the amount left over. This lets simplex work with equalities while preserving the original feasible choices.

Drag the decision point: \(s_i=b_i-\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\) is the unused amount of resource \(i\). A slack of \(0\) means the constraint is binding.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A zero slack means the constraint is binding at that solution.
  • The introduced slack has zero coefficient in the original objective.
  • With nonnegative right-hand sides, slack variables can form an initial feasible basis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\le10\) becomes \(2x_1+x_2+s_1=10\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A spanning tree of a connected undirected network contains every original vertex and a subset of its edges that forms a tree. If the network has \(n\) vertices, every spanning tree has \(n-1\) edges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: All locations remain connected, but enough edges are removed to eliminate every cycle. Different edge selections may produce different spanning trees.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Spanning refers to including all vertices, not all edges.
  • Adding another original edge to a spanning tree creates a cycle.
  • The minimum spanning tree problem compares the total lengths of spanning trees.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A network with seven vertices needs six edges in each spanning tree.
  • The Euclidean example selects \(1-7\), \(1-4\), \(4-3\), \(3-6\), \(6-2\), and \(6-5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A surplus variable \(S_i\ge0\) transforms a lower-bound constraint into an equality:

\[ \begin{gathered} \sum_ja_{ij}x_j\ge b_i\\ \Longleftrightarrow\\ \sum_ja_{ij}x_j-S_i=b_i,\quad S_i\ge0. \end{gathered} \]

It measures the excess of the left-hand side over the required minimum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A surplus is subtracted because it represents an amount above the minimum requirement. This differs from the added slack used for an upper-bound constraint.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course uses capital \(S_i\) for surplus and lower-case \(s_i\) for slack.
  • A surplus variable alone generally does not produce an initial feasible slack-style basis.
  • An artificial variable may be added for the first simplex phase.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(2x_1+x_2\ge4\) becomes \(2x_1+x_2-S_1=4\).
  • At \((x_1,x_2)=(3,0)\), this surplus is 2.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In task quota assignment, each task is assigned to exactly one agent and agent \(i\) must receive exactly \(q_i\) tasks. For binary assignment variables \(x_{ij}\) and times or costs \(c_{ij}\), the model is

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_i\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad \sum_ix_{ij}=1,\\ \sum_jx_{ij}=q_i,\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}. \end{gathered} \]

The quotas sum to the number of tasks.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Quotas impose a workload distribution while the objective minimizes the combined cost or time. The household exercise assigns two tasks to each person.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In the later Hungarian-method treatment, duplicate each agent row \(q_i\) times to represent its available task slots.
  • Each task remains assigned exactly once.
  • Minimizing summed execution time is different from minimizing the latest completion time.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Eve receives marketing and dishwashing; Steven receives cooking and laundry, totalling 18.4 hours.
  • In week 5 practice 3, two identical rows per machine represent its two required jobs.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The transportation problem chooses shipments \(x_{ij}\ge0\) from plants \(i\) to distribution centres \(j\) to minimize total transport cost. With unit costs \(c_{ij}\), plant capacities \(s_i\), and required deliveries \(d_j\), a formulation is

\[ \begin{gathered} \min\sum_i\sum_j c_{ij}x_{ij},\\ \sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i\ \text{for every }i,\\ \sum_ix_{ij}=d_j\ \text{for every }j. \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Each shipment consumes origin capacity and contributes to one destination's demand. The course example has more total production capacity than required demand, so unused capacity is permitted.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The decision variables are shipment quantities on routes.
  • Plant capacities are upper bounds rather than mandatory production amounts.
  • For the example with positive transport costs, allowing deliveries above demand cannot improve the optimum.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The diagram is a separate balanced illustration with total supply and demand both 50. Green-edge labels mean shipment quantity @ unit cost; their total is \(15\cdot2+15\cdot1+20\cdot4=125\). For a feasible transportation LP with integer supplies and demands, an integral optimal shipment plan exists. The illustration’s demand lower bounds are equivalent to exact delivery here because total supply equals total required demand.

  • The plants have capacities 5,000, 6,000, and 2,500; destination demands total 12,000.
  • The illustrated optimum has transport cost 35,000.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A tree is a connected undirected network containing no cycles. In the course, a tree can be formed by choosing a subset of the vertices and edges of a larger network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A tree connects its selected vertices without redundant loops. This makes it the basic structure for minimum-cost connection problems.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A finite tree with \(n\) vertices has \(n-1\) edges.
  • There is exactly one path between any two distinct vertices of a tree.
  • A spanning tree additionally includes every vertex of the original network.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The edges A-B and B-C form a tree on three vertices.
  • A tree on 77 vertices has 76 edges, as reinforced by the final-week statements exercise.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The two-phase method initializes and solves an LP using artificial variables \(R_i\ge0\). Phase I maximizes

\[ r=-\sum_iR_i \]

subject to the augmented constraints. If its optimum is negative, the original LP is infeasible. If its optimum is zero, restore the original objective, remove artificial variables from the working model, put the objective row in canonical form for the resulting feasible basis, and apply simplex in Phase II.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The first phase finds a point satisfying the original constraints. The second phase improves the objective from that feasible starting point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Eliminate basic artificial variables from the initial phase-I objective row before pivoting.
  • The phase-I objective can never exceed zero.
  • A zero-valued artificial variable still in the basis needs basis cleanup before its column is removed; the supplied worked example avoids this case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(x_1+x_2\le10\) and \(2x_1+3x_2=25\), Phase I finds \((0,25/3)\).
  • Phase II for objective \(3x_1+2x_2\) reaches \((5,5)\) and value 25.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A maximization LP has an unbounded objective if feasible solutions attain objective values greater than any prescribed finite bound. For minimization, feasible values can be arbitrarily negative. In a feasible maximization tableau, an improving entering column with no strictly positive constraint coefficient certifies unboundedness.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
There is no finite best value: a feasible improvement can continue indefinitely. In a practical model, this can point to a missing restriction.

The region is open towards the upper right, and \(z=x_1+x_2\) keeps improving along it. Change the objective or add a constraint to get a finite optimum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite optimum for a particular objective.
  • The simplex certificate requires an improving objective coefficient and an unrestricted feasible increase together.
  • Do not confuse unboundedness with infeasibility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure maximizes \(x_1+x_2\) subject to \(2x_1+x_2\ge40\) and \(x\ge0\). Taking \(x_1=t\), \(x_2=0\) for \(t\ge20\) gives feasible values growing without bound. In an applied model, such a result can indicate a missing restriction rather than automatically proving a modelling error.

  • In week 2 practice 1(c), \(x_1=0\), \(x_2=t\ge0\) satisfies \(3x_1-2x_2\le8\) and gives \(z=t\).
  • In the week 3 example, \(x_1=x_2=t\) is feasible and yields \(2x_1+x_2=3t\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The underage cost in the newsvendor model is the foregone margin on one unit of demand that cannot be served:

\[ b=p-c>0, \]

where \(p\) is selling price and \(c\) is unit cost. Expected underage cost is \(b\mathbb E[(D-y)^+]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A stockout loses the opportunity to earn the margin, rather than the full selling price. The purchase cost that would have been paid must be subtracted.

Each unit of unmet demand loses the margin \(b=p-c\). Raise \(p\) and watch \(y^*\) move up.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only demand above the available quantity contributes to underage loss.
  • Increasing selling price increases underage cost when unit cost is fixed.
  • The course assumes no additional per-unit stockout penalty beyond the lost margin.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The illustrated newspaper data give overage cost \(h=2\) and underage cost \(b=1.5\), hence critical ratio \(\beta=1.5/3.5=3/7\). These are single-period per-unit losses, rather than EOQ cost rates.

  • Newspapers sold for 5 and purchased for 3.50 have \(b=1.50\).
  • Meals sold for 5.50 and costing 2.20 have \(b=3.30\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An undirected network is a network in which edges have no prescribed orientation. An edge joining vertices \(i\) and \(j\) may be traversed in either direction.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This represents connections whose availability is symmetric. The course uses undirected networks for spanning trees, Euler tours, the Chinese postman problem, and shortest paths.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The pair \(i-j\) describes one undirected connection.
  • A path can traverse its edges in either direction.
  • Connectedness requires a path between every pair of vertices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
An undirected edge may be written \(\{i,j\}\); roads, cables and other symmetric links provide examples. The degree counts incident edge ends.

  • A two-way road connects two towns.
  • A cable connecting two sites can be selected as part of a spanning tree.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course's uniform demand model assumes \(D\) is uniformly distributed on a known interval \([a,u]\), with \(a<u\). Its CDF inside the interval is \(F(y)=(y-a)/(u-a)\), with values 0 below \(a\) and 1 above \(u\). Thus the continuous newsvendor quantity is

\[ y^*=a+(u-a)\beta. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Demand is spread uniformly across the stated interval. The relevant inventory calculation is a linear interpolation to the critical quantile.

With demand uniform on \([50,150]\) the optimal stock interpolates linearly: \(y^*=a+(u-a)\beta\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distribution is used as an application of probability prerequisites; the course does not develop a general distribution theory.
  • For \(\beta=1/2\), the quantity is the midpoint.
  • The quantile lies within the demand interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For meal demand on \([80,120]\) and \(\beta=0.6\), order 104.
  • For that same interval, \(F(100)=0.5\) and \(F(104)=0.6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An unrestricted variable \(x_j\) can be replaced everywhere by the difference of two nonnegative variables:

\[ x_j=x_j^+-x_j^-,\qquad x_j^+,x_j^-\ge0. \]

If \(x_j\le0\) is required, use \(x_j=-x_j^-\) with \(x_j^-\ge0\) instead.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The substitution allows simplex to use nonnegative variables while preserving the original variable's ability to take negative values. Recover the original decision after solving.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Apply the substitution to both the objective and every constraint.
  • The difference representation is not unique; it is not necessary to impose a nonlinear restriction preventing both parts from being positive.
  • The optimal original variable is the difference of the computed parts.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The two replacement columns are opposites and hence linearly dependent. They cannot both belong to one basis, although a nonbasic feasible representation may have both component values positive.

  • \(x_2^+=0\) and \(x_2^-=10\) give \(x_2=-10\).
  • The other-model-forms exercise transforms its nonpositive \(x_1\) as \(-x_1^-\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's vehicle routing problem asks for a minimum-distance route plan that starts at a depot, visits eight required locations, and returns to the depot. The vehicle can travel at most 100 miles between refuelling stops, and refuelling is possible only at the depot.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The fuel limit may require several depot-to-depot trips. This example illustrates how a feasible heuristic and a relaxed problem give complementary information.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every required location must be visited and every trip must respect the fuel limit.
  • Joining successive visits can improve a plan if feasibility is retained.
  • Removing the fuel limit gives a lower bound, not automatically a feasible route for the original problem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Separate visits from the depot produce the stated 232-mile heuristic plan.
  • The improved plan has length 214; the relaxed optimum has length 202.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The degree of a vertex in the undirected networks considered in the course is the number of edges incident to it. Parallel edges are counted separately. A vertex has even or odd degree according to the parity of that count.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Degree counts how many edge ends meet at a vertex. Its parity determines whether a closed traversal can use every incident edge exactly once.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• At a vertex on an Euler tour, arrivals and departures pair the incident edges.
  • Duplicating a path reverses degree parity at its endpoints and preserves it at internal vertices.
  • Odd-degree vertices are the vertices matched in the Chinese postman construction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
In the figure, the degrees sum to \(\sum_v\deg v=2|E|=18\), since each of the nine edges contributes two ends. Thus the number of odd-degree vertices is even; the illustrated odd vertices are \(B\) and \(E\).

  • In the introduction network, A has degree 3 and C has degree 5.
  • In the five-vertex Chinese postman example, A, B, D, and E are odd-degree vertices.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Weibull demand distribution in the exercise has shape \(k>0\), scale \(\lambda>0\), and nonnegative support. For \(x\ge0\),

\[ \begin{gathered} F(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-(x/\lambda)^k},\\ f(x)=\frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}\mathrm{e}^{-(x/\lambda)^k}. \end{gathered} \]

For the newsvendor critical ratio \(0<\beta<1\), inversion gives

\[ y^*=\lambda[-\ln(1-\beta)]^{1/k}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The exercise supplies the density and CDF, so the required task is to solve the CDF equation at the cost-based probability. No broader Weibull theory is needed for this application.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Use the given shape and scale parametrization.
  • The CDF is zero below zero.
  • The scale parameter has the same units as demand.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Bananas have \(k=2\), \(\lambda=50\), \(b=1.3\), \(h=0.2\), so \(\beta=13/15\).
  • The optimum is \(50\sqrt{-\ln(2/15)}\approx70.97\) kilograms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: To obtain a maximum zero-cost matching, create a source \(S\), one vertex for each matrix row, one for each column, and a sink \(T\). Add source-to-row edges, row-to-column edges exactly where the matrix entry is zero, and column-to-sink edges. Give every edge capacity 1 and compute an integral maximum flow.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A unit of flow selects a zero-cost row-column pair. Unit capacities ensure that no row or column is assigned twice.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The maximum flow value is the maximum number of simultaneous zero-cost assignments.
  • Read selected pairs from row-to-column edges carrying flow 1.
  • The augmenting path algorithm starting at zero preserves integrality for these integer capacities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The figure’s zero pairs are \((1,2),(2,1),(2,2),(2,3),(3,2)\). Its integral maximum flow is 2, so only two independent zeros can be assigned, fewer than the three required for a complete assignment. The minimum cut also determines a minimum zero cover; further Hungarian adjustment is needed.

  • The five-job practice matrix admits four zero-cost pairs.
  • One such matching is jobs 1, 2, 3, 4 to machines 1, 4, 3, 2.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
In the course's uncapacitated dynamic lot-size special case, assume no shortages or lead time, nonincreasing marginal production and holding costs, and zero initial inventory. There exists an optimal policy with

\[ y_ix_i=0\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n). \]

Thus a positive order is placed only when starting stock is zero, and it covers the exact demand of one or more consecutive periods.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The property reduces the number of order quantities that need to be examined. Candidate orders are cumulative demands, rather than every integer quantity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The statement guarantees an optimal policy of this form; it need not describe every tied optimum.
  • The special case is not justified for increasing marginal ordering costs, as in the general example.
  • The course handles positive initial stock by subtracting it from successive demands until exhausted.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In the four-period example, initial stock 15 reduces first-period demand from 76 to 61.
  • The optimal orders \((61,116,0,67)\) cover period 1, periods 2-3, and period 4, at total cost 860.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The 2-argument arctangent, denoted as \(\text{atan2}\), is a function defined by

\[ \begin{gathered} \text{atan2}(y,x)=\\ \begin{cases} \displaystyle \,\arctan(y/x),& x>0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\arctan(y/x)+\pi,& x<0 \text{ and }y\geq 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\arctan(y/x)-\pi,& x<0 \text{ and }y< 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\pi/2,& x=0 \text{ and }y> 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,-\pi/2,& x=0 \text{ and }y< 0,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \,\text{undefined},&x=0 \text{ and }y= 0. \end{cases} \end{gathered} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The function \(\text{atan2}\) computes the principal argument of the complex number, correctly covering all four quadrants and avoiding division‑by‑zero issues.

For the nonzero point \((x,y)\) drawn, \(\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)\in(-\pi,\pi]\) gives the argument of \(x+yi\). It retains the quadrant information that the ratio \(y/x\) alone loses.

Drag the point \((x,y)\) into the left half-plane: \(\arctan(y/x)\) only sees the slope, while \(\text{atan2}(y,x)\) adds or subtracts \(\pi\) to give the true direction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The range of \(\text{atan2}(y, x)\) is \((-\pi, \pi]\), covering all four quadrants.
  • \(\text{atan2}(y, x)\) is continuous for all \((x, y) \neq (0, 0)\), except along the negative real axis where it has a jump discontinuity of \(2\pi\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\text{atan2}(1, -1) = 3\pi/4\) (second quadrant).
  • \(\text{atan2}(-1, -1) = -3\pi/4\) (third quadrant, within range \((-\pi, \pi]\)).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Aleph null, denoted \(\aleph_0\), is the cardinality of the natural numbers:

\[\aleph_0=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb N).\]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
It is the standard symbol for countable infinity.

The diagram pairs \(n\) with \(2n\), showing that the natural numbers and the even natural numbers have the same cardinality. Likewise, \(\mathbb N\times\mathbb N\) has cardinality \(\aleph_0\); in cardinal arithmetic, \(\aleph_0+1=\aleph_0+\aleph_0=\aleph_0\cdot\aleph_0=\aleph_0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set has cardinality \(\aleph_0\) exactly when it is countably infinite.
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb N\), \(\mathbb Z\), and \(\mathbb Q\) all have cardinality \(\aleph_0\).
  • The natural numbers \(\mathbb N\) are the standard example of a countably infinite set.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
If the characteristic polynomial factors as \(c(\lambda-\lambda_1)^{k_1}\cdots(\lambda-\lambda_l)^{k_l}\) with distinct \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_l\), then \(k_i\) is the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\), written \(am(\lambda_i)\).

The geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is the maximal number of linearly independent eigenvectors associated with \(\lambda\), written \(gm(\lambda)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Algebraic multiplicity counts how often an eigenvalue appears as a root of the characteristic polynomial. Geometric multiplicity counts how many independent eigendirections it actually has.

\(p(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I-A)=(\lambda-1)^2(\lambda-3)\) for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}\): \(\lambda=1\) has algebraic multiplicity \(2\) but only one independent eigenvector.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For every eigenvalue of an \(n\times n\) matrix, \(1\leq gm(\lambda)\leq am(\lambda)\leq n\).
  • A matrix is diagonalizable iff \(gm(\lambda)=am(\lambda)\) for every eigenvalue, the eigenvalues being taken in \(\mathbb{C}\) so that the characteristic polynomial factors completely. A real matrix is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb{R}\) only if, in addition, all its eigenvalues are real.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \((\lambda-2)^3(\lambda+1)\), eigenvalue \(2\) has algebraic multiplicity \(3\).
  • For \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), eigenvalue \(1\) has algebraic multiplicity \(2\) but geometric multiplicity \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An algebraic structure consists of a set together with one or more operations on that set.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For nonzero vectors \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\), the angle \(\theta\) between them satisfies \(x\cdot y=\|x\|\|y\|\cos\theta\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The inner product determines whether two vectors point in similar, opposite, or perpendicular directions.

For the vectors drawn, \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{x\cdot y}{\|x\|\,\|y\|}=\dfrac{4+3}{\sqrt{17}\sqrt{10}}\approx0.54\), so \(\theta\approx57^\circ\). Two nonzero vectors are perpendicular when their inner product is zero and parallel when their angle is \(0\) or \(180^\circ\).

Drag \(x\) and \(y\) and read \(\theta\) from \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{x\cdot y}{\|x\|\|y\|}\). The sign of \(x\cdot y\) tells acute from obtuse.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(x\cdot y>0\), the angle is acute.
  • If \(x\cdot y=0\), the angle is right and the vectors are orthogonal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) have angle \(\pi/2\).
  • \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\) have a positive inner product, so their angle is acute.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The argument of a nonzero complex number \(z\), denoted \(\arg z\), is the angle between the positive real axis and the line joining the origin and \(z\). It is a multivalued function due to the periodicity of the angle in the polar coordinate system. The principal argument, denoted as \(\operatorname{Arg} z\), is the unique value of the argument that lies in the interval \((-\pi, \pi].\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For a nonzero complex number \(z\), if \(\varphi\) is a polar angle, then \(\varphi + 2\pi k\) also represents a valid polar angle for any integer \(k\).

For a nonzero complex number \(z\), its argument is the angle from the positive real axis, defined modulo \(2\pi\). The principal value \(\operatorname{Arg}z\) lies in \((-\pi,\pi]\); here \(\varphi_2=-130^\circ\) rather than \(230^\circ\).

Drag \(z\) and change \(k\): \(\operatorname{Arg} z\) is the angle in \((-\pi,\pi]\), and adding whole turns \(2\pi k\) gives the other values of \(\arg z\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each nonzero complex number has a unique principal argument. The argument of \(0\) is undefined.
  • For \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), the principal argument of \(a+\mathrm{i} b\) is \(\text{atan2}(b,a)\), where \(\text{atan2}\) is the 2-argument arctangent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Arg} \mathrm{i}=\pi /2\).
  • \(\operatorname{Arg}(1-\mathrm{i})=-\pi/4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The augmented matrix of a linear system \(Ax=b\) is the matrix formed by adjoining the right-hand side vector \(b\) to the coefficient matrix \(A\), often written \((A\mid b)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An augmented matrix contains all numerical information needed to solve a linear system.

The augmented matrix \([A\,|\,b]\) keeps the coefficients and right-hand side together during row operations. Row reduction gives the solution set; if \(\operatorname{rank}[A|b]>\operatorname{rank}A\), the system has no solution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Elementary row operations on the augmented matrix correspond to elementary operations on the equations.
  • Gauss-Jordan elimination is performed on augmented matrices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(2x+y=3\), \(x-y=1\), the augmented matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\1&-1&1\end{pmatrix}\).
  • The vertical bar in \((A\mid b)\) is visual; the augmented matrix is still a matrix.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A basis of a vector space \(V\) is a collection of vectors that is linearly independent and spans \(V\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A basis is a minimal generating collection and a non-redundant coordinate system for the vector space.

The vector \(w\) drawn has coordinates \([w]_{\mathcal B}=(2,1)\), so \(w=2b_1+b_2\). Because \((b_1,b_2)\) is a basis, every vector in the plane has a unique pair of coordinates in this grid.

Drag \(w\): it is reached in exactly one way as \(c_1b_1+c_2b_2\). Drag \(b_1\) and \(b_2\) to make a new grid, and line them up to see the basis fail.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every vector in \(V\) can be written uniquely as a linear combination of basis vectors.
  • Any two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have the same length.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The standard basis of \(\mathbb R^2\) is \(((1,0),(0,1))\).
  • In \(\mathbb R^2\), vectors such as \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) illustrate the concept concretely.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A block matrix is a matrix viewed as being partitioned into smaller matrices called blocks or submatrices.

A block diagonal matrix is a square block matrix of the form

\[ \begin{pmatrix} A_1&0&\cdots&0\\ 0&A_2&\cdots&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ 0&0&\cdots&A_k \end{pmatrix}, \]

where \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) are square matrices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Block notation lets us calculate with large matrices by treating compatible submatrices as entries. Block diagonal matrices represent independent components that do not interact across blocks.

The four blocks have sizes \(2\times2\) for \(A_{11}\), \(2\times3\) for \(A_{12}\), \(1\times2\) for \(A_{21}\), and \(1\times3\) for \(A_{22}\). When the inner partitions match, block multiplication uses the same row-by-column rule as scalar matrix multiplication; for example, the top-left block of \(AB\) is \(A_{11}B_{11}+A_{12}B_{21}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compatible block matrices can be added and multiplied block-by-block using the usual matrix rules.
  • If \(A\) is block diagonal with diagonal blocks \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\), then
\[ \det(A)=\det(A_1)\det(A_2)\cdots\det(A_k). \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}A_{11}&A_{12}\\A_{21}&A_{22}\end{pmatrix}\) is a matrix written in four blocks.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0\\0&A_2\end{pmatrix}\) is block diagonal.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Cantor's diagonal argument shows that there is no bijection between \(\mathbb N\) and the interval \([0,1]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If a list claimed to contain every binary expansion in \([0,1]\), one can construct a new sequence by flipping the diagonal entries. This new sequence differs from the \(i\)th listed sequence in its \(i\)th digit, so it cannot be on the list. Strictly, a few numbers have two binary expansions (\(0.0111\ldots=0.1000\ldots\)), which is why the lecture says that each 0-1 sequence corresponds more or less to a unique number. Every number has at most two expansions, so a list of all numbers in \([0,1]\) would still give a list of all 0-1 sequences, and the conclusion stands.

The decimal illustration highlights diagonal digits \(3,7,1,0,3\), which can be changed to \(4,8,2,1,4\), giving a new number with prefix \(0.48214\ldots\). At every subsequent position, choose either \(1\) or \(2\) so that the chosen digit differs from the corresponding diagonal digit. The resulting expansion is neither eventually all \(0\) nor eventually all \(9\), so it avoids the ambiguity of two decimal representations. It therefore represents a number different from every \(r_i\) in the proposed list.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The interval \([0,1]\) is uncountable.
  • The real numbers have strictly larger cardinality than the natural numbers.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• From a list \(s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots\), define \(s^*\) by making its \(i\)th digit different from the \(i\)th digit of \(s_i\).
  • The natural numbers \(\mathbb N\) are the standard example of a countably infinite set.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Cantor's theorem states that for every set \(A\),

\[\operatorname{card}(A)<\operatorname{card}(2^A),\]

where \(2^A\) is the power set of \(A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
No function from a set to its power set can be surjective. Thus the power set is always strictly larger than the original set.

Cantor's theorem gives \(\operatorname{card}(A)<\operatorname{card}(\mathcal P(A))\) for every set \(A\). An injection exists, but no map \(f\colon A\to\mathcal P(A)\) is surjective, since it misses \(\{x\in A:x\notin f(x)\}\). Thus \(\aleph_0<2^{\aleph_0}<2^{2^{\aleph_0}}<\cdots\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There is an infinite staircase of larger and larger infinities: \(A,2^A,2^{2^A},\ldots\).
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(A=\mathbb N\), the power set \(2^{\mathbb N}\) has larger cardinality than \(\mathbb N\).
  • The natural numbers \(\mathbb N\) are the standard example of a countably infinite set.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The cardinality of the continuum, often denoted \(\mathfrak c\), is the cardinality of the real numbers:

\[\mathfrak c=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb R).\]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The continuum is the size of the real line, and it is larger than countable infinity.

\(\tan\colon(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)\to\mathbb{R}\) is a bijection, so \(\operatorname{card}(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb{R})=\mathfrak{c}\). Moreover \(\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_0}>\aleph_0\), and every non-degenerate interval, \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})\) all have cardinality \(\mathfrak{c}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{card}(2^{\mathbb N})=2^{\aleph_0}=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb R)=\mathfrak c\).
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The interval \([0,1]\) has cardinality \(\mathfrak c\).
  • The natural numbers \(\mathbb N\) are the standard example of a countably infinite set.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Two sets \(A\) and \(B\) have the same cardinality, written

\[ \operatorname{card}(A)=\operatorname{card}(B), \]

if there exists a bijection \(f\colon A\to B\text{.}\)

The empty set has cardinality \(0\text{.}\) A set \(A\) has finite cardinality \(n\) if it has the same cardinality as \(\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Cardinality measures the size of a set through one-to-one correspondence. For finite sets this reproduces ordinary counting; for infinite sets it provides a precise way to compare sizes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Having equal cardinality is an equivalence relation on sets.
  • A finite set with \(n\) distinct elements has cardinality \(n\text{.}\)
  • Infinite sets can have the same cardinality even when one is a proper subset of the other.
  • Cantor's theorem shows that every set has strictly smaller cardinality than its power set.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\{1,2,3\}\) and \(\{a,b,c\}\) have the same cardinality.
  • \(\mathbb N\) and the even natural numbers have the same cardinality because \(n\mapsto 2n\) is a bijection.
  • \(\mathbb N\), \(\mathbb Z\), and \(\mathbb Q\) are countably infinite, whereas \(\mathbb R\) is uncountable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Cartesian product of two sets \(A\) and \(B\) is the set of all ordered pairs whose first component comes from \(A\) and whose second component comes from \(B\):

\[ A \times B = \{(a,b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Cartesian product lists every possible pairing of an element of \(A\) with an element of \(B\).

The figure has \(|A\times B|=3\cdot2=6\) ordered pairs. The order matters: \((a,1)\ne(1,a)\), so the two illustrated sets satisfy \(A\times B\ne B\times A\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A\) and \(B\) are finite, then \(\operatorname{card}(A\times B)=\operatorname{card}(A)\operatorname{card}(B)\).
  • Cartesian products are used to define binary operations, since a binary operation on \(A\) is a function from \(A\times A\) to \(A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{x,y\}\), then \(A\times B=\{(1,x),(1,y),(2,x),(2,y)\}\).
  • The set \(\mathbb R^2\) can be understood as \(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\), the set of all ordered pairs of real numbers.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For vectors \(x\) and \(y\) in an inner product space, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality states \(|x\cdot y|\leq\|x\|\|y\|\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The inner product of two vectors cannot exceed the product of their lengths in absolute value.

For the nonzero vector \(x\) drawn, the projection of \(y\) onto its line is no longer than \(y\). This gives \(|x\cdot y|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|\), with equality when \(y\) is a multiple of \(x\) and the projection reaches the arc.

Drag \(x\) and \(y\): \(|x\cdot y|\) never exceeds \(\|x\|\|y\|\), because the shadow of \(x\) is never longer than \(x\). Equality holds exactly when the vectors lie on one line.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Cauchy-Schwarz justifies the formula for the angle between vectors.
  • It can be used to prove the triangle inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For orthogonal vectors, the left side is \(0\).
  • For \(x=y\), equality holds.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a square matrix \(A\), the characteristic polynomial is \(\det(A-\lambda I)\), viewed as a polynomial in \(\lambda\). The equation \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) is called the characteristic equation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The characteristic polynomial packages the eigenvalue problem into a polynomial equation.

Change the entries of \(A\): the roots of \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) on the right are the eigenvalues, and their eigenvector lines are dashed on the left.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The eigenvalues of \(A\) are exactly the roots of the characteristic polynomial, equivalently the solutions of the characteristic equation.
  • For an \(n\times n\) matrix, the characteristic polynomial has degree \(n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&b\end{pmatrix}\), the characteristic polynomial is \((a-\lambda)(b-\lambda)\).
  • For \(I_n\), the characteristic polynomial is \((1-\lambda)^n\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For a square matrix \(A\), let \(A_{ij}\) be the matrix obtained by deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\). The number \(\det(A_{ij})\) is the minor of entry \((i,j)\), and

\[ C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\det(A_{ij}) \]

is the corresponding cofactor.

The determinant can be computed by expanding along any row or column:

\[ \det(A)=\sum_k a_{ik}C_{ik} \]

for expansion along row \(i\), or

\[ \det(A)=\sum_k a_{kj}C_{kj} \]

for expansion along column \(j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Cofactor expansion reduces the determinant of an \(n\times n\) matrix to determinants of smaller matrices.

\(\det A=a_{11}C_{11}+a_{12}C_{12}+a_{13}C_{13}\) with \(C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\det A_{ij}\), where \(\det A_{11}\) is the minor of \(a_{11}\). Any row or column works, so pick the one with the most zeros.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Cofactor expansion can be performed along any row or column.
  • Choosing a row or column with many zeros makes the computation shorter.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a \(3\times3\) matrix, expanding along the first row gives three \(2\times2\) determinants.
  • For a diagonal matrix, expanding along sparse rows quickly gives the product of diagonal entries.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A binary operation \(\star\) on \(A\) is commutative if

\[a\star b=b\star a\]

for all \(a,b\in A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Commutativity means that changing the order of the two inputs does not change the result.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An Abelian group is a group whose operation is commutative.
  • Associativity, identity elements, and inverse elements determine which algebraic structure is present.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Addition of real numbers is commutative. Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative.
  • \((\mathbb R,+)\) is a standard example where the operation is ordinary addition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a complex number \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) where \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), the absolute value or modulus of \(z\) is denoted as \(|z|\) is a real number and is calculated by \(|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The absolute value of a complex number is simply its distance from the origin on the complex plane​.

\(|z|\) is the distance from \(0\) to \(z\) (Pythagoras); \(|z|^2=z\bar z\) and \(|zw|=|z|\,|w|\).

Drag \(z\): \(|z|\) is its distance from \(0\), the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs \(|a|\) and \(|b|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• While it is true that \(|z| = \sqrt{z^2}\) when \(z\) is real number, it does not hold whenever \(z\) is a non-real complex number, i.e., \(|z| \neq \sqrt{z^2}\) for \(z\in (\mathbb C\setminus \mathbb R)\).
  • Complex numbers extend the real numbers by adding a solution of \(x^2=-1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(|1+\mathrm{i}|=\sqrt 2\).
  • \(|z|=1\) represents a unit circle in the complex plane.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given two complex numbers \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) and \(w=c+\mathrm{i}d\) where \(a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}\), the sum of complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\) is defined as \(z+w=(a+c)+\mathrm{i}(b+d).\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Adding complex numbers is like adding two vectors: you simply add their real parts together and their imaginary parts together.

For \(z=a+b\mathrm{i}\) and \(w=c+d\mathrm{i}\): \(z+w=(a+c)+(b+d)\mathrm{i}\). Real and imaginary parts add separately, which is the parallelogram rule for arrows.

Drag \(z\) and \(w\): real parts add, imaginary parts add, just like vector addition.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The addition identity for complex numbers is \(0_\mathbb{C} = 0 + 0\mathrm{i},\) which is the real number \(0.\)
  • Complex addition has commutativity: \(z_1 + z_2 = z_2 + z_1.\)
  • Complex addition has associativity: \((z_1 + z_2) + z_3 = z_1 + (z_2 + z_3)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((2+\mathrm{i}) + (3+4\mathrm{i}) = 5+5\mathrm{i}\).
  • \((1-\mathrm{i})+(-1+\mathrm{i}) = 0_{\mathbb{C}}=0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: If \(P\) is a polynomial in one variable with real coefficients, and \(a + \mathrm{i} b\) is a root of \(P\) with \(a\) and \(b\) being real numbers, then its complex conjugate \(a − \mathrm{i} b\) is also a root of \(P\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Complex roots of real polynomials come in pairs.

The plotted roots belong to \(p(z)=z^4+2z^3+2z^2+10z+25\). Because its coefficients are real, its non-real roots come in conjugate pairs, reflected across the real axis.

With real coefficients the roots are mirrored in the real axis. Give \(a_0\) an imaginary part and the symmetry breaks: the theorem needs real coefficients.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If the degree of a real polynomial is odd, it must have at least one real root.
  • Any real square matrix of odd degree has at least one real eigenvalue.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(x^2-2x+5\) has real coefficients and the root \(1+2\mathrm{i}\), so \(1-2\mathrm{i}\) is also a root.
  • \(x-\mathrm{i}\) has the root \(\mathrm{i}\) but not \(-\mathrm{i}\): its coefficients are not all real, so the theorem does not apply.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a complex number \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) where \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), the conjugate of the complex number \(z\) is defined as \(\overline{z}=a-\mathrm{i}b.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The conjugate of a complex number retains the original real part while inverting the sign of the imaginary part.

Conjugation reflects \(z\) across the real axis and preserves its modulus: \(|\bar z|=|z|\) and \(z\bar z=|z|^2\). For \(z\ne0\), its argument changes sign modulo \(2\pi\).

Drag \(z\): \(\overline z\) is its mirror image in the real axis, with the angle \(-\varphi\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• We have \(\overline{z + w} = \overline{z} + \overline{w},\) \(\overline{-z} = -\overline{z},\) and \(\overline{zw} = \overline{z} \cdot \overline{w}.\)
  • \(z\) and \(\overline z\) are symmetric about the real axis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\overline{1+\mathrm{i}}=1-\mathrm{i}\).
  • \(\overline{-2-3\mathrm{i}}=-2+3\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For any two complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\) (where \(w \neq 0\)), the quotient of complex numbers \(z/w\) is defined as \(z/w = z \cdot w^{-1} = \dfrac{z\overline{w}}{|w|^2}.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
To divide one complex number by another, you multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which turns the denominator into a real number you can divide by.

For \(w\ne0\), moduli divide and arguments subtract modulo \(2\pi\): \(|z/w|=|z|/|w|\), and \(\arg(z/w)=\arg z-\arg w\) when \(z\ne0\). Multiplying by the conjugate gives \(z/w=z\bar w/|w|^2\).

Drag \(z\) and \(w\): the lengths divide and the angles subtract.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(|z/w|=|z|/|w|\).
  • \(\overline{z/w}=\overline z /\overline w\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \((1+\mathrm{i})/(2-\mathrm{i})=\dfrac{(1+\mathrm{i})(2+\mathrm{i})}{(2-\mathrm{i})(2+\mathrm{i})}=\dfrac{1+3\mathrm{i}}{5}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(z\in\mathbb{C}\). The complex exponential function \(\mathrm{e}^z\) is defined as

\[ \mathrm{e}^z=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{z^n}{n!}=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2!}+\frac{z^3}{3!}+\cdots, \]

where \(z^n\) denotes the \(n\)-fold complex product of \(z\) with itself (with \(z^0=1\)), which can be evaluated in polar form by De Moivre's formula.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The complex exponential is defined based on the Taylor series of the real exponential, extending its definition using powers of complex numbers.

The modulus \(\mathrm{e}^{x}\) comes from the real part and the angle \(y\) from the imaginary part: the line \(x=c\) wraps onto the circle of radius \(\mathrm{e}^{c}\), once per height \(2\pi\) (dashed), and the green point \(c+\mathrm{i}\theta\) lands at \(\mathrm{e}^{c+\mathrm{i}\theta}\). So \(\mathrm{e}^{z}\) is \(2\pi\mathrm{i}\)-periodic and never \(0\).

Drag \(z\) and raise \(N\): the terms \(z^n/n!\) are laid tip to tail, and the partial sums spiral into \(\mathrm{e}^z\) (ringed).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The series converges for all \(z \in \mathbb{C}\) (infinite radius of convergence).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(\displaystyle \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}}=1+\mathrm{i}-\frac{1}{2!}-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{3!}+\frac{1}{4!}+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{5!}+\cdots\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(z\neq 0\) and \(w\) be complex numbers. The complex power \(z^w\) is defined as \(\mathrm{e}^{w \log z}\), where the complex logarithm \(\log z\) is a multivalued function. The principal value of the complex exponentiation \(z^w\) is \(\mathrm{e}^{w \operatorname{Log}z}\), where \(\operatorname{Log}z\) denotes the principal value of the complex logarithm.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Raising a complex number to a complex power is done by taking a logarithm of the base, multiplying it by the exponent \(w\), and then applying the complex exponential function. Because \(\log z\) has infinitely many values, \(z^w\) generally does too.

For \(z=re^{\mathrm i\varphi}\), the power \(z^n=r^ne^{\mathrm i n\varphi}\) has modulus \(r^n\) and argument \(n\varphi\) modulo \(2\pi\). The figure uses \(r=1.25\) and \(\varphi=\pi/6\).

\(z^{1/n}\) has \(n\) values, evenly spaced on a circle of radius \(|z|^{1/n}\). The highlighted one is the principal value \(\mathrm{e}^{\frac1n\operatorname{Log}z}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Complex exponentiation is generally multivalued. For an integer exponent \(m\), changing \(\log z\) by \(2\pi\mathrm{i} k\) multiplies the result by \(\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i} km}=1\), so \(z^m\) is single-valued.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \[\displaystyle \begin{aligned}\mathrm{i}^{1/2}&= \left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\pi/2+2\pi k)}\right)^{1/2}\\&= \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\left(\pi k+\pi/4\right)}\\&=\left\{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathrm{i},\right.\\&\qquad\left.-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathrm{i}\right\}.\end{aligned}\]
  • \(\displaystyle \mathrm{i}^\mathrm{i} = \left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\pi/2+2\pi k) }\right)^\mathrm{i} = \mathrm{e}^{-\pi/2-2k\pi}\in\mathbb{R},\) where \(k\in\mathbb{Z}.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A complex logarithm of a nonzero complex number \(z\), defined to be any complex number \(w\) for which \(\mathrm{e}^{w}=z\). Such a number \(w\) is denoted by \(\log z\). If \(z\) is given in polar form as \(z=re^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}\), where \(r>0\) and \(\varphi\) are real numbers, then \(\ln r+\mathrm{i} \varphi\) is one logarithm of \(z\), and all the complex logarithms of \(z\) are exactly the numbers of the form \(\ln r+\mathrm{i}\left(\varphi +2\pi k\right)\) for integers \(k.\) For each nonzero complex number \(z\), the principal value of the complex logarithm \(\operatorname{Log} z\) is the logarithm whose imaginary part lies in the interval \((-\pi ,\pi].\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The complex logarithm is a multivalued function since the complex exponential function is not bijective.

For \(z\ne0\), the complex logarithm has values \(\log z=\ln|z|+\mathrm i(\arg z+2\pi k)\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\). These values are \(2\pi\mathrm i\) apart, and the principal value \(\operatorname{Log}z\) uses \(\operatorname{Arg}z\in(-\pi,\pi]\).

Drag \(z\): its logarithms (right) lie on one vertical line, \(2\pi\) apart. \(\operatorname{Log} z\) is the one in the shaded strip; move \(z\) across the negative real axis and it jumps.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • For nonzero \(z,w\), the identity \(\operatorname{Log}(zw)=\operatorname{Log}z+\operatorname{Log}w\) is not valid in general: the sum of principal arguments may lie outside \((-\pi,\pi]\). For example, taking \(z=w=-1\) gives \(\operatorname{Log}(zw)=0\), whereas \(\operatorname{Log}z+\operatorname{Log}w=2\pi\mathrm{i}\). For positive real \(z,w\), the identity does hold.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\log 1=2\pi\mathrm{i} k\) while \(\operatorname{Log} 1=0.\)
  • \(\log (-1)=\mathrm{i} (\pi+2\pi k)\) while \(\operatorname{Log} (-1)=\mathrm{i}\pi.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given two complex numbers \(z=a+\mathrm{i}b\) and \(w=c+\mathrm{i}d\) where \(a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}\), the product of complex numbers \(z\) and \(w\) is defined as \(zw = (a+\mathrm{i}b)(c+\mathrm{i}d) = (ac-bd) + \mathrm{i}(ad+bc).\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Multiplying two complex numbers is similar to multiplying two binomials.

Complex multiplication multiplies the moduli, \(|zw|=|z|\,|w|\). When \(z\) and \(w\) are nonzero, their arguments add modulo \(2\pi\), so multiplication combines a stretch and a rotation.

Drag \(z\) and \(w\): the length of \(zw\) is the product of the lengths, and its angle is the sum of the angles.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The multiplicative identity for complex numbers is \(1_\mathbb{C} = 1 + 0\mathrm{i},\) which is the real number \(1.\)
  • Complex multiplication has commutativity, associativity, and distributivity over complex addition.
  • In polar form, complex multiplication combines stretching, because \(|zw|=|z|\,|w|\), with rotation, because arguments add modulo \(2\pi\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1+2\mathrm{i})(2-\mathrm{i})=4+3\mathrm{i}=(2-\mathrm{i})(1+2\mathrm{i})\).
  • \((3+4\mathrm{i})1_\mathbb{C}=(3+4\mathrm{i})(1+0\mathrm{i})=3+4\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A complex number is of the form \(a + \mathrm{i}b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are real numbers, and \(\mathrm{i}\) is the imaginary unit. The number \(a\) is the real part of the complex number \(a + \mathrm{i}b\) and is denoted by \(a = \operatorname{Re}(a+\mathrm{i}b)=\Re(a+\mathrm{i}b)\). Similarly, \(b\) is the imaginary part and is represented as \(b = \operatorname{Im}(a+\mathrm{i}b)=\Im(a+\mathrm{i}b).\) If the real part of a complex number \(a+\mathrm{i}b\) is zero, we term the number \(0+\mathrm{i}b\) as a purely imaginary number. The set of all complex numbers is denoted by \(\mathbb{C}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Essentially, a complex number is an ordered pair of two real numbers.

Drag \(z\): the real part \(a\) is measured along the horizontal axis and the imaginary part \(b\) along the vertical one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Complex numbers do not have trichotomy, e.g., we cannot say \(1-\mathrm{i}> 0\) or \(1-\mathrm{i} < 0.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The complex plane or \(\boldsymbol{z}\)-plane is the plane formed by the complex numbers, with a Cartesian coordinate system such that the horizontal \(x\)-axis, called the real axis, is formed by the real numbers, and the vertical \(y\)-axis, called the imaginary axis, is formed by the purely imaginary numbers. The form \(a+\mathrm{i} b\) is called the Cartesian form of a complex number.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The complex plane can be seen as the Cartesian plane \(\mathbb R^2\) equipped with a number of additional structures (e.g., complex multiplication).

Each complex number \(a+\mathrm{i}b\) is the point \((a,b)\). Drag \(z\) along the axes to see the real and the purely imaginary numbers.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Each complex number \(a+\mathrm{i} b\) corresponds to unique coordinates \((a,b).\)
  • In the Cartesian coordinate system, the addition of complex numbers can be visualized as vector addition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(1+\mathrm{i}\) and \(2-\mathrm{i}\) are elements in the complex plane \(\mathbb C\).
  • For \(z=3+4\mathrm{i}\), the real part is \(3\), the imaginary part is \(4\), and \(|z|=5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The polar coordinate system for complex numbers specifies each complex number by its modulus \(r\) and polar angle \(\varphi\) (known as the argument). The form \(z=r(\cos \varphi+\mathrm{i}\sin\varphi)\) is called the polar form of a complex number.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The polar form of a complex number describes it using its distance from the origin and the angle it makes with the positive real axis.

For the nonzero point drawn, its modulus \(r\) and argument \(\varphi\) locate it just as well as its Cartesian coordinates. Adding \(2\pi k\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\), to the argument gives the same point.

Set the modulus \(r\) and the angle \(\varphi\), or drag \(z\): \(z=r(\cos\varphi+\mathrm{i}\sin\varphi)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Complex multiplication in polar form combines stretching (multiplying moduli) with rotation (adding arguments).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The complex number \(1+\mathrm{i}\) has polar coordinates \((\sqrt 2, \pi/4)\).
  • The complex number \(3+4\mathrm{i}\) has polar coordinates \((5, \operatorname{atan2}(4,3))\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The reciprocal of the complex number \(z\neq 0\) is defined as \(z^{-1} = |z|^{-2} \overline{z}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The reciprocal of a complex number is found by dividing its conjugate by the square of its absolute value.

For \(z\ne0\), \(1/z=\bar z/|z|^2\) lies in the direction of \(\bar z\) and has modulus \(1/|z|\). Points outside the unit circle map inside it, and nonzero points inside map outside.

Drag \(z\): \(z^{-1}\) lies on the ray of \(\overline z\) at distance \(1/|z|\), inside the unit circle when \(z\) is outside it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • We have \(|z^{-1}|=1/|z|\) and \(\arg(z^{-1})=-\arg z\) modulo \(2\pi\). For the principal argument, \(\operatorname{Arg}(z^{-1})=-\operatorname{Arg}z\) unless \(z\) is a negative real number, in which case both equal \(\pi\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The reciprocal of \(z = 1 + 2\mathrm{i}\) is \(\displaystyle z^{-1} = \frac{1}{5} - \frac{2}{5}\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(z\in\mathbb{C}\). The complex sine function \(\sin z\) and the complex cosine function \(\cos z\) are defined as

\[ \begin{aligned} \sin z&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n} z^{2 n+1}}{(2 n+1) !}\\ &=z-\frac{z^3}{3!}+\frac{z^5}{5!}-\cdots,\\ \cos z&=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n} z^{2 n}}{(2 n) !}\\ &=1-\frac{z^2}{2!}+\frac{z^4}{4!}-\cdots. \end{aligned} \]

where the power functions \(z^n\)'s are defined according to De Moivre's formula.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The complex sine and cosine functions are defined based on their Taylor series.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The complex sine and cosine functions remain periodic with period \(2\pi\).
  • All fundamental algebraic identities from real trigonometry continue to hold for complex arguments

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(\displaystyle \sin \mathrm{i}=\mathrm{i}+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{3!}+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{5!}+\cdots=\mathrm{i}\left(1+\frac{1}{3!}+\frac{1}{5!}+\cdots\right)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The continuum hypothesis is the hypothesis that there is no set whose cardinality is strictly between \(\aleph_0\) and \(\mathfrak c\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
It asks whether there is an intermediate size of infinity between the natural numbers and the real numbers.

Equivalently, the continuum hypothesis states \(\mathfrak c=\aleph_1\), the next cardinal after \(\aleph_0\). Assuming the standard ZFC axioms are consistent, they can neither prove nor refute this hypothesis (Gödel, 1940; Cohen, 1963).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In symbols, it denies the existence of a set \(A\) such that \(\aleph_0<\operatorname{card}(A)<\mathfrak c\).
  • A bijection is the main tool for proving that two sets have the same cardinality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The question compares the size of \(\mathbb N\) with the size of \(\mathbb R\).
  • The natural numbers \(\mathbb N\) are the standard example of a countably infinite set.

\[v=(v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n),\]

then \(v_i\) is called the \(i\)th coordinate of \(v\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A set is countably infinite if it has the same cardinality as the natural numbers, equivalently if there is a bijection between the set and \(\mathbb N\text{.}\)

A set is countable if it is finite or countably infinite. A set that is not countable is called uncountable.

Course convention

In Math II: Linear Algebra, countable includes finite sets. Use countably infinite when the set must be infinite and in bijection with \(\mathbb N\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A countable set can be listed without missing any element. An uncountable set is too large to be exhausted by a sequence indexed by the natural numbers.

The zig-zag numbers every pair \((i,j)\in\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\): a bijection \(\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\), so \(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\) (and likewise \(\mathbb{Q}\), via \(i/j\)) is countably infinite. \(\mathbb{R}\) cannot be listed this way (Cantor's diagonal argument): it is uncountable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every finite set is countable.
  • Every subset of a countable set is countable.
  • \(\mathbb N\), \(\mathbb Z\), and \(\mathbb Q\) are countably infinite.
  • Cantor's diagonal argument shows that \([0,1]\) and \(\mathbb R\) are uncountable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\{1,2,3\}\) is countable because it is finite.
  • The even natural numbers are countably infinite: \(n\mapsto 2n\) gives a bijection from \(\mathbb N\).
  • The real interval \([0,1]\) is uncountable.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: If \(A\) is a nonsingular \(n\times n\) matrix, then the unique solution of \(Ax=b\) is given by \(x_j=\frac{\det(B_j)}{\det(A)}\), where \(B_j\) is obtained from \(A\) by replacing column \(j\) with \(b\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Cramer's rule expresses each unknown of a square linear system using determinants.

For the illustrated system \(Ax=b\), \(A=(a_1\ a_2)=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(b=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\end{pmatrix}\). Cramer's rule gives \(x_1=\dfrac{\det(b,a_2)}{\det(a_1,a_2)}=2\) and \(x_2=\dfrac{\det(a_1,b)}{\det(a_1,a_2)}=1\). Replacing \(a_1\) by \(b=x_1a_1+x_2a_2\) multiplies the area by \(x_1\), while the \(a_2\) component only shears it.

Each unknown is a ratio of determinants: \(x_j=\det(B_j)/\det(A)\), where \(B_j\) has \(b\) in column \(j\). Make \(\det(A)=0\) and the rule breaks down.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Cramer's rule applies only when \(A\) is nonsingular.
  • It gives an explicit formula for the unique solution of \(Ax=b\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a \(2\times2\) nonsingular system, \(x_1=\det(B_1)/\det(A)\) and \(x_2=\det(B_2)/\det(A)\).
  • If \(\det(A)=0\), Cramer's rule cannot be used.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For any integer \(n\), and any complex number \(z = r(\cos\varphi + \mathrm{i}\sin\varphi)\), it holds that:

\[ z^n = r^n(\cos(n\varphi) + \mathrm{i}\sin(n\varphi)). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
To raise a complex number in polar form to an integer power \(n\), raise its modulus to the power \(n\) and multiply its angle by \(n\).

Drag \(z\) and change \(n\): each power multiplies the modulus by \(r\) and adds \(\varphi\) to the angle, so the powers lie on a spiral.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The formula converts integer powers of a complex number into powers of its modulus and multiples of its argument.
  • It is closely related to Euler's formula.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1+\sqrt{3}\mathrm{i})^8=2^8(\cos(8\pi/3)+\mathrm{i}\sin(8\pi/3))\).
  • \((-1+\mathrm{i})^4=(\sqrt2)^4(\cos(3\pi)+\mathrm{i}\sin(3\pi))=-4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a real symmetric matrix. The definiteness of \(A\) classifies the sign of the quadratic form \(x^T A x\):

  • Positive definite: \(x^TAx>0\) for every nonzero vector \(x\).
  • Positive semidefinite: \(x^TAx\ge 0\) for every vector \(x\).
  • Negative definite: \(x^TAx<0\) for every nonzero vector \(x\).
  • Negative semidefinite: \(x^TAx\le 0\) for every vector \(x\).
  • Indefinite: \(x^TAx\) takes both positive and negative values.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Definiteness tells whether the quadratic form determined by a symmetric matrix is always positive, always nonnegative, always negative, always nonpositive, or changes sign.

The four panels show level curves of \(x^\top Ax\) for \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\), \(A=\operatorname{diag}(-1,-2)\), \(A=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\), and \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), respectively. The first form is positive for every nonzero \(x\), the second is negative, the third is nonnegative but zero along a line, and the fourth takes both signs.

Positive definite means \(x^TAx>0\) for every \(x\neq0\): the curve on the right stays above \(0\). Try the examples, and look for directions where the form vanishes.

A positive definite \(A\) gives a bowl, a negative definite one a cap, and an indefinite one a saddle; the eigenvalues are shown below.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A symmetric matrix is positive definite iff all its eigenvalues are positive.
  • A symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite iff all its eigenvalues are nonnegative.
  • A symmetric matrix is negative definite iff all its eigenvalues are negative.
  • A symmetric matrix is negative semidefinite iff all its eigenvalues are nonpositive.
  • A symmetric matrix is indefinite iff it has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(I_n\) is positive definite, while \(-I_n\) is negative definite.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) is positive semidefinite, and \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\) is indefinite.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For a real symmetric matrix \(A\), definiteness is completely determined by the signs of the eigenvalues: positive definite means all eigenvalues are positive, positive semidefinite means all are nonnegative, negative definite means all are negative, negative semidefinite means all are nonpositive, and indefinite means both positive and negative eigenvalues occur.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Eigenvalues reveal the sign behavior of a symmetric matrix's quadratic form.

In eigen-coordinates \(c=Q^\top x\), the illustrated quadratic form is \(x^\top Ax=\lambda_1c_1^2+\lambda_2c_2^2\). Both eigenvalues are positive, so its level curve is an ellipse. Changing just one eigenvalue to a negative value gives a hyperbola; changing it to zero gives a semidefinite form.

On the unit circle \(x^TAx\) runs between the two eigenvalues, reached along the eigenvectors. Their signs decide the definiteness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• This theorem converts a quadratic-form problem into an eigenvalue problem.
  • It applies to real symmetric matrices.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A diagonal matrix with diagonal entries \(2\) and \(3\) is positive definite.
  • A diagonal matrix with diagonal entries \(2\) and \(-3\) is indefinite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The determinant of a square matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\) of size \(n\times n\), denoted \(\det(A)\) or \(|A|\), is the scalar defined recursively by \(\det(a)=a\) for a \(1\times1\) matrix and, for \(n\geq2\),

\[\det(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}(-1)^{1+j}a_{1j}\det(A_{1j}),\]

where \(A_{1j}\) is the \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) matrix obtained from \(A\) by deleting row \(1\) and column \(j\) (cofactor expansion along the first row). It detects invertibility and encodes the volume scaling of the associated linear transformation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The determinant summarizes important information about a square matrix in one number.

The columns of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0.5\\0.5&1.5\end{pmatrix}\) are \(Ae_1\) and \(Ae_2\). Its determinant is \(2\cdot1.5-0.5\cdot0.5=2.75\). A negative determinant would reverse the orientation, while a zero determinant would collapse the parallelogram to zero area and make the matrix singular.

The unit square becomes a parallelogram of area \(|\det(A)|\). It flips colour when \(\det(A)<0\) (orientation reversed) and collapses when \(\det(A)=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A square matrix is invertible if and only if \(\det(A)\neq0\).
  • \(\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)\) for square matrices of the same size.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), \(\det(A)=ad-bc\).
  • \(\det(I_n)=1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A diagonal matrix is a square matrix whose off-diagonal entries are all zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A diagonal matrix only acts separately on each coordinate.

The matrix \(D=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&\tfrac12\end{pmatrix}\) stretches the first coordinate by \(2\) and shrinks the second by \(\tfrac12\). The axes are eigendirections, its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries, and \(D^k=\operatorname{diag}(2^k,2^{-k})\).

A diagonal matrix scales each axis on its own: \(Ae_1=a_{11}e_1\) and \(Ae_2=a_{22}e_2\). Allow off-diagonal entries to see the axes turn.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The determinant of a diagonal matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.
  • The product and sum of diagonal matrices of the same size are diagonal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\) is diagonal.
  • \(I_n\) and \(0_n\) are diagonal.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A square matrix \(A\) is diagonalizable if there exists an invertible matrix \(P\) such that \(P^{-1}AP\) is diagonal.

docs.title: Non-diagonalizable (defective) matrices
docs.text: A square matrix that is not diagonalizable is called non-diagonalizable or defective. This means it does not have enough linearly independent eigenvectors to form an eigenbasis. Jordan normal form is the tool used for such matrices.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A diagonalizable matrix becomes diagonal after changing to a suitable basis.

On the left, \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) has two independent eigenvectors and is diagonalizable: \(P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\). On the right, the shear \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) has only one eigendirection, so it is defective and not diagonalizable.

Choose the examples: two eigenvector lines give an eigenbasis; a shear has only one, and a rotation has none over \(\mathbb R\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A matrix is diagonalizable if it has enough linearly independent eigenvectors to form a basis.
  • If an \(n\times n\) matrix has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues, it is diagonalizable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Every diagonal matrix is diagonalizable.
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) is not diagonalizable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Diagonalization is the process of finding an invertible matrix \(P\) and a diagonal matrix \(D\) such that \(A=PDP^{-1}\), equivalently \(P^{-1}AP=D\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Diagonalization rewrites a linear transformation in an eigenbasis, where its action is simple coordinate-wise scaling.

\(P^{-1}\) changes to the eigenvector basis, \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\) only scales, \(P\) changes back: \(A=PDP^{-1}\) with the eigenvectors as columns of \(P\) and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of \(D\). Hence \(A^k=PD^kP^{-1}\), and \(A\) is diagonalizable \(\iff\) it has a basis of eigenvectors.

Move \(t\): the grid drawn along the eigenvectors \(p_1,p_2\) keeps its directions and only stretches, by \(\lambda_1\) along \(p_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) along \(p_2\). That is \(A=PDP^{-1}\) read in the basis \(p_1,p_2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A=PDP^{-1}\), then \(A^k=PD^kP^{-1}\).
  • The columns of \(P\) are eigenvectors of \(A\), and the diagonal entries of \(D\) are the corresponding eigenvalues.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A diagonal matrix is already diagonalized with \(P=I\).
  • If \(A\) has a basis of eigenvectors, then it is diagonalizable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space is the length of any basis of that vector space. It is denoted by \(\dim(V)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Dimension counts how many independent directions are needed to describe every vector in the space.

\(\dim V\) is the number of vectors in any basis of \(V\): one arrow spans the line, two the plane, three all of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Any two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have the same length.
  • Every basis of \(\mathbb R^n\) contains exactly \(n\) vectors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb R^2\) has dimension \(2\).
  • The vector space of polynomials of degree at most \(2\) has dimension \(3\), with basis \((1,x,x^2)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(V_1,V_2,\ldots,V_m\) be subspaces of \(V\), and let \(W=V_1+V_2+\cdots+V_m\). If every \(w\in W\) can be written in exactly one way as

\[w=v_1+v_2+\cdots+v_m,\]

with \(v_i\in V_i\), then \(W\) is the direct sum of the subspaces, denoted

\[W=V_1\oplus V_2\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m.\]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A direct sum is a sum of subspaces without overlap that would create non-unique decompositions.

In a direct sum \(W=V_1\oplus V_2\), every \(w\in W\) has exactly one expression \(w=v_1+v_2\) with \(v_i\in V_i\). Equivalently, \(W=V_1+V_2\) and \(V_1\cap V_2=\{0\}\); the figure shows this decomposition for \(\mathbb R^2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For two subspaces, \(V_1+V_2\) is direct exactly when \(V_1\cap V_2=\{\boldsymbol 0\}\).
  • Many questions about the concept reduce to solving equations involving linear combinations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The \(x\)-axis and \(y\)-axis form a direct sum equal to \(\mathbb R^2\).
  • Let \(V_1=\{(a,0):a\in\mathbb R\}\) and \(V_2=\{(0,b):b\in\mathbb R\}\). The vector \((3,-2)\) has the decomposition \((3,0)+(0,-2)\). Any decomposition \((a,0)+(0,b)=(3,-2)\) forces \(a=3\) and \(b=-2\), so it is unique.

  • Dimension: for finite-dimensional subspaces, \(\dim(V_1\oplus V_2)=\dim V_1+\dim V_2\).

docs.title: Distance Between a Point and a Line
Definition
docs.text: The distance between a point \(A\) and a line \(\ell(t)\) is the shortest distance between \(A\) and all points on the line.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Geometrically, it is the length of the perpendicular segment from the point to the line.

The distance from \(A\) to the line through \(B\) in the nonzero direction \(v\) is \(d=\left\|(A-B)-\dfrac{(A-B)\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v\right\|\). In \(\mathbb R^3\), it is also \(d=\dfrac{\|(A-B)\times v\|}{\|v\|}\). The closest point is the foot of the perpendicular.

Move \(t\) along the line through \(B\): the distance from \(A\) to \(\ell(t)\) (right panel) is smallest at the foot \(F\) of the perpendicular.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distance is zero if and only if the point lies on the line.
  • In coordinates, the distance can be found by minimizing \(\|\ell(t)-A\|\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\ell(t)=(1+t,2t,-1,2-t)\), a point on the line gives minimum distance \(0\).
  • A point not on the line has positive distance.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: If \(A\) is a linear operator with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\) and corresponding eigenvectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\), then \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) is linearly independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Different eigenvalues produce genuinely different eigendirections.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An \(n\times n\) matrix with \(n\) distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable.
  • The theorem is a main reason eigenvectors can form useful bases.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A \(2\times2\) diagonal matrix with diagonal entries \(2\) and \(3\) has two independent eigenvectors.
  • A \(3\times3\) matrix with three distinct eigenvalues has three independent eigenvectors.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An eigenbasis is a basis of a vector space consisting entirely of eigenvectors of a linear operator.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
In an eigenbasis, the matrix of the operator is diagonal.

The vectors \((p_1,p_2)\) form an eigenbasis of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\). In these coordinates its matrix is \(\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\), so each grid direction is stretched by its eigenvalue.

In the eigenbasis \(p_1,p_2\) the map only scales each basis vector, so its matrix is diagonal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when an eigenbasis exists.
  • The change-of-basis matrix \(P\) in diagonalization has eigenbasis vectors as its columns.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The standard basis is an eigenbasis for a diagonal matrix.
  • If two independent eigenvectors span \(\mathbb R^2\), they form an eigenbasis.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a linear operator or square matrix \(A\), a nonzero vector \(p\) and scalar \(\lambda\) satisfying \(Ap=\lambda p\) give an eigenvector \(p\) and corresponding eigenvalue \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For a real eigenvector with a real eigenvalue, the line it spans is invariant under the transformation. A positive eigenvalue preserves its direction, a negative eigenvalue reverses it, and a zero eigenvalue maps it to the zero vector. The equation \(Ap=\lambda p\) also defines eigenvectors and eigenvalues over the complex numbers.

\(Ap=\lambda p\) with \(p\neq0\): \(A\) only rescales \(p\), by the eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Here \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) has \(\lambda_1=3\) on \(p_1=\binom11\) and \(\lambda_2=1\) on \(p_2=\binom1{-1}\); a vector \(v\) off these lines is turned.

Turn the unit vector \(x\) with \(\varphi\): usually \(Ax\) points elsewhere, but on the dashed eigenvector lines \(Ax=\lambda x\). A quarter turn has no real eigenvector.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero vector is excluded from being an eigenvector.
  • Eigenvalues of triangular or diagonal matrices are their diagonal entries.
  • For a real-valued matrix, nonreal complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors occur in complex conjugate pairs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\), \((1,0)\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(2\).
  • For the same matrix, \((0,1)\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(3\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For any square matrix \(A\), the eigenvalues of \(A\) are exactly the roots of its characteristic polynomial \(\det(A-\lambda I)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The eigenvalue equation \(Ap=\lambda p\) has a nonzero solution \(p\) exactly when \(A-\lambda I\) is singular, that is, when \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue iff \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\).
  • Every eigenvalue has at least one corresponding eigenvector.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a diagonal matrix, the roots are precisely the diagonal entries.
  • For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\), the eigenvalues are \(1\pm2\mathrm{i}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An elementary row operation is one of three reversible operations on a system or matrix: adding a multiple of one row to another, interchanging two rows, or multiplying a row by a nonzero scalar.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Elementary row operations transform a system without changing its solution set.

Each operation is undone by another of the same kind, so the transformed system is equivalent to the original. Each operation can also be written as multiplication on the left by an elementary matrix.

Replace \(R_2\) by \(R_2+kR_1\): the second line swings about the solution, which never moves. The button picks the \(k\) that eliminates \(x_1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Elementary row operations preserve equivalence of systems.
  • Gauss-Jordan elimination consists of applying elementary row operations until reduced row echelon form is reached.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Replace \(R_2\) by \(R_2-3R_1\).
  • Swap \(R_1\) and \(R_3\).
