docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) over a scalar field \(\mathbb{F}\) (commonly \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb C\)) is a collection of vectors equipped with the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication that satisfy the following properties:

Let \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z}\in \boldsymbol{V}\).

  1. Closure under addition: \(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}\in\boldsymbol{V}\).
  2. Associativity of addition: \(\boldsymbol{x} + (\boldsymbol{y} + \boldsymbol{z}) = (\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{y}) + \boldsymbol{z}\).
  3. Additive identity: There exists a zero vector \(\boldsymbol{0}\in \boldsymbol{V}\) such that \(\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{0} = \boldsymbol{x}\).
  4. Commutativity of addition: \(\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{y} + \boldsymbol{x}\).
  5. Additive inverse: There exists \(-\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{V}\) such that \(\boldsymbol{x} + (-\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{0}\).

Let \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}\) and \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in \boldsymbol{V}\).

  1. Closure under scalar multiplication: \(\alpha \boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{V}\).
  2. Associativity of scalar multiplication: \(\alpha(\beta\boldsymbol{x}) = (\alpha\beta)\boldsymbol{x}\).
  3. Distributive property over vector addition: \(\alpha(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}) = \alpha\boldsymbol{x} + \alpha\boldsymbol{y}\).
  4. Distributive property over scalar addition: \((\alpha+\beta)\boldsymbol{x} = \alpha\boldsymbol{x} + \beta\boldsymbol{x}\).
  5. Scalar multiplication identity: For the multiplication identity \(1\in\mathbb F\), we have \(1\boldsymbol x=\boldsymbol x\).

docs.title: Real and complex vector spaces
docs.text: A real vector space is a vector space over the field \(\mathbb R\). A complex vector space is a vector space over the field \(\mathbb C\), so its scalars may be complex numbers.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A vector space is a collection of objects you can add together and multiply by numbers, with all the usual algebraic rules you would expect.

It is the basic setting for linear algebra.

In the diagram, adding \(x\) and \(y\) gives \(x+y\), and multiplying \(x\) by \(-1/2\) reverses its direction and halves its length. Both results remain in \(V=\mathbb{R}^2\). The same axioms also apply to polynomial and function spaces and to the solution set of \(Ax=0\); every subspace is itself a vector space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The additive identity is unique.
  • If \(\boldsymbol x + \boldsymbol y = \boldsymbol x + \boldsymbol z\), then \(\boldsymbol y = \boldsymbol z\). This is known as the cancellation law.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the most common vector space.
  • The set of all \(m \times n\) real matrices, under matrix addition and scalar multiplication, is also a vector space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A vector is an element of a vector space. In coordinate spaces such as \(\mathbb R^n\), a vector is often represented as an ordered list of coordinates.

A vector written vertically as an \(n\times1\) matrix is called a column vector. A vector written horizontally as a \(1\times n\) matrix is called a row vector.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Vectors can represent points, arrows, displacements, or lists of numerical information. Column vectors are the standard matrix representation for vectors in systems like \(Ax=b\), while row vectors often appear as transposes of column vectors.

The vector in \(\mathbb R^2\) is represented by an ordered pair of coordinates and drawn as an arrow. Moving the arrow to another starting point preserves the vector if its direction and length stay the same.

Drag the tip of \(v\): its two coordinates are the steps along the axes, and the same vector can be written as a column or, transposed, as a row.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Vectors can be added and multiplied by elements of the underlying field when they belong to a vector space.
  • The transpose of a column vector is a row vector, and the transpose of a row vector is a column vector.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}\) is a column vector in \(\mathbb R^3\).
  • \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\end{pmatrix}\) is a row vector.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The zero vector \(\boldsymbol 0\) is the additive identity of a vector space: for every \(v\in V\),

\[v+\boldsymbol 0=v.\]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: It is the vector that leaves all vectors unchanged under vector addition.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The zero vector is unique.
  • For every vector \(v\), \(0v=\boldsymbol 0\), where the \(0\) on the left is the zero scalar.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb R^n\), the zero vector is \((0,0,\ldots,0)\).
  • For \(v=(2,-3)\) in \(\mathbb R^2\), \(v+(0,0)=(2,-3)\) and \(v+(-v)=(2,-3)+(-2,3)=(0,0)\). This checks the identity property and shows that a vector plus its additive inverse gives the zero vector.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\{N_t:t\ge 0\}\) be a Poisson process. The arrival rate is the parameter \(\lambda>0\) such that the expected number of arrivals in a time interval of length \(t\) equals \(\lambda t\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The arrival rate tells how quickly events occur on average. A larger rate means arrivals are more frequent, while a smaller rate means longer waiting times are typical.

For the Poisson process shown, the rate \(\lambda\) is the expected number of arrivals per unit time: \(\mathbb{E}[N_t]=\lambda t\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(N_t)=\lambda t\). The mean interarrival time is \(1/\lambda\).

Raise \(\lambda\): the staircase \(N_t\) climbs faster around the line \(\lambda t\), and the average gap between arrivals shrinks to about \(1/\lambda\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\), \(\mathbb{E}[N_t]=\lambda t\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(N_t)=\lambda t\).
  • The first waiting time in a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) has an exponential distribution with mean \(1/\lambda\).
  • If independent Poisson processes have rates \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\), their superposition has rate \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Customer arrivals at a help desk can be modeled with rate \(12\) per hour, giving an expected \(6\) arrivals in half an hour.
  • If failures occur at rate \(0.02\) per machine-hour, then \(100\) machine-hours give an expected \(2\) failures.
  • Radioactive decays with larger arrival rate have shorter expected waiting times between successive decays.

docs.title: Axiom
docs.text:
Let \(S\) be a sample space, let \(\mathcal F\) be a collection of events, and let \(P:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\). The function \(P\) satisfies the axioms of probability if:

  1. \(\mathbb{P}(A)\ge 0\) for every event \(A\).
  2. \(\mathbb{P}(S)=1\).
  3. If \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\) are pairwise disjoint events, then
\[ \mathbb{P}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}A_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(A_i). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: These axioms set the basic rules that every probability model must obey. They say probabilities cannot be negative, certainty has probability one, and mutually exclusive possibilities can be added.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• From the axioms, \(\mathbb{P}(A^c)=1-\mathbb{P}(A)\) for every event \(A\).
  • If \(A\subseteq B\), then \(\mathbb{P}(A)\le \mathbb{P}(B)\).
  • Finite additivity follows from countable additivity: for pairwise disjoint \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\) take \(A_{n+1}=A_{n+2}=\cdots=\emptyset\) in axiom 3 and use \(\mathbb{P}(\emptyset)=0\), which gives \(\mathbb{P}(A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_n)=\mathbb{P}(A_1)+\cdots+\mathbb{P}(A_n)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In a fair die model, nonnegativity assigns no negative chance to any face, and the sample space has probability one.
  • If the events 'roll a one' and 'roll a two' are disjoint, their union has probability equal to the sum of their probabilities.
  • For nested events such as 'roll at most two' and 'roll at most four', monotonicity gives the smaller event no larger probability.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events with \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\). Bayes' rule states that

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Bayes' rule explains how to update a belief after new evidence is observed. It is useful when one conditional probability is easier to understand than the reverse conditional probability.

In the illustrated screening model, \(\mathbb{P}(D)=0.01\), \(\mathbb{P}(+\mid D)=0.9\) and \(\mathbb{P}(+\mid D^c)=0.05\). Bayes' rule gives \(\mathbb{P}(D\mid+)=\frac{0.9\cdot0.01}{0.9\cdot0.01+0.05\cdot0.99}=\frac{90}{90+495}\approx0.15\). Thus only about \(15\%\) of positive tests correspond to disease, because healthy people are much more numerous.

With a rare condition, even a good test produces many false positives. Change the prior \(\mathbb{P}(A)\), the sensitivity and the false positive rate, and watch \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Bayes' rule is obtained by writing \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)\) in two ways using conditional probability.
  • With a partition \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\), Bayes' rule becomes \(\mathbb{P}(A_i\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\mid A_i)\mathbb{P}(A_i)}{\sum_j \mathbb{P}(B\mid A_j)\mathbb{P}(A_j)}\).
  • Base rates enter through the prior probabilities and can strongly affect posterior probabilities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A diagnostic test with high sensitivity (it detects most people who have the disease) can still have a low positive predictive value (few of its positive results are true cases) when the disease is rare.
  • In spam filtering, the probability that a message is spam is updated after observing words in the message.
  • In reliability analysis, a component type can be inferred from an observed failure pattern using prior component frequencies.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(0\le p\le1\). A random variable \(X\) has a Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(p\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(p)\), if

\[ \mathbb{P}(X=1)=p,\qquad \mathbb{P}(X=0)=1-p. \]

We write \(q=1-p\). The endpoints \(p=0\) and \(p=1\) give degenerate distributions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Bernoulli variable models one success-or-failure observation, with success represented by one.

Move \(p\): the two bars always add up to \(1\), and the mean \(\mathbb{E}X=p\) sits between them. At \(p=0\) or \(p=1\) the distribution is degenerate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)\).
  • \(M_X(t)=1-p+pe^t\) for every real \(t\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair coin indicator has mean \(1/2\) and variance \(1/4\).
  • A defect indicator with \(p=0.02\) has \(\mathbb{P}(X=0)=0.98\) and variance \(0.0196\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: An indicator of an event with probability \(p\) has this distribution; sums of independent Bernoulli variables produce binomial counts.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,k\in\mathbb N\) with \(0\le k\le n\). The binomial coefficient \(\binom nk\) is the number of ways to form a combination of \(k\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects without regard to order, and is given by

\[ \binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A binomial coefficient counts selections where order does not matter. It appears whenever a problem asks how many groups of a fixed size can be chosen.

Choosing \(k\) objects from \(n\) gives \(\binom nk=n!/(k!(n-k)!)\) subsets. In the highlighted part of Pascal's triangle, \(\binom52=\binom41+\binom42=4+6=10\). Each row sums to \(2^n\), as follows by setting \(a=b=1\) in the binomial theorem.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\binom nk=\binom n{n-k}\), since choosing \(k\) objects is equivalent to leaving out \(n-k\) objects.
  • \(\binom n0=\binom nn=1\) and \(\binom n1=n\).
  • Binomial coefficients use factorials and appear in the expansion \((a+b)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a^k b^{n-k}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• From \(10\) applicants, the number of possible interview groups of size \(3\) is \(\binom{10}{3}\).
  • The number of ways to choose \(5\) cards from a \(52\) card deck is \(\binom{52}{5}\).
  • In a binomial distribution, \(\binom nk\) counts the number of ways to choose which \(k\) of the \(n\) trials are successes, which is why it appears in \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n\) be a nonnegative integer, \(0\le p\le1\) and \(q=1-p\). A discrete random variable \(X\) has a binomial distribution with parameters \(n\) and \(p\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\), if

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^kq^{n-k},\\ k=0,1,\ldots,n, \end{gathered} \]

and the PMF is zero elsewhere. Equivalently, \(X\) is the sum of \(n\) iid Bernoulli variables with success probability \(p\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A binomial variable counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability.

The diagram shows \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(10,0.3)\), the number of successes in ten independent trials with success probability \(0.3\). Its PMF is \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom{10}{k}0.3^k0.7^{10-k}\) for \(k=0,\ldots,10\). Its mean is \(3\) and variance is \(2.1\).

Change \(n\) and \(p\): the bars sit around \(\mathbb{E}X=np\) with spread \(\sqrt{npq}\). Use \(c\) and \(d\) to add up \(\mathbb{P}(c\le X\le d)\), and hover over a bar for its formula.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=np\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)\).
  • \(M_X(t)=(1-p+pe^t)^n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For three fair tosses, \(\mathbb{P}(X=2)=\binom32(1/2)^3=3/8\).
  • For \(n=10\), \(p=0.2\), the count has mean \(2\), variance \(1.6\), and no-success probability \(0.8^{10}\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: The binomial count is a sum of independent Bernoulli trials. In the rare-event limit \(n\to\infty\), \(p_n\to0\), and \(np_n\to\lambda\), its distribution converges to \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Consider a group of \(n\) people and assume that each person's birthday is independently and uniformly distributed over \(365\) possible days. The birthday problem asks for the probability that at least two people in the group share a birthday.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The birthday problem shows that coincidences can happen much sooner than intuition suggests. It is usually easier to solve by first finding the chance that no match occurs.

Under the model of independent birthdays uniformly distributed over 365 days, the probability of a shared birthday among \(n\le365\) people is \(1-365\cdot364\cdots(365-n+1)/365^n\). With 23 people there are \(\binom{23}{2}=253\) pairs that could match, and the probability exceeds one half.

Move \(n\): the chance of no shared birthday is a product of fractions that shrinks quickly, and a match becomes more likely than not from \(23\) people on.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Computing the complement usually gives the simplest formula for at least one match.
  • For \(n\) draws from \(m\) equally likely labels, the no-match probability is \(\frac{m(m-1)\cdots(m-n+1)}{m^n}\).
  • The same calculation applies to hash collisions, repeated IDs, and sampled labels.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In a group of \(23\) people, the probability of at least one shared birthday is already above one half under the usual simplified assumptions.
  • If \(1000\) IDs are sampled with replacement from a million possible IDs, the collision probability can be found from the no-repeat probability.
  • A database using short random codes faces a birthday-type collision risk.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) be a finite set with \(n\) elements, and let \(k\le n\). A combination is a selection of \(k\) elements from \(A\) in which order is not taken into account.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Combinations are used when only the chosen group matters. Rearranging the same chosen objects does not create a new outcome.

Each unordered pair corresponds to \(2!\) orderings, so \(\binom nk=\dfrac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!}=\dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}\); combinations count subsets (hands of cards, committees), permutations count arrangements.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Combinations ignore order, while permutations count order.
  • The number of \(k\)-combinations from \(n\) distinct objects is \(\binom nk\).
  • Combinations are used in sampling without regard to sequence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Choosing three committee members from twelve people is a combination problem.
  • A five-card poker hand is counted as a combination because the order of the cards in the hand does not matter.
  • Selecting two spare parts from a box of ten distinct parts is counted by \(\binom{10}{2}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be an event in a sample space \(S\). The complement of \(A\), denoted \(A^c\), is the event

\[ A^c=\{\omega\in S:\omega\notin A\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The complement is the event that the original event does not happen. It is often easier to calculate the chance of the opposite situation.

For four independent fair die rolls, the complement of at least one six is no six on any roll. Hence \(\mathbb{P}(\text{at least one six})=1-(5/6)^4\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(A^c)=1-\mathbb{P}(A)\).
  • \(A\cup A^c=S\) and \(A\cap A^c=\emptyset\).
  • The complement method is useful for events described by 'at least one'.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The complement of 'at least one machine fails' is 'no machine fails'.
  • The complement of rolling an even number on a die is rolling an odd number.
  • In the birthday problem, the complement of a shared birthday is that all birthdays are different.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be an event with \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\) and let \(Y\) be integrable. Its conditional expectation given \(A\) is the average under the conditional probability model:

\[ \mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbf{1}_A]}{\mathbb{P}(A)}. \]

For discrete \(Y\), this equals \(\sum_y y\,\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid A)\). When the conditional law has a density \(f_{Y\mid A}\), it equals \(\int_{\mathbb R}y f_{Y\mid A}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\). Conditioning on an event gives a number; conditioning on a random variable gives a random variable and is treated separately in PD.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This is the average value after restricting the probability model to an event that occurred.

For \(B=\{X\ge3\}\) in the diagram, \(\mathbb{P}(B)=0.7\). The remaining values \(3\) and \(4\) have conditional probabilities \(3/7\) and \(4/7\), so \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid B]=3(3/7)+4(4/7)=25/7\approx3.57\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]=\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbf{1}_A]/\mathbb{P}(A)\).
  • For constants \(a,b\) and integrable \(Y,Z\), \(\mathbb{E}[aY+bZ\mid A]=a\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]+b\mathbb{E}[Z\mid A]\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die conditioned to be even, the mean is \((2+4+6)/3=4\).
  • For \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) conditioned on \(Y>1/2\), the mean is \(\int_{1/2}^12y\,\mathrm{d}y=3/4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) be events with \(\mathbb{P}(C)>0\). The events \(A\) and \(B\) are conditionally independent given \(C\) if

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\cap B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(A\mid C)\mathbb{P}(B\mid C). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditional independence means two events stop influencing each other once certain information is known. It is a statement about independence inside a restricted situation.

The diagram chooses a fair coin or a coin with head probability \(0.9\), each with probability \(1/2\), and tosses the chosen coin twice. Given its identity \(C\), the two heads events are independent. Without this conditioning, \(\mathbb{P}(H_1\cap H_2)=\frac12(0.25)+\frac12(0.81)=0.53\), whereas \(\mathbb{P}(H_1)\mathbb{P}(H_2)=0.7^2=0.49\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Conditional independence is not the same as ordinary independence.
  • Two variables can be dependent marginally but conditionally independent after a common cause is known.
  • Conditional independence is central in graphical and hierarchical probability models.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two symptoms may be dependent overall but conditionally independent given the disease status.
  • Two students' answers may become conditionally independent once their preparation levels are known.
  • Machine failures in different locations may be conditionally independent given the weather condition.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A,B\) be events with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\). The conditional probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}. \]

This definition restricts and renormalizes the probability model to \(B\). It cannot be used by dividing by the probability of an exact continuously distributed observation, because that probability is zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditioning restricts outcomes to an event known to have happened and rescales their probabilities to sum to one.

Knowing that \(B\) happened keeps only the outlined region. \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\) is the share of that region taken up by \(A\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B)\).
  • For fixed \(B\) of positive probability, \(A\mapsto\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\) is a probability measure.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(\mathbb{P}(X=6\mid X\text{ is even})=(1/6)/(3/6)=1/3\).
  • If \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=0.12\) and \(\mathbb{P}(B)=0.4\), then \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=0.3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable and let \(B\) be an event with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\). The conditional variance of \(X\) given \(B\) is

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X\mid B)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X\mid B])^2\mid B], \]

provided the conditional expectations exist.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditional variance measures remaining uncertainty after some information is known. It describes how spread out the values are within the restricted situation.

For \(B=\{X\ge3\}\) in the diagram, the conditional mean is \(25/7\). The conditional variance measures spread around this mean: \(\operatorname{Var}(X\mid B)=\frac37(\frac47)^2+\frac47(\frac37)^2=\frac{12}{49}\approx0.24\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Conditional variance measures spread after conditioning on information.
  • The law of total variance decomposes total variability into within-condition and between-condition parts.
  • Conditional variance is zero when the condition determines the random variable exactly.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Delivery time may have smaller variance after conditioning on the shipping method.
  • Exam score variability may differ between students who studied and students who did not.
  • In a mixture distribution, each component can have its own conditional variance.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Under the course's absolutely continuous convention, a real-valued random variable \(X\) is continuous if it has a nonnegative integrable density \(f_X\) such that

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\int_A f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x \]

for every interval \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\). Necessarily \(\int_{\mathbb R}f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1\). A continuous CDF by itself does not guarantee the existence of a density.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: In this course, a continuous random variable means one whose probabilities can be computed from a density. Single values have zero probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)=0\) for every real \(x\).
  • Its CDF is absolutely continuous and equals the integral of its density.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A uniform variable on \((0,1)\) has density \(1\) there and no atom at \(1/2\).
  • An exponential waiting time has \(\mathbb{P}(a<X<b)=\int_a^b\lambda \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\,\mathrm{d}x\) for \(0\le a<b\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) be a finite set. Counting is the process of determining the number of elements of \(A\), usually by using systematic rules such as addition, multiplication, permutations, or combinations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Counting methods help determine how many outcomes are possible. They are essential when probabilities are based on equally likely outcomes.

The diagram pairs each of two shirts with each of three pairs of trousers, giving \(2\cdot3=6\) outfits. Multiplying the numbers of choices counts these ordered combinations; whether order matters determines when permutations or combinations are appropriate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The counting multiplication rule multiplies the number of choices at successive stages: if every first-stage choice has \(m\) second-stage choices and there are \(n\) first-stage choices, there are \(nm\) ordered outcomes.
  • The addition rule counts alternatives that do not overlap.
  • Counting arguments support naive probability models when outcomes are equally likely.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A password with two letters followed by three digits has \(26^2\cdot10^3=676{,}000\) possibilities when all 26 letters and 10 digits are allowed at each position and repetition is permitted.
  • If a menu offers either a soup or a salad but not both, the addition rule counts the first-course choices.
  • Counting favorable poker hands and total poker hands gives a naive probability.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a real-valued random variable \(X\), its cumulative distribution function is

\[ F_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X\le x),\qquad x\in\mathbb R. \]

It is nondecreasing and right-continuous, with \(\lim_{x\to-\infty}F_X(x)=0\) and \(\lim_{x\to\infty}F_X(x)=1\). These limits describe the notation \(F_X(-\infty)=0\) and \(F_X(\infty)=1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The CDF gives the probability of being at or below a threshold. It works for discrete, continuous, and mixed distributions.

Move \(x\): \(F_X(x)\) collects all probability at or below \(x\). Masses give a staircase, a density a smooth curve, and the mixed example both a jump and a smooth rise.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a)\).
  • \(\mathbb{P}(X=x)=F_X(x)-F_X(x-)\), where \(F_X(x-)\) is the left limit.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)\), the CDF is \(0\) for \(x<0\), \(0.7\) for \(0\le x<1\), and \(1\) for \(x\ge1\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(F_X(0.4)=0.4\) and \(\mathbb{P}(0.2<X\le0.4)=0.2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A real-valued random variable \(X\) is discrete if there is a finite or countably infinite set \(D\) such that \(\mathbb{P}(X\in D)=1\). Its distribution is determined by the masses \(p_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X=x)\) on this set.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A discrete variable places all probability on finitely or countably many values. Probabilities are computed by adding the masses of those values.

In the illustrated example, \(X\) takes the values \(0\), \(1\) and \(2\). Their probability masses sum to \(1\), and the probability of any set of these values is the sum of its masses.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There is a countable set \(D\) with \(\mathbb{P}(X\in D)=1\).
  • For any set \(A\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\sum_{x\in A\cap D}p_X(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair die has values \(1,\ldots,6\), each with probability \(1/6\).
  • A Poisson count has possible values \(0,1,2,\ldots\), so a discrete support need not be finite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\) be a nonempty finite set of distinct real values. A variable is discrete uniform on \(A\) if \(p_X(a_i)=1/n\) for each \(i\) and its PMF is zero outside \(A\).

The course's integer-range case has \(A=\{a,a+1,\ldots,b\}\), where \(a\le b\) are integers, and

\[ p_X(k)=\frac1{b-a+1},\qquad k=a,\ldots,b. \]

The mean and variance formulas below apply to this consecutive-integer case; for an arbitrary finite set, average its listed values and squared deviations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Every value in a specified finite set is equally likely. Consecutive integers give the familiar fair-die model and have simple mean and variance formulas.

Move the ends \(a\) and \(b\): every value gets the same mass \(1/(b-a+1)\), and the mean \((a+b)/2\) sits in the middle.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=(a+b)/2\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=((b-a+1)^2-1)/12\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair die has mean \(3.5\) and variance \(35/12\).
  • A uniform integer on \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\) has \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge1)=2/5\) and mean \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events. The events \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint or mutually exclusive if

\[ A\cap B=\emptyset. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Disjoint events cannot happen at the same time. Once one occurs, the other is ruled out.

For a fair die, the disjoint events \(A=\{1,2\}\) and \(B=\{6\}\) have \(\mathbb{P}(A\cup B)=2/6+1/6\). Disjointness differs from independence: two disjoint events with positive probabilities cannot be independent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Disjoint events have empty intersection.
  • For disjoint events, \(\mathbb{P}(A\cup B)=\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)\).
  • Independence and disjointness are different unless one event has probability zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• On one die roll, rolling a one and rolling a six are disjoint events.
  • Drawing a red card and drawing a black card on a single draw are disjoint.
  • Passing and failing the same exam attempt are mutually exclusive outcomes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable on a probability space. The distribution of \(X\) is the probability measure on \(\mathbb R\) defined by assigning to each suitable set \(B\) the probability

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\in B). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A distribution describes where the probability of a random variable is located. It tells which values or ranges are likely and which are unlikely.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distribution of a real-valued random variable is uniquely determined by its CDF.
  • Different random variables can have the same distribution.
  • Discrete, continuous, and mixed distributions describe different ways probability can be allocated.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two independent fair coin indicators have the same Bernoulli distribution but are not the same random variable.
  • The distribution of a delivery time describes the probabilities of different time intervals.
  • A mixture of customer types can create a distribution with several peaks.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space. An event is a subset \(A\subseteq S\) whose occurrence can be assigned a probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An event is a statement about the outcome of an experiment. It happens exactly when the realized outcome belongs to the event.

For a fair die, the event of an even outcome is \(A=\{2,4,6\}\) and has probability \(3/6=1/2\). The empty event never occurs, whereas the whole sample space is certain.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Events are subsets of the sample space.
  • Events can be combined using union, intersection, and complement.
  • A probability function assigns probabilities to events, not to informal statements outside the model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In a die roll, the event 'roll an even number' is the set of outcomes two, four, and six.
  • In a reliability model, the event 'system fails before noon' is a subset of possible histories.
  • In a survey, the event 'respondent is under thirty' collects all outcomes with that property.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an integrable real-valued random variable \(X\), its expectation is the probability-weighted mean. The formulas are

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}X&=\sum_x x\,p_X(x) \quad\text{for discrete }X,\\[4pt] \mathbb{E}X&=\int_{\mathbb R}x f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &\qquad\text{when }X\text{ has a density}. \end{aligned} \]

Finite expectation requires \(\mathbb{E}|X|<\infty\): respectively \(\sum_x|x|p_X(x)<\infty\) or \(\int_{\mathbb R}|x|f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x<\infty\). More generally, write \(X=X^+-X^-\); the extended expectation is defined if at least one of \(\mathbb{E}X^+\) and \(\mathbb{E}X^-\) is finite. If both are infinite, \(\mathbb{E}X\) is undefined.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Expectation describes the center of a distribution by weighting each outcome by its probability. Sums and integrals express the same idea for discrete variables and variables with densities.

For the illustrated masses, the mean is \(\mathbb{E}[X]=1(0.1)+2(0.2)+3(0.3)+4(0.4)=3\). This probability-weighted average is the balance point of the masses and the long-run average of iid draws.

Treat the probabilities as weights on a seesaw and move the fulcrum \(c\): it balances exactly at \(c=\mathbb{E}X=\sum_x x\,p_X(x)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For nonnegative \(X\), expectation is well-defined in \([0,\infty]\), even when it is not finite.
  • For \(X\ge0\), \(\mathbb{E}X=\int_0^\infty\mathbb{P}(X>t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), possibly \(+\infty\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(\mathbb{E}X=(1+2+3+4+5+6)/6=3.5\).
  • If \(f_X(x)=2x\) for \(0<x<1\) and zero elsewhere, then \(\mathbb{E}X=\int_0^1 2x^2\,\mathrm{d}x=2/3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda>0\). A continuous random variable \(X\) has an exponential distribution with rate \(\lambda\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), if its density is

\[ \begin{aligned} f_X(x)&=\lambda \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\quad(x>0),\\ f_X(x)&=0\quad(x\le0). \end{aligned} \]

The parameter \(\lambda\) is a rate, not a scale: \(\mathbb{E}X=1/\lambda\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/\lambda^2\). Assigning any nonnegative density value at \(x=0\) does not change the distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An exponential variable models a memoryless waiting time. Its rate parameter is the inverse of its mean waiting time.

Raise the rate \(\lambda\): the density starts higher and falls faster, and the mean waiting time \(1/\lambda\) shrinks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(x\ge0\), \(F_X(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X>x)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}X=1/\lambda\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/\lambda^2\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\lambda=2\), the mean is \(1/2\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X>1)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}\).
  • At rate \(\lambda=1/5\) per minute, the mean wait is \(5\) minutes and \(\mathbb{P}(X\le5)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-1}\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: In a homogeneous Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\), interarrival times are independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(0<p\le1\) and \(q=1-p\). A discrete random variable \(T\) has a first success distribution with parameter \(p\), written \(T\sim\operatorname{FS}(p)\), if \(T\) counts the trial on which the first success occurs in independent trials with success probability \(p\):

\[ \mathbb{P}(T=k)=q^{k-1}p,\qquad k=1,2,\ldots. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This convention counts the successful trial itself. It is one larger than the geometric failure count.

The same shape as the geometric distribution, moved one step to the right because the successful trial is counted: \(\mathbb{E}T=1/p\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(G\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)\), then \(T=G+1\) has the first success distribution.
  • \(\mathbb{E}T=1/p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)=(1-p)/p^2\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(p=1/2\), \(\mathbb{P}(T=3)=1/8\).
  • For \(p=0.2\), the expected trial number of the first success is \(5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(Y\) be a normally distributed random variable. The random variable \(X=|Y|\) has a folded normal distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A folded normal distribution is obtained by reflecting negative normal values to the positive side. It is useful when only the magnitude of a normally distributed quantity matters.

The illustrated calculation gives \(X=|Y|\). The sign is lost, so the density of \(Y\) on the negative side is folded onto the positive side and all mass lands on \([0,\infty)\).

Move \(\mu\) towards \(0\): more of the normal density of \(Y\) lies below zero and gets reflected, and the density of \(X=|Y|\) is the sum of the two dashed curves.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A folded normal variable is the absolute value of a normal variable.
  • Its support is nonnegative.
  • When the underlying normal mean is zero, it becomes a half-normal distribution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The absolute measurement error from a normally distributed error has a folded normal distribution.
  • The distance from zero of a one-dimensional normal displacement is folded normal.
  • Quality-control deviations recorded only by magnitude can follow a folded normal model.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable and let \(g\) be a real-valued function. The function of a random variable determined by \(g\) is the random variable \(Y=g(X)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A function of a random variable transforms the original random outcome into a new quantity. This is useful when the observed value is derived from another random value.

In this diagram, \(Y=g(X)\) is again a random variable: \(\mathbb{P}(Y=y)=\sum_{x:\,g(x)=y}\mathbb{P}(X=x)\); e.g. \(\mathbb{E}[Y]=0\cdot\tfrac15+1\cdot\tfrac25+4\cdot\tfrac25=2\) (also computable by LOTUS).

Apply \(g\) to a fair die: when several faces are sent to the same value, their probabilities add up in the distribution of \(Y=g(X)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is a random variable and \(g\) is a function on its values, then \(g(X)\) is again a random variable.
  • The distribution of \(g(X)\) may differ substantially from the distribution of \(X\).
  • LOTUS can compute expectations of \(g(X)\) without first deriving the full distribution of \(g(X)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is temperature in Celsius, then a linear function of \(X\) gives temperature in Fahrenheit.
  • If \(X\) is a return, then \(X^2\) measures squared return magnitude.
  • If \(X\) is a waiting time, then an indicator of whether it exceeds ten minutes is a function of \(X\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For any event \(A\), let \(\mathbf{1}_A\) equal one on \(A\) and zero outside \(A\). The fundamental bridge is

\[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_A]=\mathbb{P}(A). \]

The expectation always exists because the indicator is bounded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An event probability is the expectation of its indicator. This connects event calculations to expectation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_A]=1\mathbb{P}(A)+0\mathbb{P}(A^c)=\mathbb{P}(A)\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}[\sum_i\mathbf{1}_{A_i}]=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(A_i)\) for finitely many events, without independence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For an even result on a fair die, \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_A]=1/2\).
  • For \(10\) components each failing with probability \(0.02\), the expected failure count is \(0.2\), even if failures are dependent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X:S\to\mathbb R\) be a random variable and let \(B\subseteq\mathbb R\). The event generated by \(X\) and \(B\) is

\[ \{\omega\in S:X(\omega)\in B\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A generated event turns a statement about a random variable into an event in the original sample space. It explains how random variables connect numerical conditions to outcomes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Generated events are preimages of numerical sets under a random variable.
  • Statements such as \(X\le x\) are events in the original sample space.
  • The distribution of a random variable is defined through probabilities of generated events.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is a die roll, the event generated by \(X\) and the set of even numbers is rolling an even value.
  • If \(X\) is waiting time, the statement 'wait at most five minutes' is a generated event.
  • If \(X\) is a test score, the event 'score at least seventy' is generated by an interval of scores.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(0<p\le1\) and \(q=1-p\). A discrete random variable \(X\) has a geometric distribution with parameter \(p\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)\), if \(X\) counts the failures before the first success in independent trials with success probability \(p\):

\[ \mathbb{P}(X=k)=q^kp,\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots. \]

At \(p=1\) the first trial is a success, so \(X=0\) almost surely.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This course counts failures before the first success. A value of zero means the first trial succeeds.

Each bar is \(q\) times the one before, starting at \(\mathbb{P}(X=0)=p\). A smaller \(p\) means a longer wait: \(\mathbb{E}X=q/p\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=(1-p)/p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=(1-p)/p^2\).
  • For integers \(m\ge0\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge m)=(1-p)^m\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(p=1/2\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=2)=1/8\).
  • For \(p=1/4\), the expected failure count is \((3/4)/(1/4)=3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a nonnegative random variable with survival function \(S_X(t)=\mathbb{P}(X>t)\). A half-life is a time \(h\) such that

\[ S_X(h)=\frac12. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Half-life is the time by which survival or remaining amount has fallen to half. It gives an easily understood summary of decay or waiting time.

For an exponential lifetime, the half-life \(h\) satisfies \(S_X(h)=e^{-\lambda h}=1/2\), hence \(h=\ln2/\lambda\). Each additional interval of length \(h\) halves the surviving proportion: \(S_X(kh)=2^{-k}\) for integers \(k\ge0\).

Change the rate \(\lambda\): the half-life \(h=\ln 2/\lambda\) is where survival drops to \(\frac12\), and each further \(h\) halves it again.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For exponential decay with rate \(\lambda\), the half-life is \(\log(2)/\lambda\).
  • Half-life is a median survival time in exponential waiting models.
  • Shorter half-life corresponds to faster decay or faster event occurrence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a drug concentration decays exponentially, the half-life is the time until the concentration is halved.
  • In radioactive decay, half-life summarizes how quickly unstable atoms decay.
  • For an exponential component lifetime, the half-life is the time by which half of components are expected to have failed.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let a population contain \(N\) objects, of which \(K\) are successes (\(0\le K\le N\)), and suppose \(n\) objects (\(0\le n\le N\)) are drawn without replacement. A random variable \(X\) has a hypergeometric distribution if \(X\) counts the number of successes in the draw, with

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}(X=k)=\frac{\binom Kk\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom Nn},\\ \max(0,\,n-N+K)\le k\le\min(n,K), \end{gathered} \]

and \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=0\) for all other \(k\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A hypergeometric distribution counts successes when sampling without replacement. The trials are dependent because each draw changes what remains.

The diagram counts successes in a sample of \(n=6\) objects drawn without replacement from \(N=20\) objects, of which \(K=8\) are successes. The PMF is \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom8k\binom{12}{6-k}/\binom{20}6\) for \(0\le k\le6\). Its variance is smaller than that of \(\operatorname{Bin}(6,0.4)\), the corresponding model with replacement.

Change \(N\), \(K\) and \(n\): drawing without replacement gives mean \(nK/N\), like the binomial, but a smaller variance because each draw changes what remains.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The hypergeometric distribution models sampling without replacement.
  • Unlike the binomial distribution, the trials are dependent.
  • Its mean is \(nK/N\) when \(K\) successes are in a population of size \(N\) and \(n\) items are drawn.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of aces in a five-card hand has a hypergeometric distribution.
  • The number of defective items in a sample drawn without replacement from a shipment is hypergeometric.
  • The number of red balls drawn from an urn without replacement is hypergeometric.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A sequence \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) is independent and identically distributed (iid) if it is mutually independent and all its variables have the same distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
IID means the observations share one distribution and do not influence each other probabilistically. Both requirements are needed in the course’s laws of large numbers and CLT.

Each variable in the diagram has the PMF of a fair die. Independence gives \(\mathbb{P}(X_1=a,X_2=b,X_3=c)=\mathbb{P}(X_1=a)\mathbb{P}(X_2=b)\mathbb{P}(X_3=c)\), so these rolls form an iid sample.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For iid \(X_i\), \(\mathbb{P}(X_1\in A_1,\ldots,X_n\in A_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n\mathbb{P}(X_i\in A_i)\) for every finite collection.
  • Identical marginal distributions alone do not imply independence; pairwise independence alone does not establish mutual independence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Repeated independent fair die rolls are iid, all with the discrete uniform law on \(\{1,\ldots,6\}\).
  • If \(X_1=X_2=Z\) with \(Z\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/2)\), the margins match but the observations are not iid: \(\mathbb{P}(X_1=1,X_2=0)=0\) rather than \(1/4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events. The inclusion-exclusion principle for two events states that

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\cup B)=\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)-\mathbb{P}(A\cap B). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Inclusion-exclusion corrects double counting. When two events overlap, the overlap is counted twice unless it is subtracted once.

The labels show how many times each region is counted by \(\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(C)\). Subtracting the pairwise intersections and adding the triple intersection gives

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\cup B\cup C)=\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(C)-\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)-\mathbb{P}(A\cap C)-\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)+\mathbb{P}(A\cap B\cap C). \]

Grow the overlap: \(\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B)\) counts \(A\cap B\) twice, so it is subtracted once to give \(\mathbb{P}(A\cup B)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For two events, inclusion-exclusion subtracts the overlap once.
  • For three events, the triple overlap must be added back after pairwise overlaps are subtracted.
  • The principle works for both counting and probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• To count students taking mathematics or statistics, add both course counts and subtract students taking both.
  • In card problems, the probability of drawing a heart or a face card requires subtracting heart face cards once.
  • To compute the chance of at least one of several alarms sounding, inclusion-exclusion adjusts for simultaneous alarms.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if

\[ \mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B). \]

For a collection of events, mutual independence requires the product identity for every finite subcollection; pairwise independence alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two events are independent when knowing one happened leaves the probability of the other unchanged.

In the illustrated example, \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=0.6\cdot0.5=0.3=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)\) \(\iff\) \(A\) and \(B\) independent equivalently \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\): inside \(B\) the band \(A\) still takes up \(60\%\).

Make \(B\) fill the same share of \(A\) as of its complement: then \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B)\) and the events are independent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\), independence is equivalent to \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\).
  • Independence of \(A,B\) implies independence of \(A^c,B\) and of \(A^c,B^c\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Heads on two independent fair tosses have intersection probability \(1/4=(1/2)(1/2)\).
  • On one fair die, \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2\}\) are disjoint but not independent: \(0\ne(1/6)(1/6)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Real-valued random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\in A,Y\in B)=\mathbb{P}(X\in A)\mathbb{P}(Y\in B) \]

for every pair of intervals \(A,B\). For a finite family, mutual independence requires the analogous product formula for every selection of sets and every subfamily, rather than merely for pairs.

For discrete variables, this is equivalent to \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)\) for every \(x,y\). For a pair with a joint density, it is equivalent to \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)\) for all \((x,y)\) except possibly on a set of zero area, for example along finitely many lines. In either case, conditional laws agree with the corresponding marginal laws wherever the conditioning denominator is positive (with density identities allowed to fail on a set of zero length or area).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Independent variables supply separate sources of randomness: learning one variable does not change the distribution of the other. PMF and PDF factorization are two ways to check the same property.

Every cell is the product of its row and column marginal, e.g. \(\mathbb{P}(X=1,Y=1)=0.5\cdot0.6=0.30\): \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, \(\mathbb{P}(X\in A,\,Y\in B)=\mathbb{P}(X\in A)\mathbb{P}(Y\in B)\) for all \(A,B\); knowing \(Y\) does not change the distribution of \(X\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For arbitrary real-valued \(X,Y\), independence is equivalent to \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)=F_X(x)F_Y(y)\) for every \(x,y\).
  • If \(X,Y\) are independent and integrable, then \(XY\) is integrable and \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two independent fair dice have \(p_{X,Y}(i,j)=1/36=(1/6)(1/6)\) for all \(i,j\in\{1,\ldots,6\}\).
  • The joint density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\) has marginals \(f_X(x)=2(1-x)\) and \(f_Y(y)=2y\) on \((0,1)\). At \((x,y)=(1/4,3/4)\) their product is \(9/4\), rather than \(2\), and this discrepancy persists on a whole neighborhood, which has positive area; hence the density does not factor.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For an event \(A\), the indicator random variable \(\mathbf{1}_{A}\) equals \(1\) if \(A\) occurs and \(0\) otherwise.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An indicator turns an event into a numerical yes-or-no observation. Counting events becomes adding random variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbf{1}_A\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\mathbb{P}(A))\).
  • \(\mathbf{1}_{A\cap B}=\mathbf{1}_A\mathbf{1}_B\) and \(\mathbf{1}_{A^c}=1-\mathbf{1}_A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair-toss heads indicator is \(1\) on heads and \(0\) on tails.
  • The number of heads in three tosses is \(\mathbf{1}_{A_1}+\mathbf{1}_{A_2}+\mathbf{1}_{A_3}\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: A sum of indicators counts the number of events that occur, even when those events are dependent.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(\{B_i\}\) be a finite or countable partition of the sample space into events. For every event \(A\),

\[ \mathbb{P}(A)=\sum_{i:\mathbb{P}(B_i)>0}\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\mathbb{P}(B_i). \]

Null partition events contribute zero to \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) and are omitted so that no undefined conditional probability is used.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Compute a probability by conditioning on each possible case and weighting by how likely that case is.

The diagram splits \(A\) into the disjoint pieces \(A\cap B_1\), \(A\cap B_2\) and \(A\cap B_3\). Their probabilities add to \(\mathbb{P}(A)\); each positive-probability case contributes \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\mathbb{P}(B_i)\).

Split the sample space into three cases and set \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i)\) in each: \(\mathbb{P}(A)\) is the total shaded area, a weighted average of the three.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(A)=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(A\cap B_i)\) for a countable partition.
  • Only terms with \(\mathbb{P}(B_i)>0\) need conditional probabilities; zero-probability cases contribute zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If factories supply \(60\%\) and \(40\%\) of products with defect rates \(0.01\) and \(0.03\), the defect probability is \(0.6(0.01)+0.4(0.03)=0.018\).
  • For a fair die, conditioning on odd or even gives \(\mathbb{P}(X=6)=0(1/2)+(1/3)(1/2)=1/6\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For integrable random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) and real constants \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), linearity of expectation states

\[ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\right]=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\mathbb{E}X_i. \]

Independence is not required. In particular, \(\mathbb{E}[aX+bY]=a\mathbb{E}X+b\mathbb{E}Y\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The average of a finite linear combination is the same linear combination of averages. Dependence does not affect this rule.

The independent variables shown have means \(2\) and \(4\), so their sum has mean \(6\). Here the sum takes the values \(3\), \(5\), \(7\) and \(9\), each with probability \(1/4\); the identity for the means itself does not require independence.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For integrable \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), \(\mathbb{E}[\sum_ia_iX_i]=\sum_ia_i\mathbb{E}X_i\).
  • \(\mathbb{E}[a+bX]=a+b\mathbb{E}X\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\mathbb{E}X=2\) and \(\mathbb{E}Y=5\), then \(\mathbb{E}[3X-Y]=1\) regardless of dependence.
  • If \(Y=X\) and \(\mathbb{E}X=4\), then \(\mathbb{E}[X+Y]=8\) despite perfect dependence.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(Y\) be normally distributed with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). The random variable \(X=\mathrm{e}^Y\) has a lognormal distribution with parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A lognormal distribution models positive quantities created by multiplicative effects. Taking logarithms turns it into a normal distribution.

In the illustrated example, \(X=\mathrm{e}^{Y}\) with \(Y\sim N(0,0.5^2)\): \(\ln X\) is normal, so \(X>0\). The density is right-skewed, with mode \(<\) median \(<\) mean (the three dashed lines, from left to right).

Change \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) of the underlying normal \(Y\): the density of \(X=\mathrm e^Y\) is skewed to the right, and more so as \(\sigma\) grows.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A lognormal random variable is always positive.
  • If \(X\) is lognormal, then \(\log X\) is normal.
  • Lognormal models often arise from products of many positive random factors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Household income is often modeled with a lognormal-type distribution.
  • Multiplicative investment growth can lead to lognormal returns over time.
  • Repair times that are positive and right-skewed may be approximated by a lognormal model.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(g\) be a real function. If \(\mathbb{E}|g(X)|<\infty\), the law of the unconscious statistician (LOTUS) gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[g(X)]&=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x)\\ &\qquad\text{for discrete }X,\\[4pt] \mathbb{E}[g(X)]&=\int_{\mathbb R}g(x)f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &\qquad\text{when }X\text{ has a density}. \end{aligned} \]

The formulas also hold as extended nonnegative expectations when \(g\ge0\). A finite signed result requires absolute integrability; no distribution of \(g(X)\) has to be computed first.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
To average a transformed variable, apply the transformation to each possible value and weight using the original distribution. This avoids deriving a new distribution merely to compute an expectation.

For the transformation \(g(x)=x^2\) shown, \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]=1(0.1)+0(0.3)+1(0.4)+4(0.2)=1.3\). The values of \(g\) are weighted by the PMF of \(X\), without deriving the PMF of \(g(X)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Choosing \(g(x)=x^k\) computes the \(k\)th moment when it exists; in particular \(g(x)=x^2\) gives the second moment.
  • Choosing \(g(x)=\mathbf{1}_{\{x\in A\}}\) gives \(\mathbb{P}(X\in A)\) by a sum or an integral.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=(1+4+9+16+25+36)/6=91/6\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\), \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{-X}]=\int_0^\infty2\mathrm{e}^{-3x}\,\mathrm{d}x=2/3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable with distribution function \(F_X\). A median of \(X\) is a real number \(m\) such that

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\le m)\ge \frac12 \quad\text{and}\quad \mathbb{P}(X\ge m)\ge \frac12. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A median is a central value that splits the distribution into two balanced parts. It is often less sensitive to extreme values than the mean.

For the illustrated density \(f(x)=xe^{-x}\) on \(x\ge0\), the median is approximately \(1.68\) and the mean is \(2\). Each shaded region has probability \(1/2\) in this continuous example.

Move the candidate \(m\) and check both conditions. For the skewed density the median is unique; for \(\operatorname{Bin}(3,\frac12)\) every \(m\in[1,2]\) is a median.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A median need not be unique: the medians of a distribution form an interval, which contains more than one point exactly when the CDF equals \(\tfrac12\) on a whole stretch (for a fair die, every point of \([3,4]\) is a median). If the CDF jumps from below \(\tfrac12\) to above \(\tfrac12\) at a point, that point is the unique median.
  • For a continuous strictly increasing CDF, the median is the point where the CDF equals one half.
  • The median is robust to extreme values compared with the mean.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The median of a symmetric normal distribution is its center.
  • For waiting times, the median is the time by which half of cases have occurred.
  • In income data, the median can better describe a typical person than the mean when there are extreme high incomes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A nonnegative waiting time is memoryless if, once it has lasted a certain time, the time still to wait has the same distribution as the original waiting time. For a nonnegative integer-valued \(G\) this means that for all nonnegative integers \(m,n\)

\[ \mathbb{P}(G\ge m+n\mid G\ge m)=\mathbb{P}(G\ge n). \]

For an absolutely continuous nonnegative \(T\) it means that for all \(s,t\ge0\)

\[ \mathbb{P}(T>s+t\mid T>s)=\mathbb{P}(T>t). \]

The conditioning events must have positive probability. The property also works in reverse. Suppose the waiting time is finite with probability \(1\) and all its tail probabilities are positive. Then a memoryless \(G\) has a \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) distribution for some \(0<p<1\) (counting the failures before the first success), and a memoryless \(T\) has an \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) distribution for some \(\lambda>0\). For the first-success distribution, which counts trials and takes the values \(1,2,\dots\), the same condition is written with strict tails: \(\mathbb{P}(X>m+n\mid X>m)=\mathbb{P}(X>n)\) for all nonnegative integers \(m,n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For a memoryless waiting time, surviving the elapsed waiting period leaves the same distribution for the remaining waiting time.

The blue curve shows the original survival probability; the red curve restarts it at time \(s\). For an exponential waiting time \(T\), the conditional probability is

\[ \mathbb{P}(T>s+t\mid T>s) =\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda s}} =\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t} =\mathbb{P}(T>t). \]

Thus surviving until \(s\) leaves the same distribution for the remaining wait. The continuous and discrete characterisations, including their assumptions, are stated in the definition above.

After waiting \(s\), the wide pale band shows the conditional survival of the remaining wait, shifted back to \(0\): it coincides with the original curve. The discrete version does the same for \(G\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(G\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counting failures, \(\mathbb{P}(G\ge m+n\mid G\ge m)=(1-p)^n\) for admissible nonnegative integers \(m,n\).
  • For \(T\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), \(\mathbb{P}(T>s+t\mid T>s)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\) for \(s,t\ge0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(G\sim\operatorname{Geo}(1/4)\), \(\mathbb{P}(G\ge5\mid G\ge2)=(3/4)^3=27/64\).
  • For \(T\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\), \(\mathbb{P}(T>4\mid T>3)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}=\mathbb{P}(T>1)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent exponential random variables with rates \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\). Then \(\min(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) is exponentially distributed with rate \(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The minimum is the first waiting time among several independent clocks. The more clocks are running, the faster the first one tends to ring.

The minimum exceeds \(t\) only if both do: \(\mathbb{P}(\min(X_1,X_2)>t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t}\,\mathrm{e}^{-2t}=\mathrm{e}^{-3t}\), again exponential, with the rates added. Moreover \(\mathbb{P}(X_1\text{ is the minimum})=\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}=\tfrac13\).

Multiply the survival curves: the minimum survives only if both clocks do, which gives rate \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2\). The simulation agrees with the exponential density.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The minimum of independent exponentials is exponential with rate equal to the sum of the rates.
  • The probability that a particular clock is first is its rate divided by the total rate.
  • This result connects competing risks with Poisson process arrivals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If two repair teams respond independently, the first response time can be modeled as the minimum of two exponential times.
  • In competing failure modes, the first failure time has rate equal to the sum of mode-specific rates.
  • If buses from two routes arrive independently, the next bus time can be the minimum of the two route waiting times.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(Z\) be a random index and let the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Z=i\) be specified for each possible value of \(i\). The distribution of \(X\) is a mixture distribution if it is obtained by averaging these conditional distributions using the probabilities of the values of \(Z\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A mixture distribution combines several simpler distributions. It represents a situation where the population is made of different hidden groups.

First pick the component \(Z\) (with \(\mathbb{P}(Z=1)=0.4\)), then draw \(X\) from that component. The density of \(X\) is the weighted average of the component densities.

Change the weight and the two group means: the mixture density is the weighted average of the group densities, and its mean is the weighted average of their means.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A mixture distribution is a weighted average of component distributions.
  • The weights are nonnegative and sum to one.
  • Mixtures can produce multimodal shapes even when each component is unimodal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Customer spending can be modeled as a mixture of business and leisure customer distributions.
  • Machine lifetime may be a mixture of lifetimes from old and new machines.
  • Exam scores can form a mixture if two preparation groups are present.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable. A mode of \(X\) is a value at which the probability mass function or probability density function attains its maximum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A mode is the most likely or most densely represented value. A distribution may have one mode, several modes, or no unique mode.

For the illustrated density \(f(x)=xe^{-x}\) on \(x\ge0\), the mode is \(1\), the median is approximately \(1.68\) and the mean is \(2\). The Poisson example has two modes, at \(2\) and \(3\).

For the lognormal density, change \(\sigma\) and watch mode, median and mean drift apart. For the Poisson distribution, set \(\lambda\) to a whole number to get two modes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A mode is a maximizer of the mass function or density function.
  • A distribution may have more than one mode.
  • For continuous distributions, density height is not itself probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair die has every face as a mode because all faces are equally likely.
  • A normal distribution has one mode at its center.
  • A mixture of two separated normal distributions can have two modes.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables with finite expectations. If \(X\le Y\) almost surely, then monotonicity of expectation states that

\[ \mathbb{E}[X]\le \mathbb{E}[Y]. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Monotonicity says that a random variable that is always no larger has no larger average. It matches the ordinary idea that bigger outcomes lead to a bigger mean.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X\le Y\) almost surely, then \(\mathbb{E}[X]\le \mathbb{E}[Y]\) when expectations exist.
  • Strict inequality is not guaranteed unless the ordering is strict with positive probability.
  • Monotonicity is often used to bound expectations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a premium service always costs at least as much as a basic service, its expected cost is at least as large.
  • If one policy always pays no more than another, its expected payout is no larger.
  • Truncating losses from above produces a random variable with no larger expectation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a compound experiment made of two stages. If the first stage has \(a\) possible outcomes and, for each of them, the second stage has \(b\) possible outcomes, then the compound experiment has

\[ a\cdot b \]

possible outcomes. This is the multiplication rule for counting. For \(k\) successive stages with \(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k\) choices it gives \(n_1n_2\cdots n_k\) ordered outcomes; in set notation, \(|A\times B|=|A|\,|B|\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The multiplication rule counts ordered outcomes stage by stage: in a tree diagram, the number of leaves is the product of the numbers of branches at each level. The same tree carries probabilities, and multiplying along a path gives the probability of that path.

Counting the ordered outcomes gives \(52\cdot51=2652\) ordered draws, \(4\cdot3=12\) of them two aces, so \(\tfrac{12}{2652}=\tfrac1{221}\). Probabilities multiply along a path in the same way: \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\,\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of choices at a stage must not depend on the outcomes of earlier stages, although the choices themselves may.
  • Probability version: for events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\); for several events the rule becomes a product of successive conditional probabilities.
  • For independent events, the conditional factor reduces to the marginal probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A code of two letters followed by three digits can be formed in \(26^2\cdot10^3=676\,000\) ways.
  • Two dice give \(6\cdot6=36\) ordered outcomes, and \(n\) distinct objects can be ordered in \(n(n-1)\cdots1=n!\) ways.
  • Two cards drawn without replacement are both aces with probability \(\frac4{52}\cdot\frac3{51}=\frac1{221}\): the chance of the first ace times the conditional chance of the second. In counts, \(4\cdot3=12\) of the \(52\cdot51=2652\) ordered draws.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(S\) be a finite sample space whose outcomes are equally likely. For an event \(A\subseteq S\), the naive probability of \(A\) is

\[ \mathbb{P}(A)=\frac{|A|}{|S|}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Naive probability counts favorable outcomes and divides by all possible outcomes. It works only when the outcomes are equally likely.

For two independent fair dice, all 36 ordered outcomes are equally likely and six have sum \(7\). Thus \(\mathbb{P}(\text{sum}=7)=6/36=1/6\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Naive probability applies only when all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely.
  • It is computed as favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
  • Counting errors in either numerator or denominator lead directly to probability errors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The probability of rolling an even number on a fair die is three favorable faces out of six.
  • The probability of drawing an ace from a well-shuffled deck is four favorable cards out of fifty-two.
  • If a random PIN is chosen uniformly from all four-digit PINs, naive probability can compute the chance of a repeated digit pattern.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(r\) be a positive integer and \(p\in(0,1]\). A random variable \(X\) has a negative binomial distribution if \(X\) counts the number of trials needed to obtain the \(r\)th success in independent Bernoulli trials with success probability \(p\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
In this trial-count convention, a negative binomial distribution generalizes the first success distribution. Instead of waiting for the first success, it waits for a fixed later success.

The diagram uses \(r=3\) and \(p=0.4\). For \(k\ge r\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{k-r}\): the first \(k-1\) trials have \(r-1\) successes, and trial \(k\) is the \(r\)th success.

Change \(r\) and \(p\): the distribution of the trial of the \(r\)th success starts at \(r\) and has mean \(r/p\). With \(r=1\) it is the first success distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• It counts waiting time until a fixed number of successes.
  • For \(r=1\), \(X\) has the first success distribution. The shifted variable \(X-1\) has the geometric distribution used in this course.
  • The failure-count convention uses \(X-r\) instead of \(X\). For \(k=r,r+1,\ldots\), the trial-count probability is \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{k-r}\); the final trial is a success, and the preceding \(k-1\) trials contain exactly \(r-1\) successes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of sales calls needed to close five sales can be negative binomial.
  • The number of coin tosses needed to obtain three heads follows a negative binomial model.
  • The number of inspected items until the tenth defective item can be modeled this way under independent constant defect probability.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\mu\in\mathbb R\) and \(\sigma>0\). A continuous random variable \(X\) has a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), written \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), if its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A normal distribution is the familiar bell-shaped distribution. It is widely used because many sums and averages behave approximately normally.

The curve is symmetric about its mean \(\mu\), and its variance is \(\sigma^2\). Approximately \(68\%\) of its probability lies within \(\mu\pm\sigma\), and \(95\%\) lies within \(\mu\pm2\sigma\).

Move \(\mu\) to shift the bell and \(\sigma\) to widen it. The interval \((\mu-\sigma,\mu+\sigma)\) always holds about \(68\%\) of the probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A normal distribution is determined by its mean and variance.
  • Standardizing a normal random variable gives a standard normal random variable.
  • Sums of independent normal random variables are normal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Measurement error is often approximated by a normal distribution.
  • The average of many small independent effects is often modeled as normal.
  • Manufacturing deviations from a target dimension are frequently modeled with a normal distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be random variables and let \(X_{(1)}\le\cdots\le X_{(n)}\) be the ordered values. The random variable \(X_{(k)}\) is called the \(k\)th order statistic.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Order statistics describe positions in a sorted sample. They include the minimum, maximum, and sample median.

The diagram relabels the same five values by rank. For iid observations with CDF \(F\), \(\mathbb{P}(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)^n\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X_{(1)}>x)=(1-F(x))^n\).

Sort a uniform sample and pick the \(k\)th smallest. Over many samples \(X_{(k)}\) clusters around \(k/(n+1)\): the minimum near \(0\), the maximum near \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The first order statistic is the sample minimum and the last is the sample maximum.
  • Order statistics are functions of a sample.
  • They are central in quantile estimation and reliability calculations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The smallest of five component lifetimes is the first order statistic.
  • The median of an odd-sized sample is a middle order statistic.
  • The maximum daily demand in a month is the largest order statistic of the daily demands.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space. An outcome is an element \(\omega\in S\) representing one possible result of the random experiment.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An outcome is one possible result of an experiment. It is the most detailed result considered by the chosen model.

In the diagram, the realised die outcome is \(4\). Thus the event \(\{2,4,6\}\) occurs and \(\{1,2\}\) does not: an event occurs exactly when it contains the realised outcome.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An outcome is a single element of the sample space.
  • The level of detail in an outcome depends on how the experiment is modeled.
  • Events are collections of outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one die roll, the outcome can be the face that appears.
  • For two coin tosses, an outcome can record the ordered pair of heads and tails.
  • For a customer-order experiment, an outcome might include purchase amount, item type, and delivery time.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A partition of a set \(E\) is a family \(\{B_i:i\in I\}\) of nonempty subsets satisfying

\[ B_i\cap B_j=\emptyset\quad(i\ne j),\qquad\bigcup_{i\in I}B_i=E. \]

In probability, take \(E=\Omega\) and require the blocks to be events. The elementary total-probability sums use finite or countable partitions. A nonempty event can still have probability zero; omit such blocks from formulas that divide by their probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A partition separates every outcome into exactly one case. This lets a probability or expectation be calculated case by case.

In the illustrated example, \(B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\neq j\) and \(B_1\cup\cdots\cup B_4=S\), so \(\mathbb{P}(B_1)+\cdots+\mathbb{P}(B_4)=1\); a partition splits any question into cases: \(\mathbb{P}(A)=\sum_i \mathbb{P}(A\cap B_i)\) (law of total probability).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every outcome belongs to exactly one partition event.
  • For any event \(A\), the events \(A\cap B_i\) are disjoint and have union \(A\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, the odd and even outcomes partition \(\{1,\ldots,6\}\).
  • For an integer-valued count \(N\), the events \(\{N=0\},\{N=1\},\ldots\) partition the outcomes if \(N\) takes finite nonnegative integer values.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) be a finite set with \(n\) elements and let \(0\le k\le n\). A \(k\)-permutation of \(A\) is an ordered selection \((a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) of \(k\) distinct elements of \(A\). For \(k=n\) it is an ordering of all of \(A\), which corresponds to a bijection \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\to A\); when \(A=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) this is a permutation of \(A\) in the Math II sense of a bijection from \(A\) onto itself.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
\(k\)-permutations count selections in which order matters: changing the order gives a different selection. Counting texts often say permutation for both cases; the \(k\) makes clear which one is meant.

An ordered selection of \(k\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects can be made in \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)=n!/(n-k)!\) ways. For example, there are \(4\cdot3=12\) ordered pairs from four letters.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of \(k\)-permutations of \(n\) distinct objects is \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)=n!/(n-k)!\).
  • In particular there are \(n!\) orderings of \(n\) distinct objects.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of possible podium finishes among eight runners is a permutation count.
  • Arranging five books on a shelf uses full permutations.
  • Assigning three distinct tasks to three ordered time slots is a permutation problem.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda>0\). A discrete random variable \(X\) has a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), if

\[ \mathbb{P}(X=k)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots, \]

and the PMF is zero elsewhere. The extension \(\lambda=0\) gives the constant-zero distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Poisson variable models a nonnegative count with a parameter equal to its mean count.

Change \(\lambda\): it is both the mean and the variance. Small \(\lambda\) piles the mass near \(0\); large \(\lambda\) gives a wider, more symmetric hump.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda\).
  • \(M_X(t)=\exp(\lambda(\mathrm{e}^t-1))\) for every real \(t\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\lambda=2\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=0)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=2\mathrm{e}^{-2}\).
  • A Poisson count with mean \(5\) has variance \(5\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt5\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: Independent Poisson counts add to a Poisson count with the sum of their parameters. A binomial model converges to this law when the number of trials tends to infinity and the success probabilities shrink so that their product tends to a fixed parameter.
