docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda>0\). A process \(\{N_t:t\ge 0\}\) with \(N_0=0\), in which \(N_t\) counts the arrivals in \([0,t]\), is a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) if it has independent increments and

\[ N_{t+s}-N_s\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t) \]

for all \(s,t\ge 0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Poisson process models random arrivals over time. It assumes arrivals occur independently and at a constant average rate.

The count \(N_t\) records arrivals in \([0,t]\). For a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\), \(N_{t+s}-N_s\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t)\) and disjoint increments are independent. Successive interarrival times are iid \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), with \(\lambda\) expected arrivals per unit time.

Each press of the button draws new arrivals at rate \(\lambda\). The number in the window \((s,s+t]\) varies from draw to draw like a \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t)\) variable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A Poisson process has independent increments.
  • The number of arrivals in an interval depends only on the interval length.
  • Interarrival times in a Poisson process are independent exponential random variables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Customer arrivals to a store can be approximated by a Poisson process during a stable period.
  • Particle emissions from a radioactive source are often modeled as a Poisson process.
  • Requests to a server may be modeled as a Poisson process over short intervals.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A probability density function of an absolutely continuous \(X\) is a nonnegative integrable function satisfying

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\int_Af_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\\ \int_{\mathbb{R}}f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1. \end{gathered} \]

Densities that agree except possibly on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points, describe the same distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A density describes how probability is spread over the real line. Areas under it are probabilities; the height at a point is not a probability.

Probabilities are areas under the density. The narrow uniform density reaches height \(2\), which is fine: only areas, never heights, are probabilities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(a<X\le b)=\int_a^bf_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  • \(F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xf_X(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), so \(F_X^\prime=f_X\) except possibly on a set of zero length.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f_X(x)=2x\) on \((0,1)\) and zero elsewhere, \(\mathbb{P}(X\le1/2)=1/4\).
  • The uniform density on \((0,1/2)\) has height \(2\), total area \(1\), and \(\mathbb{P}(X=1/4)=0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space and let \(\mathcal F\) be a collection of events. A probability function is a function \(P:\mathcal F\to[0,1]\) that assigns probabilities to events and satisfies the axioms of probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A probability function is the rule that assigns chances to events. It turns a sample space into a usable probability model.

For the fair die in the diagram, the disjoint events \(\{1,3\}\) and \(\{6\}\) have probabilities \(1/3\) and \(1/6\). Their union therefore has probability \(1/2\). Different events can have the same probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A probability function assigns numbers to events according to the probability axioms.
  • The full sample space has probability one.
  • Disjoint unions are handled by adding probabilities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, the probability function assigns probability one sixth to each single-face event.
  • In a reliability model, the probability function assigns a probability to the event that the system fails.
  • For a deck of cards, the probability function assigns probabilities to events such as drawing a heart.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable. The probability mass function of \(X\) is the function \(p_X\) defined by

\[ p_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X=x). \]

It is zero except on the countable set of values that \(X\) can take.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A PMF assigns a probability to each discrete value. Its nonnegative masses account for all outcomes.

The diagram shows \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,1/2)\), with masses \(1/8\), \(3/8\), \(3/8\) and \(1/8\), which sum to \(1\). The two red bars give \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge2)=3/8+1/8=1/2\).

Each bar is a value of \(p_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X=x)\); together they add up to \(1\). Set \(c\) and \(d\) to add the masses of a range of values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(p_X(x)\ge0\) and \(\sum_xp_X(x)=1\).
  • \(F_X(t)=\sum_{x\le t}p_X(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(p_X(3)=1/6\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X\le3)=3/6\).
  • If \(p_X(0)=0.7\) and \(p_X(1)=0.3\), then \(\mathbb{P}(X>0)=0.3\).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The prosecutor's fallacy is the error of confusing the probability of observing evidence under a hypothesis with the probability that the hypothesis is true given the evidence.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This fallacy reverses a conditional probability. It can make evidence sound much stronger than it actually is.

In the illustrated population, one culprit matches and about ten innocent people match. Thus \(\mathbb{P}(\text{innocent}\mid\text{match})\approx10/11\approx0.91\), despite \(\mathbb{P}(\text{match}\mid\text{innocent})=0.00001\). The fallacy confuses these conditional probabilities and overlooks the large number of innocent people.

A tiny chance of an innocent match, spread over a large population, still produces several innocent matches. Compare \(\mathbb{P}(\text{match}\mid\text{innocent})\) with \(\mathbb{P}(\text{innocent}\mid\text{match})\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The fallacy confuses \(\mathbb{P}(E\mid H)\) with \(\mathbb{P}(H\mid E)\).
  • Bayes' rule shows that posterior probabilities require prior probabilities and alternative explanations.
  • Rare evidence is not automatically decisive if it can also occur under competing hypotheses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A rare DNA match probability is not the same as the probability that a defendant is innocent.
  • A rare disease test result is not the same as the probability of disease without considering prevalence.
  • A suspicious transaction pattern must be compared against both fraud and non-fraud explanations.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a CDF \(F\) and \(0<u<1\), its generalized inverse is

\[ F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x\in\mathbb{R}:F(x)\ge u\}. \]

It need not be an ordinary inverse: \(F\) can have flat portions or jumps. Endpoint values at \(u=0,1\) are irrelevant when using a continuous uniform input.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The generalized inverse converts a probability level into a threshold. Applied to a uniform input, it simulates a variable with the desired distribution.

In this diagram, \(Q(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge u\}\) reads the CDF backwards: the smallest value whose CDF reaches the probability \(u\). \(Q(0.5)\) is the median and \(Q(0.25)\), \(Q(0.75)\) are the quartiles.

Pick a level \(u\) and read the CDF backwards. At a jump many levels share one quantile, and where \(F\) is flat the infimum picks the left end.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(0<u<1\), \(F^{-1}(u)\le x\) if and only if \(u\le F(x)\).
  • Consequently, if \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(\mathbb{P}(F^{-1}(U)\le x)=F(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\), \(F^{-1}(u)=-\log(1-u)/2\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)\), \(F^{-1}(u)=0\) for \(0<u\le0.7\) and \(1\) for \(0.7<u<1\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: The median is a quantile at probability level \(1/2\). Other probability levels define percentiles. The generalized inverse is useful even when an ordinary inverse does not exist.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be random variables with \(A\le B\). A random interval is an interval whose endpoints are random, such as \([A,B]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A random interval is an interval that changes from one outcome to another. It is useful when uncertainty affects the bounds rather than just a single value.

In the illustrated example, \(A\le B\) are random, so \([A,B]\) changes from run to run. \(\mathbb{P}(A\le\theta\le B)\) is the probability that the random interval covers the fixed \(\theta\) (the idea behind confidence intervals); here \(5\) out of \(6\) runs cover it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A random interval has endpoints that are random variables.
  • Events can be formed from statements about whether a fixed value lies inside the interval.
  • Random intervals are useful for uncertainty bands and coverage statements.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A confidence interval computed from data is a random interval before the data are observed.
  • The interval between two random arrival times is random.
  • A forecast range with random lower and upper bounds is a random interval.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(S\) be a sample space. A random variable is a function \(X:S\to\mathbb R\) that assigns a real number to each outcome in \(S\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A random variable converts outcomes into numerical values. It lets probability questions be studied using functions and distributions.

The diagram counts heads in two independent fair coin tosses: \(X(HH)=2\), \(X(HT)=X(TH)=1\) and \(X(TT)=0\). The outcome probabilities give \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=\mathbb{P}(\{HT,TH\})=1/2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A random variable is a function from outcomes to real numbers.
  • Random variables generate events such as threshold events.
  • The distribution of a random variable describes probabilities of its numerical values or ranges.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a die roll, the displayed face is a random variable.
  • For a customer order, the order value is a random variable.
  • For a machine, the time until failure is a random variable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\sigma>0\). A continuous random variable \(X\) has a Rayleigh distribution with parameter \(\sigma\) if its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\frac{x}{\sigma^2}\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad x\ge 0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Rayleigh distribution often describes the magnitude of a two-dimensional random vector. It appears naturally when two independent normal components are combined into a distance.

For independent \(Y_1,Y_2\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma>0\), the radius \(X=\sqrt{Y_1^2+Y_2^2}\) has density \(f_X(x)=\frac{x}{\sigma^2}\exp(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2})\) for \(x\ge0\). The dashed lines mark its mode and mean, respectively.

Change \(\sigma\): the density peaks at \(x=\sigma\) and the mean sits a little further out, at \(\sigma\sqrt{\pi/2}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Rayleigh distribution is supported on nonnegative values.
  • It arises as the magnitude of a two-dimensional normal vector with independent centered components of equal variance.
  • Its density starts at zero, rises to a peak, and then decays.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Wind speed magnitude can sometimes be modeled with a Rayleigh distribution.
  • The distance error from two independent normal coordinate errors can be Rayleigh.
  • Signal envelope amplitudes in some noise models follow a Rayleigh distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let a random experiment be specified. The sample space \(S\) is the set of all possible outcomes of that experiment.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The sample space is the universe of possible results in the model. Choosing it carefully determines what events and probabilities can be discussed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sample space must include every possible outcome in the model.
  • Different modeling choices can lead to different sample spaces for the same real situation.
  • Events are subsets of the sample space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one coin toss, the sample space can be heads and tails.
  • For two dice, the sample space can be ordered pairs of die faces.
  • For a waiting-time experiment, the sample space can be all nonnegative times.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(Z\) has the standard normal distribution, written \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), if its density is \(\phi\); its CDF is \(\Phi\):

\[ \phi(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\mathrm{e}^{-z^2/2},\qquad \Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^z\phi(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. \]

In \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) the second parameter is the variance.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The standard normal law provides the reference scale for normal approximations: a centered value is measured in standard deviations.

In this diagram, \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) has density \(\varphi(z)=\dfrac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\mathrm{e}^{-z^2/2}\) and CDF \(\Phi(z)=\mathbb{P}(Z\le z)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{z}\varphi(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), the shaded area. By symmetry, \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\).

Move \(c\) and \(d\) and read probabilities as differences \(\Phi(d)-\Phi(c)\); try \(c=-1.96\), \(d=1.96\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}Z=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1\), and \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\).
  • If \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma>0\), then \((Y-\mu)/\sigma\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\).
  • Quantiles transform the same way: the \(p\)-quantile of \(Y\) is \(\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p)\). Printed normal tables list the left-tail probabilities \(\Phi(z)\), so a quantile is read off the table in reverse and then transformed back.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(Z\le1)=\Phi(1)\approx0.8413\).
  • For \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(10,4)\), \(\mathbb{P}(Y\le12)=\Phi((12-10)/2)=\Phi(1)\approx0.8413\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma>0\). The standardization of \(X\) is

\[ Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Standardization expresses a value relative to its mean and spread. It makes variables with different units or scales easier to compare.

The illustrated calculation gives \(Z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\). Subtracting \(\mu\) centres the distribution at \(0\) and dividing by \(\sigma\) rescales the spread to \(1\), so \(\mathbb{E}[Z]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1\). The \(z\)-score measures the distance from the mean in units of \(\sigma\).

Change \(\mu\), \(\sigma\) and \(x\): the standardized value \(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\) cuts off exactly the same probability under the standard normal.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation.
  • The standardized variable has mean zero and variance one when the original mean and variance exist.
  • For normal variables, standardization produces a standard normal variable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A student's score can be standardized relative to the class mean and standard deviation.
  • A product weight can be standardized to see how many standard deviations it lies from the target.
  • Standardizing normal measurement errors allows probabilities to be computed from a standard normal table.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Let \(n,k\in\mathbb N\). Stars and bars is a counting method for the number of ways to distribute \(k\) identical objects among \(n\) distinct boxes, often by representing objects as stars and dividers as bars.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Stars and bars turns a problem of distributing identical objects among boxes into an arrangement problem. It is useful when objects are identical and only the counts in each box matter.

The six stars and two bars in the figure represent \((x_1,x_2,x_3)=(2,1,3)\). Every arrangement of six stars and two bars corresponds to one nonnegative integer solution of \(x_1+x_2+x_3=6\). Choosing the two bar positions among eight positions gives \(\binom{8}{2}=28\) distributions. In the general notation below, \(k\) objects and \(n\) boxes require \(n-1\) bars.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Stars and bars counts nonnegative integer solutions to \(x_1+\cdots+x_n=k\).
  • The number of such solutions is \(\binom{k+n-1}{n-1}\).
  • Positive integer solutions can be counted by first giving one object to each box.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of ways to distribute ten identical candies among four children is a stars-and-bars count.
  • The number of nonnegative solutions to \(x_1+x_2+x_3=8\) is counted by stars and bars.
  • Allocating identical spare parts among labeled warehouses can use stars and bars.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(T\) be an index set. A stochastic process is a collection of random variables \(\{X_t:t\in T\}\) defined on a common probability space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A stochastic process describes randomness that evolves over an index such as time. Instead of one random value, it studies a whole family of related random values.

In this diagram, \(\{X_t:t\in T\}\) lives on one probability space. Fixing \(t\) gives a random variable (the vertical slice); fixing the outcome \(\omega\) gives a sample path \(t\mapsto X_t(\omega)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A stochastic process is a family of random variables indexed by time or another set.
  • The index set may be discrete or continuous.
  • Sample paths describe how one realization of the process evolves across the index set.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Daily demand over a year can be modeled as a discrete-time stochastic process.
  • The number of arrivals up to time \(t\) in a queue is a continuous-time stochastic process.
  • Stock prices observed over time form a stochastic process.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent random variables. The sum of independent random variables is the random variable \(X+Y\), whose distribution is determined by combining the distributions of \(X\) and \(Y\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Sums of independent random variables combine separate sources of randomness. Many important distributions arise from adding independent components.

For the independent fair dice shown, convolution gives \(\mathbb{P}(X+Y=7)=6/36\). Their sum has mean \(\mathbb{E}[X]+\mathbb{E}[Y]=7\). Independence also gives \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

Add dice one at a time: each new distribution is a convolution of the previous one with a single die. Means and variances add, and the shape becomes bell-like.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distribution of a sum of independent variables is obtained by convolution in many common settings.
  • Means add whenever expectations exist.
  • Variances add for independent variables with finite variances.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The total number of heads from two independent sets of tosses is a sum of independent binomial variables.
  • The total waiting time for independent service stages is a sum of waiting-time variables.
  • The total claim amount from independent claims is a sum of independent losses.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable with a distribution. Summary measures of a distribution are numerical quantities, such as center, spread, and shape measures, that describe important features of that distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Summary measures condense a distribution into interpretable numbers. They help compare distributions without listing every probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Location measures describe center.
  • Spread measures describe variability.
  • Shape measures describe asymmetry, tail weight, or modality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Mean and median summarize the center of delivery times.
  • Variance and standard deviation summarize variability in demand.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The course uses \(\{x:p_X(x)>0\}\) for a discrete support and a positive-density region for standard continuous models. The topological support, which depends only on the distribution, is

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{supp}(X)=\{x:{}&\mathbb{P}(|X-x|<\varepsilon)>0\\ &\text{ for every }\varepsilon>0\}. \end{aligned} \]

For the usual continuous densities, this is the closure of the positive-density region. If a density has been changed on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points, use the neighborhood definition: such changes do not change the support.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The support records where values with positive probability occur, or where probability can be found arbitrarily nearby. It prevents using a PMF or PDF outside its intended range.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The course discrete support is \(\{x:p_X(x)>0\}\).
  • The topological support consists of points whose every open neighborhood has positive probability, including boundary and accumulation points.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Bern}(p)\) with \(0<p<1\), the support is \(\{0,1\}\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), a positive-density region is \((0,1)\), while the topological support is \([0,1]\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(X\) be a random variable and let \(a\in\mathbb R\). The distribution of \(X\) is symmetric about \(a\) if \(X-a\) and \(a-X\) have the same distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A symmetric distribution has matching behavior on both sides of its center. The left and right sides mirror each other in probability.

The illustrated density is symmetric about \(a\), so \(f_X(a-t)=f_X(a+t)\) and the two shaded tails have equal probability. The value \(a\) is a median and is the mean when it exists; any finite odd central moment is zero.

Pick a centre \(a\) and a distance \(t\): the distribution is symmetric about \(a\) when the two tails match for every \(t\). The exponential distribution fails for every \(a\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Symmetry about a center means left and right deviations have the same distribution.
  • For many symmetric distributions, mean and median coincide when they exist.
  • A symmetric distribution need not be normal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean.
  • A fair die distribution is symmetric around three and a half.
  • A two-point distribution with equal mass at negative one and one is symmetric about zero.

docs.title: Transformation of a Continuous Random Variable
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X\) have a density on an interval \(I\). Suppose \(g:I\to J\) is a continuously differentiable bijection with \(g^\prime(x)\ne0\) on \(I\). For the transformed variable \(Y=g(X)\),

\[ f_Y(y)=f_X(g^{-1}(y))\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}g^{-1}(y)\right|,\qquad y\in J, \]

and the density is zero outside \(J\). Density values at endpoints do not affect probabilities. The absolute derivative accounts for interval stretching; non-strict monotonicity alone is insufficient for this formula. For transformations with suitable monotone branches, add the contributions from each inverse branch.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A monotone transformation changes a density by stretching or compressing intervals. The absolute inverse derivative compensates for this change of scale.

In the illustrated example, \(f_Y(y)=f_X\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\Big|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}g^{-1}(y)\Big|=1\cdot\dfrac1{2\sqrt y}\) on \((0,1]\) for \(g(x)=x^2\). The derivative factor rescales the density so that each strip keeps its probability and the total area stays \(1\).

A small interval of \(X\) and its image under \(g\) carry the same probability. Where \(g\) stretches intervals, the density of \(Y\) drops by the factor \(\left|\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(Y=a+bX\) with \(b\ne0\), then \(f_Y(y)=f_X((y-a)/b)/|b|\).
  • For a suitable finite collection of monotone branches, sum \(f_X(x)/|g^\prime(x)|\) over the preimages \(g(x)=y\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y=2X+1\), then \(f_Y(y)=1/2\) on \((1,3)\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y=X^2\), then \(f_Y(y)=1/(2\sqrt y)\) on \((0,1)\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: The transformed density integrates to one. In higher-dimensional transformations, a Jacobian determinant provides the corresponding volume adjustment.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For real numbers \(a<b\), a random variable \(X\) has the uniform distribution on \((a,b)\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(a,b)\), if its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\begin{cases}1/(b-a),&a<x<b,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} \]

Including the endpoints in the density interval does not change the distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A continuous uniform variable has constant density over an interval. Equal-length subintervals have equal probability.

Widen or narrow \((a,b)\): the density height \(1/(b-a)\) adjusts so that the total area stays \(1\), and equal-length subintervals get equal probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=(a+b)/2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=(b-a)^2/12\).
  • For \(a\le c\le d\le b\), \(\mathbb{P}(c<X<d)=(d-c)/(b-a)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(2,6)\), \(\mathbb{P}(3<X<5)=2/4=1/2\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(\mathbb{E}X=1/2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/12\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A distribution is unimodal if its probability mass function or density function has a single peak (one local maximum), and multimodal if it has several separated peaks; with two peaks it is called bimodal. Here every peak is called a mode, although only the highest peak is a mode in the strict sense of a global maximizer.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A unimodal distribution has one main peak. A multimodal distribution has several peaks, which may indicate several groups or mechanisms.

Pull the two group means apart, or shrink \(\sigma\): at some point a single peak splits into two.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A unimodal distribution has a single peak, which is then its mode.
  • A multimodal distribution has several peaks; they need not be equally high.
  • Mixtures can create multimodal distributions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A normal distribution is unimodal.
  • A mixture of weekday and weekend demand distributions may be bimodal.
  • Exam scores from two very different preparation groups can form a multimodal distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events in a sample space. The union \(A\cup B\) is the event that at least one of \(A\) or \(B\) occurs, and the intersection \(A\cap B\) is the event that both \(A\) and \(B\) occur.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The union combines events by allowing either event to happen. The intersection focuses only on outcomes shared by both events.

Adding the probabilities of the two discs counts their overlap twice, so its probability must be subtracted once. De Morgan's identities relate these operations to complements: \((A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c\) and \((A\cap B)^c=A^c\cup B^c\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(A\cup B\) occurs when at least one of the events occurs.
  • \(A\cap B\) occurs when both events occur.
  • Inclusion-exclusion connects the probability of a union to the probabilities of the two events and their intersection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The event 'draw a heart or a king' is a union of two events.
  • The event 'draw a red king' is an intersection of two events.
  • The event that a customer buys online and uses a coupon is an intersection.

docs.title: Universality of the Uniform and CDF Realizability
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(F:\mathbb R\to[0,1]\) be nondecreasing and right-continuous, with \(\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0\) and \(\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x)=1\). Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and define \(Q(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge u\}\) for \(0<u<1\). Then

\[ X=Q(U)\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\mathbb{P}(X\le x)=F(x). \]

Thus every function satisfying the CDF conditions is realizable as a distribution, and a uniform input can generate that distribution. The construction allows jumps and flat portions of \(F\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A uniform draw selects a probability level; the quantile function converts it into an outcome. This both proves that valid CDFs describe genuine random variables and provides inverse transform simulation.

The equally spaced probability levels map to quantiles \(x=Q(u)\). These quantiles are closer together where \(F\) is steep, illustrating how a uniform input produces the target distribution.

Press the button to draw uniform levels \(U\): pushed through \(Q\), they produce a sample whose histogram follows the target distribution, including the jumps of a discrete one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The monotonicity, right-continuity, and endpoint-limit conditions are necessary and sufficient for a function to be a CDF.
  • For \(0<u<1\), \(Q(u)\le x\) exactly when \(u\le F(x)\), so \(\mathbb{P}(Q(U)\le x)=\mathbb{P}(U\le F(x))=F(x)\).
  • Conversely, if \(X\) has a continuous CDF \(F\), then \(F(X)\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\); this direction is the probability integral transform. It fails when \(F\) has jumps, because \(F(X)\) then takes some values with positive probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the step CDF \(F(x)=0\) when \(x<c\) and \(F(x)=1\) when \(x\ge c\), \(Q(u)=c\) and the construction gives \(X=c\) almost surely.
  • For \(F(x)=0\) when \(x<0\) and \(F(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-2x}\) when \(x\ge0\), the construction gives \(X=-\log(1-U)/2\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable with \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]<\infty\), and let \(\mu=\mathbb{E}X\). The variance of \(X\) is

\[ \operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2, \]

and the standard deviation is \(\sigma_X=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Variance measures average squared distance from the mean. Its square root measures spread in the original units.

The arrows mark one standard deviation on either side of the mean for each curve. Standard deviation has the same units as \(X\), whereas variance uses squared units.

Spread the mass out and the variance grows; shift the whole distribution and it hardly changes. Darker bars contribute more to \(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Var}(a+bX)=b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=0\) if and only if \(X=\mathbb{E}X\) almost surely.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)\), the variance is \(0.3(0.7)=0.21\).
  • If \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=4\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(5-3X)=36\) and its standard deviation is \(6\).

docs.title: Accumulation Point in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text:
Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) be a metric space and let \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\). A point \(\boldsymbol{x}\in \boldsymbol{X}\) is called an accumulation point (or cluster point, limit point) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if every metric ball around \(\boldsymbol{x}\) contains a point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) different from \(\boldsymbol{x}\), i.e.,

\[ \forall \varepsilon>0,\quad \left(\boldsymbol{B}_d(\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon)\setminus\{\boldsymbol{x}\}\right)\cap \boldsymbol{E}\neq\varnothing. \]

Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) be a metric space and let \((\boldsymbol{x}_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence in \(\boldsymbol{X}\). A point \(\boldsymbol{x}\in \boldsymbol{X}\) is called an accumulation point (or cluster point) of \((\boldsymbol{x}_n)\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist infinitely many \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(\boldsymbol{x}_n\in \boldsymbol{B}_d(\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon)\), i.e.,

\[ \forall \varepsilon>0,\quad \left|\{n\in\mathbb{N}\colon \boldsymbol{x}_n\in \boldsymbol{B}_d(\boldsymbol{x},\varepsilon)\}\right|=\infty. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An accumulation point of a set is a location you can approach arbitrarily closely using other points from the set.

For a sequence, it is a value that the sequence visits infinitely often, no matter how tight a neighbourhood you pick.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A limit point can be characterized as an adherent point that is not an isolated point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E=\{1,\,1/2,\,1/3,\, \dots,\}\), the only accumulation point is \(0\). Each point \(1/n\) is isolated.
  • The sequence \(a_n=(−1)^n\) has accumulation points 1 and -1. It does not converge.

  • Consider the sequence \((a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) that is defined by \(a_n=\sin n\). We can show that any number \(A\in[-1,1]\) is an accumulation point of this sequence.

    Among the first \(50\) terms, four lie in the band \([0.4,0.6]\) (red); infinitely many terms fall in every band around \(0.5\), so \(0.5\) is an accumulation point.

docs.title: Adherent Point and Closure of a Set
Definition
docs.text: Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) be a metric space and let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be a subset of \(\boldsymbol{X}\). A point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is termed an adherent point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), the ball \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0, \varepsilon)\) intersects \(\boldsymbol{E}\) nonemptily. The set of all adherent points of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) constitutes the closure of \(\boldsymbol{E}\), denoted as \(\overline{\boldsymbol{E}}\) or \(\mathrm{cl}\boldsymbol{E}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An adherent point of a set is one that you can get arbitrarily close to from inside the set.

The closure is the original set together with all its adherent points, meaning everything you can touch or approach.

An adherent point has every ball meeting \(\boldsymbol E\): the points of the closed disc and the isolated point \(\boldsymbol p\). Switching the metric does not change the answer.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• We have \(\overline{\boldsymbol{E}} = \mathrm{int}\boldsymbol{E} \cup \partial \boldsymbol{E} = \boldsymbol{E} \cup \partial \boldsymbol{E} = \boldsymbol{X} \setminus \mathrm{ext}\boldsymbol{E}.\)
  • A set is closed if and only if it contains all its adherent points.
  • The closure of a set \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is the intersection of all closed sets which contain \(\boldsymbol{E}\), or equivalently, the smallest closed set that contains \(\boldsymbol{E}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closure of \((0,1)\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is \([0,1]\). The endpoints \(0\) and \(1\) are adherent points even though they are not in the open interval.
  • If \(E = \{1/n \colon n \in \mathbb{N}^+\}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\), the closure is \(E \cup {0}\). Zero is an adherent point approached by the sequence.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,\,k \in\mathbb N^+\). A function \(\boldsymbol f\colon \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R^k\) is an affine map (or affine transformation) if there are a \(k\times n\) real matrix \(\boldsymbol A\) and a vector \(\boldsymbol b\in\mathbb R^k\) such that

\[ \boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol x)=\boldsymbol A \boldsymbol x+ \boldsymbol b\qquad\text{for all }\boldsymbol x\in\mathbb R^n. \]

A real-valued affine map \(f\colon \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R\) (\(k=1\)) is an affine function:

\[ \begin{aligned} &f(x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)\\ &\quad=a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_nx_n+b. \end{aligned} \]

An affine map is a linear map exactly when \(\boldsymbol b=\boldsymbol 0\), that is, when \(\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol 0)=\boldsymbol 0\).

Terminology

The Math III lecture notes, like much of economics and calculus, call an affine function a linear function and reserve linear transformation for the case \(\boldsymbol b=\boldsymbol 0\). In linear algebra linear always means \(\boldsymbol b=\boldsymbol 0\), so this wiki says affine for the general case.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An affine map is a linear map followed by a shift: if one argument is increased by \(c\) units, the value changes by \(c\) times a fixed vector, wherever the starting point is.

The blue linear map \(f(x)=2x\) passes through the origin. The red affine map \(g(x)=f(x)+1\) is shifted upwards by \(1\), so \(g(0)=1\) rather than \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The graph \(\{(\boldsymbol x,f(\boldsymbol x))\colon\boldsymbol x\in\mathbb R^n\}\) of an affine function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is an affine hyperplane of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\); it passes through the origin exactly when \(b=0\text{.}\)
  • The level sets \(\{\boldsymbol x\colon f(\boldsymbol x)=c\}\) of a non-constant affine function are parallel affine hyperplanes of \(\mathbb R^n\).
  • A composition of affine maps is affine.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x + 2y - 1\) is affine but not linear, since \(f(0,0)=-1\); \(x+2y\) is both.
  • \(g(x,y) = x + xy\) and \(h(x,y) = 2^x + \sin y\) are not affine.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider two functions \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(g\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(a\in[-\infty,+\infty]\).

  • We say that \(f(x)\) is big-\(\boldsymbol{O}\) of \(g(x)\) as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) and write \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) if there is a constant \(M>0\) such that \(|f(x)|\le M\,|g(x)|\) for all \(x\) near \(a\text{:}\) for \(0<|x-a|<\delta\) (a punctured neighbourhood of \(a\)) when \(a\) is finite, for \(x>N\) when \(a=+\infty\text{,}\) and for \(x<-N\) when \(a=-\infty\text{,}\) for some \(\delta>0\) or \(N\text{.}\)
  • Assume that \(g(x)\neq0\) for all \(x\) near \(a\) in the same sense. We say that \(f(x)\) is little-\(\boldsymbol{o}\) of \(g(x)\) as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) and write \(f(x)=o(g(x))\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) if \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: • Big-\(O\) means that near \(a\) the size of \(f\) is at most a constant multiple of the size of \(g\text{;}\) little-\(o\) means that \(f\) is negligible compared with \(g\) near \(a\text{.}\) When \(g\to0\text{,}\) this reads: \(f\) goes to zero at least as fast as \(g\) (big-\(O\)), or faster than \(g\) (little-\(o\)).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The little-\(o\) notation makes a stronger assertion than the big-\(O\) notation: every function that is little-\(o\) of \(g\) is also big-\(O\) of \(g\text{,}\) but not all functions that are big-\(O\) of \(g\) are little-\(o\) of \(g\text{.}\)
  • If \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) are asymptotically equivalent as \(x\) tends to \(a\text{,}\) i.e., \(f(x)\sim g(x)\) as \(x\to a\text{,}\) then we have \(f(x)=O(g(x))\) and \(g(x)=O(f(x))\text{,}\) as \(x\to a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• As \(x\to 0\), \(x^2\) is both \(O(x)\) and \(o(x)\) since \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{x^2}{x} = 0\).
  • As \(x\to 0\), \(\sin (x^2)\) is \(O(x^2)\) but not \(o(x^2)\) since \(\displaystyle \lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin(x^2)}{x^2} = 1\).

  • In the following graph, we have \(g(x)=o(f(x))\) and \(g(x)=o(h(x))\) as \(x\to 0\):

    Near \(0\) the parabola \(g\) is much flatter than \(f\) and \(h\): \(g(x)/f(x)\to0\) and \(g(x)/h(x)\to0\) as \(x\to0\).

Zoom in towards \(0\): \(f=O(g)\) when some \(M\) keeps \(|f|\le M|g|\) near \(0\); \(f=o(g)\) when the ratio \(f/g\) (right) tends to \(0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Each bounded sequence in the Euclidean space \((\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)\) has a convergent subsequence.

Equivalently, a subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\) of the Euclidean space is sequentially compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Even if a sequence wanders around without settling down, as long as it stays within a bounded region you can always pick out a subsequence that eventually homes in on some point.

In Euclidean space, closedness and boundedness guarantee enough crowding to force a convergent subsequence.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit of a convergent subsequence is an accumulation point of the original sequence.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), every Cauchy sequence is bounded, so by Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem it has a convergent subsequence. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence must itself converge. This gives another proof that \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is complete.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \(x_n = (-1)^n\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\). It does not converge, but it has two convergent subsequences: the even terms \(x_{2n}=1\) converge to \(1\), and the odd terms \(x_{2n-1}=-1\) converge to \(-1\).
  • The sequence \(x_n = 1/n\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is bounded in \([0,1]\). It already converges to \(0\), so every subsequence also converges to \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is a boundary point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if it's neither an interior nor an exterior point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) We denote the set of boundary points of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) as \(\partial \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The boundary is the dividing line between inside and outside.

The boundary consists of points that are neither interior nor exterior: \(\partial\boldsymbol E=\overline{\boldsymbol E}\setminus\operatorname{int}(\boldsymbol E)\).

On the unit circle, and at the isolated point \(\boldsymbol p\), every ball meets both \(\boldsymbol E\) and its complement, however small \(\varepsilon\) is.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A boundary point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) may or may not be in \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)
  • For a boundary point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{,}\) any balls centered at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) will contain points both inside and outside \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The boundary of \((0,1)\) is \(\{0,1\}\). Every neighborhood around \(0\) contains points in \((0,1)\) and points not in \((0,1)\).
  • The boundary of \(\mathbb{Q}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) is all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Bounded Set in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text: Given a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\text{,}\) a set \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\) is termed bounded if there exists \(M>0\) such that the ball \(\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})} (\boldsymbol{x},M)\) contains \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) Here, \(\boldsymbol{x}\) can be any point in \(\boldsymbol{X}\) (usually chosen to be the origin or a particular point in \(\boldsymbol{E}\)).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A bounded set is one that fits entirely inside some large enough ball.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set is bounded if and only if \(\displaystyle \sup_{\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y\in \boldsymbol E} d_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)\) is finite.
  • Any subset of a bounded set is bounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A unit sphere \(\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3\colon x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}\) is bounded.
  • A parabola curve \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\colon y=x^2\}\) is unbounded.

docs.title: Cauchy Sequence in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text: For a sequence of points \((\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) in a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\), it is termed a Cauchy sequence if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists an integer \(N\geq 1\) such that the distance \(d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k)<\varepsilon\) for all \(j, k \geq N\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
It is the same idea as a Cauchy sequence of real numbers, but with the absolute value replaced by a general metric.

The terms get closer to each other, but a Cauchy sequence need not converge to a point of \(\boldsymbol X\) unless the space is complete.

Raise \(N\) until all tail points lie within \(\varepsilon\) of each other, without using the limit at all.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • While all convergent sequences are Cauchy, not every Cauchy sequence converges because a sequence can cluster together (Cauchy property) around a limit that does not exist within the current space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The sequence \(a_n=\left(1+\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^n\) is a Cauchy sequence in \((\mathbb Q, d)\), but it does not converge to any point in this space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\), a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), and \(r > 0\), the closed metric ball \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), centered at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) with radius \(r\) in metric \(d\), is defined as the following set:

\[ \overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r) = \{\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{X} \colon d(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) \leq r\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A closed metric ball is the set of all points whose distance from the center is less than or equal to the radius.

The closed ball also contains its sphere \(\{d(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol x_0)=r\}\). Drag \(\boldsymbol x\) onto the boundary to see the difference.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The closed metric ball is a closed set.
  • In a normed vector space, in particular in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with any \(p\)-metric, the closed metric ball is the closure of the open metric ball with the same center and radius. This can fail for a metric that is merely topologically equivalent to these, such as \(\min(|x-y|,1)\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) with radius \(1\).
  • In a general metric space, we do not have \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\varepsilon)=\overline{\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\varepsilon)}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual distance, \(\overline{\boldsymbol B}((0,0),1)\) is the closed disc of radius \(1\) centered at the origin. Points with \(x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\) are elements of this ball.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a space \(\boldsymbol{X}\) in which open sets are defined. A subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is called compact if every open cover of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) has a finite subcover.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: No matter how you try to cover a compact set with open patches, you only ever need finitely many of them to do the job.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The set \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \mathbb R ^n\) is compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.
  • Let \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) \(\boldsymbol{f} \colon \boldsymbol{E} \to \mathbb{R}^k\) be a function, and \(\boldsymbol{X} \subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\) be a compact set. If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuous on \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) then the image \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{X})\) is also compact. This result is known as continuity preserves compactness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball \(\{x\in \mathbb R^n\colon \|x\|\leq 1\}\) is compact.
  • Any finite set in any metric space is compact. You can always pick one open set for each point; finitely many suffice.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d)\) is termed complete if each Cauchy sequence contained within converges in \((\boldsymbol{X}, d)\). When a complete normed vector space is encountered, it's also referred to as a Banach space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A complete metric space is one with no “missing points”: every sequence that looks like it should converge actually lands inside the space.

The displayed Cauchy sequence converges to \(\sqrt2\) in \(\mathbb R\). It has no limit in \(\mathbb Q\) because \(\sqrt2\notin\mathbb Q\), illustrating the incompleteness of the rational numbers.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Every Cauchy sequence converges in the completion of the space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^n\) is a complete normed vector space.
  • The open interval \((0,1)\) with the usual metric \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\) is not complete: \((1/n)_{n\ge2}\) is a Cauchy sequence whose limit \(0\) does not belong to \((0,1)\text{.}\)
  • The \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space equipped with the discrete metric is complete: a Cauchy sequence is eventually constant, because \(d(\boldsymbol{x}_j,\boldsymbol{x}_k)<\tfrac12\) forces \(\boldsymbol{x}_j=\boldsymbol{x}_k\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a space \(\boldsymbol{X}\) in which openness is defined. A subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\) is called disconnected if \(\boldsymbol{E}\) possesses a disjoint open cover \(\{\boldsymbol{V},\boldsymbol{W}\}\) (i.e., \(\boldsymbol{V}\cap\boldsymbol{W}=\varnothing\) and \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{V} \cup \boldsymbol{W}\)) such that both \(\boldsymbol{E} \cap \boldsymbol{V}\) and \(\boldsymbol{E} \cap \boldsymbol{W}\) are nonempty. If \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is nonempty and not disconnected, it is connected.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A set is disconnected if you can split it into two nonempty open pieces that do not touch each other.

A set is connected if it comes in one piece without such a split.

On the left, the dark set \(\boldsymbol E\) meets both disjoint open sets \(\boldsymbol U\) and \(\boldsymbol V\) and is contained in their union, so it is disconnected. The right-hand set cannot be split into two nonempty parts by disjoint open sets, so it is connected.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The only type of connected subsets of \(\mathbb R\) is interval.
  • Consider metric spaces \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) and \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\text{.}\) Let \(\boldsymbol{f}:\boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\) be a continuous function, and let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be a connected subset of \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\) Then \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{E})\) is a connected subset of \(\boldsymbol{Y}\text{.}\) This result is known as continuity preserves connectedness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any singleton set is connected.
  • \(\mathbb Q\) is a disconnected subset of \(\mathbb R\).
  • In a discrete metric space, any set with at least two points is disconnected because each singleton is open.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider two metric spaces \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) and \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\text{,}\) and a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\) where \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\) Let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\) Assume there exists an \(r>0\) such that \(\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)\subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) We say that \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuous at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) if, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a \(0<\delta \leq r\) such that whenever \(d_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)<\delta\text{,}\) we have \(d_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}),\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0))<\varepsilon\text{.}\)

We say that \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuous on \(\boldsymbol{E}\) (or simply continuous) if it is continuous at every point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) At a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\boldsymbol{E}\) that has no such ball inside \(\boldsymbol{E}\) (a boundary point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\)), the same condition is required only for \(\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is continuous at a point if you can make the outputs as close as you want to the value at that point by taking inputs sufficiently close to it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If two paths approaching a point give different limits, then the limit of the function at that point does not exist, so the function is not continuous there. More generally, if along some path approaching \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) the values \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})\) do not tend to \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\text{,}\) then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is not continuous at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{.}\)
  • A vector-valued function is continuous if and only if each of its component functions is continuous.
  • Most properties of real-valued functions of one real variable are preserved under continuity. In particular, continuity is preserved under addition, subtraction, multiplication, division (where the denominator is nonzero), as well as taking the maximum, minimum, and composition of functions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). At \((0,0)\), if you want \(f\) within \(\varepsilon\) of \(0\), choose \(\delta=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\). Then \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<\delta\) gives \(x^2+y^2<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d)\), a sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) and a point \(\boldsymbol{x}\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), the sequence is said to converge to \(\boldsymbol{x}\) under metric \(\boldsymbol{d}\) if \(\displaystyle \lim_{i\to\infty}d(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{x}) = 0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This is just like convergent sequences of real numbers, but with a general notion of distance.

For each \(\varepsilon\) there is an \(N\) after which every \(\boldsymbol x_i\) lies in the \(\varepsilon\)-ball around the limit. Change the metric: \(N\) changes, the limit does not.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A convergent sequence in a metric space must be a Cauchy sequence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) where \(\boldsymbol{x}_i = (1/i, 1/i)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) converges to \((0,0)\) under the Euclidean metric \(d_2\).
  • The sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i})_{i=1}^\infty\) where \(\boldsymbol{x}_i = (1/i, 1/i)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) also converges to \((0,0)\) under the taxicab metric \(d_1\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Consider a power series \(\displaystyle f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) with a radius of convergence \(R > 0\text{.}\) For any chosen \(r\) such that \(0 < r < R\):

  • The series converges pointwise on the open interval \((a-R, a+R)\text{.}\)
  • It converges uniformly on the closed interval \([a-r, a+r]\text{.}\)
  • The limit function \(f\) is differentiable on \((a-R, a+R)\text{.}\)
  • The derivative series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty nc_n (x-a)^{n-1}\) converges uniformly to the derivative, \(f'\text{,}\) on \([a-r, a+r]\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The derivative of a power series within its radius of convergence can be found by differentiating each term individually, and the resulting series converges to the correct derivative.

For every \(0<r<R\), the power series and its termwise derivative converge uniformly on \([a-r,a+r]\): \(\sum_n c_n(x-a)^n\rightrightarrows f(x)\) and \(\sum_{n\ge1}nc_n(x-a)^{n-1}\rightrightarrows f'(x)\).

On every closed interval \([a-r,a+r]\) with \(r<R\) the partial sums approach the sum uniformly; near the ends of the interval they need many more terms.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Term-by-term differentiation is valid inside the radius of convergence.
  • Locally (on \([a-r,a+r]\)), a power series behaves like a polynomial: it is smooth and uniformly controlled.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) with \(R = 1/2\) centered at \(a = 3\text{,}\) converges pointwise on \((5/2, 7/2)\) and uniformly on any closed interval within it.
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = 0\) centered at \(a = -2\text{,}\) converges solely at its center \(x = -2\text{.}\)
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{-n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = +\infty\) centered at \(a = -2\text{,}\) converges pointwise over the entire real line \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Uniform convergence for this series over \(\mathbb{R}\) needs further analysis.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a (topological) space \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\) Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be a subset of \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) and let \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}=\{\boldsymbol{G}_i\colon i\in I\}\) be a collection of subsets \(\boldsymbol{G}_i\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) indexed by an arbitrary index set \(I\text{.}\) The collection \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}\) is called a cover of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \bigcup_{i\in I} \boldsymbol{G}_i\text{.}\)

  • An open cover is a cover where each "patch" \(\boldsymbol{G}_i\) is open.
  • A finite cover consists of a collection \(\{\boldsymbol{G}_i\colon i\in I\}\) where \(I\) is finite. A cover is called a countable cover when \(I\) is a countable set, e.g., \(\mathbb{N}\text{.}\)
  • A subcover is a cover that is a subset of another cover.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A cover is just a collection of sets that together contain the set you care about.

Think of it as laying patches over the set so every point is under at least one patch.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any set \(\boldsymbol E\subseteq \boldsymbol X\) is covered by the space \(\boldsymbol X\). So covers always exist.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \((0,1)\) in \(\mathbb R\) can be covered by the collection of open sets \(\{(1/n,1−1/n)\colon n≥3\}\). This is an infinite open cover.
  • The set \(\{1,2,3\}\) is covered by the three singletons \(\{1\}\), \(\{2\}\), \(\{3\}\). That is a finite cover.
  • The set of rational numbers \(\mathbb Q\) in \(\mathbb R\) can be covered by open intervals centered at each rational with radius \(1\). That's a countable cover because \(\mathbb Q\) is countable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}^k\). Let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) be an interior point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}\) be a unit vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (note: some authors only require \(\boldsymbol{v}\) to be a nonzero vector). If the limit

\[ \lim_{t\to 0^+}\frac{\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0+t\boldsymbol{v})-\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)}{t} \]

exists, then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is said to be differentiable in the direction \(\boldsymbol{v}\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\). This limit is termed the directional derivative and is denoted by \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}} \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The directional derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function as you move from a point in a specific direction.

It generalizes the one-sided derivative to functions of several variables by looking at how the function changes along a straight line in that direction.

For a differentiable \(f\) and a unit direction \( oldsymbol v\), the directional derivative is \(D_{ oldsymbol v}f( oldsymbol x_0)= abla f( oldsymbol x_0)\cdot oldsymbol v\). For the nonzero gradient drawn, it is largest when the direction follows the gradient and zero in a tangent direction to the level curve.

Turn the direction \( oldsymbol v\) with \( heta\): the slope of \(f\) along \( oldsymbol v\) is \( abla f( oldsymbol x_0)\cdot oldsymbol v\), largest along the gradient and zero along the level curve.

Turn \( oldsymbol v\): the slice of the graph through \( oldsymbol x_0\) in direction \( oldsymbol v\) has slope \(\mathrm{D}_{ oldsymbol v}f( oldsymbol x_0)= abla f( oldsymbol x_0)\cdot oldsymbol v\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{,}\) then the directional derivative \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exists for every direction \(\boldsymbol v\) and equals the total derivative at \(\boldsymbol v\text{,}\) \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}(\boldsymbol{v})\text{.}\)
  • A function is totally differentiable at a point implies that this function is directionally differentiable in any direction. The converse is incorrect.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • For the function \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x^2,y^2)\), consider \(\boldsymbol{x}_0=(1,2)\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}=(3/5,4/5)\). We have \(\displaystyle \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) =\left(\frac{6}{5},\frac{16}{5}\right)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider the space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with its elements \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{y}\). We define a discrete metric \(d_{\text{disc}}\) as:

\[ d_{\text{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = \begin{cases} \displaystyle \;1, & \text{if } \boldsymbol{x} \neq \boldsymbol{y}, \\[2pt] \displaystyle \;0, & \text{if } \boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{y}. \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The discrete metric is the simplest possible distance: distinct points are always exactly 1 unit apart, and a point is 0 units from itself.

It treats every pair of different points as equally far.

The discrete distance is \(0\) between a point and itself, and \(1\) between distinct points. A ball of radius less than \(1\), such as the radius \(1/2\) drawn around \(\boldsymbol x\), contains only its centre, so every point is isolated and every subset is open.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The discrete metric is not strongly equivalent to any of the \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(d_{\text{disc}}(2,5)=1\) since \(2\neq 5\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) and \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\) be metric spaces, and let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\) be a function. The following statements are equivalent:

  • \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuous.
  • For every \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\boldsymbol{X}\) and every convergent sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) in \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) converging to \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\), its image under \(\boldsymbol{f}\), \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\), also converges to \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\).
  • The preimage of any open set in \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\) is open in \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\).
  • The preimage of any closed set in \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\) is closed in \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is continuous if and only if the preimage operation preserves openness and closedness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • At a fixed point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{,}\) the sequential condition is equivalent to continuity at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{.}\) In metric spaces it is often the easiest to work with when proving discontinuity. To show \(f\) is not continuous at a point, find one sequence converging to that point whose image does not converge to the function value.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A continuous function \(f\) might map an open set \(V\) to a non-open set \(f(V)\). For example, let \(V=(0,1)\) with \(f(x)=1\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). Then \(f(V)=\{1\}\) isn't open under usual metrics.
  • A continuous function \(f\) might map a closed set \(F\) to a non-closed set \(f(F)\). For example, let \(F=[1,+\infty)\) and \(f(x)=1/x\) for all \(x>0\). Then \(f(F)=(0,1]\) isn't closed under usual metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Two norms \(\|\cdot\|_p\) and \(\|\cdot\|_q\) on a vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) are termed equivalent if there exist constants \(a, b > 0\) such that for every \(\boldsymbol{v} \in \boldsymbol{V}\), we have:

\[ a \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p \leq \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q \leq b \|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Equivalent norms are different ways of measuring length that are comparable up to fixed scaling factors.

On \(\mathbb R^2\), the illustrated norms satisfy \(\|\boldsymbol x\|_\infty\le\|\boldsymbol x\|_2\le\sqrt2\,\|\boldsymbol x\|_\infty\), so they are equivalent.

Pick \(p\) and \(q\): the \(q\)-circles of radius \(a\) and \(b\) squeeze the \(p\)-unit circle between them, so \(a\|\boldsymbol v\|_p\le\|\boldsymbol v\|_q\le b\|\boldsymbol v\|_p\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any two norms \(\|\cdot\|_p\) and \(\|\cdot\|_q\) on a finite-dimensional vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) are equivalent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The Euclidean norm and the taxicab norm are equivalent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is an exterior point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\varepsilon) \cap \boldsymbol{E} = \varnothing\) for some \(\varepsilon > 0\text{.}\) We denote the set of exterior points of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) as \(\mathrm{ext} \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An exterior point is one that has a ball around it completely missing the set.

The ambient space is the disjoint union \(\boldsymbol X=\operatorname{int}(\boldsymbol E)\cup\partial\boldsymbol E\cup\operatorname{ext}(\boldsymbol E)\). The exterior is \(\operatorname{ext}(\boldsymbol E)=\operatorname{int}(\boldsymbol X\setminus\boldsymbol E)\).

Outside the closed disc (and away from \(\boldsymbol p\)) a small enough ball misses \(\boldsymbol E\) entirely.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • An exterior point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) can never be in \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E = (0,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), the point \(x = 2\) is an exterior point. A small ball around \(2\), say \((1.9,2.1)\), avoids \((0,1)\).
  • For \(E = \{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\colon x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\}\), the point \((3,0)\) is an exterior point. A small disc around it stays entirely outside the unit disc.

docs.title: Extreme Value Theorem on Compact Sets
Theorem
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) \(f \colon \boldsymbol{E} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function, and \(\boldsymbol{X} \subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\) be a compact set. If \(f\) is continuous on \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) then \(f\) attains both its maximum and minimum on \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A continuous function on a compact set cannot sneak off to infinity or skip its highest and lowest values. It must actually hit both a maximum and a minimum somewhere inside that set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If the domain is not compact, the conclusion may fail. For example, \(f(x)=1/x\) on \((0,1)\) is continuous but has no maximum (it blows up as \(x\to0^+\)) and no minimum (its values decrease towards \(1\) as \(x\to1^-\text{,}\) but \(1\) is never attained, since \(1\notin(0,1)\)).
  • This theorem is used to prove existence of solutions in optimization problems.
  • Together with the intermediate value theorem, it gives a complete picture of the range of a continuous function on a connected compact set (a closed interval in \(\mathbb R\)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The function \(f(x,y)=x+y\) on the closed unit disc \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\colon x^2+y^2\leq 1\}\) attains maximum \(\sqrt{2}\)​ at \((1/\sqrt{2},1/\sqrt{2})\) and minimum \(-\sqrt{2}\)​ at \((-1/\sqrt{2},-1/\sqrt{2})\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Consider a function \(\boldsymbol f\colon \boldsymbol X \to\boldsymbol Y\) where \(\boldsymbol X\) is set in an \(n\)-dimensional space (e.g., \(\mathbb R^n\)) and \(\boldsymbol Y\) in an \(k\)-dimensional space (e.g., \(\mathbb R^k\)). We have the following terminologies:

  • it is called a univariate function (also known as single variable function, function of one variable) if \(n=1\);
  • it is called a bivariate function (also known as function of two variables) if \(n=2\);
  • it is called a multivariable function (also known as multivariate function, function of several variables) if \(n\geq 2\);
  • it is called a real-valued function if its codomain is a subset of \(\mathbb R\);
  • it is called a vector-valued function if \(k\geq 2\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is classified by how many numbers go in and how many come out.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A multivalued function is neither a multivariable function nor a vector-valued function.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is a bivariate real valued function.
  • \(\boldsymbol{F}(x,y) = (x+y, x-y, xy)\) from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a multivariable vector valued function.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(f \colon \boldsymbol{E} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a real-valued function. If \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is an interior point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\), the gradient \(\nabla f (\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) of \(f\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is given as the \(n\)-dimensional column vector:

\[ \begin{aligned} \nabla f (\boldsymbol{x}_0) &= \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(\boldsymbol{x}_0),\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(\boldsymbol{x}_0),\right.\\ &\qquad\left.\ldots,\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\right)^\intercal. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
When \( abla f ( oldsymbol{x}_0)= oldsymbol{0}\), we say that \( oldsymbol{x}_0\) is a stationary point of \(f\) (possibly a local extremum point).

When \(f\) is totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{x}_0\) and \( abla f ( oldsymbol{x}_0) eq oldsymbol{0}\), the gradient gives two things: the direction \( oldsymbol{u}= abla f( oldsymbol{x}_0)/\| abla f( oldsymbol{x}_0)\|\) of steepest ascent, and the maximal rate of increase \(\| abla f( oldsymbol{x}_0)\|=\max_{\| oldsymbol{u}\|=1}\mathrm{D}_{ oldsymbol{u}}f( oldsymbol{x}_0) ext{,}\) by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

The gradient arrows point uphill, perpendicular to the level curves, and are longer where the curves are close together. Drag \( oldsymbol x_0\) to a stationary point.

The red path climbs the surface along \( abla f\); on the floor it crosses the level curves at right angles.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f\) is totally differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{,}\) the gradient is the vector whose dot product with any unit vector \(\boldsymbol{v}\) equals the directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) along \(\boldsymbol{v}\), i.e.,
\[ \nabla f (\boldsymbol{x}_0) \cdot \boldsymbol{v} = \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_0). \]
  • The existence of the gradient (all partial derivatives at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\)) alone does not guarantee this formula.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f(x,y) = \mathrm{e}^{x+y}\). Then \(\displaystyle \nabla f(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{e}^{x+y} \\ \mathrm{e}^{x+y} \end{pmatrix}\).
  • Let \(f(x,y) = x^2 y + y^3\). Then \(\nabla f(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 2xy \\ x^2 + 3y^2 \end{pmatrix}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be a subset of the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\text{.}\) The set \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is compact if and only if it is both closed and bounded.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A set in Euclidean space is compact exactly when it contains all its limit points and stays within some finite distance from the origin. Closedness keeps the boundary in, boundedness keeps it from running off to infinity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The continuous image of a compact set is compact. This yields the extreme value theorem.
  • Any closed subset of a compact set in \(\mathbb R^n\) is itself compact.
  • Finite unions of compact sets are compact. Arbitrary intersections of compact sets are compact.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A closed metric ball \(\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r) = \{\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{X} \colon d_2(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) \leq r\}\) in the Euclidean space is closed and bounded, so compact.
  • Any finite set \(\{\boldsymbol x_1,\dots,\boldsymbol x_k\}\subset \mathbb R^n\) is closed (finite sets are closed) and bounded, so compact.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(a < b\) be real numbers, and consider a function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) that is continuous on \([a, b]\text{.}\) Then, \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \([a, b]\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• A continuous function on a closed interval can’t "escape" or behave wildly near the edges because the interval includes its endpoints.
  • This prevents sudden jumps or unbounded growth, ensuring that the function's small changes near one point apply uniformly across the whole interval.

Because \(f\) is continuous on the compact interval \([a,b]\), it is uniformly continuous. For any prescribed vertical tolerance, one horizontal tolerance works at every point, as illustrated by windows of the same width and height.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• This theorem has a generalized version if \([a,b]\) is replaced by a compact set.
  • This theorem does not imply that uniform continuity holds only on closed intervals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^2+\sin x}{\mathrm{e}^x}\) is uniformly continuous on any closed interval since we know it is continuous everywhere.
  • The function \(g(x)=x\) is uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\) though \((0,1)\) is not a closed interval. This does not contradict with the theorem since the "closed interval" condition is sufficient but not necessary.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n,\,k \in\mathbb N^+\) and \(m\in \mathbb Z\). A function \(\boldsymbol f\colon \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R^k\) is homogeneous of degree \(\boldsymbol m\) if

\[ \boldsymbol f(cx_1,\,cx_2,\,\dots,\,cx_n)=c^m \boldsymbol f(x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n) \]

for every \((x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)\) and \(c\neq 0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If each of the homogeneous function's arguments is multiplied by the same scalar, then the function's value is multiplied by some power of this scalar.

Scale the point by \(c\): the value is multiplied by \(c^m\), so the level curves are scaled copies of each other along rays from the origin.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f\) is homogeneous of degree \(m\) and differentiable, then each partial derivative is homogeneous of degree \(m-1\).
  • The sum of two functions that are homogeneous of the same degree \(m\) is homogeneous of degree \(m\text{;}\) the product of functions homogeneous of degrees \(m\) and \(\ell\) is homogeneous of degree \(m+\ell\text{,}\) and the composition of functions homogeneous of degrees \(m\) and \(p\) is homogeneous of degree \(mp\text{.}\) A sum of homogeneous functions of different degrees, such as \(xy+x\text{,}\) is not homogeneous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 + xy\) is homogeneous as \(f(cx, cy) = c^2 f(x,y)\).
  • \(g(x,y) = xy + x\) is said to be inhomogeneous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A polynomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is called homogeneous of degree \(\boldsymbol k\) if all of its non-zero terms have degree \(k\). Such a polynomial is also called a (algebraic) form.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A homogeneous polynomial is one where every term has the same total degree.

Scaling all variables by a factor scales the polynomial by that factor raised to that degree.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The sum of two homogeneous polynomials of the same degree is homogeneous of that degree.
  • The product of a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(k\) and one of degree \(\ell\) is homogeneous of degree \(k+\ell\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(P(x) = 2x^5\) is a homogeneous polynomial of degree 5.
  • \(P(x,y) = x^2 + xy + y^2\) is homogeneous of degree 2. Each term has total degree 2.

docs.title: Image and Preimage of a Set
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and \(\boldsymbol{Y}\) be sets (in this course usually subsets of metric spaces), and let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\) be a function. Let \(\boldsymbol{C}\) be a subset of the domain \(\boldsymbol{X}\), the image of \(\boldsymbol{C}\) under \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is defined as:

\[ \begin{aligned} &\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{C})=\{\boldsymbol{y}\in\boldsymbol{Y}\colon \text{there exists some }\\ &\qquad\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{C} \text{ such that } \boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})\}. \end{aligned} \]

Let \(\boldsymbol{V}\) be a subset of the codomain \(\boldsymbol{Y}\), the preimage of \(\boldsymbol{V}\) under \(\boldsymbol{f}\) includes all points in the domain that give results in \(\boldsymbol{V}\):

\[ \boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{V})=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}\colon\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})\in\boldsymbol{V}\}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Image is the set of all outputs you actually get from the function when you put in points from a specific set.

Preimage is the set of all inputs that the function sends into a chosen target set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\boldsymbol{V}\) only needs to be a part of the codomain of \(\boldsymbol{f}\). This means there might be some \(\boldsymbol{y}\) in \(\boldsymbol{V}\) that doesn't match any \(\boldsymbol{x}\) in the domain \(\boldsymbol{X}\).
  • We have \(\boldsymbol{C} \subseteq \boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{C}))\) and \(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{f}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{V})) \subseteq \boldsymbol{V}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x+y\). Image of the unit square \([0,1]\times[0,1]\) under \(f\) is \([0,2]\). Preimage of \(\{0\}\) under \(f\) is the line \(y=-x\).
  • Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x,y)=x\). Image of the disc \(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\colon x^2+y^2 \leq 1\}\) under \(f\) is \([-1,1]\). Preimage of \([2,3]\) under \(f\) is the vertical strip \([2,3]\times\mathbb{R}\).
