docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider a sequence of functions \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) from \(X\) to \(\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) If the sequence of partial sums \(\displaystyle S_N(x) = \sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)\) converges to \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) pointwise or uniformly on \(X\) as \(N \to \infty\text{,}\) then we say the infinite series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\) converges pointwise/uniformly to \(\boldsymbol{f}\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) denoted as \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The infinite sum of functions is defined by its partial sums, and if these partial sums converge to a function, we say the series itself converges to that function.

Raise \(N\): the partial sums \(S_N(x)=\sum_{n=1}^N f_n(x)\) settle on the limit function (dashed).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(f_n\)'s are (continuously) differentiable, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n \rightarrow f\text{,}\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f'_n\rightrightarrows g\) on \((a,b)\text{,}\) then \(f\) is (continuously) differentiable on \((a, b)\) with \(f' = g\text{,}\) i.e.,
\[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty f'_n(x_0)=\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\right)'(x_0),\quad x_0\in(a,b). \]
  • On a finite closed interval \([a,b]\) with \(a<b\), if every \(f_n\) is Riemann integrable and \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\) converges uniformly, then its sum is Riemann integrable and
\[ \int_a^b \left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\right) \, \mathrm{d}x = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \int_a^b f_n(x) \, \mathrm{d}x. \]

The finite interval matters: the integral of a uniform error is at most \((b-a)\) times that error. Uniform convergence alone does not provide this bound for an improper integral on an unbounded interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n/n!\) converges uniformly on every fixed interval \([-R,R]\), where \(R>0\): \(|x^n/n!|\le R^n/n!\), and \(\sum_n R^n/n!=\mathrm{e}^R\). It converges pointwise on \(\mathbb R\), but not uniformly there; for each finite partial sum, the difference from \(\mathrm{e}^x\) is unbounded as \(x\to+\infty\).
  • The geometric series \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n\) converges uniformly on \([-r,r]\) for every fixed \(0<r<1\), because \(|x^n|\le r^n\) and \(\sum_n r^n<\infty\). On \((-1,1)\) it converges pointwise to \(1/(1-x)\), but not uniformly: the remainder \(x^{N+1}/(1-x)\) is unbounded as \(x\to1^-\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\text{,}\) and a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\text{,}\) a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) is an interior point of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if there exists some \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,\varepsilon) \subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) We denote the set of interior points of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) as \(\mathrm{int} \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An interior point is one that has a little ball around it completely contained in the set.

The green ball lies entirely inside \(\boldsymbol E\), so its centre \(\boldsymbol x_0\) is an interior point. Every ball around the red edge point leaves \(\boldsymbol E\), so that point is not interior. The interior is the largest open subset of \(\boldsymbol E\).

\(\boldsymbol E\) is the open unit disc together with one extra point \(\boldsymbol p\). Drag \(\boldsymbol x_0\) and shrink \(\varepsilon\): an interior point has some ball inside \(\boldsymbol E\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An interior point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is always in \(\boldsymbol{E}\) since balls centered at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) include \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{.}\)
  • The interior of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is the largest open subset of \(\boldsymbol{E}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(E = (0,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), every point in \((0,1)\) is interior. Pick a small enough interval around any point and it stays inside \((0,1)\).
  • For \(E = \{1,2,3\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), no point is interior. Any ball around \(1\) contains numbers other than \(1,2,3\).

docs.title: Intermediate Value Theorem on Connected Sets
Theorem
docs.text: Let \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) be a continuous real-valued function. Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be any connected subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\text{,}\) and let \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\) be any two points in \(\boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\) If \(y\) is a real number between \(f(\boldsymbol{a})\) and \(f(\boldsymbol{b})\text{,}\) then there exists a \(\boldsymbol{c} \in \boldsymbol{E}\) such that \(f(\boldsymbol{c}) = y\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A continuous function on a connected set cannot skip values: if it takes two different numbers, it must also take every number in between.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Continuous image of a connected set is connected.
  • If \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is path‑connected, the theorem can be proved by composing \(f\) with a path and applying the one‑dimensional intermediate value theorem.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be the closed unit disk in \(\mathbb R^2\) and \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\)​. The image is \([0,1]\) which is also a connected set.
  • Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\) be the unit sphere in \(\mathbb R^3\) and \(f(x,y,z)=z\) (height). The image is \([−1,1]\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X} \to \mathbb R\) be a real-valued function defined on a set \(\boldsymbol{X}\subseteq \mathbb R^n\). A level set is defined as the preimage of a singleton set \(\{k\}\), i.e.,

\[ \begin{aligned} L_k(f)&=f^{-1}(\{k\})\\ &=\{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\\ &\qquad f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)=k\}. \end{aligned} \]

When the number of independent variables is two, a level set is called a level curve, also known as contour line.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A level curve is the set of all real-valued solutions of an equation in two variables \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Different level sets for distinct values are disjoint, and the union over all possible values covers the entire domain where the function is defined.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Let \(f\colon \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\). Level sets are circles centered at the origin for \(k>0\), a single point \((0,0)\) for \(k=0\), and empty for \(k<0\).

    The level curves \(x^2+y^2=k\) are circles of radius \(\sqrt k\) for \(k>0\). They appear in red on the graph of \(f\) and in blue in the \(xy\)-plane.

Move \(k\) to highlight the level curve \(L_k(f)\). Drag \(\boldsymbol x_0\) to read off \(f\); nearby level curves crowd together where \(f\) changes fast.

Move \(k\): the plane \(z=k\) cuts the graph along the level curve \(L_k(f)\), drawn again on the floor.

  • Let \(f\colon \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x,y)=x+y\). Level sets are straight lines of slope \(−1\): \(x+y=k\). All level sets are parallel lines.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n=0}^{\infty}\) be a sequence. For each \(N\in\mathbb{N}\text{,}\) consider the supremum and infimum of the terms from \(a_N\) onward: \(\displaystyle s_N = \sup_{n\geq N} a_n\) and \(\displaystyle i_N = \inf_{n\geq N} a_n\text{.}\) The limit superior and limit inferior of \((a_n)_{n=0}^{\infty}\) are defined as:

\[ \begin{aligned} \limsup_{n\to \infty}a_n &:= \lim_{N\to\infty} s_N = \inf_{N\geq 0} s_N\\ &=\inf_{N\geq 0}\sup_{n\geq N} a_n, \\ \liminf_{n\to \infty}a_n &:= \lim_{N\to\infty} i_N = \sup_{N\geq 0} i_N\\ &=\sup_{N\geq 0}\inf_{n\geq N} a_n. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The limit superior and limit inferior describe the largest and smallest "long-run" accumulation points of a sequence, essentially capturing its eventual upper and lower bounds.

Move \(N\): \(s_N=\sup_{n\ge N}a_n\) can only decrease and \(i_N=\inf_{n\ge N}a_n\) can only increase. Their limits are \(\limsup a_n\) and \(\liminf a_n\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit superior and limit inferior of a sequence always exist.
  • A sequence converges if and only if its \(\limsup\) and \(\liminf\) are equal and finite; otherwise, it's divergent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(a_n = (-1)^n\): \(\limsup\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = 1\text{,}\) \(\liminf\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = -1\text{.}\)
  • For \(a_n = 1/2^n\): \(\limsup\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = \liminf\limits_{n\to \infty}a_n = 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The maximum norm of \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space \(\mathbb R^n\) with fixed Cartesian coordinate system is:

\[ \|\boldsymbol x\|_\infty=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i|. \]

Correspondingly, the Chebyshev distance between \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol y=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\) is calculated as:

\[ d_\infty(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i-y_i|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The maximum norm is the limiting case of the \(p\)-norm when \(p\to+\infty\).

With \(\|\boldsymbol x\|_\infty=\max(|x_1|,|x_2|)\) the unit circle is a square. Drag \(\boldsymbol x\) and compare the three norms.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball in the maximum norm is an axis-aligned hypercube
\[ \overline{\boldsymbol B}_{d_\infty}(\boldsymbol 0,1)=[-1,1]^n. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d)\) consists of a set of points \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and a distance function (or metric) \(d\colon \boldsymbol{X} \times \boldsymbol{X} \to [0,+\infty)\) that maps pairs of points to nonnegative real values. The metric adheres to the following properties:

  1. Non-negativity: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \geq 0\) for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)
  2. Identity of indiscernibles: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = 0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}\text{.}\)
  3. Symmetry: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = d(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x})\) for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)
  4. Triangle inequality: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{z}) \leq d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) + d(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z})\) for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{z} \in \boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A metric space is just a set of points with a clear and reasonable rule for measuring the distance between any two of them.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Metrics are always nonnegative. The only point at a zero distance from a point \(\boldsymbol{x}\) is \(\boldsymbol{x}\) itself.
  • Metrics are symmetric and adhere to the triangle inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean distance in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined as \(\displaystyle d(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}) = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2\right)^{1/2}\text{.}\)
  • The complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\) with the distance function (based on modulus) \(d(z,w) = |z-w|\) form a metric space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A monomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is a function from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R\) is a product of real coefficients and variables raised to nonnegative integer powers, i.e., a monomial has the general expression

\[ f(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n) = a x_1^{k_1} x_2^{k_2} \cdots x_n^{k_n}, \]

with constant \(a \in \mathbb{R}\) and exponents \(k_1,\, \dots,\, k_n \in \mathbb{N}\). The total degree of a monomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is the sum of the exponents of all variables appearing in that monomial, i.e., \(k_1+\cdots+k_n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A monomial is a simple expression made by multiplying a constant with each variable raised to a whole number power.

Its total degree is the sum of those powers, telling you how many factors of variables appear in total.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The product of two monomials is again a monomial. The exponents add componentwise, and the constant multiplies.
  • Every monomial is a homogeneous function whose degree equals its total degree.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y)=-2x^2y\)  is a monomial with exponents \(k_1=2\), \(k_2=1\), total degree \(3\).
  • The monomial \(f(x,y)=x^4\) has \(k_1=4\), \(k_2=0\), total degree \(4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A norm on a vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) over the scalar field \(\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\) (in this course \(\mathbb{R}\)) is a function \(\|\cdot\|\colon \boldsymbol{V}\to[0,+\infty)\) that adheres to the following criteria:

  1. Non-negativity and definiteness: For any \(\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{V}\), \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\| \geq 0\), and \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\| = 0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{0}\).
  2. Positive homogeneity: For any scalar \(c \in \mathbb{F}\) and any \(\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{V}\), \(\|c\boldsymbol{x}\| = |c|\cdot\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\), where \(|c|\) is the absolute value (modulus) of \(c\).
  3. Triangle inequality: For any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{V}\): \(\|\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{y}\| \leq \|\boldsymbol{x}\| + \|\boldsymbol{y}\|\).

A normed vector space \((\boldsymbol{V}, \|\cdot\|)\) is a vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) over \(\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\), equipped with a norm \(\|\cdot\|\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A norm is a rule that assigns a length to every vector in a consistent way.

A normed vector space is just a vector space where every vector has such a length, and scaling or adding vectors behaves as you would expect.

Each \(p\ge1\) gives a norm on \(\mathbb R^2\) with its own unit circle; all of them are convex and symmetric about \(\boldsymbol 0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Given a normed vector space \((\boldsymbol{V}, \|\cdot\|)\), one can define the metric as \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = \|\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{y}\|,\) making \((\boldsymbol{V}, d)\) inherently a metric space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The real line \(\mathbb{R}\) with the absolute-value norm forms a normed vector space over \(\mathbb{R}\).
  • The plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the Euclidean norm is similarly a normed vector space. Using the taxicab norm, \(\mathbb{R}^2\) remains a normed vector space.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of bounded functions on \(X\). We say the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\) is normally convergent if the series of uniform norms of the terms of the series converges, i.e., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty<+\infty.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Normal convergence means the functions are so well controlled that their worst-case contributions are summable.

\(\sum_n\|f_n\|_\infty=\sum_n 1/n^2\) converges, so the partial sums stay within the shrinking band around the limit.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Normal convergence implies uniform absolute convergence, which in turn implies uniform convergence, which in turn implies pointwise convergence, i.e.,
\[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty<+\infty &\implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty |f_n(x)|\rightrightarrows g\\ &\implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\rightrightarrows f\\ &\implies \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\to f. \end{aligned} \]

Here \(g\) is the sum of the absolute series; it differs from \(f\) unless every \(f_n\ge0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Uniform absolute convergence does not imply normal convergence. Consider $\(f(x)=\begin{cases} \displaystyle \, 1/n, &x=n,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \, 0, &x\neq n.\end{cases}\)$Then the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |f_n(x)|\) is uniformly convergent, however the series of uniform norms is the harmonic series and thus diverges.

docs.title: Open and Closed Sets in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) and its subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\):

  • \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is closed if it includes all of its boundary points, i.e., \(\partial \boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is open if it doesn't include any of its boundary points, i.e., \(\partial \boldsymbol{E} \cap \boldsymbol{E} = \varnothing\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is neither open nor closed if it includes some but not all of its boundary points.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Open sets keep their boundaries out. Closed sets keep their boundaries in. Sets that include some boundary points but not others are neither open nor closed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is open if and only if \(\boldsymbol{E} = \mathrm{int}\boldsymbol{E}\).
  • A set \(\boldsymbol F\) is closed if and only if every convergent sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^{\infty}\) within \(\boldsymbol{F}\) converges to a limiting point lying in \(\boldsymbol{F}\).
  • A set \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is open if and only if its complement \(\boldsymbol{E}^\complement=\boldsymbol{X}\setminus \boldsymbol{E}\) is closed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The open metric ball \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0, \varepsilon)\) is open.
  • \(\varnothing\) is both open and closed. It has no boundary points to include or exclude.
  • Under the discrete metric, every set is both open and closed. Each singleton set has a ball containing only itself.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\), a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), and \(r > 0\), the open metric ball \(\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), centered at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) with radius \(r\) in metric \(d\), is defined as the following set:

\[ \boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r) = \{\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{X} \colon d(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) < r\}. \]

If the context is clear, we'll abbreviate this as \(\boldsymbol{B}_d(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)\) or simply \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r).\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An open metric ball is the set of all points whose distance from the center is strictly less than the radius.

It is the basic building block for defining open sets and continuity in metric spaces.

Change the centre, the radius \(r\) and the metric: the ball contains the points at distance less than \(r\). Points on the dashed sphere are not included.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Open balls are open sets.
  • A subset of a metric space is open if and only if it can be written as a union of open balls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual distance, \(\boldsymbol B((0,0),1)\) is the open disc of radius \(1\) centered at the origin. Points with \(x^2 + y^2 < 1\) are elements of this ball.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with \(d_1\), \(\boldsymbol B((0,0),1)\) is a diamond shape with vertices at \((\pm1,0)\) and \((0,\pm1)\).
  • In any set with the discrete metric, \(\boldsymbol B(\boldsymbol x,1) = \{\boldsymbol x\}\) and \(\boldsymbol B(\boldsymbol x,0.5) = \{\boldsymbol x\}\), but \(\boldsymbol B(\boldsymbol x,2)\) is the whole space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2, \ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(p\in[1,+\infty)\), the \(\boldsymbol{p}\)-norm, denoted \(\|\cdot\|_p\), is defined on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) by:

\[ \|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}. \]

For \(p=+\infty\) one sets \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_\infty=\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}|x_i|\), which is the limit of \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p\) as \(p\to+\infty\).

Correspondingly, the \(p\)-metric \(d_p\) is defined as \(d_p(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=\|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol y\|_p\), that is,

\[ \begin{aligned} d_p(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)&=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i-y_i|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\\ &\qquad(1\le p<+\infty),\\ d_\infty(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)&=\max_{1\le i\le n}|x_i-y_i|. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The \(p\)-norm is a way of measuring the size of a vector by raising each coordinate's absolute value to the \(p\)-th power, summing them, and taking the \(p\)-th root.

The figure compares the unit balls \(\{\boldsymbol x:\|\boldsymbol x\|_p\le1\}\) for \(p=1,2,4,\infty\). As \(p\) increases, these balls expand from the diamond towards the square.

Move \(p\): the unit circle \(\{\boldsymbol x:\|\boldsymbol x\|_p=1\}\) swells from the diamond at \(p=1\) through the circle at \(p=2\) towards the square at \(p=\infty\). Drag \(\boldsymbol x\) to compare its norms.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The smallest permissible value for \(p\) in the \(p\)-norm is \(1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean distance \(d_2\) is a particular \(p\)-metric when \(p=2\).
  • The taxicab distance \(d_1\) is a particular \(p\)-metric when \(p=1\).
  • The maximum norm \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) is a particular \(p\)-norm when \(p=+\infty\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and consider a function \(\boldsymbol{f} \colon \boldsymbol{E} \to \mathbb{R}^k\). For an interior point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) and an integer \(1 \leq j \leq n\), the partial derivative of \(\boldsymbol{f}\) with respect to the \(x_j\)-variable at \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}_0\), denoted by \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\), is given by

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) &= \lim_{{t\to0}} \frac{\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{e}_j) - \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)}{t}\\ &= \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{e}_j)\,\right|_{t=0}, \end{aligned} \]

where \(\boldsymbol{e}_j\) represents the unit vector in the positive direction of the \(j\)-th coordinate, provided the limit exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The partial derivative measures how the function changes when you nudge only one coordinate while keeping all others fixed.

It is like taking an ordinary derivative in the direction of that coordinate axis.

Choose \(j\): along the line \(\boldsymbol x_0+t\boldsymbol e_j\) the function becomes a one-variable function (right), and \(\partial f/\partial x_j\) is its slope at \(t=0\).

Freeze one variable: the graph is cut along a line through \(\boldsymbol x_0\), and \(\partial f/\partial x_j\) is the slope of that slice. Edit \(f\) to try your own function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The partial derivative \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exists if and only if both \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) and \(\mathrm{D}_{-\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exist and are negatives of each other. In such a scenario, we have \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0).\)
  • If \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\text{,}\) then for every vector \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{v} = (v_1,\,\ldots,\,v_n)= \sum_{j=1}^n v_j\boldsymbol{e}_j\) we have \(\displaystyle \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \frac{\partial }{\partial x_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0).\) Without total differentiability this can fail even when all partial derivatives exist.
  • If all the partial derivatives are both existent within a neighborhood and continuous at the center, then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at this point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The partial derivative of \(f(x,y) = 3x^2y^2 + 4xy^3 + 7y\) with respect to the first variable is \(\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}f(x,y) = 6xy^2 + 4y^3.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\text{,}\) a subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is termed path-connected if, for any two distinct points \(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b} \in \boldsymbol{E}\text{,}\) a path \(\boldsymbol{p}\colon [0,1] \to \boldsymbol{E}\) exists such that \(\boldsymbol{p}(0) = \boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{p}(1) = \boldsymbol{b}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: You can walk from any point to any other point in a path-connected set without ever leaving the set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In the metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\text{,}\) any path-connected subset of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is connected.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The topologist's sine curve is connected but not path-connected:

    \[ \{(0,0)\}\cup \{(x,\sin (1/x)) \colon x\in (0,+\infty)\}. \]

    As \(x\to0^+\) the graph oscillates ever faster between \(-1\) and \(1\); the set is connected, but no path inside it reaches \((0,0)\).

  • The collection of line segments joining the origin to points \((1, 1/n)\) for all positive integers \(n\), together with the point \((1,0)\) is also connected but not path-connected.

    Segments from the origin to \((1,1/n)\) crowd towards the missing segment to \((1,0)\); only its endpoint \((1,0)\) belongs to the set, and no path inside the set reaches it.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\), a path is a continuous function \(\boldsymbol{p}\colon [0,1] \to \boldsymbol{X}\). If for two points \(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b} \in \boldsymbol{X}\), the path \(\boldsymbol{p}\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{p}(0) = \boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{p}(1) = \boldsymbol{b}\), it is termed as a path from \(\boldsymbol{a}\) to \(\boldsymbol{b}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A path is a continuous journey from one point to another within the space.

It is like drawing a curve without lifting your pencil, with the curve entirely contained in the space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol p\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol a\) to \(\boldsymbol b\) and \(\boldsymbol q\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol b\) to \(\boldsymbol c\), then it is possible to construct a path from \(\boldsymbol a\) to \(\boldsymbol c\) using \(\boldsymbol p\) and \(\boldsymbol q\). This is called the concatenation.
  • For any path \(\boldsymbol p\) from \(\boldsymbol a\) to \(\boldsymbol b\), the reverse path \(\boldsymbol p(1−t)\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol b\) to \(\boldsymbol a\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In Euclidean space, the function \(p(t)=(1−t)a+tb\) is a path from \(a\) to \(b\).
  • The function \(p(t)=(\cos⁡(2\pi t),\sin(⁡2\pi t))\) is a path from \((1,0)\) back to itself (a loop).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence of functions \(f_n\colon X\to \mathbb{R}\) and \(f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be another function. We say that \((f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) converges pointwise to \(\boldsymbol{f}\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and write \(f_n\to f\text{,}\) if for every \(x \in X\text{,}\) \(\displaystyle \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} f_n(x) = f(x)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Pointwise convergence means that for each fixed point, the function values get closer to a limit as the index goes to infinity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pointwise convergence guarantees that the limit exists at each individual point.
  • Pointwise convergence does not preserve boundedness, limits/continuity, differentiability, or integrals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f_n(x) = \dfrac{n}{nx + 1}\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=1/x\) on \((0,+\infty)\text{.}\)
  • \(f_n(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+1 / n}}\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=|x|.\)

For each fixed \(x\), \(f_n(x)\to|x|\); at \(x=-1\) the values \(f_n(-1)\) (dots) increase to \(f(-1)=1\).

Point at a value \(x\): the numbers \(f_n(x)\) (right) enter the \(\varepsilon\)-band from some \(N(x)\) on. For \(x^n\) that \(N(x)\) grows without bound as \(x\to1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A polynomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is a real-valued function that is a finite sum of monomials on \(\mathbb R^n\). The degree of a polynomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is defined as the maximum, over all its monomials, of the total degree of each monomial.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A polynomial in several variables is a finite combination of monomials added together.

Its degree is the highest total degree among all the monomials that appear with nonzero coefficient.

The plotted polynomial \(p(x_1,x_2)=x_1^3-3x_1x_2^2\) is the sum of two monomials, each of total degree \(3\).

Drag the picture to turn it. \(x_1^3-3x_1x_2^2\) has degree \(3\); compare it with the degree-\(2\) examples, whose graphs are bowls and saddles.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The degree of the sum of two polynomials is at most the maximum of their degrees. The degree of the product of two polynomials is the sum of their degrees.
  • Polynomials are infinitely differentiable. All partial derivatives of all orders exist and are themselves polynomials (or zero).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + 2xy + y^2 + x + 1\) is a polynomial of degree 2. Its highest total degree comes from \(x^2\), \(xy\), and \(y^2\), all degree 2.
  • \(f(x,y) = x^3 + xy + y^2\) has degree 3 from the \(x^3\) term.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(a \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) A power series centered at \(\boldsymbol{a}\) is expressed as \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\text{,}\) where \((c_n)_{n=0}^\infty\) is a sequence of real numbers, independent of \(x\text{.}\) We refer to \(c_n\) as the \(\boldsymbol{n}\)-th coefficient of the power series.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A power series is an infinite sum of power functions.

Raise \(N\): inside the shaded interval of convergence the partial sums settle on the sum; outside they run away.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • This is the formal definition of power series since it is not discussed whether such a series is convergent or divergent for different \(x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any polynomial is a special case of a power series, since the coefficients \(c_n\) are allowed to be zero.
  • \(1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots\) is a power series.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a given power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\text{,}\) its radius of convergence \(R\) is a nonnegative real number or \(+\infty\) such that the series converges if \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges if \(|x-a|>R\text{.}\) The interval of convergence is the set of all values of \(x\) for which the series converges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The radius of convergence tells you how far from the center point a power series will reliably converge.

Each series converges for \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges for \(|x-a|>R\); what happens at the endpoints differs from series to series.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The convergence of \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) at \(x=a-R\) and \(x=a+R\) is to be determined case-by-case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) with \(R = 1/2\) centered at \(a = 3\), converges pointwise on \(\left(5/2, 7/2\right)\) and uniformly on any closed interval within it. Its convergence interval is \(\left(5/2, 7/2\right)\) since the series diverges at both endpoints.
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = 0\) centered at \(a = -2\), converges solely at its center \(x = -2.\)

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) where \(a_n\in\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\text{,}\) then:

  • If \(L < 1\text{,}\) the series converges. Moreover, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) also converges.
  • If \(L > 1\text{,}\) the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\) or the limit does not exist, the test is inconclusive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The ratio test states that a series converges if the limit of the ratio of consecutive terms is less than 1, and diverges if it is greater than 1.

\(\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=\dfrac{n+1}{2n}\to L=\tfrac12<1\). For \(n\ge3\), \(a_{n+1}\le\tfrac23a_n\), so \(a_n\le a_3(\tfrac23)^{n-3}\) and \(\sum a_n\) converges by comparison.

Move \(x\): the ratios \(|a_{n+1}/a_n|\) (right) settle at \(L=|x-a|/R\). The series converges for \(L<1\) and diverges for \(L>1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • For the power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x - a)^n\text{,}\) the radius of convergence \(R\) can be found using \(\displaystyle R = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{c_{n}}{c_{n+1}} \right|\) if the limit exists or tends to infinity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n}\) is convergent since \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{(n+1)/\mathrm{e}^{n+1}}{n/\mathrm{e}^n} \right| =\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{e}}<1\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n}\) diverges since \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{2^{n+1}/(n+1)}{2^n/n} \right| =2>1\text{.}\)
  • When \(L=1\text{,}\) both convergent and divergent series exist, e.g., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges while \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\) converges for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{(n+1)!}{n!} \right|=+\infty\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^n(x-3)^n\) converges for \(|x-3|<1/2\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{2^{n}}{2^{n+1}} \right|=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n!(x+1)^n\) diverges for all \(x\) except \(x=-1\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{n!} {(n+1)!}\right|=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon E \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function where \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) We say:

  • \(f\) is real analytic at \(\boldsymbol{x=a}\) if \(a\) is an interior point of \(E\) and there exists a power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) centered at \(a\) and an open interval \((a-r, a+r) \subseteq E\) (for some \(r > 0\)) where this series converges to \(f\text{.}\)
  • \(f\) is real analytic on \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if \(E\) is an open set and \(f\) is real analytic at every point \(a \in E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is real analytic at a point if it can be represented by a power series that matches the function exactly in a small interval around that point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The convergence type here is not limited, but if we consider a closed subinterval of \((a-r,a+r)\text{,}\) then it is the uniform convergence.
  • Sums, products, and compositions of real analytic functions are also real analytic.
  • A real analytic function is always infinitely differentiable, and all of its higher-order derivatives are real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Almost all common functions are real analytic.
  • Most piecewise functions are not real analytic, though they can be even infinitely differentiable. For instance, the following function is a particular non-analytic but infinitely differentiable function.

Every derivative of \(f\) at \(0\) is \(0\), so its Taylor series at \(0\) is the zero series, yet \(f(x)>0\) for \(x>0\): \(f\) is infinitely differentiable but not real analytic at \(0\).

A real analytic function equals its Taylor series near each point \(a\). Move \(a\): the interval of convergence moves and changes size with it.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) where \(a_n \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(\displaystyle L = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\), then:

  • If \(L < 1\text{,}\) the series converges. Moreover, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) also converges.
  • If \(L > 1\text{,}\) the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\text{,}\) the test is inconclusive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The root test determines convergence by comparing the limit of the \(n\)-th root of the terms' absolute values to 1.

The \(n\)th roots \(|a_n|^{1/n}\) (right) approach \(L=|x-a|/R\); compare with \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• One of the differences between the ratio test and the root test is that the limit in the ratio test may not exist, while the limit in the root test always exists.
  • The radius of convergence of a power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) is given by
\[ R=\frac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n\to\infty} |c_n|^{1/n}}. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n}\) is convergent since \(\displaystyle L=\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\left| \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n} \right|} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}<1\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n}\) diverges since \(\displaystyle L=\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\left|\frac{2^n}{n} \right|} = 2>1\text{.}\)
  • When \(L=1\text{,}\) both convergent and divergent series exist, e.g., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges while \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) is convergent for \(|x-3|<\dfrac{1}{2}\) since \(R = \dfrac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n \to\infty}|n\left(-2\right)^{n}|^{1/n}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) is divergent except at \(x=-2\) since \(R= \dfrac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n \rightarrow \infty}|2^{n^{2}}|^{1/n}}= 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) be a metric space. A subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is termed sequentially compact if for every sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) with each \(\boldsymbol{x}_i \in \boldsymbol{E}\text{,}\) there exists a convergent subsequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i_j})_{j=1}^\infty\) that converges to a point \(\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A set is sequentially compact if every infinite sequence drawn from it has a subsequence that converges to a point still inside the set.

It captures the idea that the set is "closed under taking limits of subsequences."

In the closed disc, the red subsequence converges to a point of \(\boldsymbol E\). In the open disc, the illustrated sequence approaches a missing rim point, and every subsequence has that same limit outside \(\boldsymbol E\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In any metric space, a set is compact if and only if it is sequentially compact. This gives two equivalent ways to think about compactness: open covers or convergent subsequences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball \(\{x\in \mathbb R^n\colon \|x\|\leq 1\}\) is sequentially compact. This fails in infinite dimensions.
  • Any finite set in any metric space is compact.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{X}\) be a metric space. The metrics \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are termed strongly equivalent, denoted \(d_p\approx d_q\), if positive constants \(a\) and \(b\) exist such that for any \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{X}\),

\[ a \cdot d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \leq d_q(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \leq b \cdot d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Equivalent metrics measure distances in different scales but agree on which points are close or far apart.

On \(\mathbb R^2\), the illustrated Euclidean and taxicab distances satisfy \(d_2\le d_1\le\sqrt2\,d_2\). Consequently, \(\boldsymbol B_{d_2}(\boldsymbol x,r/\sqrt2)\subseteq\boldsymbol B_{d_1}(\boldsymbol x,r)\subseteq\boldsymbol B_{d_2}(\boldsymbol x,r)\), so they induce the same open sets and convergent sequences.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The strong equivalence relation possesses symmetry (\(d_p\approx d_q\) if and only if \(d_q\approx d_p\)), reflexivity (\(d_p\approx d_p\)) and transitivity (if \(d_p\approx d_q\) and \(d_q\approx d_r\), then \(d_p\approx d_r\)).
  • Strongly equivalent metrics induce the same notion of convergence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any two \(p\)-metrics on \(\mathbb R^n\) are strongly equivalent.
  • The discrete metric, \(d_{\text{disc}}\), is not strongly equivalent to any of the \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The taxicab distance between points \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol y=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space \(\mathbb R^n\) with fixed Cartesian coordinate system is:

\[ d_1(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i-x_i|. \]

The taxicab norm, or known as \(\ell^1\) norm, of \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) is calculated as:

\[ \|\boldsymbol x\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_i|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The taxicab distance represents the distance a taxi would travel between two points when restricted to cardinal directions (north, south, east, west) without moving diagonally or in any other curved path.

The red staircase has taxicab length \(d_1(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=5+4=9\). Any monotone staircase between the points has the same length, whereas the blue straight segment has Euclidean length \(d_2(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=\sqrt{5^2+4^2}\approx6.4\).

In the taxicab norm \(\|\boldsymbol x\|_1=|x_1|+|x_2|\) the unit circle is a diamond. Drag \(\boldsymbol x\): the \(1\)-norm is always at least the Euclidean norm.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The closed unit ball in the taxicab norm is an \(n\)-dimensional cross-polytope, e.g., a diamond in \(\mathbb R^2\) and a regular octahedron in \(\mathbb R^3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The polynomial that emerges from Taylor's theorem is termed the \(\boldsymbol{k}\)-th order Taylor polynomial for the function \(f\) at \(x=a\):

\[ \begin{aligned} P_{k}(x) &= f(a) + f^{\prime}(a)(x-a) + \cdots\\ &\quad + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^{k}. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial of \(f\) captures the initial \(k+1\) terms of its Taylor series (given existence) centered at the same point.
  • If \(f\) is \(k\) times differentiable at \(a\text{,}\) then \(P_k\) is the unique polynomial of degree at most \(k\) with \(f(x)-P_k(x)=o\big((x-a)^k\big)\) as \(x\to a\text{;}\) in this sense it is the best polynomial approximation of order \(k\) near \(x=a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial and the function \(f\) have the same value and the same derivatives up to order \(k\) at \(x=a\text{:}\) \(P_k^{(j)}(a)=f^{(j)}(a)\) for \(j=0,1,\dots,k\text{.}\) Away from \(a\) they generally differ.
  • One can write a Taylor polynomial for a function just from its first few derivatives, but the full Taylor series exists if the function is smooth, and the full series converges to the function only if it's real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The 3rd order Taylor polynomial of \(\sin x\) around \(x=0\) is \(P_3(x) = x - \dfrac{x^3}{3!}\).

    The two panels compare Taylor polynomials of \(\sin x\) about \(0\). The cubic \(P_3\) on the right follows \(\sin x\) over a wider interval than the linear polynomial \(P_1\) on the left.

Raise the order \(k\) and move the centre \(a\): \(P_k\) matches \(f\) and its first \(k\) derivatives at \(a\), and fits over a wider range.

  • The 1st order Taylor polynomial of \(1/x\) around \(x = 1\) is \(P_1(x)=2-x\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(a\) be an interior point of \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and let \(f\colon E\to\mathbb{R}\) be real analytic at \(x=a\text{.}\) Then \(f\) has the power series expansion around \(x=a\):

\[ \begin{gathered} f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n\\ \text{for all } x \in (a-r,a+r), \end{gathered} \]

known as the Taylor series of \(f\) around \(x=a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If a function is so smooth that it behaves exactly like an infinite polynomial near a point, then that polynomial is built entirely from its derivatives at that point.

For \(\ln(1+x)\) and \(1/(1-x)\) the Taylor polynomials converge to \(f\) inside the shaded interval and not beyond it; for \(\mathrm{e}^x\) and \(\sin x\) everywhere.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Taylor series centered at the origin is called the Maclaurin series.
  • For any smooth function you can write down its Taylor series, but that series is guaranteed to converge to the function only if the function is real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Taylor series of the natural exponential function at the origin:
\[ \displaystyle \mathrm{e}^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!} = 1 + x + \dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \cdots. \]
  • The generalized binomial expansion at the origin, valid for \(|x|<1\) and any real exponent \(\alpha\) (and for all \(x\) when \(\alpha\) is a nonnegative integer, since the series then terminates):
\[ \begin{aligned} &(1+x)^\alpha = \sum_{i=0}^\infty \binom{\alpha}{i} x^i \\ &\quad= 1 + \alpha x + \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}{2}x^2\\ &\qquad + \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)}{6}x^3 + \cdots, \end{aligned} \]

where \(\displaystyle\binom{\alpha}{i}=\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)\cdots(\alpha-i+1)}{i!}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(k \geq 1\) be an integer and assume that the function \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(k\)-times differentiable (not necessarily real analytic) at \(x=a\text{.}\) There exists a function \(\displaystyle h_k \colon \mathbb{R} \to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to a} h_k(x) = 0\) and

\[ \begin{aligned} f(x) &= f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots\\ &\quad + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^k + R_k(x) \end{aligned} \]

where \(R_k(x)= h_k(x)(x-a)^k\) is called the Peano form of the remainder.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
One can approximate a smooth function near a point using a polynomial, and the error term behaves like \((x−a)^k\) multiplied by something that tends to \(0\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\).

The right panel shows \(h_k(x)=R_k(x)/(x-a)^k\): it tends to \(0\) as \(x\to a\), which is the Peano form of the remainder.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Using the little-\(o\) notation, the statement in Taylor's theorem reads as \(R_k(x)=o((x-a)^k)\text{,}\) as \(x\to a\text{.}\) In this case, we have the \(k\)-th order Taylor expansion:
\[ \begin{aligned} f(x) &= f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots\\ &\quad + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^{k}\\ &\quad + o((x-a)^{k}). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathrm{e}^x=1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+h_2(x)x^2\), where \(\displaystyle h_2(x)=\sum_{n=3}^\infty \dfrac{x^{n-2}}{n!}\).
  • \(\dfrac{1}{1-x}=1+x+x^2+h_2(x) x^2\), where \(\displaystyle h_2(x)=\sum_{n=3}^\infty x^{n-2}\), for \(|x|<1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two metrics \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) on a space \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are termed (topologically) equivalent if they produce identical topology (the set of open subsets of \(\boldsymbol{X}\)) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\), i.e., a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\) is open with respect to \(d_p\) if and only if it's open under \(d_q\). This relationship is expressed as \(d_p \sim d_q.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two metrics are topologically equivalent if they determine the same collection of open sets.

They may measure distances differently, but they agree on which points are close enough to be in the same open set.

Around every point of a \(d_p\)-ball fits a \(d_q\)-ball, and vice versa, so a set is \(d_p\)-open \(\iff\) it is \(d_q\)-open: the same topology.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • If two metrics are strongly equivalent, then they are topologically equivalent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• On the interval \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\text{,}\) the metric \(d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|\) is topologically equivalent to the absolute value metric, but they are not strongly equivalent: the ratio \(|\tan x-\tan y|/|x-y|\) is unbounded near \(\pm\pi/2\text{.}\)
  • The discrete metric is not topologically equivalent to any \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A topology on a set \(\boldsymbol{X}\), often denoted by \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\), is a collection of subsets of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) that satisfies the following properties:

  1. Both the empty set and the entire set \(\boldsymbol{X}\) belong to \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\).
  2. Any union of elements in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) also belongs to \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\).
  3. The intersection of any finite number of elements in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) remains in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\).

The pair \((\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol \tau)\) is called a topological space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A topology is a collection of open sets that tells you which points are close to which without using a distance.

It is the most general setting for studying continuity and convergence.

\(\boldsymbol{\tau}=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{a,b\},\boldsymbol{X}\}\) is a topology on \(\boldsymbol{X}\): it contains \(\varnothing\) and \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and is closed under unions and finite intersections (e.g. \(\{a\}\cup\{a,b\}=\{a,b\}\), \(\{a\}\cap\{a,b\}=\{a\}\)); the members of \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) are the open sets.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Metric spaces are topological spaces. Every metric space induces a topology where open sets are unions of open metric balls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The trivial topology is the topology with the least possible number of open sets, namely the empty set and the entire space, i.e., \(\boldsymbol{\tau}=\{\varnothing, \boldsymbol X\}\).

docs.title: Total Derivative as a Linear Map
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a function, let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\mathrm{int}\boldsymbol{E}\), and let \(\boldsymbol{L}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a linear transformation. We say that \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is (totally) differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_{\boldsymbol{0}}\) with (total) derivative \(\boldsymbol{L}\) if:

\[ \lim_{\substack{\boldsymbol{x}\to\boldsymbol{x}_0}}\frac{\|\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})-(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_0))\|}{\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_0\|}=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Total differentiability means the function can be approximated near the point by a linear transformation, with the error shrinking to zero faster than the distance to the point.

It is the multidimensional version of the Newton's approximation, which is an equivalent formulation of differentiability.

The first-order approximation is \(\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol x_0+\boldsymbol h)=\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol x_0)+\boldsymbol L\boldsymbol h+o(\|\boldsymbol h\|)\), where \(\boldsymbol L=\boldsymbol{Df}(\boldsymbol x_0)\). Locally, \(\boldsymbol f\) acts like this linear map, so small squares become approximate parallelograms.

Move \(\boldsymbol x_0\) and zoom in: near \(\boldsymbol x_0\) the graph is almost the plane \(f(\boldsymbol x_0)+\mathrm{D}f_{\boldsymbol x_0}(\boldsymbol h)\), with an error that shrinks faster than \(\|\boldsymbol h\|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For the function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\), its derivative, \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}\), is a \(k\times n\) matrix or an equivalent linear transformation from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^k\).
  • \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}(\boldsymbol{h})\), where \(\boldsymbol{h}\) is an infinitesimal vector, provides an approximation of the shift in \(\boldsymbol{f}\) (a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^k\)) arising from the change \(\boldsymbol{h}\) in \(\boldsymbol{x}\) around \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) (a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = (x^2,y^2)\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}=(1,2)\) with the derivative \(\boldsymbol{L}(x,y) = (2x,4y)\).
  • The function \(f(x,y) = \sin(x^2+y)\) is differentiable at \((x,y)=(0,0)\) and the derivative is \(L(x,y)=y\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider metric spaces \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) and \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\), and a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\). We say \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is uniformly continuous on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) if, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_2\in\boldsymbol{X}\) with \(d_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_2)<\delta\), it holds that \(d_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_1),\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_2))<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
This is the general definition of uniform continuity where the metric functions are allowed to be potentially different metrics on possibly different spaces.

For a given \(\varepsilon>0\), the same \(\delta>0\) works at every point: \(d_{\boldsymbol X}(\boldsymbol x_1,\boldsymbol x_2)<\delta\) implies \(d_{\boldsymbol Y}(\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol x_1),\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol x_2))<\varepsilon\). Each \(\delta\)-ball is therefore mapped inside the \(\varepsilon\)-ball around its centre's image.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any continuous function defined on a compact set is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Every constant function is uniformly continuous regardless of the metrics.
  • Every function from a discrete space is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A function \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) is said to be uniformly continuous if, for every \(\varepsilon >0\text{,}\) there exists a \(\delta >0\) such that for all pairs of points \(x_1, x_2\in X\) with \(|x_1-x_2|<\delta\text{,}\) it holds that \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|<\varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Uniform continuity means one fixed rule for “how small is small” works everywhere, while ordinary continuity may need different rules at different points.

For a fixed \(\varepsilon\) the right panel shows the largest admissible \(\delta\) at each \(x_0\). Uniform continuity means one positive \(\delta\) works everywhere; for \(1/x\) the admissible \(\delta\) shrinks to \(0\) near \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every uniformly continuous function is continuous, the converse doesn't necessarily hold.
  • \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(X\) if and only if given two equivalent sequences \((x_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((y_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) in \(X\) (that is, \(|x_n-y_n|\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\)), the sequences \((f(x_n))_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((f(y_n))_{n=1}^\infty\) are also equivalent.
  • A continuous function \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \((a, b)\) if and only if the right limit \(\displaystyle f(a^+)\) and the left limit \(\displaystyle f(b^-)\) both exist and are finite. In other words, continuous functions can fail to be uniformly continuous if they are unbounded on a bounded domain.
  • A differentiable function \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \((a,b)\) if \(f'\) is bounded. Boundedness of \(f'\) is sufficient, not necessary: \(\sqrt{x}\) is uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\) although its derivative is unbounded there. A typical failure on an unbounded domain is \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\text{,}\) whose slope is unbounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=1/x\) is uniformly continuous on \((1,2)\), but not uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\).
  • The function \(g(x)=\sin x\) is uniformly continuous on any interval in this domain.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of functions defined on \(X \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) and \(f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be another function. We say that \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges uniformly to \(\boldsymbol{f}\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and write \(f_n\rightrightarrows f\text{,}\) if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a positive integer \(N\) such that for all \(n > N\text{,}\) the inequality \(|f_n(x) - f(x) | < \varepsilon\) holds for all \(x \in X\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Uniform convergence means that the function values get close to the limit at the same speed for all points, not one point at a time.

Uniform convergence \(f_n\to f\) means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the graph of \(f_n\) lies in the \(\varepsilon\)-tube around \(f\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Thus \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) holds for all \(x\) at once, equivalently \(\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0\).

Uniform convergence asks for one \(n\) that puts the whole graph of \(f_n\) inside the \(\varepsilon\)-band. Compare \(\sin(nx)/n\) with \(x^n\) and the moving bump.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence.
  • Uniform convergence preserves boundedness and continuity (uniform limit theorem). On a closed bounded interval \([a,b]\) it preserves Riemann integrability and allows \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n=\int_a^b f\text{.}\) It does not preserve differentiability: for that, the derivatives \(f_n'\) must converge uniformly as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sequence \(f_n(x) = x/n\) converges uniformly to \(f(x)=0\) on every bounded interval \([-R,R]\) (since \(|x/n|\le R/n\)), but only pointwise on \(\mathbb R\text{.}\)
  • The functions \(f_n(x) = \dfrac{n}{nx + 1}\) on \((0,1]\) converge pointwise, but not uniformly, to \(f(x)=1/x\text{,}\) because \(|f_n(x)-1/x|=\dfrac{1}{x(nx+1)}\) is unbounded near \(0\) for every \(n\text{.}\) (On \([0,1]\) there is no pointwise limit at all, since \(f_n(0)=n\to\infty\text{.}\))

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The uniform norm \(\|f\|_\infty\) of a bounded functions \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) is defined as:

\[ \|f\|_\infty = \sup_{x \in X} |f(x)|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The uniform norm is the supremum of the absolute value of the function over its entire domain.

The red segment marks the largest gap between \(f_n\) and \(f\): that is \(\|f_n-f\|_\infty\). Uniform convergence means it tends to \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A sequence of functions \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges uniformly to a function \(f\) on \(X\) if and only if:
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \|f_n - f\|_\infty = 0. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the function \(f\colon (0,+\infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x) = \mathrm{e}^{-x}\), we have \(\|f\|_\infty = 1.\)
  • For the function \(g\colon \mathbb R \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(g(x) = \sin x\), we have \(\|g\|_\infty = 1.\)

docs.title: Union and Intersection of Closed Sets
Proposition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) and a collection of closed subsets \((\boldsymbol{E}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\), the countable intersection \(\displaystyle\bigcap_{i=1}^\infty \boldsymbol{E}_i\) and the finite union \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{i=1}^k \boldsymbol{E}_i\) are also closed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Closed sets are preserved under finite unions and arbitrary intersections.

Infinite unions can break closedness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) are always closed (and also open).
  • In fact any intersection of closed sets, not just countably many, is closed. This holds for uncountable families as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty [-1/n, 1/n] = {0}\) is closed. Shrinking closed intervals collapse to a single closed point.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty [0, 1-1/n] = [0,1)\) is not closed. It is missing the endpoint \(1\).

docs.title: Union and Intersection of Open Sets
Proposition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) and a collection of open subsets \((\boldsymbol{E}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\), the countable union \(\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \boldsymbol{E}_i\) and the finite intersection \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^k \boldsymbol{E}_i\) are also open.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Open sets are preserved under finite intersections and arbitrary unions.

Infinite intersections can break openness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) are always open (and also closed).
  • In fact any union of open sets, not just countably many, is open. This holds for uncountable families as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (0, 1-1/n) = (0,1)\) is open. Even though each interval misses the right endpoint, the union still does not include 1.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty (-1/n, 1+1/n) = [0,1]\) is closed. The intersection includes the endpoints 0 and 1, which are not interior points.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For a continuous function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a polynomial \(P\colon [a, b]\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\|P-f\|_\infty < \varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Any continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated as closely as desired by a polynomial.

Raise the degree \(n\) of the Bernstein polynomial until it lies within \(\varepsilon\) of \(f\) on all of \([0,1]\), even at the kink of \(|x-\tfrac12|\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Polynomials are dense in \(C^0([a,b])\) with respect to the uniform norm.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any polynomial can be "approximated" by itself accurately.
  • Continuous functions, e.g., \(f(x)=\mathrm{e}^x\), over the entirety of \(\mathbb{R}\) aren't always uniformly approximable by polynomials.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Weierstrass function is defined as

\[ f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a^n \cos(b^n x) \]

where \(0<a<1\) and \(ab>1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Weierstrass function is one of the most famous examples of continuous but nowhere differentiable functions. In the original paper, this function is defined as \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a^n \cos(b^n \pi x)\) where  \(0<a<1\text{,}\) \(b\) is a positive odd number, and \(ab>1+\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\text{.}\)

The Weierstrass function is based on the earlier Riemann function \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{\sin(n^2 x)}{n^2}\text{,}\) which has also been called the Weierstrass function in some textbooks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Weierstrass function is continuous everywhere as long as \(0<a<1\text{.}\)
  • The Weierstrass function is nowhere differentiable if \(ab>1\text{.}\)

The figure plots the finite partial sum \(\sum_{n=1}^{8}a^n\cos(b^nx)\) with \(a=1/2\) and \(b=3\). The right panel magnifies the red window and illustrates the repeated roughness; the claim about the infinite limit function is stated above.

With \(0<a<1\) and \(ab>1\), add terms and zoom in: the graph keeps its wiggles at every scale, so it has no tangent anywhere.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n} \cos(3^n x)\) is a particular Weierstrass function.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Suppose \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) is a sequence of bounded functions on \(X\) such that the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty\) converges. Then, the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\rightrightarrows f\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bound \(|f_n(x)|\le M_n\) must hold for every \(x\in X\), with \(M_n\) independent of \(x\), and the numerical series \(\sum_n M_n\) must converge. For partial sums \(S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N f_n\), the same estimate controls every tail: \(|S_M(x)-S_N(x)|\le\sum_{n=N+1}^M M_n\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(M>N\). The right-hand side tends to zero independently of \(x\). Completeness of the real numbers gives a pointwise limit, and the common tail bound makes convergence uniform.

Here \(|f_n(x)|\le M_n=1/n^2\) for every \(x\). The tail bound \(\sum_{n>N}M_n\) is one band width for all \(x\) at once, which gives uniform convergence.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit function \(f\) is also bounded on \(X\).
  • Due to the uniform limit theorem, if each \(f_n\) is continuous, then the limit function \(f\) is continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• On \(X=\mathbb R\), take \(f_n(x)=2^{-n}\cos(3^nx)\). Since \(|\cos(3^nx)|\le1\) for every real \(x\), the bound \(|f_n(x)|\le M_n=2^{-n}\) holds simultaneously for all \(x\). The numerical series of bounds sums to \(1\), so the function series converges uniformly on \(\mathbb R\):
\[ \sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|f(x)-S_N(x)|\le\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty 2^{-n}=2^{-N}. \]

For example, \(N=10\) makes the error at most \(2^{-10}=1/1024\) at every real \(x\), using the same number of terms everywhere.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an inequality constraint written as \(g_i(x)\le b_i\), the constraint is binding at a feasible point \(x^\ast\) if

\[ g_i(x^\ast)=b_i. \]

It is nonbinding or slack at \(x^\ast\) if

\[ g_i(x^\ast)<b_i. \]

The same idea applies to constraints written in other equivalent sign conventions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A binding constraint is tight at the chosen point. A nonbinding constraint still has room left and does not directly limit the current choice.

At the illustrated optimum, \(g_1(x^\ast)=3.9\) binds and has multiplier \(\lambda_1>0\), while \(g_2(x^\ast)=2.2<3\) is slack and has \(\lambda_2=0\). In this example, relaxing the first constraint increases the maximum, whereas relaxing the second does not change it.

The constraint is binding when the optimum lies on the line \(x+y=b\) and slack when the peak is already feasible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Only binding inequality constraints can carry nonzero multipliers in standard Kuhn-Tucker conditions.
  • The set of binding constraints is often called the active set.
  • Changing a nonbinding constraint slightly usually does not change the optimum locally.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x\le 10\) and the optimum has \(x=10\), the constraint is binding.
  • If \(x+y\le 5\) and the chosen point is \((1,2)\), the constraint is nonbinding because \(1+2<5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an equality-constrained problem with Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda)\) and constraint Jacobian \(Dg(x^\ast)\), the bordered Hessian matrix is the block matrix

\[ \begin{pmatrix} 0 & Dg(x^\ast)\\ Dg(x^\ast)^\top & H_xL(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast) \end{pmatrix}, \]

with the exact block orientation depending on whether gradients are written as rows or columns.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bordered Hessian packages the constraint linearization and the objective curvature into one matrix for second-order constrained tests.

The constraint gradient borders the Hessian block; the determinant of the bordered matrix carries the second-order constrained test.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The grey \(m\times m\) zero block corresponds to the multiplier variables; the red \(m\times n\) border contains the constraint gradients.
  • The blue \(n\times n\) Hessian block is taken with respect to the choice variables, so the full matrix has size \((m+n)\times(m+n)\).
  • Determinants of selected bordered submatrices are used in bordered matrix tests.

For \(m<n\) equality constraints with independent gradients at a first-order candidate, the second-order sufficient conditions inspect the last \(n-m\) leading principal minors. Alternating signs starting with \((-1)^{m+1}\) give a strict local maximum; signs all equal to \((-1)^m\) give a strict local minimum. These tests check the curvature of \(L\) along directions tangent to the constraints.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one constraint \(g(x,y)=0\), a common bordered Hessian has first row and column built from \(g_x\) and \(g_y\).
  • For two equality constraints in three variables, the bordered Hessian has a \(2\) by \(2\) zero block and a \(3\) by \(3\) Hessian block.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(Q(x)=x^\top Ax\) with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) symmetric, and let the independent linear constraint set be \(Bx=0\) with \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=m\). The bordered matrix is

\[ H= \begin{pmatrix} 0_m & B\\ B^\top & A \end{pmatrix}. \]

Ignore the first \(2m\) leading principal minors. For \(k=2m+1,\ldots,m+n\):

  • If \((-1)^m\det(H_k)>0\) for all relevant \(k\), then \(Q\) is positive definite on the constraint set.
  • If \((-1)^{k-m}\det(H_k)>0\) for all relevant \(k\), then \(Q\) is negative definite on the constraint set.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The bordered matrix test checks curvature after linear constraints remove some directions. It is the constrained version of reading definiteness from determinant signs.

With one constraint in two variables, the sign of \(\det(H_3)\) decides definiteness on the constraint set, matching the sign of the form along the highlighted line \(T\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Definiteness on the whole space can change after restricting to a constraint set.
  • For positive definiteness, all relevant signs match \((-1)^m\).
  • For negative definiteness, relevant signs alternate and the full determinant has sign \((-1)^n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The form \(x_1^2-x_2^2\) is indefinite on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) but positive on the line \(x_1=2x_2\).
  • When \(n=2\) and \(m=1\), there is just one relevant minor: \(\det H<0\) gives positive definiteness of \(Q\) on the constraint line.
  • When \(n=3\) and \(m=1\), inspect \(\det(H_3)\) and \(\det(H_4)\) after ignoring the first two leading minors.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an interval and let \(\gamma\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a differentiable curve. Its velocity at \(t_0\) is

\[ \gamma'(t_0)= \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_1'(t_0)\\ \vdots\\ \gamma_n'(t_0) \end{pmatrix}. \]

If \(f\colon B\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at \(\gamma(t_0)\in B\), then

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(f\circ\gamma)(t_0) &=Df(\gamma(t_0))\gamma'(t_0)\\ &=\nabla f(\gamma(t_0))^\top\gamma'(t_0). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A curve describes motion through a multivariable state space. The chain rule says the value changes by combining the system's velocity with the local sensitivity of the value function.

The chain rule gives \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}f(\gamma(t))\big|_{t=t_0}=\nabla f(\gamma(t_0))\cdot\gamma'(t_0)\). In the figure, the velocity has a positive component along the gradient, so \(f\) increases along the curve at \(t_0\). The grey circles are level sets of \(f\).

Move \(t\): the rate of change of \(f(\gamma(t))\) (right) equals \(\nabla f(\gamma(t))^\top\gamma'(t)\), the gradient dotted with the velocity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The derivative of \(f(\gamma(t))\) is the total derivative of \(f\) applied to the velocity of \(\gamma\).
  • If the velocity is a unit vector, the formula is a directional derivative.
  • The curve case is the one-dimensional input version of the multivariable chain rule.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) and \(\gamma(t)=(t,2t)\), then \((f\circ\gamma)'(t)=10t\).
  • If \(f(x,y)=xy\) and \(\gamma(t)=(\mathrm{e}^t,t^2)\), then \((f\circ\gamma)'(t)=\mathrm{e}^t(t^2+2t)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an inequality constraint written as \(c_i(x)\le 0\) with multiplier \(\lambda_i\ge 0\), complementary slackness is the condition

\[ \lambda_i c_i(x^\ast)=0. \]

Equivalently, either the constraint is binding or its multiplier is zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Complementary slackness says that a constraint can matter through its multiplier only when it is actually tight.

On the left, the binding constraint holds back the maximum, with \(\nabla f=\lambda\nabla c\), \(\lambda>0\), and \(c=0\). On the right, the optimum lies in the interior and the multiplier is zero. The grey curves are objective level sets and the blue region is feasible.

Move \(b\) and the peak: either the constraint binds, or its multiplier is \(0\), so the product \(\lambda\,(b-g(x^*))\) is always \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(c_i(x^\ast)<0\), then \(\lambda_i=0\).
  • If \(\lambda_i>0\), then \(c_i(x^\ast)=0\).
  • The condition is part of the Kuhn-Tucker system for inequality-constrained optimization.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(x\le 4\) is written as \(x-4\le 0\) and the optimum has \(x=3\), then the multiplier must be \(0\).
  • If a multiplier for \(x\le 4\) is positive, then the optimum must satisfy \(x=4\).

Definition
docs.text:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A function \(f\colon C\to\mathbb R\) is convex if for all \(x,y\in C\) and all \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),

\[ f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y) \le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y). \]

It is concave if the inequality is reversed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A convex function lies below the straight interpolation of its values. A concave function lies above that interpolation.

The two graphs illustrate the segment test: on a convex domain \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), apply the defining inequality to every segment joining \(x,y\in C\). Reversing the inequality gives concavity; equivalently, \(f\) is concave if and only if \(-f\) is convex. For a twice continuously differentiable function on an open convex domain, the Hessian test checks positive semidefiniteness for convexity and negative semidefiniteness for concavity.

Along the segment from \(y\) to \(x\) (right), a convex function stays below the chord and a concave one above it.

Drag \(x\) and \(y\): for a convex \(f\) the surface along the segment stays below the chord between \(f(x)\) and \(f(y)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For convex functions, every local minimum is a global minimum.
  • For concave functions, every local maximum is a global maximum.
  • Strict convexity or strict concavity usually gives uniqueness of the corresponding optimum when it exists.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2\) is convex on \(\mathbb R^2\).
  • The function \(u(x,y)=\log x+\log y\) is concave on \((0,\infty)^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex if for every \(x,y\in C\) and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),

\[ \lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in C. \]

Equivalently, the whole line segment between any two points of \(C\) lies inside \(C\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A convex set has no inward gaps when viewed along straight lines. Moving directly between two feasible points stays feasible.

Drag \(x\) and \(y\) inside the set and move \(\lambda\): a set is convex when every such segment stays inside. Find a segment that leaves the L-shape.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Intersections of convex sets are convex.
  • Open balls, closed balls, half-spaces, and affine subspaces are convex.
  • A feasible region described by linear equality and weak linear inequality constraints is convex.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The set \(\{(x,y):x+y\le 1\}\) is convex because it is a half-space.
  • The unit disk \(\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le 1\}\) is convex, but the unit circle \(\{(x,y):x^2+y^2=1\}\) is not.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
In a parametric problem, the value function is the optimized objective value

\[ F(\alpha)=f(\gamma(\alpha);\alpha), \]

where \(\gamma(\alpha)\) is an optimizer. For equality constraints, define

\[ L(x,\mu;\alpha)=f(x;\alpha)+\sum_j\mu_jh_j(x;\alpha). \]

If smooth optimizer and multiplier functions satisfy the first-order conditions, then

\[ \frac{\partial F}{\partial\alpha_\ell}(\alpha) = \frac{\partial L}{\partial\alpha_\ell}(x,\mu;\alpha) \bigg|_{(x,\mu)=(\gamma(\alpha),\widetilde\mu(\alpha))}. \]

For mixed constraints, the same formula holds with the Lagrangian including the binding inequalities and equality constraints, provided the relevant bordered Hessian is nonsingular and the active set is smooth. In the special equality case \(h_j(x;\alpha)=\alpha_j-\widetilde h_j(x)\) with \(f\) independent of \(\alpha\), the multiplier is the shadow price:

\[ \frac{\partial F}{\partial\alpha_j}(\alpha)=\widetilde\mu_j(\alpha). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The envelope theorem computes how the best attainable value changes when a parameter changes. It avoids separately differentiating every movement of the optimizer.

In the illustrated example, the feasible choices do not depend on \(\alpha\), and \(V(\alpha)=\max_x f(x;\alpha)\) is the upper envelope of the grey curves obtained by fixing \(x\). At \(\alpha_0\), it touches the curve for \(x^\ast(\alpha_0)\) and shares its slope: \(V'(\alpha_0)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha}(x^\ast(\alpha_0);\alpha_0)\). The theorem above gives the corresponding formula when the constraints depend on the parameter.

The derivative of the optimal value \(F(\alpha)\) equals the partial derivative of the Lagrangian with respect to \(\alpha\) at the optimum, here the multiplier \(\mu\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The value function records the optimum as a function of parameters.
  • The envelope derivative is the direct parameter derivative of the Lagrangian at the optimal solution.
  • A shadow price is the marginal value of relaxing a constraint in the stated equality-constraint setup.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(f(x;\alpha)=\alpha x-x^2\), the envelope derivative is \(x^\ast(\alpha)\).
  • In utility maximization with income as a parameter, the multiplier on the budget equation measures marginal utility of income.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In an equation system \(F(x,y)=0\), the variables in \(x\) are called exogenous variables if they are treated as freely chosen inputs. The variables in \(y\) are called endogenous variables if the equation system is used to solve for them as functions of \(x\).

When possible, the implicit function theorem gives a local function \(g\) such that

\[ F(x,g(x))=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Exogenous variables are the knobs set from outside the system. Endogenous variables are the quantities the system determines in response.

The model takes the exogenous variables as inputs and solves for the endogenous variables. Under the local invertibility assumptions of the implicit function theorem, \(m\) equations determine \(m\) endogenous variables locally once the inputs are fixed. The split is a modelling choice: prices are endogenous in an equilibrium model but exogenous for a price-taker.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The distinction depends on how the equation system is being used, not only on the symbols.
  • The implicit function theorem requires the partial Jacobian with respect to the endogenous variables to be invertible in the square case.
  • Comparative statics studies how endogenous variables change when exogenous variables are perturbed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(x+y=10\), if \(x\) is chosen externally, then \(y=10-x\) is endogenous.
  • In supply and demand equilibrium, a tax can be exogenous while price and quantity are endogenous equilibrium variables.
