docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable and \(a\in\mathbb{R}\). For every \(t>0\) at which the MGF \(M_X(t)\) is finite,

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(X\geq a)\leq \mathrm{e}^{-ta}M_X(t). \end{aligned} \]

Optimizing over such \(t>0\) gives the tightest bound. The optimization must stay within the region where the MGF is finite, and the infimum need not be attained.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An exponential transformation turns a tail probability into an MGF bound. Optimizing the transformation parameter can yield a useful bound without finding the exact tail.

For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) and threshold \(a=3\), each \(t\in(0,1)\) gives the bound \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge3)\le e^{-3t}M_X(t)\). Minimising over \(t\) gives the tightest bound in this family.

Every \(t>0\) gives a bound \(\mathrm{e}^{-ta}M_X(t)\) (right). Move \(t\), or press the button, to find the \(t\) that makes it smallest.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\le\inf_{\{t>0:M_X(t)<\infty\}}\mathrm{e}^{-ta}M_X(t)\).
  • For \(t<0\) with finite MGF, \(\mathbb{P}(X\le a)\le \mathrm{e}^{-ta}M_X(t)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(2)\) and \(a=4\), choose \(t=\log2\): \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge4)\le \mathrm{e}^{-4\log2+2(2-1)}=\mathrm{e}^2/16\approx0.4618\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) and \(a=3\), choose \(t=2/3\): \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge3)\le \mathrm{e}^{-2}/(1-2/3)=3\mathrm{e}^{-2}\approx0.4060\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(\lambda>0\), \(0\le p\le1\) and \(q=1-p\). If \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\) and, given \(N=n\), \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\) for every \(n\ge0\), then \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda p)\) and \(N-X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda q)\), and \(X\) and \(N-X\) are independent.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A Poisson total divided by binomial labeling produces two independent Poisson counts, even though their sum is the original total.

With a Poisson total the two counts are independent, e.g. \(\lambda=10\), \(p=0.3\) gives \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(3)\) and \(N-X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(7)\). For a fixed total \(n\) they are dependent, since they must add up to \(n\).

\(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\) eggs each hatch with probability \(p\). The hatched and unhatched counts are independent Poisson variables.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(Y=N-X\), then \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda p)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda(1-p))\) independently.
  • Given \(N=n\), the two counts add to \(n\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y\mid N=n)=-np(1-p)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(10)\) and \(p=0.3\), then \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(3)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(7)\) independently.
  • With \(\lambda=4\), \(p=1/2\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=0,Y=0)=\mathrm{e}^{-2}\mathrm{e}^{-2}=\mathrm{e}^{-4}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be continuous random variables with joint density \(f_{X,Y}\), and let \(y\) satisfy \(f_Y(y)>0\). The conditional CDF of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y) =\int_{-\infty}^x f_{X\mid Y}(t\mid y)\,\mathrm{d} t. \end{aligned} \]

Here

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{X\mid Y}(t\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(t,y)}{f_Y(y)}. \end{aligned} \]

We write \(F_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq x\mid Y=y)\). Note that for continuous \(Y\), this cannot be defined by the elementary formula \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)/\mathbb{P}(B)\), because \(\mathbb{P}(Y=y)=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A conditional CDF gives threshold probabilities within a specified conditional distribution.

The diagram shows \(X\mid Y=y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,y)\) for \(0<y<1\), with \(F_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=x/y\) for \(0<x<y\). For each fixed \(y\), this is an ordinary CDF in \(x\), and \(F_{X\mid Y}(y/2\mid y)=1/2\).

Fix \(y\) and move \(x\): \(F_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) accumulates the conditional density up to \(x\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For every \(y\) with \(f_Y(y)>0\), it is a nondecreasing, right-continuous CDF in \(x\).
  • Where differentiation is justified, \(\partial F_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)/\partial x=f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) except possibly on a set of zero length.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the uniform conditional law on \((0,y)\), \(F_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=x/y\) for \(0<x<y\), so \(F_{X\mid Y}(y/2\mid y)=1/2\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) is independent of \(Y\), then \(F_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-2x}\) for \(x\ge0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(Y\) be a continuous random variable and \(A\) an event with \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\). The conditional CDF of \(Y\) given \(A\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{Y\mid A}(y)=\mathbb{P}(Y\leq y\mid A). \end{aligned} \]

Where the derivative exists, the conditional density of \(Y\) given \(A\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{Y\mid A}(y)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} y}F_{Y\mid A}(y). \end{aligned} \]

Equivalently, by Bayes' rule,

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{Y\mid A}(y)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\mid Y=y)f_Y(y)}{\mathbb{P}(A)}. \end{aligned} \]

Here \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid Y=y)\) is the conditional probability given the value \(y\), determined except possibly on a set of values \(y\) of probability zero, where it may be chosen arbitrarily; it is not an elementary ratio, whose denominator \(\mathbb{P}(Y=y)\) would be zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditioning on an event reweights the original density by how compatible each value is with that event.

In the illustrated example, \(Y\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) and \(A=\{Y>1\}\): keep the part of the density on \(A\) and divide by \(\mathbb{P}(A)\), so \(f_{Y\mid A}(y)=f_Y(y)/\mathrm{e}^{-2}\) for \(y>1\) and \(0\) elsewhere.

Move \(c\): on \(A=\{Y>c\}\) the density is divided by \(\mathbb{P}(A)\), and outside \(A\) it is \(0\). For \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) the result is the same density shifted to start at \(c\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A=\{Y\in B\}\), then \(f_{Y\mid A}(y)=\mathbf{1}_{B}(y)f_Y(y)/\mathbb{P}(Y\in B)\) except possibly on a set of zero length.
  • The conditional density integrates to one whenever \(\mathbb{P}(A)>0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(A=\{Y>1/2\}\), the conditional density is \(2\) on \((1/2,1)\).
  • For \(Y\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) and \(A=\{Y>1\}\), the conditional density is \(2\mathrm{e}^{-2(y-1)}\) for \(y>1\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: Let \(\mathbb{E}|Y|<\infty\). If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent (\(X\perp Y\)), then \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=\mathbb{E}[Y]\) almost surely.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
If the response is independent of the observed variable, observing that variable cannot change the response’s expected value.

The red lines show \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\). For independent fair dice this equals \(3.5\). A constant conditional mean does not imply independence: if \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)\) and \(X=Y^2\), then \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=0\) almost surely, yet \(X\) and \(Y\) are dependent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Independence gives \(\mathbb{E}[h(Y)\mid X]=\mathbb{E}[h(Y)]\) for every integrable \(h(Y)\).
  • The converse for the identity map fails: a constant conditional mean does not by itself imply independence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent fair dice \(X,Y\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=3.5\).
  • For \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)\) and \(X=Y^2\), symmetry gives \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=0=\mathbb{E}Y\), yet \(X\) and \(Y\) are dependent.

docs.title: Conditional Expectation Given a Random Variable
Definition
docs.text:
For integrable \(Y\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) is a function \(g(X)\) of \(X\) satisfying the averaging identity for every event determined by \(X\). When a conditional PMF or PDF exists,

\[ \begin{aligned} &g(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\\ &=\begin{cases}\sum_y y\,p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x),\\ \quad Y\text{ discrete},\\[4pt] \int_{\mathbb{R}}y\,f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\,\mathrm{d}y,\\ \quad Y\text{ has a conditional density}.\end{cases} \end{aligned} \]

The sum or integral is selected by the conditional law of \(Y\), not by whether the conditioning variable \(X\) is discrete or continuous.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditioning on a variable produces a new random variable: the predicted average changes with the value observed. Evaluating it at a fixed value gives an ordinary number.

In the illustrated triangular model, the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=x\) is uniform on \((0,x)\), with mean \(g(x)=x/2\). Evaluating this function at the random \(X\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=g(X)=X/2\).

Each value of \(X\) has its own conditional mean \(g(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\) (right); \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=g(X)\) is a random variable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=g(X)\) is determined up to almost-sure equality.
  • For every interval \(B\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mathbf{1}_{\{X\in B\}}]=\mathbb{E}[g(X)\mathbf{1}_{\{X\in B\}}]\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Pois}(x)\) with \(X\ge0\) integrable, then \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=X\).
  • For joint density \(2\) on \(0<y<x<1\), \(Y\mid X=x\) is uniform on \((0,x)\), so \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]=X/2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) have joint density \(f_{X,Y}\), and let \(y\) satisfy \(0<f_Y(y)<\infty\). The conditional PDF of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}. \end{aligned} \]

The denominator is the density \(f_Y(y)\), not \(\mathbb{P}(Y=y)=0\). On a set of conditioning values \(y\) of probability zero, for example finitely many points, conditional laws may be chosen arbitrarily.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A conditional density describes one variable after a continuous value of another is observed. It uses a ratio of densities, rather than dividing by the probability of a zero-probability event.

In the illustrated triangular model, \(X\mid Y=y\) is uniform on \((0,y)\) for \(0<y<1\). Dividing the joint density by \(f_Y(y)\) rescales the horizontal slice to have total area \(1\).

Move \(y\): the slice \(f_{X,Y}(\cdot,y)\) divided by \(f_Y(y)\) is the conditional density, with total area \(1\). On the triangle it is uniform on \((0,y)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For every \(y\) with \(0<f_Y(y)<\infty\), \(\int f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,\mathrm{d}x=1\).
  • \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)f_Y(y)\) except possibly on a set of zero area.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For joint density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=1/y\) on \(0<x<y\): a uniform conditional law.
  • For independent \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Exp}(3)\), \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=2\mathrm{e}^{-2x}\) for \(x>0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) and a value \(y\) with \(p_Y(y)>0\), the conditional PMF of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)}, \quad p_Y(y)>0. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A conditional PMF rescales the part of a joint table consistent with the observed discrete value.

For the column \(Y=1\) in the diagram, \(\mathbb{P}(Y=1)=0.6\). Dividing each joint mass in that column by \(0.6\) gives the conditional probabilities, which sum to \(1\).

Fix \(Y=y\): keep that row of masses and divide by \(p_Y(y)\) so that they sum to \(1\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(p_Y(y)>0\), \(\sum_xp_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=1\).
  • \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)p_Y(y)\).

docs.title: Conditional Variance Given a Random Variable
Definition
docs.text:
For \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2]<\infty\), conditional variance is

\[ \begin{aligned} &\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\\ &\quad=\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])^2\mid X]\\ &\quad=\mathbb{E}[Y^2\mid X]-(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])^2. \end{aligned} \]

These identities hold almost surely.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Conditional variance measures the remaining spread of a response once the observed information is fixed. It is itself a random variable.

The diagram shows \(Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Pois}(x)\). Its conditional standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=x)}=\sqrt{x}\), so larger \(x\) gives more spread. Evaluating at the random \(X\) gives the random variable \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=X\).

\(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=x)\) is the spread within group \(x\) (right); averaged over \(X\) it gives \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\ge0\) almost surely.
  • For real constants \(a,b\), \(\operatorname{Var}(a+bY\mid X)=b^2\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\) with \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]<\infty\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=X\).
  • If \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,X)\) with \(0\le X\le1\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=nX(1-X)\).

docs.title: Method
docs.text: When \(Y\) has a natural conditional structure, for example \(Y\mid X=x\sim\operatorname{Pois}(x)\), compute \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) by decomposing it with Eve's law (total variance). This is a calculation method rather than a separate theorem; it needs \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2]<\infty\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Choose information that makes a response’s mean and variance easy, then combine them using total variance. This avoids finding the marginal distribution.

For equally likely \(X=1\) and \(X=3\) with \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\), the average conditional variance is \((1+3)/2=2\). The variance of the conditional means \(1\) and \(3\) is \(1\). The total variance is therefore \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2+1=3\), without first deriving the distribution of \(Y\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Compute \(m(X)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) and \(v(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\) first; then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[v(X)]+\operatorname{Var}(m(X))\).
  • For \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\) with finite second moment of \(X\), \(\mathbb{E}Y=\mathbb{E}X\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}X+\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is equally likely to be \(1\) or \(3\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\), then \(\mathbb{E}Y=2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2+1=3\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/2)\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(4,0.2+0.6X)\), the within variance is \(0.64\), the conditional-mean variance is \(1.44\), and total variance is \(2.08\).

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
When approximating \(\mathbb{P}(X\leq k)\) for an integer-valued random variable \(X\) by a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma>0\), use

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(X\leq k)\approx\Phi\!\left(\frac{k+1/2-\mu}{\sigma}\right) \end{aligned} \]

(and similarly for \(\geq\)). The half-unit shift is an approximation rule, not an exact identity.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A normal area approximating an integer-valued probability should cover the half-unit cells around the included integers.

In the illustrated example, \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.5)\) with the \(\mathcal{N}(50,25)\) density. The bar of \(k\) covers \([k-\tfrac12,k+\tfrac12]\), so \(\mathbb{P}(45\le X\le55)\approx\Phi(1.1)-\Phi(-1.1)\approx0.7287\) (exact: \(0.7287\)).

The bars for \(X\le k\) end at \(k+\tfrac12\), not at \(k\). Compare both normal answers with the exact probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge k)\approx1-\Phi((k-1/2-\mu)/\sigma)\).
  • For integers \(a\le b\), \(\mathbb{P}(a\le X\le b)\approx\Phi((b+1/2-\mu)/\sigma)-\Phi((a-1/2-\mu)/\sigma)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.5)\), \(\mathbb{P}(X=50)\approx\Phi(0.1)-\Phi(-0.1)\approx0.0797\).
  • For the same \(X\), \(\mathbb{P}(45\le X\le55)\approx\Phi(1.1)-\Phi(-1.1)\approx0.7287\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) and an observed value \(x\) with \(0<f_X(x)<\infty\),

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,f_Y(y)}{f_X(x)}. \end{aligned} \]

Equalities between conditional densities may fail on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Bayes’ rule reverses a conditional density: likelihood times prior density, normalized by the marginal density of the observation.

The illustrated joint density equals \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\). For the observation \(X=0.4\), the prior density \(f_Y(y)=2y\) and likelihood \(f_{X\mid Y}(0.4\mid y)=1/y\) for \(0.4<y<1\) have a constant product. The posterior is therefore uniform on \((0.4,1)\); more generally, \(f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=1/(1-x)\) for \(0<x<y<1\).

Observe \(x\): the prior \(f_Y\) is reweighted by \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) and divided by \(f_X(x)\), giving the posterior \(f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The normalizing density is \(f_X(x)=\int f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)f_Y(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\).
  • For fixed \(x\), \(f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\) is proportional in \(y\) to likelihood times prior.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=1/(1-x)\) on \(x<y<1\).
  • For independent \(X,Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), likelihood and marginal cancel, so the posterior density of \(Y\) remains \(1\) on \((0,1)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) for which the conditional density \(f_{X\mid Y}\) exists,

\[ \begin{aligned} f_X(x)=\int f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,f_Y(y)\,\mathrm{d} y \end{aligned} \]

for every \(x\) except possibly on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An unconditional density is a weighted mixture of conditional densities, using the density of the conditioning variable as the weight.

For \(X\mid Y=y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,y)\) and \(f_Y(y)=2y\) on \((0,1)\), averaging the conditional densities gives \(f_X(x)=\int_x^1(1/y)2y\,\mathrm{d}y=2(1-x)\) for \(0<x<1\).

Cut the range of \(Y\) into \(m\) slices: each contributes \(f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y_j)f_Y(y_j)\Delta y\). Raise \(m\) and the sum becomes \(f_X\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The event form is \(\mathbb{P}(X\in A)=\int\mathbb{P}(X\in A\mid Y=y)f_Y(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\).
  • Integrating the conditional density mixture over \(x\) gives total probability one.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(f_X(x)=\int_x^1(1/y)(2y)\,\mathrm{d}y=2(1-x)\) for \(0<x<1\).
  • If \(Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(X\mid Y=y\sim\operatorname{Bern}(y)\), then \(\mathbb{P}(X=1)=\int_0^1y\,\mathrm{d}y=1/2\), using the event form.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A sequence of random variables \(X_n\) converges in distribution to \(X\) if the CDFs of the \(X_n\) converge to the CDF of \(X\) wherever the latter is continuous:

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x) \end{aligned} \]

for every point \(x\) at which \(F_X\) is continuous. This is written as \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}X\). Convergence at the jump points of \(F_X\) is not required, and the variables may be defined on different probability spaces.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The distributions approach a limiting distribution through their CDFs. The variables need not approach one another along the same sample paths.

The illustrated calculation gives \(X_n=1/n\). \(F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)\) for every \(x\ne0\), so \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}0\). At the jump \(x=0\) of the limit, \(F_{X_n}(0)=0\not\to1=F_X(0)\); convergence is only required where \(F_X\) is continuous.

Raise \(n\) and watch the CDF of \(Z_n\) close in on \(\Phi\). For a discrete start the CDF keeps its jumps, yet the largest gap still shrinks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution.
  • Convergence in distribution to a constant \(c\) implies convergence in probability to \(c\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X_n=1/n\), its CDF converges to the CDF of the constant \(0\) at every continuity point \(x\ne0\), so \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}0\).
  • For \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and \(X_n=(-1)^nZ\), every \(X_n\) has the law of \(Z\), so \(X_n\xrightarrow{d}Z\), but \(X_n\) does not converge in probability to \(Z\): odd-index differences are \(2|Z|\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) and \(X\) be random variables on a common probability space. The sequence converges in probability to \(X\), written \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}X\), if for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[ \mathbb{P}(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }n\to\infty. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The probability of a fixed-size error tends to zero. The definition concerns each sample size’s error probability, rather than convergence of every sample path.

In the illustrated example, \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}c\) means: for every tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n-c|>\varepsilon)\to0\). The shaded tails outside the band \([c-\varepsilon,c+\varepsilon]\) shrink as \(n\) grows.

Here \(X_n=\bar X_n\) and \(X=\mu\). Pick any \(\varepsilon\): the probability of an error larger than \(\varepsilon\) tends to \(0\), which is exactly the definition.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability.
  • Convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution; the converses generally fail.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X_n=1/n\), then for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n|>\varepsilon)=0\) for sufficiently large \(n\), so \(X_n\xrightarrow{P}0\).
  • If \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/n)\), then for \(0<\varepsilon<1\), \(\mathbb{P}(|X_n|>\varepsilon)=1/n\to0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For independent continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the density of \(X+Y\) is the convolution of their densities; independence is what lets the joint density factor into the two marginal densities:

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{X+Y}(t)=\int f_X(x)\,f_Y(t-x)\,\mathrm{d} x. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A sum can reach a value in many ways. Convolution integrates over the possible first summand and the matching second summand.

For independent \(X,Y\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), the density of their sum at \(t=2\) is the green area: \(f_{X+Y}(2)=\int_0^2e^{-x}e^{-(2-x)}\,\mathrm{d}x=2e^{-2}\), marked by the red point. More generally, \(f_{X+Y}(t)=te^{-t}\) for \(t>0\).

Move \(t\): \(f_Y(t-x)\) is \(f_Y\) flipped and shifted, and the area of its product with \(f_X\) is \(f_{X+Y}(t)\), traced on the right.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For independent discrete variables, \(p_{X+Y}(t)=\sum_xp_X(x)p_Y(t-x)\).
  • For independent variables with densities, the integral is over \(x\) for which both density factors are nonzero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) variables, \(f_{X+Y}(t)=\int_0^t\mathrm{e}^{-x}\mathrm{e}^{-(t-x)}\,\mathrm{d}x=t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) for \(t>0\).
  • For independent fair Bernoulli variables, the sum has masses \(1/4,1/2,1/4\) at \(0,1,2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with \(0<\operatorname{Var}(X)<\infty\) and \(0<\operatorname{Var}(Y)<\infty\), the correlation of \(X\) and \(Y\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}\in[-1,1]. \end{aligned} \]

Correlation is undefined if either variance is zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Correlation standardizes covariance into a unit-free measure of linear association. Zero correlation rules out linear association but can coexist with dependence.

The left panel shows the exact decreasing relation \(Y=5-2X\). The middle panel shows a positive but imperfect linear association. In the right panel, \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)\) and \(Y=X^2\) are uncorrelated but dependent, illustrating that correlation measures linear association.

Change the slope and the noise: the correlation measures how tightly the points follow a line. With \(Y=X^2\) it is \(0\), although \(Y\) depends on \(X\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(-1\le\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)\le1\).
  • Absolute correlation is \(1\) exactly when \(Y=a+bX\) almost surely for constants \(a,b\) with \(b\ne0\); its sign is the sign of \(b\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y=5-2X\) and \(X\) has positive finite variance, the correlation is \(-1\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1)\) and \(Y=X^2\), symmetry gives \(\mathbb{E}X=\mathbb{E}[X^3]=0\), so correlation is \(0\) although \(Y\) is determined by \(X\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For square-integrable \(X,Y\), covariance is

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)&=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}X)(Y-\mathbb{E}Y)]\\ &=\mathbb{E}[XY]-\mathbb{E}X\,\mathbb{E}Y. \end{aligned} \]

Independence implies zero covariance; the converse generally fails.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Covariance measures whether two variables tend to deviate from their means in the same direction. It also accounts for dependence in the variance of a sum.

Points in the green quadrants contribute positive products of deviations, while points in the red quadrants contribute negative products. Covariance averages these products, taking both their magnitudes and probabilities into account.

Points where \(X\) and \(Y\) are on the same side of their means count positively, the others negatively; the covariance averages these products.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Cov}(a+bX,c+dY)=bd\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y=2X\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=3\), then \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=6\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=27\).
  • For independent fair Bernoulli variables, \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=1/4\) and \(\mathbb{E}X\mathbb{E}Y=1/4\), so covariance is zero.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be iid continuous random variables with PDF \(f\) and CDF \(F\), let \(X_{(1)}\le\cdots\le X_{(n)}\) be their order statistics, and write \(\bar F=1-F\). For \(1\le k\le n\), the \(k\)th order statistic has density

\[ \begin{aligned} f_{X_{(k)}}(x)= n f(x) {\binom{n-1}{k -1}} F(x)^{k-1} \bar F(x)^{n-k}. \end{aligned} \]

The formula holds for every \(x\) except possibly on a set of zero length, for example at finitely many points.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An order statistic is a sorted observation. Its density combines the chance of an observation near a value with the chances that the required numbers of observations fall below and above it.

For three iid \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) observations, the \(k\)th order statistic has density \(f_{X_{(k)}}(x)=3\binom{2}{k-1}x^{k-1}(1-x)^{3-k}\) for \(0<x<1\) and \(k=1,2,3\). The factors account for one observation near \(x\), \(k-1\) below it and \(3-k\) above it.

Change \(n\) and \(k\): the \(k\)th smallest of \(n\) draws has density \(nf(x)\binom{n-1}{k-1}F(x)^{k-1}\bar F(x)^{n-k}\), moving right as \(k\) grows.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the maximum of three iid \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) variables, the density is \(3x^2\) on \((0,1)\) and \(\mathbb{P}(X_{(3)}\le1/2)=1/8\).
  • The minimum of four independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) variables has tail \(\mathrm{e}^{-8x}\) for \(x\ge0\), hence distribution \(\operatorname{Exp}(8)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2]<\infty\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]+\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]). \end{aligned} \]

Consequence: the residual \(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) is uncorrelated with every function \(h(X)\) that has \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)^2]<\infty\) (or satisfies another assumption that makes the products integrable):

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X],\,h(X))=0. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Total spread consists of average spread within conditional groups plus spread between their conditional means.

The first term in the total-variance identity measures the average spread within groups around the red group means. The second measures the spread of those means around \(\mathbb{E}Y\).

Move the group means and spreads: \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) is the average spread within the groups plus the spread of the group means.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])\le\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).
  • The residual \(R=Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) has mean zero and \(\operatorname{Cov}(R,h(X))=0\) for every square-integrable \(h(X)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}X+\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/2+1/4=3/4\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,X)\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=n/6+n^2/12=n(n+2)/12\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For every real \(x\),

\[ \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{x}{n}\right)^n = \mathrm{e}^x. \]

Here \(1+x/n>0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), which the usual logarithm argument needs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Many small multiplicative changes combine into an exponential. This limit also explains how rare-event binomial probabilities approach Poisson probabilities.

For each fixed \(x\), \((1+x/n)^n\to e^x\). Taking \(x=-\lambda\) gives \((1-\lambda/n)^n\to e^{-\lambda}\), the limiting zero-count probability for rare-event binomials.

Raise \(n\): the curve \((1+x/n)^n\) approaches \(\mathrm{e}^x\) for every \(x\). Point at the plot to compare the values at one \(x\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For fixed \(x\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+x/n)^n=\mathrm{e}^x\).
  • For fixed \(\lambda>0\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}(1-\lambda/n)^n=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \((1+1/n)^n\to \mathrm{e}\).
  • If \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,3/n)\) for \(n\ge3\), then \(\mathbb{P}(X_n=0)=(1-3/n)^n\to \mathrm{e}^{-3}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For shape \(r>0\) and rate \(\lambda>0\), \(X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(r,\lambda)\) has density

\[ f_X(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\lambda^r}{\Gamma(r)}x^{r-1}\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x},&x>0,\\0,&x\le0.\end{cases} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The gamma family extends exponential waiting times. For a positive integer shape, it is the distribution of a sum of independent exponential waits with a common rate.

The diagram shows gamma densities with rate \(\lambda=1\). For a positive integer shape \(r\), a \(\operatorname{Gamma}(r,\lambda)\) variable is the sum of \(r\) independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) waiting times, with mean \(r/\lambda\) and variance \(r/\lambda^2\).

Change the shape \(r\) and the rate \(\lambda\). At \(r=1\) the density is \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\); integer \(r\) gives the waiting time for \(r\) exponential events.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In shape-rate notation, \(\mathbb{E}X=r/\lambda\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=r/\lambda^2\).
  • \(M_X(t)=(\lambda/(\lambda-t))^r\) for \(t<\lambda\); shape \(r=1\) gives the exponential law.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For shape \(r=2\) and rate \(\lambda=1\), the density is \(x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) on \(x>0\), the mean is \(2\), and the variance is \(2\).
  • The sum of three independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) waits has \(\operatorname{Gamma}(3,2)\) distribution, with mean \(3/2\) and variance \(3/4\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be nonnegative and nondecreasing on a domain containing the values of \(X\) and the threshold \(a\). If \(f(a)>0\) and \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]<\infty\), then

\[ \mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb{E}[f(X)]}{f(a)}. \]

This follows from \(f(X)\ge f(a)\mathbf{1}_{\{X\ge a\}}\). For ordinary Markov, take \(f(x)=x\) on \([0,\infty)\) and require \(X\ge0\), \(a>0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A nonnegative transformed average bounds the chance of a large value. Choosing different increasing transformations produces different tail bounds.

For nonnegative nondecreasing \(f\), \(f(x)\ge f(a)\mathbf{1}_{\{x\ge a\}}\) for all \(x\). Taking expectations gives \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\ge f(a)\,\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\). A steeper \(f\) (dashed) uses a higher moment and can give a smaller bound.

Compare \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\) with \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]/f(a)\) for \(f(x)=x\) and \(f(x)=x^2\): the faster-growing \(f\) gives the sharper bound far out in the tail.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(X\ge0\) and \(a>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\le\mathbb{E}X/a\).
  • For \(X\ge0\) and \(r>0\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge a)\le\mathbb{E}[X^r]/a^r\) whenever the moment is finite.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A nonnegative loss with mean \(10\) satisfies \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge50)\le10/50=0.2\).
  • If \(X\ge0\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=9\), then \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge6)\le9/36=1/4\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be an integrable random variable taking values in an interval on which \(g\) is convex. If \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) exists (in the finite-valued form, \(\mathbb{E}|g(X)|<\infty\)), then

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[g(X)]\geq g(\mathbb{E} X). \end{aligned} \]

The inequality reverses for concave \(g\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For a convex function, averaging before applying the function gives no larger a value than applying it first and then averaging.

For a convex function, the chord shown lies above the graph. In the uniform example, \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=1/3\ge1/4=(\mathbb{E}X)^2\).

\(X\) takes two values; \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) lies on the chord and \(g(\mathbb{E}X)\) on the curve. Convex \(g\) puts the chord above, concave \(g\) below.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a concave function, the inequality reverses.
  • If \(g\) is strictly convex and both sides are finite, equality holds exactly when \(X\) is constant almost surely.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(g(x)=x^2\) and \(X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), \(g(\mathbb{E}X)=1/4\le\mathbb{E}[X^2]=1/3\).
  • For \(X=1\) or \(3\) with equal probability, concavity of \(\log\) gives \(\mathbb{E}\log X=\frac12\log3\le\log2=\log\mathbb{E}X\).

docs.title: Joint CDF of Continuous Random Variables
Definition
docs.text:
The joint CDF of a random pair \((X,Y)\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{X,Y}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq x,Y\leq y). \end{aligned} \]

It exists for every random pair, including pairs without a joint PDF.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The joint CDF accumulates probability in a lower-left region of the plane. A joint density allows it to be calculated by a double integral.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With a joint density, \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)=\int_{-\infty}^x\int_{-\infty}^yf_{X,Y}(u,v)\,\mathrm{d}v\,\mathrm{d}u\).
  • Rectangle probabilities follow by inclusion-exclusion: \(F(b,d)-F(a,d)-F(b,c)+F(a,c)\) for \((a,b]\times(c,d]\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) variables, \(F_{X,Y}(0.4,0.5)=0.2\).
  • If \(Y=X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), then \(F_{X,Y}(0.4,0.5)=0.4\); this pair has no joint PDF.

docs.title: Joint CDF of Discrete Random Variables
Definition
docs.text:
The joint CDF of a random pair \((X,Y)\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{X,Y}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq x,Y\leq y). \end{aligned} \]

The definition applies to any random pair; this page develops its discrete form.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The joint CDF measures the probability that two variables simultaneously lie below specified thresholds.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(F_{X,Y}(x,y)=\sum_{u\le x}\sum_{v\le y}p_{X,Y}(u,v)\).
  • \(F_X(x)=\lim_{y\to\infty}F_{X,Y}(x,y)\) and similarly for \(Y\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent fair dice, \(F_{X,Y}(2,3)=(2/6)(3/6)=1/6\).
  • If \(X=Y\) is Bernoulli with parameter \(0.4\), then \(F_{X,Y}(0,0)=0.6\), rather than \(0.6^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random pair \((X,Y)\) is jointly continuous with joint PDF \(f_{X,Y}\) if, for every region \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\), such as a rectangle, a disc or a half-plane,

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}((X,Y)\in B)=\iint_B f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} y. \end{aligned} \]

Continuous marginals alone do not guarantee a joint density: with \(Y=X\) both marginals can be continuous while all the probability lies on a line.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A joint density spreads probability over the plane. Probability of a region is its integral over that region.

The illustrated density has height \(2\) over a triangle of area \(1/2\), so its total volume is \(2(1/2)=1\). The probability of a subregion is the volume under the surface above that region.

Choose \(a\) and \(b\): \(\mathbb{P}(X\le a,Y\le b)\) is the volume under \(f_{X,Y}\) over the shaded rectangle. Try the course examples.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(f_{X,Y}\ge0\) and \(\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=1\).
  • A region of planar area zero has probability zero under a joint density.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For density \(1\) on \((0,1)^2\), \(\mathbb{P}(X<1/2,Y<1/3)=1/6\).
  • For density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(\mathbb{P}(Y<1/2)=\int_0^{1/2}\int_0^y2\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=1/4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the joint PMF is

\[ \begin{aligned} p_{X,Y}(x,y)=\mathbb{P}(X=x,Y=y). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A joint PMF assigns probability to each pair of discrete values and describes how the variables behave together.

Each disc is a mass \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\). Choose \(a\) and \(b\) and add the masses in the corner to get \(\mathbb{P}(X\le a,Y\le b)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\ge0\) and \(\sum_x\sum_yp_{X,Y}(x,y)=1\).
  • For a set \(B\) of pairs, \(\mathbb{P}((X,Y)\in B)=\sum_{(x,y)\in B}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two independent fair dice have \(p_{X,Y}(i,j)=1/36\) for \(i,j=1,\ldots,6\).
  • If \(X=Y\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/2)\), the masses at \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\) are \(1/2\), and all other masses are zero.

docs.title: Law of Total Expectation over a Partition
Theorem
docs.text:
If \(\{A_i\}\) is a finite or countable partition of the sample space and \(Y\) is integrable, then

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[Y]=\sum_i\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A_i]\,\mathbb{P}(A_{i}), \end{aligned} \]

where terms with \(\mathbb{P}(A_i)=0\) are omitted. The law of total probability (LOTP) is the special case \(Y=\mathbf{1}_B\) of this law of total expectation (LOTE).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The overall average is a weighted average of the averages within disjoint cases.

In the diagram, the two cases have probabilities \(0.3\) and \(0.7\) and conditional means \(10\) and \(2\). Their weighted mean is \(0.3\cdot10+0.7\cdot2=4.4\). The dashed level has the same total area as the two bars.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a partition \(\{A_i\}\), \(\mathbb{E}Y=\sum_{i:\mathbb{P}(A_i)>0}\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A_i]\mathbb{P}(A_i)\).
  • Putting \(Y=\mathbf{1}_B\) gives the law of total probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If two equally likely customer groups have mean spending \(20\) and \(50\), overall mean spending is \(35\).
  • If \(\mathbb{P}(A)=0.3\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A]=10\), and \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid A^c]=2\), then \(\mathbb{E}Y=0.3(10)+0.7(2)=4.4\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For a jointly continuous pair \((X,Y)\) and a function \(g\) with \(\iint |g(x,y)|f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y<\infty\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]=\iint g(x,y)\,f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} y. \end{aligned} \]

For \(g\ge0\) the formula also holds without this assumption, as an extended (possibly infinite) expectation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A function of a continuous pair is averaged by integrating it against the joint density. The pair need not be independent.

The illustrated calculation gives \(\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]=\iint g(x,y)f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\). Weight each value of \(g\) by the joint density. Here \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1xy\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=\tfrac14\), without finding the distribution of \(XY\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(g(x,y)=xy\), the integral gives \(\mathbb{E}[XY]\).
  • For an indicator of a region \(B\), it gives \(\mathbb{P}((X,Y)\in B)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent uniform coordinates on \((0,1)\), \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\int_0^1\int_0^1xy\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=1/4\).
  • For density \(2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), \(\mathbb{E}X=\int_0^1\int_0^y2x\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y=1/3\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For a discrete pair \((X,Y)\) and a function \(g\) with \(\sum_{x,y}|g(x,y)|p_{X,Y}(x,y)<\infty\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]=\sum_x\sum_y g(x,y)\,p_{X,Y}(x,y). \end{aligned} \]

For \(g\ge0\) the formula also holds without this assumption, as an extended (possibly infinite) expectation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function of two variables can be averaged directly using their joint PMF, even when the variables are dependent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Choosing \(g(x,y)=xy\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[XY]\).
  • Choosing \(g(x,y)=\mathbf{1}_{\{x+y\le c\}}\) gives \(\mathbb{P}(X+Y\le c)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For independent fair Bernoulli variables, \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=1(1/4)=1/4\).
  • For independent fair dice, \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{\{X+Y=7\}}]=6(1/36)=1/6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a jointly continuous pair \((X,Y)\) with joint density \(f_{X,Y}\), the marginal PDF of \(X\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} f_X(x)=\int f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y, \end{aligned} \]

where the integral runs over the values allowed for the other coordinate; the density is zero outside the joint support.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Integrating out one coordinate of a joint density leaves the density of the other coordinate.

For the illustrated triangular density, integrating over the other coordinate gives \(f_X(x)=\int_x^1 2\,\mathrm{d}y=2(1-x)\) for \(0<x<1\) and \(f_Y(y)=\int_0^y2\,\mathrm{d}x=2y\) for \(0<y<1\). The red and green slices represent these two integrals.

Move \(x\): integrating the joint density along the vertical slice gives \(f_X(x)\). For the triangle example this is \(2(1-x)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(f_Y(y)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  • Each marginal integrates to one, since the joint density does.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)=2\) on \(0<x<y<1\), then \(f_X(x)=2(1-x)\) for \(0<x<1\).
  • For the same triangle, \(f_Y(y)=\int_0^y2\,\mathrm{d}x=2y\) for \(0<y<1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a discrete random pair \((X,Y)\) with joint PMF \(p_{X,Y}\), the marginal PMF of \(X\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} p_X(x)=\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y), \end{aligned} \]

where the sum runs over all possible values \(y\) of \(Y\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A marginal PMF describes one component of a random pair after the other component has been summed out.

Move \(x\): \(p_X(x)\) adds the masses in the column \(X=x\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(p_X(x)=\sum_yp_{X,Y}(x,y)\) and \(p_Y(y)=\sum_xp_{X,Y}(x,y)\).
  • Marginalization preserves normalization: \(\sum_xp_X(x)=1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If the masses at \((0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\) are \(0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\), then \(p_X(0)=0.3\) and \(p_Y(1)=0.6\).
  • For independent fair dice, summing the six masses \(1/36\) in a row gives \(p_X(i)=1/6\).

docs.title: Location and Scale Property of the MGF
Proposition
docs.text:
For real constants \(a\) and \(b\) (no positivity is needed for \(b\)),

\[ \begin{aligned} M_{a+bX}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{a t}M_X(b t) \end{aligned} \]

for every \(t\) at which \(M_X(bt)\) is finite.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A shift contributes an exponential factor to an MGF, while a scale changes its argument.

For the illustrated standard normal \(Z\), \(M_Z(t)=e^{t^2/2}\). Shifting and scaling gives \(M_{5+2Z}(t)=e^{5t}M_Z(2t)=e^{5t+2t^2}\), the MGF of \(\mathcal{N}(5,4)\).

Change \(a\) and \(b\): \(M_{a+bX}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{at}M_X(bt)\), and the slope at \(0\) becomes \(a+b\,\mathbb{E}X\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The formula is valid where \(M_X(bt)\) is finite.
  • For \(b=0\), \(M_{a+bX}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{at}\), the MGF of the constant \(a\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(p)\), \(M_{2+3X}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{2t}(1-p+p\mathrm{e}^{3t})\).
  • For \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), \(M_{5+2Z}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{5t+2t^2}\), so \(5+2Z\sim\mathcal{N}(5,4)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent (\(X\perp Y\)), then for every \(t\) at which both MGFs are finite,

\[ \begin{aligned} M_{X+Y}(t)=M_X(t)\cdot M_Y(t). \end{aligned} \]

Independence is essential.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Adding independent variables corresponds to multiplying their MGFs. This often identifies the distribution of a sum.

For the independent Poisson variables shown, multiplying the MGFs gives \(e^{2(e^t-1)}e^{3(e^t-1)}=e^{5(e^t-1)}\). This identifies the sum as \(\operatorname{Pois}(5)\).

For independent \(X\) and \(Y\) the MGF of \(X+Y\) is the product of the two curves, which identifies the distribution of the sum.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For independent \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), \(M_{\sum_iX_i}(t)=\prod_iM_{X_i}(t)\).
  • For iid variables, \(M_{\sum_iX_i}(t)=M_{X_1}(t)^n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The sum of independent Poisson variables with parameters \(2\) and \(3\) has MGF \(\exp(5(\mathrm{e}^t-1))\), so it is \(\operatorname{Pois}(5)\).
  • The sum of two independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) variables has MGF \((1-t)^{-2}\) for \(t<1\), identifying \(\operatorname{Gamma}(2,1)\) in rate notation.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: If the MGFs of \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite and equal, \(M_X(t)=M_Y(t)\), on an open interval around \(0\), then \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two finite MGFs agreeing around zero identify the same distribution. They do not establish that the variables are equal as outcomes or independent.

The Poisson and normal laws shown both have mean \(3\) and variance \(3\), so their MGFs have the same value and first two derivatives at \(0\). Their MGFs differ away from \(0\), reflecting different distributions; agreement of just these first derivatives is insufficient.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equality on an open interval containing zero is sufficient; equality only at zero is not.
  • Matching a computed MGF to a known MGF identifies the distribution under the same finiteness condition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(M_X(t)=\exp(3(\mathrm{e}^t-1))\) near zero, then \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(3)\).
  • If \(M_X(t)=\mathrm{e}^{2t+9t^2/2}\) near zero, then \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(2,9)\), with variance \(9\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The moment generating function (MGF) of a random variable \(X\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]. \end{aligned} \]

The course assumes it is finite on a neighborhood of \(t=0\): there is \(\delta>0\) with \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]<\infty\) for every \(|t|<\delta\). Finiteness only at \(t=0\), where \(M_X(0)=1\) always, is not enough for the moment and uniqueness theorems.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An MGF encodes a distribution through exponential averages. When finite near zero, it can generate moments and identify distributions.

The illustrated exponential MGF is finite for \(t<1\) and grows without bound as \(t\) approaches \(1\). Finiteness at \(t=0\) alone does not give the neighbourhood required by the moment and uniqueness theorems.

Move \(t\) along the curve \(M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]\). Every MGF passes through \((0,1)\); for \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\) it is finite only for \(t<\lambda\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(M_X(0)=1\).
  • Discrete variables use \(M_X(t)=\sum_x\mathrm{e}^{tx}p_X(x)\); density models use \(M_X(t)=\int \mathrm{e}^{tx}f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Bern}(p)\), \(M_X(t)=1-p+p\mathrm{e}^t\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\), \(M_X(t)=\lambda/(\lambda-t)\) for \(t<\lambda\); it is infinite for \(t\ge\lambda\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If the MGF \(M_X\) is finite on an open interval containing \(0\), then all moments of \(X\) are finite and, for every nonnegative integer \(n\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[X^n]=M_X^{(n)}(0), \end{aligned} \]

where \(M_X^{(n)}\) denotes the \(n\)th derivative of \(M_X\). The assumption is what justifies differentiating under the expectation.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Differentiating the MGF at zero extracts the corresponding powers of the random variable, giving its moments.

In the illustrated example, \(M_X(t)=1+\mathbb{E}[X]\,t+\mathbb{E}[X^2]\dfrac{t^2}{2!}+\cdots\) near \(0\), so the \(n\)th derivative at \(t=0\) is the \(n\)th moment: \(\mathbb{E}[X^n]=M_X^{(n)}(0)\). For \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\): \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=2-1^2=1\).

The tangent at \(t=0\) has slope \(\mathbb{E}X\), and the parabola \(1+\mathbb{E}X\,t+\mathbb{E}[X^2]\,t^2/2\) hugs the curve near \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}X=M_X^\prime(0)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]=M_X^{\prime\prime}(0)\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=M_X^{\prime\prime}(0)-(M_X^\prime(0))^2\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(M_X(t)=1-p+p\mathrm{e}^t\), the first two derivatives at zero both equal \(p\), giving variance \(p-p^2\).
  • For \(M_X(t)=\lambda/(\lambda-t)\), the first two moments are \(1/\lambda\) and \(2/\lambda^2\), giving variance \(1/\lambda^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(n\ge0\) be an integer and \(\mathbf p=(p_1,\dots,p_k)\) with \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_{j=1}^kp_j=1\). A random vector \(\mathbf X=(X_1,\dots,X_k)\) has a multinomial distribution, written \(\mathbf X\sim\mathrm{Mult}(n,\mathbf p)\), if for all integers \(n_j\ge0\) with \(\sum_jn_j=n\)

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(\mathbf X=\mathbf n)=\frac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_k!}p_1^{n_1}\cdots p_k^{n_k}, \end{aligned} \]

with \(0^0=1\) when a category probability is zero; the PMF is zero otherwise. The margins are binomial: \(X_j\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p_j)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A multinomial vector counts outcomes in several categories across a fixed number of independent trials. Its category counts must add to the fixed total.

The diagram uses \(n=3\) trials with category probabilities \((1/2,1/4,1/4)\). Each disc represents a count vector \((n_1,n_2,n_3)\) whose entries sum to \(3\), and its area is proportional to the probability given by the PMF above. The red disc marks \((1,1,1)\), with probability \(3/16\), calculated in the first example below. The counts are dependent because their total is fixed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(X_j\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p_j)\), so \(\mathbb{E}X_j=np_j\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_j)=np_j(1-p_j)\).
  • For \(i\ne j\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=-np_ip_j\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(n=3\) and category probabilities \((1/2,1/4,1/4)\), \(\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}=(1,1,1))=6(1/2)(1/4)(1/4)=3/16\).
  • For \(n=10\) and probabilities \((0.2,0.3,0.5)\), \(\mathbb{E}X_1=2\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=-0.6\).

docs.title: Approximation
docs.text:
For \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\) with fixed \(p\in(0,1)\), as \(n\to\infty\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{X_n-np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(0,1). \end{aligned} \]

For a finite \(n\) the normal approximation can be inaccurate when \(np\) or \(n(1-p)\) is small; there is no universal finite-\(n\) accuracy guarantee.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A large binomial count can be approximated by a normal variable with the same mean and variance, as a consequence of the CLT for Bernoulli sums.

The diagram compares \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.2)\) with a normal law of mean \(20\) and variance \(16\). The highlighted binomial tail is \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge25)\approx0.131\); the continuity correction places the corresponding normal threshold at \(24.5\).

Change \(n\) and \(p\): once \(np(1-p)\) is large the bars follow the normal density with mean \(np\) and variance \(np(1-p)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For fixed \(0<p<1\), \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\) has \(\mathbb{E}X_n=np\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_n)=np(1-p)\).
  • For a finite-\(n\) threshold \(k\), a continuity-corrected approximation is \(\mathbb{P}(X_n\le k)\approx\Phi((k+1/2-np)/\sqrt{np(1-p)})\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.5)\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\le60)\approx\Phi(2.1)\approx0.9821\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.2)\), \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge25)\approx1-\Phi((24.5-20)/4)\approx0.1303\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: If \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_2)\) are independent, then \(X+Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\). Independence is needed: Poisson marginals alone do not make the sum Poisson.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Independent Poisson sources combine into a Poisson total whose parameter is the sum of the source parameters.

For independent \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_2)\), the sum has distribution \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\). Independence is essential.

Two independent Poisson sources together give \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For finitely many independent Poisson variables, \(\sum_iX_i\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\sum_i\lambda_i)\).
  • For independent \(X,Y\) with positive parameters, \(X\mid X+Y=n\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,\lambda_X/(\lambda_X+\lambda_Y))\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Independent arrival counts with means \(3\) and \(7\) combine to a \(\operatorname{Pois}(10)\) count.
  • Two independent counts with means \(2\) and \(4\) have total-zero probability \(\mathrm{e}^{-2}\mathrm{e}^{-4}=\mathrm{e}^{-6}\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), and give each of the \(N\) items a label, independently of each other and of \(N\): type 1 with probability \(p\) and type 2 with probability \(q=1-p\). Then the numbers of type-1 and type-2 items are independent, with distributions \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda p)\) and \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda q)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Independent labels divide a Poisson count into independent Poisson category counts. Fixed totals do not have this unconditional independence.

Independent labels split a \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\) count into independent counts \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda p)\) and \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda(1-p))\), whose parameters add up to \(\lambda\).

Each item is type 1 with probability \(p\). The two counts are independent, with distributions \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda p)\) and \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda q)\); press New sample to see them vary.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The two parameters add to the original parameter: \(\lambda p+\lambda(1-p)=\lambda\).
  • For \(k\) independent categorical labels with probabilities \(p_i\), the category counts are independent \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda p_i)\) variables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A Poisson arrival count of mean \(20\), labeled urgent with probability \(0.1\), yields independent counts of means \(2\) and \(18\).
  • For mean \(12\) and label probabilities \(1/6,1/3,1/2\), the three counts are independent Poisson variables of means \(2,4,6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) and \(n\ge1\), their sample mean is

\[ \bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The sample mean summarizes observations by their arithmetic average. As a random variable it has its own expectation, variance, and sampling distribution.

The eight observations shown have mean \(\bar x=(2.1+3.4+3.9+4.6+5.0+5.8+6.7+8.5)/8=5.0\). Their deviations balance: \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0\). The sample mean estimates the population mean \(\mathbb{E}[X]\).

The sample mean has its own distribution: centred at \(\mu\), with variance \(\sigma^2/n\). Raise \(n\) to see it narrow.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If every \(X_i\) has mean \(\mu\), then \(\mathbb{E}\bar X_n=\mu\) without independence.
  • If the observations are independent with common variance \(\sigma^2\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For observations \(2,4,9\), the observed sample mean is \((2+4+9)/3=5\).
  • For \(100\) iid \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) observations, the sample mean has expectation \(1/2\) and variance \(1/(4\cdot100)=1/400\).

docs.title: Further Properties
docs.text: For realized observations \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), the observed average is \(\bar x_n=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i\). A sample proportion is the sample mean of success indicators.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be iid with \(\mathbb{E}|X_1|<\infty\) and mean \(\mu=\mathbb{E}X_1\). Then the sample mean \(\bar X_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) satisfies

\[ \begin{aligned} \bar X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}\mu. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The running average of an integrable iid sequence settles at the population mean with probability one.

The diagram shows three simulated sequences of fair die rolls. The strong law states that the running average converges to the mean along sample paths with probability \(1\): \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}\mu\).

Each path is one sequence of draws. Every path eventually enters the band \(\mu\pm\varepsilon\) and stays there; show more steps or narrow the band to test it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Finite \(\mathbb{E}|X_1|\) is sufficient; finite variance is not required.
  • The almost-sure conclusion also implies \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{P}\mu\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For iid fair die rolls, the running average converges almost surely to \(3.5\).
  • For iid variables with density \(f(x)=\frac32x^{-5/2}\) for \(x\ge1\) and zero elsewhere, the mean is \(3\) and the second moment is infinite; the running average still converges almost surely to \(3\).

docs.title: Sum of Two IID Uniform Variables
Proposition
docs.text:
If \(X,Y\) are independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) variables, then \(S=X+Y\) has density

\[ f_S(s)=\begin{cases}s,&0<s\le1,\\2-s,&1<s<2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} \]

The density peaks at \(s=1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two independent uniform values have more ways to add up near the center than near either endpoint. Their sum therefore has a triangular density.

For independent \(X,Y\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), more pairs contribute to a sum near \(1\) than near either endpoint \(0\) or \(2\), giving a triangular density for \(S=X+Y\). Its probabilities satisfy \(\mathbb{P}(S\le1/2)=1/8\) and \(\mathbb{P}(1/2<S<3/2)=3/4\).

Move \(s\): \(f_S(s)\) is the length of the overlap of \((0,1)\) and \((s-1,s)\), which grows to \(1\) at \(s=1\) and then shrinks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}(X+Y)=1\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=1/6\).
  • The CDF is \(s^2/2\) on \(0<s\le1\) and \(1-(2-s)^2/2\) on \(1<s<2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a random variable \(X\) with CDF \(F\), the survivor function is

\[ \begin{aligned} \overline{F}(x) = 1 - F(x) = \mathbb{P}(X > x). \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The survivor function gives the probability of exceeding a threshold. It is useful for waiting times, reliability, and tail probabilities.

The illustrated \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) distribution has survivor function \(\overline F(x)=e^{-x}\) for \(x\ge0\). For rate \(\lambda>0\), this becomes \(e^{-\lambda x}\).

Move \(x\): \(\overline F(x)=\mathbb{P}(X>x)\) is the shaded tail. For a discrete variable the strict inequality matters at the jumps.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\overline{F}(x)=1-F(x)\) is nonincreasing and right-continuous.
  • For a discrete variable, \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge x)=1-F(x-)\), which can differ from \(\overline{F}(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(\operatorname{Exp}(3)\), \(\overline{F}(2)=\mathrm{e}^{-6}\).
  • For \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.4)\), \(\mathbb{P}(X>0)=0.4\) but \(\mathbb{P}(X\ge0)=1\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(h\) be a function, and let \(Y\) and \(h(X)Y\) be integrable (for example, \(h\) bounded). Then, almost surely,

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[h(X)\,Y\mid X]=h(X)\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]. \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Once a variable is observed, any function of it is known and acts as a constant inside the conditional average.

In the illustrated example, \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\). Once \(X=x\) is observed, \(h(x)\) is a constant and moves outside the conditional average: \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)Y\mid X]=h(X)\,\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\); here \(\mathbb{E}[XY\mid X]=X\cdot X=X^2\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)\mid X]=h(X)\) when \(h(X)\) is integrable.
  • Combining the rule with Adam’s law gives \(\mathbb{E}[h(X)Y]=\mathbb{E}[h(X)\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(X)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]<\infty\), then \(\mathbb{E}[XY\mid X]=X^2\).
  • If \(A=\{X>0\}\), then \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_AY\mid X]=\mathbf{1}_A\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(C\) be an event with \(\mathbb{P}(C)>0\) and \(\{B_i\}\) a partition, and write \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i,C)\) for \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i\cap C)\). Then, omitting the terms with \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\cap C)=0\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(A\mid C)=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i,C)\,\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid C). \end{aligned} \]

Analogous versions hold for expectations, PMFs, and PDFs.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Case-by-case probability calculations remain valid after additional background information is fixed. Both the case weights and case probabilities must use that background.

Within the event \(C\), the diagram weights the conditional case probabilities by \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid C)\). The contributions \(0.14\) and \(0.15\) give \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid C)=0.29\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B_i\cap C)/\mathbb{P}(C)\).
  • Only cases with \(\mathbb{P}(B_i\cap C)>0\) need conditional probabilities \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B_i\cap C)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Within known rainy days \(C\), suppose \(\mathbb{P}(B_1\mid C)=0.7\), with delay probabilities \(0.2\) and \(0.5\) in the two routes. Then \(\mathbb{P}(A\mid C)=0.7(0.2)+0.3(0.5)=0.29\).
  • For a fair die conditioned to be even, partition into \(B_1=\{X\le3\}\) and \(B_2=\{X>3\}\). Then \(\mathbb{P}(X=6\mid C)=0(1/3)+(1/2)(2/3)=1/3\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be independent and identically distributed, with \(\mathbb{E}|X_1|<\infty\) and mean \(\mu\). Then their sample mean satisfies

\[ \bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\xrightarrow{P}\mu. \]

Probability Distributions uses the sufficient finite-variance case \(\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\sigma^2<\infty\), which admits the explicit Chebyshev proof below. Finite variance is not required for the more general integrable iid statement.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
For a large iid sample with a finite mean, the average is close to the population mean with high probability. Finite variance additionally supplies a quantitative probability bound.

In this diagram, \(\bar X_n=(X_1+\cdots+X_n)/n\) has standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) (here \(\sigma=1\)), so its distribution concentrates around \(\mu\): by Chebyshev, \(\mathbb{P}(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\to0\).

For a fixed \(\varepsilon\), \(\mathbb{P}(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\) (right) falls to \(0\) as \(n\) grows, always below the Chebyshev bound \(\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\) used in the proof.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n\).
  • Chebyshev gives \(\mathbb{P}(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\to0\) for each \(\varepsilon>0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For iid \(\operatorname{Bern}(0.4)\) variables, the proportion of successes converges in probability to \(0.4\).
  • For iid \(\operatorname{Exp}(2)\) variables and \(n=1000\), the probability that the sample mean differs from \(0.5\) by at least \(0.1\) is at most \(0.25/(1000(0.1)^2)=0.025\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The actuarial present value (APV) of an insurance cash flow is the expectation of its random present value \(Z\): \(\operatorname{APV}=\mathbb E[Z]\), when integrable. For a benefit \(b(T_x)\) paid at death under constant force of interest \(\delta\), \(Z=b(T_x)e^{-\delta T_x}\). Define \(v=(1+i)^{-1}\) and \(\delta=\log(1+i)\) for annual effective interest \(i>-1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The payment timing is uncertain even when the benefit amount is fixed. Discount each possible payment first, then average over the mortality model.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A non-negative benefit paid at death has APV \(\int_0^\infty b(t)v^tf_x(t)\,dt\).
  • For payments \(b_k\) at fixed times \(t_k\) conditional on survival, APV is \(\sum_k b_kv^{t_k}{}_{t_k}p_x\).
  • Scaling benefits by \(B\) scales APV by \(B\) and variance by \(B^2\).
  • A net single premium covers expected discounted benefits under the chosen basis; expenses and risk loading require additional treatment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A payment of 100 at time 5 with survival probability \(0.9\) and \(i=0.04\) has APV \(100(1.04)^{-5}(0.9)\approx73.97\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a life aged \(x\) with future lifetime \(T_x\), define \({}_tp_x=\mathbb P(T_x>t)\) and \({}_tq_x=\mathbb P(T_x\le t)\) for \(t\ge0\). The deferred death probability is

\[ {}_{u|t}q_x=\mathbb P(u<T_x\le u+t)={}_up_x-{}_{u+t}p_x. \]

Here \(u\ge0\) is the deferment and \(t\ge0\) the subsequent coverage period. An omitted left-hand duration means one year: \(p_x={}_1p_x\), \(q_x={}_1q_x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: These symbols encode the age, waiting period and coverage period of a survival event. Reading those three parts prevents confusion between dying within a period and surviving until it begins.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_tp_x+{}_tq_x=1\).
  • \({}_{t+u}p_x={}_tp_x\,{}_up_{x+t}\).
  • \({}_{u|t}q_x={}_up_x\,{}_tq_{x+u}\) when survival to \(x+u\) has positive probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \({}_5p_{40}=0.98\) and \({}_{10}p_{40}=0.95\), then \({}_{5|5}q_{40}=0.03\). This is an unconditional probability at age 40, not the conditional five-year death probability at age 45.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An annuity certain makes specified payments independently of survival. For \(n\) annual unit payments, the annuity-due pays at \(0,\ldots,n-1\), whereas the annuity-immediate pays at \(1,\ldots,n\). Their present values are \(\ddot a_{\angl{n}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v^k\) and \(a_{\angl{n}}=\sum_{k=1}^nv^k\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This is the deterministic building block for life annuities. The due/immediate distinction describes payment timing, not uncertainty.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With \(d=1-v\ne0\), \(\ddot a_{\angl{n}}=(1-v^n)/d\) and \(a_{\angl{n}}=v\ddot a_{\angl{n}}\).
  • A continuous unit-rate annuity has value \(\bar a_{\angl{n}}=(1-e^{-\delta n})/\delta\), with limit \(n\) at \(\delta=0\).
  • Paying \(1/m\) in advance every \(1/m\) year gives \(m^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{mn-1}v^{k/m}\).
  • At positive interest, the infinite-duration versions are perpetuities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At \(v=0.9\), three unit payments in advance have value \(1+0.9+0.81=2.71\). Moving all payments one year later gives \(0.9(2.71)=2.439\).

docs.title: Constant Force Within a Year of Age
Definition
docs.text: For integer age \(x\), constant-force interpolation assumes \(\mu_{x+s}=\mu_x^*\) for \(0\le s<1\). If the annual survival probability is \(p_x>0\), the required force is \(\mu_x^*=-\log p_x\). Different years may have different forces.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Survival declines exponentially within each annual interval. A piecewise constant force can match all integer-age entries without assuming one exponential lifetime distribution over every age.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_sp_x=p_x^s\) and \(l_{x+s}=l_xp_x^s\) for \(0\le s\le1\).
  • Within one interval, \({}_tp_{x+s}=p_x^t\) for \(s+t\le1\).
  • For an interval crossing an integer age, multiply survival probabilities for its successive pieces.
  • CFM and UDD agree at integer ages but generally differ at fractional ages.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(p_{60}=0.9\), half-year survival is \(\sqrt{0.9}\approx0.94868\) under CFM, compared with \(0.95\) under UDD.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A continuous life annuity pays at rate one per year while the annuitant is alive. Its present value is \(Y=\int_0^{T_x}e^{-\delta t}\,dt\). A temporary version stops at \(\min(T_x,n)\) instead.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Continuous payments provide a tractable idealisation of a frequent payment stream. Payment rate one means an amount \(dt\) over an interval of length \(dt\), not a unit payment at every instant.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\bar a_x=\int_0^\infty v^t{}_tp_x\,dt\) and \(\bar a_{x:\angl{n}}=\int_0^n v^t{}_tp_x\,dt\).
  • For \(\delta\ne0\), \(Y=(1-v^{T_x})/\delta\) and \(\bar A_x+\delta\bar a_x=1\).
  • At constant mortality force \(\lambda>0\) and \(\delta\ge0\), \(\bar a_x=1/(\lambda+\delta)\).
  • At zero interest, \(Y=T_x\) and the APV is the complete expectation of life.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At \(\lambda=0.02\) and \(\delta=0.03\), a continuous benefit rate of 100 per year has APV \(100/0.05=2000\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The curtate future lifetime of a life aged \(x\) is \(K_x=\lfloor T_x\rfloor\), the number of complete future years lived. It takes values \(0,1,2,\ldots\). Under the continuous lifetime assumption,

\[ \mathbb P(K_x=k)={}_kp_x-{}_{k+1}p_x={}_kp_xq_{x+k}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Annual insurance payments often depend on the year of death rather than its exact time. A death after 3.7 years has \(K_x=3\) and an end-of-year death payment at time 4.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\{K_x\ge k\}=\{T_x\ge k\}\) for integer \(k\); strict versus weak inequalities have the same probability under continuous lifetimes.
  • \(\mathbb E[K_x]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}{}_kp_x\).
  • \(\mathbb E[K_x^2]=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(2k-1){}_kp_x\), when finite.
  • A mass function for \(K_x\) gives probabilities; a density for \(T_x\) does not.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At constant force \(\lambda\), \(\mathbb P(K_x=k)=e^{-\lambda k}(1-e^{-\lambda})\) and \(\mathbb E[K_x]=1/(e^\lambda-1)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit annual life annuity-due deferred \(u\) years, for integer \(u\ge0\), begins payments at time \(u\) conditional on survival and then continues while the annuitant lives. Its present value is \(Y=\sum_{k=u}^{\infty}v^k\mathbf1_{\{T_x>k\}}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A pension can be viewed as an annuity whose first payment waits until retirement. Survival to retirement and discounting both affect its issue-date value.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_{u|}\ddot a_x={}_uE_x\ddot a_{x+u}\).
  • \({}_{u|}\ddot a_x=\ddot a_x-\ddot a_{x:\angl{u}}\).
  • The first identity follows by writing \({}_{u+j}p_x={}_up_x{}_jp_{x+u}\) in the payment sum.
  • For a deferred annuity-immediate, specify that the first payment is at \(u+1\); the factorisation uses \(a_{x+u}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \({}_{20}E_{40}=0.3\) and \(\ddot a_{60}=12\), a unit pension starting at age 60 has issue-date APV \(0.3(12)=3.6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A death insurance deferred \(u\) years pays only for a death after duration \(u\). For a unit deferred whole life benefit paid at death, \(Z=v^{T_x}\mathbf1_{\{T_x>u\}}\). The discount is from the original issue date, not from the end of the deferment.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The insured must first survive the waiting period. Conditional on doing so, the remaining contract is a whole life insurance issued at the older age.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_{u|}\bar A_x=v^u{}_up_x\bar A_{x+u}={}_uE_x\bar A_{x+u}\).
  • Whole life APV equals term APV over \(u\) years plus the \(u\)-year deferred whole life APV.
  • The same factorisation applies to annual settlement for integer \(u\).
  • A deferred term policy additionally ends coverage after a finite period.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \({}_5E_x=0.7\) and the unit whole life APV at age \(x+5\) is \(0.4\), the deferred contract has APV \(0.7(0.4)=0.28\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An \(n\)-year endowment insurance pays a unit benefit at death within the term or at time \(n\) on survival. With immediate death settlement, \(Z=v^{\min(T_x,n)}\). With annual death settlement and integer \(n\), \(Z=v^{\min(K_x+1,n)}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Every lifetime leads to a payment. The uncertainty concerns when that payment occurs, up to the fixed maturity time.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• APV equals the APV of an \(n\)-year term insurance plus \({}_nE_x\).
  • Death and survival benefits occur on disjoint events; their product is zero. Their covariance is generally negative, not zero.
  • To calculate the second moment, square each discounted payment on its own event. Do not add component variances without a covariance term.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At \(\lambda=0.02\), \(\delta=0.03\) and \(n=10\), immediate death-or-survival APV is \(0.4(1-e^{-0.5})+e^{-0.5}\approx0.76392\).

docs.title: Complete and Curtate Expectation of Life
Definition
docs.text: The complete expectation of life at age \(x\) is \(\mathring e_x=\mathbb E[T_x]\), whereas the curtate expectation is \(e_x=\mathbb E[K_x]\). Their \(n\)-year term versions are \(\mathbb E[\min(T_x,n)]\) and \(\mathbb E[\min(K_x,n)]\), respectively.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The complete quantity includes fractions of the final year. The curtate quantity counts only completed years. A term expectation stops accumulating lifetime after a fixed horizon.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathring e_x=\int_0^{\infty}{}_tp_x\,dt\) and \(\mathbb E[\min(T_x,n)]=\int_0^n{}_tp_x\,dt\).
  • \(e_x=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}{}_kp_x\) and \(\mathbb E[\min(K_x,n)]=\sum_{k=1}^n{}_kp_x\) for integer \(n\).
  • When expectations are finite, \(0\le\mathring e_x-e_x\le1\). Under UDD at integer age the difference is \(1/2\).
  • \(\mathbb E[T_x^2]=2\int_0^\infty t\,{}_tp_x\,dt\) when finite.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At force \(\lambda=0.1\), the complete expectation is 10 years, while the curtate expectation is \(1/(e^{0.1}-1)\approx9.508\) years.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Under the course's absolutely continuous survival model, the force of mortality at attained age \(x+t\) is

\[ \mu_{x+t}={f_x(t)\over S_x(t)}=-{d\over dt}\log S_x(t), \]

where \(S_x(t)>0\) and the derivative exists. Equivalently, it is the limit of \(\mathbb P(t<T_x\le t+h\mid T_x>t)/h\) as \(h\downarrow0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Mortality is measured per unit of time among those still alive. The force can exceed one; it is a rate and must be multiplied by a short duration to approximate a probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_tp_x=\exp(-\int_0^t\mu_{x+s}\,ds)\) and \(f_x(t)={}_tp_x\mu_{x+t}\).
  • A constant force \(\lambda>0\) gives \({}_tp_x=e^{-\lambda t}\).
  • An increasing force expresses positive duration dependence; a decreasing force expresses negative duration dependence.
  • For a finite force at \(x\), \({}_hq_x=\mu_xh+o(h)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At constant force \(0.02\) per year, the one-year death probability is \(1-e^{-0.02}\approx0.01980\), rather than exactly \(0.02\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a life currently aged \(x\ge0\), the future lifetime \(T_x\) is the remaining time until death, conditional on being alive at age \(x\). If \(T_0\) denotes age at death and \(S_0(x)=\mathbb P(T_0>x)>0\), then

\[ \mathbb P(T_x>t)={S_0(x+t)\over S_0(x)},\qquad t\ge0. \]

The course assumes an absolutely continuous lifetime distribution. Thus \(T_x\) is a continuous random variable, rather than an expected lifetime.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The model updates the lifetime distribution when a person survives to a specified age. Two people at different ages generally have different remaining-lifetime distributions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Writing \(S_x(t)=\mathbb P(T_x>t)\), conditioning gives \(S_x(t+u)=S_x(t)S_{x+t}(u)\) whenever the conditioning probability is positive.
  • The density is \(f_x(t)=-S_x'(t)\) almost everywhere.
  • Age independence of \(T_x\) is a special property of constant-force mortality, not a general assumption.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(T_0\) is uniform on \((0,100)\), a survivor aged 60 has \(T_{60}\) uniform on \((0,40)\). Their probability of surviving another 10 years is \(30/40=0.75\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a policy still in force at duration \(t\), let \(Z_t\), \(H_t\) and \(Y_t\) be present values at time \(t\) of future benefits, expenses and premium income. The gross future loss is \(L_t^g=Z_t+H_t-Y_t\). The net loss omits expenses. All quantities refer to the policy conditional on its being in force at \(t\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The insurer faces random future obligations and random future premium income. Positive loss means future outgo exceeds income; negative loss means a future surplus.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The time-\(t\) discount origin differs from the issue-date discount origin.
  • A policy ended by death before \(t\) does not have an in-force future-loss distribution at \(t\).
  • The course normally measures the loss after any benefit at \(t\) but before the premium at \(t\). Annuity timing must be specified separately.
  • An equivalence premium gives \(\mathbb E[L_0^g]=0\) only under the same valuation and expense basis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If future benefit PV is 100, expense PV 5 and premium-income PV 80 in a realised scenario, the gross future loss is 25. These realised quantities need not equal their expectations.
