docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An annual life annuity-due with an \(n\)-year guarantee pays at times \(0,\ldots,n-1\) irrespective of survival. Payments at \(n,n+1,\ldots\) are made only while the annuitant survives. After an early death, guaranteed payments continue to the designated recipient.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The guarantee protects against losing the entire payment stream through early death. It converts the first part into an annuity certain and leaves a deferred life annuity afterwards.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• APV is \(\ddot a_{\angl{n}}+{}_{n|}\ddot a_x\).
  • With the same unit payment and timing, APV is at least that of a whole life annuity-due without a guarantee.
  • The guarantee is not the same as a temporary annuity: a temporary annuity stops on death, while guaranteed payments do not.
  • Beneficiary and payment-timing conventions must be stated in the contract.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If five certain payments have PV \(4.5\) and the five-year deferred life annuity has APV \(8\), the guaranteed contract has APV \(12.5\).

docs.title: Death Benefits Payable at Fractional-Year Boundaries
Definition
docs.text: A unit death benefit payable at the end of the \(1/m\)-year interval of death is paid at \(\tau_m=\lceil mT_x\rceil/m\), for a positive integer \(m\). Its APV is \(A_x^{(m)}=\mathbb E[v^{\tau_m}]\). Mortality is continuous, so death exactly on a payment boundary has probability zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Increasing settlement frequency reduces the waiting time after death. Unlike an annuity payable \(m\) times a year, this is one benefit payment, not \(m\) instalments of \(1/m\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(A_x^{(m)}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty v^{(k+1)/m}({}_{k/m}p_x-{}_{(k+1)/m}p_x)\).
  • As \(m\to\infty\), \(A_x^{(m)}\to\bar A_x\) for non-negative interest.
  • Under UDD in each year and \(i>0\), \(A_x^{(m)}=[i/i^{(m)}]A_x\), where \(i^{(m)}=m((1+i)^{1/m}-1)\).
  • The continuous limit is \(\bar A_x=(i/\delta)A_x\) under UDD, with \(\delta=\log(1+i)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For quarterly settlement (\(m=4\)), death at \(T_x=2.13\) leads to payment at time 2.25. Annual settlement would pay at time 3.

docs.title: Variance of an Insurance Present Value
Definition
docs.text: For a discounted insurance benefit \(Z\), its variance is \(\mathbb E[Z^2]-(\mathbb E[Z])^2\), provided the second moment is finite. For a unit benefit paid once on event \(D\) at time \(\tau\), \(Z=e^{-\delta\tau}\mathbf1_D\) and \(Z^2=e^{-2\delta\tau}\mathbf1_D\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The second moment uses twice the interest force because the discount factor is squared. Mortality and the covered event stay the same.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a unit benefit, a second-moment symbol such as \({}^2\bar A_x\) means valuation at force \(2\delta\), not \((\bar A_x)^2\).
  • If annual effective interest is \(i\), the double-force equivalent rate is \((1+i)^2-1\), not \(2i\).
  • For benefit \(B\), the second moment is multiplied by \(B^2\).
  • If benefits vary with time, both the benefit function and the discount factor must be squared.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For unit whole life insurance with \(\lambda=0.02\) and \(\delta=0.03\), the second moment is \(0.02/(0.02+0.06)=0.25\). Variance is \(0.25-0.4^2=0.09\).

docs.title: Life Annuities Payable Several Times a Year
Definition
docs.text: A life annuity payable \(m\) times a year pays instalments of \(1/m\) at intervals of \(1/m\) year while the annuitant survives. The due version starts at time zero and has APV \(\ddot a_x^{(m)}=m^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^\infty v^{k/m}{}_{k/m}p_x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The annual benefit rate stays one as frequency changes. Fractional-age survival must be calculated from a continuous mortality model or an explicit table interpolation rule.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The immediate version starts at time \(1/m\), so \(a_x^{(m)}=\ddot a_x^{(m)}-1/m\).
  • A temporary due version with integer term \(n\) stops its sum at \(mn-1\).
  • Under suitable finiteness conditions, the limit as \(m\to\infty\) is the continuous life annuity.
  • UDD and CFM can produce different values from the same annual table. Woolhouse's formula is excluded by the supplied course outline.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: An annuity paying monthly at annual rate 1200 pays 100 at each payment date. Its APV is \(100\sum_{k\ge0}v^{k/12}{}_{k/12}p_x\) for payments in advance.

docs.title: Equivalence Principle for Life Insurance Premiums
Definition
docs.text: The equivalence principle chooses a premium so that expected discounted premium income equals expected discounted benefits and, for gross valuation, expenses. Let \(Z\) be benefit PV, \(H\) expense PV and \(Y\) the PV of a unit premium stream. For a level premium \(P\), the gross equation is \(P\mathbb E[Y]=\mathbb E[Z+H]\). Net valuation omits \(H\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This balances expected cash flows at issue under a specified mortality and interest basis. It does not guarantee that every policy or every portfolio has zero realised loss.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\mathbb E[Y]>0\) and expenses do not themselves depend on \(P\), \(P=\mathbb E[Z+H]/\mathbb E[Y]\).
  • An annual net whole life premium payable in advance while alive is \(P=A_x/\ddot a_x\) for unit annual-settlement death benefit.
  • If premiums are payable for at most \(m\) years, the denominator is \(\ddot a_{x:\angl{m}}\).
  • Premium-related expenses must remain in the equation and be solved together with \(P\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If expected benefit PV is 40 and the unit premium-stream APV is 10, the net annual premium is 4. Expenses with APV 5, independent of the premium, raise the gross premium to 4.5.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
For annual unit whole life insurance, conditioning on the first year gives the valuation recursion

\[ A_x=vq_x+vp_xA_{x+1}, \]

where \(v\) is the annual discount factor and \(p_x=1-q_x\). The first term represents death during the year; the second represents survival followed by the remaining contract.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A long contract can be valued one year at a time. This also explains why product decompositions have both financial and survival discount factors.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Let \(A_{x:\angl{n}}\) denote annual-settlement unit \(n\)-year endowment APV. Then \(A_{x:\angl{n}}=v[q_x+p_xA_{x+1:\angl{n-1}}]\), with \(A_{x:\angl{0}}=1\).
  • Annual term insurance uses the same recursion but a terminal value of zero.
  • Backward numerical valuation requires a terminal age or a justified tail treatment.
  • The recursion concerns conditional values at successively older ages, not independent new policies.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A life table specifies survivor numbers \(l_x\) at ages \(x\) for a hypothetical cohort with a chosen initial size, the radix. Annual deaths are \(d_x=l_x-l_{x+1}\). Within the mortality model represented by the table, for \(l_x>0\),

\[ {}_tp_x={l_{x+t}\over l_x},\qquad q_x={d_x\over l_x}. \]

Fractional ages require an interpolation assumption if only integer-age entries are supplied.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The table expresses a survival model through cohort counts. Its numbers may be modelled or estimated; the displayed ratios do not remove sampling or projection uncertainty.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_{u|t}q_x=(l_{x+u}-l_{x+u+t})/l_x\).
  • Scaling all entries by the same positive constant leaves survival probabilities unchanged.
  • A population table and an insured-life table can differ through selection. Choose the table appropriate to the covered population.
  • Use table ratios only when a table is given or a corresponding table model has been specified.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Makeham's law specifies the force of mortality at age \(y\ge0\) as \(\mu_y=A+Bc^y\). In the standard increasing-age model, \(A\ge0\), \(B>0\) and \(c>1\). These constants determine both an age-independent component and an exponentially increasing age component.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The constant term allows a background mortality rate, while the exponential term models increasing mortality at older ages. This is a model assumption, not a universal law of human mortality.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a life aged \(x\),

    \[ {}_tp_x=\exp\left[-At-{Bc^x(c^t-1)\over\log c}\right]. \]

  • Setting \(A=0\) gives the Gompertz form.

  • Mortality depends on attained age \(x+t\), so the starting age must be retained in calculations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(A=0.001\), \(B=0.0001\) and \(c=1.1\), the force at age 40 is \(0.001+0.0001(1.1)^{40}\approx0.00553\). The survival formula integrates this changing force over the entire future interval.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The prospective gross policy value at duration \(t\) is \(V_t=\mathbb E[L_t^g\mid\text{policy in force at }t]\). Equivalently, it is expected time-\(t\) PV of future benefits and expenses minus expected time-\(t\) PV of future premiums, under the selected valuation basis and timing convention.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The value measures the expected remaining liability of an active policy. It changes as the insured ages and as benefits and premium payments approach or pass.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(V_t+\mathbb E[Y_t\mid\text{in force}]=\mathbb E[Z_t+H_t\mid\text{in force}]\).
  • Net policy values omit expenses and use the corresponding net premium.
  • A value at issue is zero under matching equivalence assumptions; this need not hold at later durations or after a change of basis.
  • An expected-liability value is not, by itself, a complete capital requirement for adverse outcomes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If expected remaining benefits and expenses are 50 and expected remaining premiums are 30, the prospective policy value is 20 at the specified valuation time.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit pure endowment pays at time \(n\ge0\) only if the life aged \(x\) survives to that time. Its present value is \(Z=v^n\mathbf1_{\{T_x>n\}}\), and its APV is denoted \({}_nE_x=v^n{}_np_x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The insurer pays for survival rather than death. The factor \({}_nE_x\) combines financial discounting with the probability that the later payment is due.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For benefit \(B\), APV is \(Bv^n{}_np_x\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=v^{2n}{}_np_x(1-{}_np_x)\) for a unit benefit.
  • \({}_{n+m}E_x={}_nE_x\,{}_mE_{x+n}\) when conditioning on survival is defined.
  • A pure endowment is the survival component of an endowment insurance.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A select mortality model records both age at selection and elapsed duration since selection. Write \(q_{[x]+s}\) for the one-year death probability of a life selected at age \(x\) and observed \(s\) years later. After a specified select period \(r\), the ultimate rate depends only on attained age: \(q_{[x]+s}=q_{x+s}\) for \(s\ge r\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Underwriting can make newly selected lives differ from other lives of the same age. The model keeps that duration effect until the assumed select period ends.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \({}_kp_{[x]}=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-q_{[x]+j})\) for integer \(k\).
  • Use select rates before duration \(r\) and ultimate rates afterwards.
  • Brackets identify selection age, not attained age. A life selected at 40 and now aged 42 is \([40]+2\).
  • The disappearance of selection after \(r\) is a modelling convention, not evidence that all real selection effects vanish.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For a two-year select period with \(q_{[40]}=0.005\), \(q_{[40]+1}=0.007\) and ultimate \(q_{42}=0.01\), three-year survival is \(0.995(0.993)(0.99)=0.97815465\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit \(n\)-year temporary life annuity pays while the life survives, for at most \(n\) payments. For integer \(n\ge1\), the due version has payments at \(0,\ldots,n-1\) and the immediate version at \(1,\ldots,n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The term limits payment duration even if the annuitant lives longer. The final immediate payment requires survival to time \(n\), whereas the due version starts with a certain payment at time zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\ddot a_{x:\angl{n}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v^k{}_kp_x\) and \(a_{x:\angl{n}}=\sum_{k=1}^nv^k{}_kp_x\).
  • \(\ddot a_{x:\angl{n}}-a_{x:\angl{n}}=1-{}_nE_x\).
  • For \(d=1-v\ne0\), \(d\ddot a_{x:\angl{n}}=1-A_{x:\angl{n}}\), where \(A_{x:\angl{n}}\) is annual-settlement endowment APV.
  • The whole life annuity is the limit as the term increases, when finite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An \(n\)-year term insurance pays a death benefit only if death occurs within the coverage period \([0,n)\). A unit benefit paid at death has present value \(Z=v^{T_x}\mathbf1_{\{T_x<n\}}\). For integer \(n\) and annual settlement, \(Z=v^{K_x+1}\mathbf1_{\{K_x<n\}}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The contract provides protection during a fixed term and pays nothing on survival to its end. The death condition and settlement time must both be specified.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Immediate-payment APV is \(\int_0^n v^tf_x(t)\,dt\).
  • Annual-settlement APV is \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v^{k+1}{}_kp_xq_{x+k}\).
  • At constant forces \(\lambda>0\) and \(\delta\ge0\), the immediate APV is \(\lambda[1-e^{-(\lambda+\delta)n}]/(\lambda+\delta)\).
  • Increasing the term increases APV for a non-negative fixed benefit.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The uniform distribution of deaths (UDD) assumption is \({}_sq_x=sq_x\) for integer age \(x\) and \(0\le s\le1\). If imposed in every subsequent year, the fractional part \(R_x=T_x-K_x\) is uniform on \((0,1)\) and independent of \(K_x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Within each year of age, deaths are spread uniformly rather than concentrated at particular dates. The assumption gives a rule for interpolating an integer-age life table.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(l_{x+s}=l_x-sd_x=(1-s)l_x+sl_{x+1}\).
  • \(\mu_{x+s}=q_x/(1-sq_x)\) where the denominator is positive.
  • For \(0\le s\le s+t\le1\), \({}_tp_{x+s}=[1-(s+t)q_x]/[1-sq_x]\).
  • UDD does not mean constant force within a year; its force increases when \(q_x>0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A varying life annuity pays predetermined amounts \(b_k\ge0\) at times \(t_k\) conditional on survival. Its present value is \(Y=\sum_k b_kv^{t_k}\mathbf1_{\{T_x>t_k\}}\). For continuous rate \(b(t)\), replace the sum by \(\int_0^{T_x}b(t)v^t\,dt\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The indicator specifies eligibility for each payment. This representation handles increasing, decreasing and stepped benefits without treating them as separate probability models.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• APV is \(\sum_k b_kv^{t_k}{}_{t_k}p_x\), or \(\int_0^\infty b(t)v^t{}_tp_x\,dt\) for continuous payments.
  • Survival indicators at different dates are dependent. Their joint probability is \({}_{\max(t_j,t_k)}p_x\).
  • Thus \(\mathbb E[Y^2]=\sum_{j,k}b_jb_kv^{t_j+t_k}{}_{\max(t_j,t_k)}p_x\), when finite.
  • Do not calculate annuity variance by assuming independent annual payments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For due payments 1 now and 2 next year, \(Y=1+2v\mathbf1_{\{T_x>1\}}\). With \(v=0.95\) and \(p_x=0.9\), APV is \(2.71\) and variance is \((1.9)^2(0.9)(0.1)=0.3249\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A varying death benefit is specified by a deterministic payment rule \(b(t)\ge0\). For payment at death, \(Z=b(T_x)v^{T_x}\); for annual settlement, \(Z=b(K_x+1)v^{K_x+1}\). A compound reversionary bonus increases the insured benefit by a fixed proportion at specified vesting dates.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The mortality model determines whether and when payment occurs; the benefit rule determines its amount. Write the vesting convention explicitly before valuing a bonus.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Immediate APV is \(\int_0^\infty b(t)v^tf_x(t)\,dt\).
  • Annual APV is \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty b(k+1)v^{k+1}{}_kp_xq_{x+k}\).
  • For annual anniversary bonuses at rate \(j\ge0\), base benefit 1 and end-of-year death settlement, the course uses \(Z=v^{K_x+1}(1+j)^{K_x}\).
  • At-death settlement needs its own rule for partial-year bonuses; do not infer one from annual settlement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With a 2% bonus vested only on completed anniversaries, death at time 3.4 gives benefit \((1.02)^3\). If settlement is at the end of the death year, discount this amount by \(v^4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit annual whole life annuity-due pays at the beginning of each year while the life aged \(x\) is alive, including a certain payment at issue. Its present value is \(Y=\sum_{k=0}^{K_x}v^k\) and APV is \(\ddot a_x=\mathbb E[Y]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Each annual payment is a pure endowment for its payment date. A longer lifetime increases the number of payments, whereas a death benefit is generally discounted more heavily when death occurs later.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\ddot a_x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}v^k{}_kp_x\).
  • For \(d=1-v\ne0\), \(Y=(1-v^{K_x+1})/d\), so \(A_x+d\ddot a_x=1\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{Var}(v^{K_x+1})/d^2\) when finite.
  • One-year recursion: \(\ddot a_x=1+vp_x\ddot a_{x+1}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(A_x=0.4\) and \(d=0.05\), the unit annuity APV is \((1-0.4)/0.05=12\). This uses annual death settlement for \(A_x\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit annual whole life annuity-immediate pays at times \(1,2,\ldots\) only while the annuitant survives. Its present value is \(Y^*=\sum_{k=1}^{K_x}v^k\) and APV is \(a_x=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}v^k{}_kp_x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: There is no guaranteed initial payment. Compared with the corresponding life annuity-due, the contract omits exactly the payment at time zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(Y^*=Y-1\), so \(a_x=\ddot a_x-1\) and both present values have the same variance.
  • \(a_x=vp_x\ddot a_{x+1}\) by conditioning on survival to the first payment.
  • Multiplying \(\ddot a_x\) by \(v\) alone is generally wrong: moving a survival-contingent payment also changes its survival condition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If the annuity-due APV is 12, the matching annuity-immediate APV is 11. Their variance is equal because the omitted initial payment is deterministic.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A unit whole life insurance pays on death whenever it occurs. For immediate payment its present value is \(Z=v^{T_x}\) and APV is \(\bar A_x\). For payment at the end of the year of death, \(Z=v^{K_x+1}\) and APV is \(A_x\), where \(v=(1+i)^{-1}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The contract covers the entire remaining lifetime. Its value depends on whether settlement occurs at death or later at an annual boundary.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\bar A_x=\int_0^\infty v^t{}_tp_x\mu_{x+t}\,dt\).
  • \(A_x=\sum_{k=0}^\infty v^{k+1}{}_kp_xq_{x+k}\).
  • For non-negative interest, \(\bar A_x\ge A_x\) because immediate settlement is earlier.
  • At constant mortality force \(\lambda>0\) and interest force \(\delta\ge0\), \(\bar A_x=\lambda/(\lambda+\delta)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(\lambda=0.02\) and \(\delta=0.03\), a benefit of 100 paid at death has APV \(100(0.02/0.05)=40\).

docs.title: Risk Insurance
docs.text:
Block 2b · Actuarial science

Coverage rules and portfolio models lead to insurance-data estimation, decisions under risk, premium principles and experience rating.

docs.title: Reading this course
docs.text:
These notes introduce course-specific concepts. Existing Year 1 concepts have one canonical page and are linked as prerequisites below. The lecture sequence follows the supplied 2026 course outline; the split within chapters or parts spanning several lectures is provisional and follows the order of the notes. Concepts appear at their first planned introduction and are reused by links afterwards.

Week 20 has no lectures in the outline and is not counted as a lecture. The sequence therefore contains 14 lectures.

Coverage boundary

The premium notes also refer to other textbook premium principles without naming them. The pages cover the explicitly supplied principles; the additional textbook scope still needs checking. The supplementary stochastic-dominance handout is used with explicit loss-versus-wealth conventions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For twice differentiable increasing utility with \(u'(w)>0\), the absolute risk aversion coefficient is \(r(w)=-u''(w)/u'(w)\). It measures local curvature relative to marginal utility at wealth \(w\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Curvature determines how much a small uncertain loss matters beyond its mean. The coefficient is unchanged by positive affine transformations of utility.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Exponential utility \(u(w)=-e^{-\alpha w}\) has constant absolute risk aversion \(r(w)=\alpha>0\).
  • Power utility \(u(w)=w^\gamma\), \(0<\gamma<1\), \(w>0\), has \(r(w)=(1-\gamma)/w\).
  • For a small mean-zero risk \(\varepsilon Z\), a certainty-equivalent wealth reduction is approximately \(\tfrac12r(w)\varepsilon^2\operatorname{Var}(Z)\), with smoothness and moment conditions for the Taylor approximation.
  • This local approximation is not an exact formula for arbitrary large losses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With exponential coefficient \(\alpha=0.01\) and a sufficiently small centred loss of variance 100, the second-order premium above the mean is approximately \(0.5(0.01)(100)=0.5\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A bonus-malus system (BMS) assigns each policyholder to a rating level, updates that level using claim history, and charges a base premium multiplied by a level-specific premium relativity. It specifies the levels, initial level, transition rules and premium scale.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Claim-free years can earn lower premiums and reported claims can trigger higher premiums. The system uses observed experience to distinguish underlying risks that are not fully captured by initial rating factors.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Let \(L_t\) be level in policy year \(t\) and \(r_l\) the price multiplier for level \(l\).
  • The notes model annual claims conditionally as \(N_t\mid\Lambda=\lambda\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\).
  • A transition rule \(T(l,n)\) maps the current level and reported annual count to next year's level.
  • Conditioning on a fixed risk rate can give a Markov chain. Mixing over unobserved risk rates does not automatically preserve the Markov property.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A two-level scheme charges \(c\) after a claim-free year and \(2c\) after a year with claims. Its next level depends on whether the reported count is zero.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: At a fixed claim rate \(\lambda\), let \(p_{ij}(\lambda)=\mathbb P(L_{t+1}=j\mid L_t=i,\lambda)\). The transition matrix \(P(\lambda)=(p_{ij})\) has non-negative entries and each row sums to one. For row-vector level probabilities \(a_t\), the next-year distribution is \(a_{t+1}=a_tP\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The state must store enough history for the transition rule. For a two-year claim-free discount, a simple high/low premium label may omit the information needed for next year.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Under a deterministic rule \(T(i,n)\) and Poisson count, \(p_{ij}(\lambda)=\sum_{n:T(i,n)=j}e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!\).
  • At a fixed rate with independent yearly claims, \(a_t=a_0P^t\).
  • The notes' three states are a claim in the latest year, one claim-free year after a claim, and at least two claim-free years.
  • Matrix orientation must match the row-vector convention.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(p=1-e^{-\lambda}\) and \(q=e^{-\lambda}\), the three-state matrix has rows \((p,q,0)\), \((p,0,q)\) and \((p,0,q)\). These rows each sum to one.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Under right censoring at a known cap \(c_i\), an exact continuous loss \(x_i<c_i\) is observed if it is below the cap; otherwise one observes only \(X_i\ge c_i\). With indicator \(\delta_i=1\) for an exact observation, its likelihood contribution is \(f_\theta(x_i)^{\delta_i}\bar F_\theta(c_i)^{1-\delta_i}\) under continuous losses and non-informative censoring.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The policy exists in the sample even when its full loss is unknown. A capped observation gives a tail event, not a point density at the cap.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Independent contributions multiply; exact observations contribute log densities and censored observations log survivor probabilities.
  • For a common exponential rate, \(\hat\lambda=r/[\sum_{\text{exact}}x_i+\sum_{\text{censored}}c_i]\), if \(r>0\) is the number of exact losses.
  • If no exact losses occur, an interior maximum need not exist.
  • An atom at the censoring boundary requires careful use of strict or weak tail events.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exact losses 20 and 30 plus one observation capped at 100, exponential log-likelihood is \(2\log\lambda-150\lambda\). Thus \(\hat\lambda=2/150\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Under coinsurance, the insurer pays a specified proportion \(a\in[0,1]\) of a covered loss and the insured or another insurer pays the rest. Without other modifications, insurer payment is \(Y=aX\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Both parties share each covered monetary unit. Combining coinsurance with a deductible or limit requires specifying the order of those operations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb E[aX]=a\mathbb E[X]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(aX)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\) when finite.
  • For \(a>0\), \(F_{aX}(y)=F_X(y/a)\).
  • \(a\min((X-d)_+,u)\) means sharing an already capped excess. It differs from \(\min((aX-d)_+,u)\).
  • A quota-share reinsurance treaty uses the same proportional split for the relevant insurer portfolio losses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(a=0.8\), \(X=1000\) and deductible 100, sharing after the deductible gives \(0.8(900)=720\). Applying the deductible after sharing gives \(800-100=700\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The collective risk model writes \(S=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i\), where \(N\) is a non-negative integer claim count and the claim severities \(X_i\) are independent, identically distributed non-negative variables, independent of \(N\). The sum is zero when \(N=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The number of claims is random, and the summands describe actual claims rather than all policies. A policy can generate more than one claim unless the frequency model rules that out.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Conditional on \(N=n\), total loss has the distribution of a sum of \(n\) severities.
  • Mean and variance follow from the random-sum formulas on the compound distribution page.
  • If severities are strictly positive, \(\mathbb P(S=0)=\mathbb P(N=0)\); otherwise zero severities also matter.
  • Frequency–severity independence is a substantive modelling assumption.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(5)\) and independent severities of mean 100 and variance 400, mean aggregate loss is 500 and variance is \(5(400+100^2)=52000\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A compound Poisson loss is \(S=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i\) with \(N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\), \(\lambda\ge0\), and iid non-negative severities independent of \(N\). The empty sum is zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Poisson frequency makes aggregate losses particularly tractable. Even with continuous positive severities, aggregate loss includes a probability of no claims at all.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb E[S]=\lambda\mathbb E[X]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=\lambda\mathbb E[X^2]\) when finite.
  • \(M_S(t)=\exp(\lambda(M_X(t)-1))\) where finite.
  • With strictly positive severity, \(\mathbb P(S=0)=e^{-\lambda}\).
  • Claim counts for disjoint severity categories are independent Poisson variables with rates \(\lambda p_j\); this uses the existing Poisson splitting result.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If each claim is 2 and \(\lambda=3\), then \(S=2N\) has mean 6 and variance 12. Its support is \(0,2,4,\ldots\), so it is not an ordinary Poisson variable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a Poisson counting process \(N(t)\) of rate \(\lambda\) and iid severities \(X_i\ge0\) independent of the entire process, the compound Poisson process is \(S(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N(t)}X_i\), \(t\ge0\). It records cumulative claims over time.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The path stays constant between claim arrivals and jumps by each arriving claim amount. A compound Poisson distribution describes one time horizon; this process describes all horizons consistently.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(S(t)\) is compound Poisson with frequency parameter \(\lambda t\).
  • It has stationary independent increments under the stated assumptions.
  • \(\mathbb E[S(t)]=\lambda t\mathbb E[X]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S(t))=\lambda t\mathbb E[X^2]\) when finite.
  • A surplus path with initial capital \(u\) and premium rate \(c\) is \(u+ct-S(t)\); ruin analysis needs additional assumptions and is not developed here.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With claim rate 2 per year and fixed severity 100, \(S(0.5)=100N(0.5)\) and \(N(0.5)\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(1)\). Mean half-year loss is 100.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let independent compound Poisson losses \(S_j\) have rates \(\lambda_j\ge0\) and severity CDFs \(F_j\), for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). If \(\lambda=\sum_j\lambda_j>0\), their sum is compound Poisson with rate \(\lambda\) and severity CDF \(F=\sum_j(\lambda_j/\lambda)F_j\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Pooling portfolios adds their claim-arrival rates. A randomly chosen pooled claim belongs to a portfolio with probability proportional to that portfolio's arrival rate.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pooled severity weights are \(\lambda_j/\lambda\), not equal portfolio weights unless rates are equal.
  • Independent losses have additive means and variances.
  • Multiplying the component MGFs yields \(\exp[\lambda(M_X(t)-1)]\) when the MGFs exist.
  • The result also holds without a finite positive MGF, by the Poisson arrival and marking construction.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Two portfolios have rates 2 and 3 and fixed claim amounts 10 and 20. Their pooled rate is 5 and severities are 10 with probability \(2/5\) and 20 with probability \(3/5\). Mean total loss is 80.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The distribution of \(S=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i\) is a compound distribution when \(N\) is a non-negative integer variable and the \(X_i\) are iid severities independent of \(N\). Let \(\mu=\mathbb E[X_1]\) and \(\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Compounding combines uncertainty in the number of claims with uncertainty in their sizes. It differs from mixing a parameter of one distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb E[S]=\mathbb E[N]\mu\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=\mathbb E[N]\sigma^2+\operatorname{Var}(N)\mu^2\), with finite second moments.
  • \(M_S(t)=G_N(M_X(t))\) where the expression is finite; for integer severities \(G_S(z)=G_N(G_X(z))\).
  • \(F_S(s)=\sum_{n\ge0}\mathbb P(N=n)F_X^{*n}(s)\), with \(F_X^{*0}\) the CDF of zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(N\) is Bernoulli with probability \(q\), then \(S\) is zero with probability \(1-q\) and otherwise has the severity law. Thus a compound Bernoulli model is also a simple mixture.

docs.title: Convex Order and More Dangerous Risks
Definition
docs.text: For integrable losses, convex order \(X\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Y\) means \(\mathbb E[h(X)]\le\mathbb E[h(Y)]\) for every convex function for which comparison is defined. For non-negative losses this is equivalent to stop-loss order together with \(\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[Y]\). The course calls the larger risk more dangerous in this equal-mean setting.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Convex order compares dispersion after removing a difference in mean. All risk-averse agents prefer the less dispersed loss when utility expectations are defined.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The order forces equal means because both \(h(x)=x\) and \(h(x)=-x\) are convex.
  • With finite second moments, \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\le\operatorname{Var}(Y)\); if the distributions differ, this inequality is strict.
  • Variance ordering alone does not imply convex order.
  • Convex order is not preserved by every convex transformation, because equal means can be lost.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: A constant loss of 1 is below the equal-probability loss on \(\{0,2\}\) in convex order. Their variances are 0 and 1.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: If the MGF \(M_X(t)=\mathbb E[e^{tX}]\) is finite in a neighbourhood of zero, the cumulant generating function is \(K_X(t)=\log M_X(t)\) on that domain. Its derivatives at zero are called cumulants.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Taking logarithms turns products of independent MGFs into sums. This makes cumulants a convenient way to describe aggregate risk.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(K_X'(0)=\mathbb E[X]\) and \(K_X''(0)=\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
  • For independent \(X,Y\) with suitable MGFs, \(K_{X+Y}=K_X+K_Y\).
  • \(K_{aX+b}(t)=bt+K_X(at)\) for constants \(a,b\) on the common domain.
  • Existence of ordinary moments does not ensure a finite MGF for positive arguments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\), \(K_X(t)=\lambda(e^t-1)\). Its first two derivatives at zero both equal \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The expected utility model compares uncertain wealth \(W\) through \(\mathbb E[u(W)]\). An increasing concave utility function \(u\) represents risk aversion: for integrable wealth with well-defined utilities, \(\mathbb E[u(W)]\le u(\mathbb E[W])\). A linear increasing utility represents risk neutrality.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A risk-averse policyholder can prefer a fixed payment to an uncertain loss with the same mean. Utility is applied to final wealth, so larger losses usually reduce utility.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Replacing \(u\) by \(au+b\) with \(a>0\) preserves preferences.
  • Concavity gives the Jensen comparison; strict preference requires suitable strict concavity and non-degenerate wealth.
  • Fractional power utility requires positive wealth. Quadratic utility is increasing only on a restricted domain.
  • The expected value of a payoff and expected utility are different criteria.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At wealth 100, a loss of 0 or 20 with equal probabilities gives expected logarithmic utility \([\log100+\log80]/2\). A certain loss of 10 gives \(\log90\), which is larger.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For integrable loss \(X\ge0\), the expected value principle sets \(\Pi(X)=(1+\theta)\mathbb E[X]\), where \(\theta\ge0\) is a fixed loading coefficient. At \(\theta=0\), it is the net premium principle, \(\Pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The loading is a constant proportion of expected loss. Different risks with the same mean receive the same price, regardless of their dispersion.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The principle is proportional and additive for integrable losses, even without independence.
  • It has non-negative loading and is monotone under stochastic or stop-loss order.
  • For \(\theta>0\), translation consistency fails: adding certain cost \(c\) adds \((1+\theta)c\) to the premium.
  • Iterativity follows from total expectation only in the net case; repeating a positive loading generally applies it twice.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For expected loss 100 and \(\theta=0.2\), premium is 120. Adding a certain 10 raises the premium to 132, rather than 130.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For non-negative losses, exponential order \(X\le_eY\) means \(\mathbb E[e^{\alpha X}]\le\mathbb E[e^{\alpha Y}]\) for every \(\alpha>0\). Comparisons may use extended values, but a finite exponential premium at a given \(\alpha\) requires the corresponding moment to be finite.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The comparison tests every exponential risk-aversion parameter. It is weaker than agreement among all increasing concave wealth utilities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Stop-loss order implies exponential order, since \(e^{\alpha x}\) is increasing and convex.
  • For \(u(w)=-e^{-\alpha w}\), exponential order gives the reverse order of expected utilities of \(w-X\) and \(w-Y\).
  • With equal means and MGFs finite near zero, a Taylor comparison gives \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\le\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).
  • If both positive MGFs are infinite, the comparison can carry little information about finite premiums.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(X=1\) and \(Y\) equal 0 or 2 with probability \(1/2\), \(M_X(\alpha)=e^\alpha\le(1+e^{2\alpha})/2=M_Y(\alpha)\) for every positive \(\alpha\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For risk-aversion parameter \(\alpha>0\) and loss \(X\) with \(\mathbb E[e^{\alpha X}]<\infty\), the exponential premium is \(\Pi_\alpha(X)=\alpha^{-1}\log\mathbb E[e^{\alpha X}]=K_X(\alpha)/\alpha\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This is the indifference price for exponential wealth utility. It gives extra weight to large losses and may be infinite for losses whose positive exponential moments do not exist.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Jensen gives \(\Pi_\alpha(X)\ge\mathbb E[X]\).
  • Translation consistency and independent additivity follow from exponential products.
  • Iterativity follows from the tower property: \(e^{\alpha\Pi_\alpha(X\mid Y)}=\mathbb E[e^{\alpha X}\mid Y]\).
  • It respects exponential order and hence stop-loss order.
  • For bounded \(X\), \(\Pi_\alpha(X)\le\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\).
  • Near \(\alpha=0\) with sufficient moments and a finite MGF, \(\Pi_\alpha(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\alpha\operatorname{Var}(X)/2+o(\alpha)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exponential severity of rate \(\lambda\) and \(0<\alpha<\lambda\), premium is \(\alpha^{-1}\log[\lambda/(\lambda-\alpha)]\). At or above \(\lambda\) it is infinite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For positive exposure \(e_i\) and claim rate \(\lambda_i=\exp(x_i^\top\beta)\), a Poisson frequency model specifies \(N_i\mid x_i,e_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(e_i\lambda_i)\). Therefore \(\log\mathbb E[N_i\mid x_i,e_i]=\log e_i+x_i^\top\beta\). The known term \(\log e_i\) is an offset, with coefficient fixed at one.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A group with twice as much insured time should have twice the expected claim count if its underlying claim rate is unchanged. The offset lets rating coefficients describe rate differences.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Expected count is \(e_i\lambda_i\); fitted rate is count mean divided by \(e_i\).
  • An offset differs from an estimated covariate coefficient.
  • Exposure must be positive and measured in a consistent unit.
  • A zero-exposure record requires separate treatment; \(\log0\) is undefined.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At rate 0.2 per policy-year, exposures 10 and 100 have expected counts 2 and 20. Both have the same fitted rate.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: With a franchise deductible \(d\ge0\), the insurer pays the entire loss once it exceeds \(d\): \(Y^L=X\mathbf1_{\{X>d\}}\). If \(X\le d\), payment is zero. Conditional on a payment, the paid amount has the law of \(X\mid X>d\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The threshold decides whether the insurer pays, but is not deducted from a qualifying loss. This creates a jump in the payment rule at the threshold.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb E[Y^L]=\mathbb E[(X-d)_+]+d\mathbb P(X>d)\) when finite.
  • Payment probability is the same as for an ordinary deductible, but qualifying payments are larger by \(d\).
  • For \(d>0\), there are no payment amounts strictly between zero and \(d\).
  • Whether equality qualifies is a contract convention; here the threshold rule is strict.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: At deductible 100, losses 80 and 150 produce franchise payments 0 and 150. The ordinary deductible would produce 0 and 50.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A generalised linear model (GLM) specifies a conditional response law from an exponential family, a mean \(\mu_i=\mathbb E[Y_i\mid x_i]\), and a link \(g\) such that \(g(\mu_i)=\eta_i=x_i^\top\beta\). Here \(x_i\) is the covariate vector, \(\beta\) the coefficient vector and \(\eta_i\) the linear predictor. The variance has form \(\phi V(\mu_i)\) under the chosen family and dispersion convention.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The predictor is linear in coefficients, while the mean can be nonlinear and the conditional variance can depend on it. This allows count or binary responses without imposing an unconstrained linear mean.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The inverse link gives \(\mu_i=g^{-1}(x_i^\top\beta)\).
  • Poisson regression uses \(g(\mu)=\log\mu\) and variance \(\mu\).
  • A Gaussian identity-link model has conditional mean \(x_i^\top\beta\) and constant variance.
  • A quasi-likelihood model specifies a mean–variance relation without necessarily specifying a complete response distribution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(\eta_i=\log 2\) under a log link, the fitted conditional mean is 2. It is an expected count, not a guarantee of exactly two claims.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Suppose independent losses are observed only as counts \(n_j\) in disjoint intervals \((c_{j-1},c_j]\), \(j=1,\ldots,k\), covering the observation space. Under CDF \(F_\theta\), interval probability is \(p_j(\theta)=F_\theta(c_j)-F_\theta(c_{j-1})\). The likelihood is proportional to \(\prod_j p_j(\theta)^{n_j}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The observed event is membership in a bin. Replacing each loss by a bin midpoint and using a density discards the actual observation mechanism.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\ell(\theta)=\sum_jn_j\log p_j(\theta)+C\), where \(C\) is independent of \(\theta\).
  • For multinomial counts, the constant factor is \(n!/\prod_jn_j!\), with \(n=\sum_jn_j\).
  • If the bins omit part of the population, include an outside bin or condition on the sampling region.
  • Grouping can reduce information compared with exact observations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If 6 exponential losses are in \((0,100]\) and 4 exceed 100, the likelihood is proportional to \((1-e^{-100\lambda})^6(e^{-100\lambda})^4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Hunger for bonus is a policyholder's incentive not to report a small covered loss when reporting would increase expected future premiums by more than the current reimbursement. It is a behavioural response to an experience-rating rule.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The reported claim record can understate accident experience. The course treats this response as a form of moral hazard; it changes the observation process on which rating relies.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A simple decision compares the current payment with the present value of extra future premiums caused by reporting.
  • The relevant future difference depends on current level, transition rules, time horizon and discounting.
  • Observed claim frequency can differ from accident frequency.
  • A reporting threshold need not equal a contractual deductible.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If reimbursement would be 80 but reporting increases expected discounted future premiums by 120, a policyholder minimising expected monetary cost prefers not to report. For reimbursement 200, the same comparison favours reporting.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The individual risk model represents total portfolio loss by \(S=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\), where \(n\) is the fixed number of policies and \(X_i\ge0\) is the loss from policy \(i\), including zero for a claim-free policy. The basic course model assumes independent policy losses, often identically distributed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The model counts policies first and models the outcome of each. Its summands may have an atom at zero even when positive claim amounts are continuous.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With independence, \(\mathbb E[S]=\sum_i\mathbb E[X_i]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(X_i)\).
  • For \(X_i=I_iB_i\) with independent Bernoulli indicator \(I_i\) of probability \(q_i\) and severity \(B_i\), the mean is \(q_i\mathbb E[B_i]\).
  • Its variance is \(q_i\operatorname{Var}(B_i)+q_i(1-q_i)(\mathbb E[B_i])^2\).
  • Dependence between policies adds covariance terms to portfolio variance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For 100 independent policies with claim probability \(0.1\) and fixed claim 10, \(S=10N\) with \(N\sim\operatorname{Bin}(100,0.1)\). Mean is 100 and variance is 900.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a fitted likelihood model with maximised log-likelihood \(\hat\ell\), \(k\) estimated parameters and sample size \(n\), Akaike's information criterion is \(\operatorname{AIC}=-2\hat\ell+2k\), and Bayesian information criterion is \(\operatorname{BIC}=-2\hat\ell+k\log n\). Smaller values are preferred when models use comparable likelihoods on the same observations.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The fit improvement from extra parameters must compensate for their penalty. Stepwise selection searches neighbouring models and need not find the best model among all possible subsets.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Count all estimated likelihood parameters, including an estimated dispersion parameter where applicable.
  • For \(n>e^2\), BIC penalises each added parameter more than AIC.
  • AIC and BIC are selection aids, not evidence of causal interpretation or predictive validation.
  • Ordinary likelihood-based AIC is not directly available from a quasi-Poisson mean–variance specification alone.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(n=100\), model A has \(\hat\ell=-50\), \(k=2\), while B has \(\hat\ell=-48\), \(k=3\). AIC values are 104 and 102, favouring B; BIC values are about 109.21 and 109.82, favouring A.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For initial policyholder wealth \(w\), strictly increasing utility \(u\) and full insurance of loss \(X\), the maximum acceptable premium \(P^+\) solves \(u(w-P^+)=\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\). For insurer wealth \(W\) and utility \(U\), its minimum acceptable premium \(P^-\) solves \(U(W)=\mathbb E[U(W+P^--X)]\), when finite solutions exist.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: One equation compares insured and uninsured wealth for the customer; the other compares taking the contract with taking no risk for the insurer. A trade is acceptable to both when the premium lies between their thresholds.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Under concavity and well-defined expectations, \(P^+\ge\mathbb E[X]\) and \(P^-\ge\mathbb E[X]\).
  • A mutually acceptable full-insurance premium exists if \(P^-\le P^+\).
  • A risk-neutral insurer has \(P^-=\mathbb E[X]\) in this expense-free model.
  • Exponential utilities with different coefficients produce different thresholds; finiteness requires the respective exponential loss moments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exponential utility parameter \(\alpha\) and loss 0 or 10 with equal probabilities, the indifference premium is \(\alpha^{-1}\log[(1+e^{10\alpha})/2]\). At \(\alpha=0.1\) it is about 6.20, above mean loss 5.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a positive differentiable stationary premium \(b(\lambda)\) at risk rate \(\lambda>0\), Loimaranta efficiency is \(e(\lambda)=\lambda b'(\lambda)/b(\lambda)=d\log b(\lambda)/d\log\lambda\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The elasticity measures the percentage change in long-run premium produced by a one-percent change in claim rate. A value near one means a proportional response locally, but does not establish accurate individual pricing.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A proportional premium \(b(\lambda)=k\lambda\) has efficiency one.
  • A flat premium has efficiency zero.
  • For the two-year discount scheme, \(e(\lambda)=2\lambda(c-a)e^{-2\lambda}/[c(1-e^{-2\lambda})+ae^{-2\lambda}]\).
  • Numerical evaluation can use nearby log-rate and log-premium differences; check sensitivity to the step size.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For a two-level one-year scheme, \(b(\lambda)=c(2-e^{-\lambda})\). At \(\lambda=0.5\), efficiency is \(0.5/(2e^{0.5}-1)\approx0.2176\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For \(0<\mathbb E[X]<\infty\) and ordinary deductible \(d\ge0\), the loss elimination ratio is

\[ \operatorname{LER}(d)={\mathbb E[X]-\mathbb E[(X-d)_+]\over\mathbb E[X]}={\mathbb E[\min(X,d)]\over\mathbb E[X]}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The ratio measures the share of expected ground-up loss removed from insurer payments. It concerns expected amounts, rather than the fraction of claims receiving no payment.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(0\le\operatorname{LER}(d)\le1\) and it increases with \(d\).
  • \(\operatorname{LER}(d)=\int_0^d\bar F_X(t)\,dt/\mathbb E[X]\).
  • It is zero at \(d=0\) and tends to one as \(d\to\infty\).
  • A zero or infinite ground-up mean makes this ratio inappropriate without further conventions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exponential losses at rate \(0.01\) and deductible 100, LER is \(1-e^{-1}\approx0.6321\). The payment probability is \(e^{-1}\approx0.3679\), a different quantity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For non-negative iid severities \(X_i\) independent of count \(N\), the maximum claim is \(M=\max(X_1,\ldots,X_N)\), with \(M=0\) if \(N=0\). Let \(F_X\) be the severity CDF and \(G_N\) the count PGF.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Aggregate loss and maximum claim measure different exposures. Conditioning on the count reduces the maximum to the probability that every claim is below a chosen threshold.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(z\ge0\), \(\mathbb P(M\le z)=G_N(F_X(z))\).
  • If \(N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\), \(\mathbb P(M\le z)=\exp[-\lambda(1-F_X(z))]\).
  • With fixed count \(n\ge1\), this becomes \(F_X(z)^n\).
  • The no-claim convention matters at zero and when evaluating moments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With Poisson mean 5 and probability \(0.1\) that one claim exceeds 1000, the probability that no claim exceeds 1000 is \(e^{-0.5}\approx0.60653\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Given a specified family of observation laws indexed by parameter \(\theta\in\Theta\), a maximum likelihood estimate maximises the likelihood of the observed data. For independent exact observations \(x_i\), \(L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^nf(x_i;\theta)\), where \(f\) is the applicable density or mass function.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The parameter varies while the observations remain fixed. Insurance data may report intervals or censoring rather than exact losses, so the likelihood must describe what was actually observed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Maximising \(L\) is equivalent to maximising \(\ell=\log L\) where \(L>0\).
  • For independent observations, \(\ell(\theta)=\sum_i\log f(x_i;\theta)\).
  • A zero derivative identifies a candidate, not automatically a maximum. Check the parameter domain, boundaries and curvature or numerical objective.
  • Grouping, censoring and truncation require different observation contributions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For positive iid exponential losses with rate \(\lambda\), \(\ell=n\log\lambda-\lambda\sum_i x_i\), so \(\hat\lambda=n/\sum_i x_i\). The second derivative is \(-n/\lambda^2<0\).

docs.title: Mixed Discrete and Continuous Loss Distribution
Definition
docs.text: A mixed discrete and continuous loss has both positive point masses and an absolutely continuous component. Its distribution can be written \(\mathbb P(X\in A)=\sum_jp_j\mathbf1_{\{a_j\in A\}}+\int_A f_c(x)\,dx\), where \(p_j>0\) and \(\sum_jp_j+\int f_c=1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A claim can be zero, a normal positive amount, or exactly a policy cap. Jumps of the CDF record point masses; the ordinary derivative between jumps records only the continuous component. This is a specific distribution structure, while a mixture describes averaging component laws.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb P(X=a)=F_X(a)-F_X(a-)\).
  • \(\mathbb E[h(X)]=\sum_jp_jh(a_j)+\int h(x)f_c(x)\,dx\) when integrable.
  • A single ordinary density with respect to length cannot represent the atoms.
  • Coverage modifications can introduce atoms even when the original loss is continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(X\) is zero with probability \(0.8\) and otherwise uniform on \((0,100)\), its continuous component density is \(0.002\) on that interval. The mean is \(0.2(50)=10\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For random risk rate \(\Lambda\) and stationary class \(L\), the unconstrained class value \(r_l\) minimising \(\mathbb E[(\Lambda-r_L)^2]\) is \(r_l=\mathbb E[\Lambda\mid L=l]\), for classes of positive probability and finite second moments. This is on a claim-frequency scale; dimensionless premium relativities require normalisation by a base rate.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Each class is priced by the average underlying rate among its members. This minimises squared prediction error, but can produce an irregular or commercially unsuitable scale.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If class probability at fixed rate is \(\pi_l(\lambda)\) and rate density is \(f_\Lambda\), then \(r_l=\int\lambda\pi_l(\lambda)f_\Lambda(\lambda)d\lambda/\int\pi_l(\lambda)f_\Lambda(\lambda)d\lambda\).
  • \(\mathbb E[r_L]=\mathbb E[\Lambda]\).
  • Under a linear restriction \(r_l=a+bl\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(L)>0\), \(b=\operatorname{Cov}(\Lambda,L)/\operatorname{Var}(L)\) and \(a=\mathbb E[\Lambda]-b\mathbb E[L]\).
  • Refining the same information partition cannot increase unconstrained minimum MSE. Merely changing the number of classes in a different system does not guarantee an improvement.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If two equally frequent classes have conditional rates 0.1 and 0.3, their optimal frequency-scale values are 0.1 and 0.3. At base rate 0.2, the dimensionless relativities are 0.5 and 1.5.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a non-negative ground-up loss \(X\) and deductible \(d\ge0\), the insurer's per-loss payment is \(Y^L=(X-d)_+=\max(X-d,0)\). The insured retains \(\min(X,d)\). The per-payment distribution is the conditional law of \(X-d\) given \(X>d\), defined only when \(\mathbb P(X>d)>0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Every loss is included in the per-loss model, with a zero payment below the deductible. The per-payment model describes only cases generating a positive payment.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb P(Y^L=0)=F_X(d)\) and \(F_{Y^L}(y)=F_X(d+y)\) for \(y\ge0\).
  • For \(y\ge0\), \(\mathbb P(Y^P>y)=\bar F_X(d+y)/\bar F_X(d)\).
  • \(\mathbb E[Y^L]=\bar F_X(d)\mathbb E[Y^P]\) when finite.
  • For continuous \(X\), \(f_{Y^P}(y)=f_X(d+y)/\bar F_X(d)\) for \(y>0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(0.01)\) and \(d=100\), the probability of payment is \(e^{-1}\). Conditional payment has mean 100, so mean payment per loss is \(100e^{-1}\approx36.79\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A conditional count model is overdispersed relative to Poisson if \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid x)>\mathbb E[Y\mid x]\). A quasi-Poisson specification uses mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\phi\mu\). A common negative binomial specification has mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\mu+\mu^2/r\), with size parameter \(r>0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Claims from apparently similar policyholders can still have different underlying rates. A gamma mixture of Poisson rates gives a negative binomial response and an extra variance term.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Quasi-Poisson has overdispersion when \(\phi>1\) and underdispersion when \(0<\phi<1\).
  • Quasi-Poisson is a mean–variance specification, not generally the literal count distribution of \(\phi\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu/\phi)\).
  • In the negative binomial model, larger \(r\) reduces excess variance; the Poisson limit is \(r\to\infty\) at fixed \(\mu\).
  • Compare dispersion conditional on predictors and exposure, rather than raw pooled mean and variance alone.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(\mu=2\) and \(r=4\), negative binomial conditional variance is \(2+4/4=3\). A quasi-Poisson fit with \(\phi=1.5\) has the same mean and variance but does not specify the same full law.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The course's Pareto loss model has survivor function \(\bar F_X(x)=[\beta/(\beta+x)]^\alpha\) for \(x\ge0\), shape \(\alpha>0\) and scale \(\beta>0\). It is the Lomax or Pareto type II convention, whose support starts at zero; an unshifted Pareto type I model has a different support.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The polynomial tail allows occasional very large losses. The shape controls which moments are finite, so a valid loss distribution need not have finite variance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(f_X(x)=\alpha\beta^\alpha/(\beta+x)^{\alpha+1}\) for \(x>0\).
  • \(\mathbb E[X]=\beta/(\alpha-1)\) for \(\alpha>1\); variance is \(\beta^2\alpha/[(\alpha-1)^2(\alpha-2)]\) for \(\alpha>2\).
  • For \(\alpha>1\), \(\pi_X(d)=\beta^\alpha(\beta+d)^{1-\alpha}/(\alpha-1)\).
  • Conditional excess over \(d\) is Lomax with the same shape and scale \(\beta+d\).
  • Every positive exponential moment is infinite, so an exponential premium is infinite.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(\alpha=2\), \(\beta=800\) and deductible 300, mean ground-up loss is 800 but variance is infinite. Mean excess per loss is \(800^2/1100\approx581.82\), and mean excess per payment is 1100.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In Poisson regression, conditionally independent counts satisfy \(Y_i\mid x_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i)\) with \(\log\mu_i=x_i^\top\beta\). Thus \(\mu_i=\exp(x_i^\top\beta)>0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid x_i)=\mu_i\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The model relates rating factors to expected claim counts through multiplicative effects. It does not directly model claim severity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Increasing covariate \(x_{ij}\) by one multiplies the mean by \(e^{\beta_j}\) if the model has no relevant interaction.
  • The independent-data log-likelihood is \(\sum_i[y_i x_i^\top\beta-e^{x_i^\top\beta}-\log(y_i!)]\).
  • Equality of conditional mean and variance is the Poisson assumption; heterogeneity across covariates does not by itself violate it.
  • Different observation durations require exposure adjustment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With intercept \(\log0.1\) and a binary rating coefficient \(\log1.5\), the two conditional means are 0.1 and 0.15 at the same exposure.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A policy limit \(u\ge0\) caps the insurer's payment. Without a deductible, payment is \(Y=\min(X,u)\). With an ordinary deductible \(d\) and maximum payment \(u\), it is \(Y=\min((X-d)_+,u)\). A maximum covered ground-up loss is a different convention and must be stated separately.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The cap creates a point mass at the maximum payment whenever losses can reach or exceed it. A deductible controls the bottom of the covered layer; a payment limit controls its width.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb E[\min(X,u)]=\int_0^u\bar F_X(t)\,dt\) for non-negative \(X\).
  • \(\mathbb E[\min((X-d)_+,u)]=\pi_X(d)-\pi_X(d+u)\).
  • For \(u>0\), the capped excess has mass \(\mathbb P(X\ge d+u)\) at \(u\).
  • For \(u>0\), its mass at zero is \(F_X(d)\); at \(u=0\) the entire payment is zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If deductible is 100 and maximum insurer payment is 500, a ground-up loss of 800 gives payment 500. A ground-up coverage cap of 500 instead would give payment 400.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A premium principle is a rule \(\Pi\) assigning a price to a loss law \(X\). The course considers non-negative loading \(\Pi(X)\ge\mathbb E[X]\), no rip-off \(\Pi(X)\le\operatorname{ess\,sup}X\), translation consistency \(\Pi(X+c)=\Pi(X)+c\), additivity for independent losses, proportionality \(\Pi(aX)=a\Pi(X)\) and iterativity \(\Pi(X)=\Pi(\Pi(X\mid Y))\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The properties describe how pricing reacts to certain cash flows, rescaling, pooling and conditioning. A plausible-looking formula need not satisfy all of them.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Iterativity applies the same rule first conditionally and then to the random conditional premium.
  • A universal property needs a proof; one counterexample disproves it.
  • An expected-value loading with positive coefficient fails translation consistency for positive constants.
  • Risk-order compatibility can be checked by expressing a premium in terms of increasing or convex functions.
  • No rip-off is only a finite upper bound when the loss is essentially bounded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(\Pi(X)=1.2\mathbb E[X]\) and deterministic \(X=10\), the premium is 12. It violates no rip-off, since the largest possible loss is only 10.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a non-negative integer-valued random variable \(N\), its probability generating function (PGF) is \(G_N(z)=\mathbb E[z^N]=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\mathbb P(N=k)z^k\), at least for \(|z|\le1\). In this power-series definition \(z^0=1\), including at \(z=0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The coefficient of each power stores a probability. PGFs are especially useful for counting claims and for composing claim frequency with claim severity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb P(N=k)=G_N^{(k)}(0)/k!\).
  • \(G_N'(1-)=\mathbb E[N]\) and \(G_N''(1-)=\mathbb E[N(N-1)]\), allowing infinite values.
  • Independent non-negative integer-valued sums have product PGFs.
  • For \(z>0\) where finite, \(G_N(z)=M_N(\log z)\). A general real-valued severity need not have a PGF.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\), \(G_N(z)=e^{\lambda(z-1)}\). Differentiating at one gives mean \(\lambda\) and second factorial moment \(\lambda^2\).

docs.title: Rating Factors and Interactions in Insurance GLMs
Definition
docs.text: A rating factor is a covariate used to distinguish expected insured risk. A categorical factor with \(k\) levels can be represented by \(k-1\) indicator variables relative to a reference level when an intercept is included. An interaction allows the effect of one factor to depend on another.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Under a log link, additive predictor terms become multiplicative rate effects. An interaction changes a rate ratio across groups rather than simply adding another independent multiplier.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• In \(\log\lambda=\beta_0+\beta_AA+\beta_BB+\beta_{AB}AB\), with binary \(A,B\), the effect of \(A\) is \(e^{\beta_A+\beta_{AB}B}\).
  • Including all category indicators plus an intercept makes the design redundant without constraints.
  • Reference categories determine coefficient interpretation but do not change fitted means under an equivalent encoding.
  • A fitted association does not establish a causal effect of a rating factor.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(\beta_A=\log1.2\) and \(\beta_{AB}=\log1.5\), the rate ratio for \(A\) is 1.2 when \(B=0\), and 1.8 when \(B=1\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For independent non-negative summands, stochastic and stop-loss orders are preserved when adding correspondingly ordered risks. For random sums, suppose iid non-negative severities \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) are independent of their respective counts \(M,N\). If severities and counts are ordered in the same stochastic or stop-loss order, the corresponding aggregate losses inherit that order, subject to required integrability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: One can compare portfolios through frequency and severity without computing their full aggregate laws. Independence from the count and non-negative severity are essential to the basic compounding statements.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X_i\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y_i\) and \(M\le_{\mathrm{st}}N\), then \(\sum_{i=1}^MX_i\le_{\mathrm{st}}\sum_{i=1}^NY_i\) under the stated model.
  • The analogous result holds for stop-loss order with finite aggregate means.
  • Exponential order also passes to these random sums when the non-negative severities and counts are exponentially ordered and the required transforms are finite: \(M_{S_X}(\alpha)=M_M(\log M_X(\alpha))\le M_N(\log M_Y(\alpha))=M_{S_Y}(\alpha)\). Non-negative severities ensure the log-MGF arguments are non-negative.
  • For iid non-negative \(X_i\) independent of \(N\), \(X_1\le_{\mathrm{sl}}\sum_{i=1}^NX_i\) when \(\mathbb E[N]\ge1\).
  • A Bernoulli-policy loss \(IX\) is below the compound sum in stop-loss order if \(\mathbb P(I=1)\le\mathbb E[N]\) and the independence assumptions hold.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: An individual policy with claim probability \(q\) and severity \(X\) is stop-loss dominated by a compound Poisson model with rate \(q\) and the same severity. Their means agree, but the Poisson model allows multiple claims.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For non-negative integrable gain or wealth variables \(X,Y\), \(Y\) has second-order stochastic dominance over \(X\) if \(\int_0^tF_X(s)\,ds\ge\int_0^tF_Y(s)\,ds\) for every \(t\ge0\). Equivalently, every increasing concave utility weakly prefers \(Y\) to \(X\), with expectations defined.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This comparison is stated for favourable outcomes. When the variables denote losses, put the minus sign inside wealth utility. A larger mean alone does not establish second-order dominance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• First-order dominance of \(Y\) over \(X\) implies second-order dominance.
  • Dominance requires \(\mathbb E[Y]\ge\mathbb E[X]\) for integrable variables.
  • At equal means, \(Y\) dominating \(X\) in second order corresponds to \(Y\le_{\mathrm{cx}}X\).
  • For losses, \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Y\) corresponds to preference for wealth \(w-X\) over \(w-Y\) by increasing concave utility.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: As gains, a certain 1 second-order dominates a fair draw of 0 or 2. As losses, the same certain 1 is the less dangerous risk. The preference direction is the same after the outcome meaning is specified.

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text: For absolutely continuous laws, suppose \(f_X(t)-f_Y(t)\) is non-negative before a threshold and non-positive afterwards, with both densities integrating to one. Then \(F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)\) for all \(t\), so \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\). The crossing criterion is sufficient; it is not a necessary requirement for stochastic order.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Integrating the signed density difference accumulates a non-negative CDF difference before the crossing and then brings it back to zero. The direction of the signs matters more than merely counting intersections.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With equal finite means, the pattern \(f_Y-f_X\ge0\), then \(\le0\), then \(\ge0\) on three consecutive intervals gives the direct thicker-tailed comparison.
  • Multiple density crossings do not by themselves decide stochastic order.
  • Density comparisons are almost-everywhere comparisons; changing a density at one point changes no probabilities.
  • For discrete laws, use cumulative masses rather than derivatives.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: On \((0,1)\), \(f_X(t)=2(1-t)\) and \(f_Y(t)=2t\) cross at \(1/2\). Their CDFs are \(2t-t^2\) and \(t^2\), confirming \(F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a loss with finite second moment, the standard deviation principle sets \(\Pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\alpha\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\), with dimensionless fixed loading \(\alpha>0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The loading is measured in the same monetary units as loss. Independent pooling generally gives a smaller loading than adding the separate standard-deviation loadings.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• It has non-negative loading, translation consistency and proportionality for positive scaling.
  • For independent losses, \(\sigma_{X+Y}=\sqrt{\sigma_X^2+\sigma_Y^2}\le\sigma_X+\sigma_Y\).
  • Therefore it is generally not additive, and it rewards diversification.
  • Equal-mean convex order raises the premium when second moments are finite; stochastic order alone need not do so.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Two independent risks each have mean 10 and standard deviation 2. At \(\alpha=1\), separate premiums sum to 24, while the pooled premium is \(20+\sqrt8\approx22.83\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A stationary distribution at risk rate \(\lambda\) is a row vector \(\pi(\lambda)\) satisfying \(\pi P=\pi\), \(\pi_l\ge0\) and \(\sum_l\pi_l=1\). With class premiums \(c_l\), the stationary mean premium is \(b(\lambda)=\sum_l\pi_l(\lambda)c_l\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The stationary distribution leaves class proportions unchanged after another year. Convergence from arbitrary initial proportions is a separate property, not a consequence of solving the stationary equation alone.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A finite irreducible chain has a unique stationary distribution; aperiodicity additionally guarantees convergence from every initial distribution.
  • \(\pi\) is a left eigenvector of \(P\) for eigenvalue one, normalised to sum to one.
  • For the three-state two-year scheme, \(\pi=(p,pq,q^2)\).
  • If the first two states cost \(c\) and the third costs \(a\), \(b(\lambda)=c(1-e^{-2\lambda})+ae^{-2\lambda}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With \(p=0.2\) and \(q=0.8\), stationary proportions are \((0.2,0.16,0.64)\). Premiums \((200,200,100)\) give mean premium \(136\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For loss variables \(X,Y\), stochastic order \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\) means \(F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)\) for every real threshold \(t\). Equivalently, \(\mathbb P(X>t)\le\mathbb P(Y>t)\) for every \(t\). Equal laws satisfy the weak order in both directions.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The larger ordered loss has at least as much probability above every threshold. For losses this is an adverse direction; for wealth or gains the same mathematical direction is favourable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\) iff \(\mathbb E[h(X)]\le\mathbb E[h(Y)]\) for all bounded increasing \(h\).
  • For increasing wealth utility \(u\), \(\mathbb E[u(w-X)]\ge\mathbb E[u(w-Y)]\) whenever defined.
  • Increasing transformations preserve stochastic order.
  • With finite means, the order implies \(\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y]\); equal means then force equal distributions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: If \(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.2)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.4)\), \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\). The result compares laws and does not require a specified joint distribution.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For integrable non-negative losses, stop-loss order \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Y\) means \(\mathbb E[(X-d)_+]\le\mathbb E[(Y-d)_+]\) for every \(d\ge0\). The course states it for \(d>0\); continuity as \(d\downarrow0\) supplies the mean comparison at zero.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Every excess-loss layer has no larger expected payment for \(X\). This order combines size and dispersion, so it does not require equal means.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• It is equivalent to increasing convex order: \(\mathbb E[h(X)]\le\mathbb E[h(Y)]\) for increasing convex \(h\) whenever the expectations are defined.
  • It implies \(\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y]\) and is transitive.
  • Stochastic order and the equal-mean thicker-tailed comparison each imply stop-loss order.
  • Without equal means, stop-loss order need not imply a variance comparison.
  • Increasing convex transformations preserve the order when the transformed quantities meet the needed integrability conditions.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Let \(X=1\) and \(Y\) equal 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. At \(d=1\), expected excesses are 0 and 0.5; their stop-loss transforms are ordered at every retention.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For non-negative integrable losses, if \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Z\) and \(\mathbb E[X]<\mathbb E[Z]\), the separation theorem guarantees a loss law \(Y\) such that \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Z\) and \(\mathbb E[Y]=\mathbb E[Z]\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The comparison can be separated into an increase in loss size followed by an equal-mean dispersion comparison. The intermediate variable describes a distribution; the theorem does not specify a unique insurance contract.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The equal-mean second step is \(Y\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Z\).
  • The theorem gives existence, not uniqueness of \(Y\).
  • If \(X\) and \(Z\) already have equal means, the intermediate law can be \(Y=X\).
  • Matching the means alone is insufficient; both order requirements must also hold.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Let \(X=0\) and \(Z\) equal 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. Choosing \(Y=1\) gives \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\), \(Y\le_{\mathrm{cx}}Z\) and matching means of 1 for \(Y,Z\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a non-negative integrable loss \(X\), its stop-loss transform at retention \(d\ge0\) is \(\pi_X(d)=\mathbb E[(X-d)_+]\). A stop-loss treaty pays the excess of an aggregate loss over its retention; the same positive-part function can describe excess-of-loss cover on an individual claim.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The transform is the expected covered tail beyond a deductible. It distinguishes risks that have the same mean but different upper-tail exposure.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\pi_X(d)=\int_d^\infty\bar F_X(t)\,dt\).
  • It is non-increasing and convex in \(d\), with \(\pi_X(0)=\mathbb E[X]\) and \(\pi_X(d)\to0\).
  • Its right derivative is \(-\mathbb P(X>d)\); its left derivative is \(-\mathbb P(X\ge d)\).
  • The retained loss \(\min(X,d)\) plus the ceded excess \((X-d)_+\) equals \(X\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exponential loss of rate \(\lambda\), \(\pi_X(d)=e^{-\lambda d}/\lambda\). This follows by integrating its survivor function from \(d\) onwards.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For integrable losses of equal mean, \(Y\) is directly thicker-tailed than \(X\) if some threshold \(t_0\) satisfies \(F_Y(t)\ge F_X(t)\) for \(t\le t_0\) and \(F_Y(t)\le F_X(t)\) for \(t\ge t_0\). This is the course's equal-mean, single-CDF-crossing comparison.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Probability shifts towards both lower and higher outcomes while keeping the mean fixed. This is a relative dispersion comparison; it does not assert a particular asymptotic heavy-tail class.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The direct single-crossing relation is not generally transitive. The notes use its transitive closure when they say indirectly thicker-tailed.
  • The direct comparison implies stop-loss order \(X\le_{\mathrm{sl}}Y\).
  • For \(0\le X\le b\) with mean \(\mu\), the constant \(\mu\) is the least dispersed and the two-point law on \(\{0,b\}\) with upper mass \(\mu/b\) is maximally dispersed in convex order.
  • Unequal means do not meet the definition.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Let \(X=1\) surely and let \(Y\) be 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. Both means are 1. The CDF of \(Y\) is above that of \(X\) below 1 and below it between 1 and 2.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Under left truncation at \(d\), only losses satisfying \(X>d\) enter the dataset. For independent exact observations drawn from that conditional population, the likelihood contribution is \(f_\theta(x_i)/\bar F_\theta(d)\) for \(x_i>d\), provided \(\bar F_\theta(d)>0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Small losses are absent altogether. The likelihood must renormalise the observed population; this differs from retaining small losses as censored observations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\ell(\theta)=\sum_i\log f_\theta(x_i)-n\log\bar F_\theta(d)\) for a fixed observed sample size.
  • For observation restricted to \((a,b]\), normalise by \(F_\theta(b)-F_\theta(a)\).
  • If a deductible dataset reports excesses \(y_i=X_i-d\), use \(f_\theta(y_i+d)/\bar F_\theta(d)\).
  • Information about the total number of excluded losses would require an additional sampling model.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For exponential losses observed only above 100, observations 120 and 150 have excesses 20 and 50. The conditional MLE is \(2/(20+50)=2/70\), rather than \(2/270\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a loss with finite second moment, the variance principle is \(\Pi(X)=\mathbb E[X]+\alpha\operatorname{Var}(X)\), with fixed coefficient \(\alpha>0\). The coefficient has units inverse to those of the monetary loss.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The loading increases with squared dispersion. Changing the monetary unit requires a corresponding change in the numerical loading coefficient if prices are to describe the same contract.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The principle has non-negative loading and translation consistency.
  • It is additive for independent losses because their variances add.
  • It is not proportional for fixed \(\alpha\): \(\Pi(aX)=a\mathbb E[X]+\alpha a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
  • It preserves equal-mean convex order, but need not preserve stochastic order when means differ.
  • Covariance matters when pricing a dependent portfolio.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: For \(\alpha=0.1\), a Bernoulli loss with probability \(0.5\) has premium \(0.5+0.1(0.25)=0.525\). Doubling the loss gives premium \(1+0.1(1)=1.1\), not \(1.05\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For increasing concave utility \(u\), the zero-utility premium \(\Pi(X)\) solves \(\mathbb E[u(\Pi(X)-X)]=u(0)\), when a finite solution exists. It is the insurer's indifference price at reference wealth zero. Utility must be defined on every relevant net outcome.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Premium income offsets the insured loss until expected utility equals the no-contract reference. The name refers to zero change in utility, not necessarily a utility function whose value is zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(u\) is strictly increasing, any finite solution is unique.
  • Concavity implies \(\Pi(X)\ge\mathbb E[X]\) under the needed integrability conditions.
  • Exponential utility gives the exponential premium principle.
  • For bounded losses, a solution is between the smallest and largest possible loss under suitable continuity and domain conditions.
  • For general utilities, reference wealth affects the indifference price.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: With risk-neutral \(u(w)=w\), the equation is \(\Pi(X)-\mathbb E[X]=0\), giving the net premium. With \(u(w)=-e^{-\alpha w}\) it gives the exponential premium.
